News.title: Brussels sprouts may be off the menu for Christmas thanks to beetle outbreak
News.content:
Brussels sprouts may be off the menu for Christmas thanks to beetle outbreak

The weather has sparked a surge in pests that are 'eating 70% of the leaves"

View 4 Images Flea beetles eating through food crops

Brussels sprouts could be off this year's Christmas menu after an outbreak of flea beetles, a farmer says. The 2026 crop of the vegetables is being decimated by the bugs and the hot weather, according to George Bennett.

‌



George, of Oxfordshire's organic Sandy Lane Farm, has raised concerns over whether the traditional Christmas food will be fit in time. He says intense summer heatwaves have created the ideal conditions for pests.

‌



Flea beetles are tiny bugs that lay eggs in the soil beneath plants, before hatching and eating holes in brassica - the leaves of leafy vegetables like cabbage and Brussels sprouts. Typically, they appear at the start of summer, and remain for around a month - but this year, due to extreme heat, the pests have been able to thrive for almost 12 weeks.

‌



View 4 Images Sprouts are a Christmas staple

George said: "Because it's been a very hot, dry summer, our brassica plants, which is the cabbage family and includes kale, Brussels sprouts and cabbage, have all been stunted and stressed. They haven't had enough moisture to get going and it's made them very vulnerable to flea beetle.

"Flea beetles nibble holes in all the leaves, and if they do too much nibbling, then they can kill the plant or limit the amount that the plant can photosynthesize, so it fails to grow and mature as it should do."

‌



George said that this year, the bugs had been "really pervasive," and added that as much as 70% of the leaves had been eaten. He added that the sprouts have been "touch and go," telling the BBC: "We will still have Brussels sprouts but they are likely to be quite small, not the big ones that are much easier to peel on your Christmas dinner."

View 4 Images Crops of Brussels sprouts are small and stunted, thanks to the weather and the beetle

George said: "Brussels sprouts grow on trees - off buttons on top of a central stalk, and the stalks themselves are about half the size they should be. At the moment, the buttons are just starting to emerge, and they really haven't had enough water and leaf cover to really start to swell up.

‌



"We're in a situation where the yield is vastly reduced because the length of the stem is so short, but also the size of the individual sprouts are going to be very small."

During this summer's heatwaves, which saw 40 days of above 30C temperatures, the beetles were able to thrive - attacking the leafy plants to get sustenance and moisture. The farm has attempted to manage the issue by covering the crops - but that raises another issue, as when the crops are covered, pests like caterpillars and aphids are protected from pigeons and wasps, allowing them to thrive.

"What do we do, or what don't we do?" said George. "Do we take the cover off and let them be ravaged by flea beetles, or do we leave them on and have caterpillar and aphid problems that build up under the covers?"

‌



View 4 Images Sprouts grow on a stalk

"Next year it is due to be hotter and drier than this year - reports say that the El Nino effect means that it's going to be a more extreme summer next year. We're definitely thinking about how we're going to change our practices so that we're more successful for next year.

"Certain crops will be very difficult - particularly the brassica family, as it needs a long time to mature over the summer months. That's the critical time for them to really get up to size.

‌



"Shorter term brassicas are easier, like pointed cabbage or broccoli, but when Brussels sprouts are in the ground for such a long time over the hot, dry summer, that is a problem. But there are some things we can do - we can change the time that we plant to try and avoid the flea beetle, and we can experiment with different crop covers that are more tightly woven so that they can't nibble through the crop covers."

Despite the problems with this year's sprouts, the farmers remain hopeful for next year - and added that the temperatures have led other crops to do "exceedingly well," meaning that crop diversifying is key. The year has been very hot and dry, and it's been a real struggle for Brussels sprouts, but we have a mixed farming system and other crops have done very well.

"Squash and pumpkins have done exceedingly well - our potatoes, leeks, onions, carrots and beetroots have all done fantastically well.

Article continues below

"Part of our resiliency and our ability to survive is by having that diversity and I suspect that a lot of farmers going into the future will not only change their practices to be more successful, but also vastly increase the range of things that they're growing, so that if one thing doesn't work, another will."

News.title: Cleveland police chief proud of force but being 'let down' by funding
News.content:
A Volkswagen Passat carrying five young men drove the wrong way down the motorway near Middlesbrough in the early hours of the morning before colliding with a marked police car.

Officers had been pursuing the car for almost seven minutes after it was connected to earlier alleged criminal activity, but the pursuit was abandoned 10 seconds before the crash when the Passat turned on to the dual carriageway, the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) said.

Fuller, whose force covers an area of north-east England that includes Middlesbrough and Teesside, recalled being asleep when the duty commander rang her with the news.

"No matter how tragic and devastated you feel, we swing into action and we do what we need to do," she said.

The home secretary announced this week that Cleveland Police would be given an extra Â£2m to deal with the fallout from the crash, with 200 officers drafted in from elsewhere.

Fuller told the BBC on Friday that she was grateful for the support the force had been given, but added: "I need that all the time."

Cleveland's Labour police and crime commissioner has previously said the force needed an extra Â£20m a year to hire more officers and crack down on organised crime.

Cleveland Police is grappling with the highest recorded crime rate of anywhere in England and Wales, Office for National Statistics (ONS) figures for the year to March show.

It also ranks highest for burglary, sexual offences, violence with injury, and criminal damage and arson.

Fuller said Cleveland Police had also experienced the largest decrease in the number of officers since 2010 and was staffed as if it were a rural force.

"It absolutely needs to change," she said.

Fuller expressed hope that reform to policing across the country was on the horizon, and that Cleveland Police would become one of the "big, strategic forces that have the resource, the flex and the capability to surge when they need to surge".

She added: "In the meantime, we need additional funding... to take us to that point."

Recent inspections show Cleveland is one of the most improved forces in England and Wales, with performance levels also judged to be some of the best in the country.

The force has recently arrested 87 people for offences linked to organised crime gangs and over the past two years 16 people have been jailed for such crimes.

Fuller denied that gangs had control over parts of Middlesbrough, describing it as a "complex" area to police, with high rates of school absence, drug addiction and mental health issues.

"We're doing the very, very best with what we've got - and we absolutely do need more."

Authorities say high deprivation and unemployment in the area are fuelling organised crime.

"When young people have little aspiration or hope, who don't have confidence in the state, then unfortunately criminals exploit these people," Fuller said.

"They give confidence, and they give them hope, and they give them aspiration. And sadly what that means is young people doing things without thought of consequences."

News.title: 'I'd rather die than ring the police': Distrust and fear in Middlesbrough after A66 crash
News.content:
All but one of the residents who speak to us do so on the condition of anonymity. They are worried that showing their faces could place them or their homes at risk.

What message do the attacks send to people on this street, I ask one.

"Well, they should be scared, shouldn't they, that something's going to happen to their property if they say anything or get involved. So we don't."

Victoria, who moved here several years ago, says the escalating violence cannot be separated from the wider condition of the town.

"This is a social problem, especially in this area. Teesside has been massively neglected and ignored," she says.

The attack in Acklam is far from Middlesbrough's only recent case of a vehicle being used as a weapon. Back in May, a tractor was driven into a house on Priory Road, and since the A66 crash Cleveland Police has investigated at least two further rammings.

Detectives have also linked their wider investigation to a caravan fire on Attlee Road in Grangetown.

"It's getting worse," a nearby resident says. "They're always balaclava-ed up as well, do you know what I mean?"

He blames drugs.

"It can't be anything else. Why would you be like you are unless it was drugs?" he says.

Whether every incident is part of a single feud has not been established. But taken together, the rammings, fires and arrests have created a powerful sense that violence is being used to intimidate, punish and send messages.

What is most unsettling for these residents is the sense that nobody is fully in control.

Grangetown and South Bank are communities still living with the void left by the decline of heavy industry. Both now rank among England's most deprived neighbourhoods.

In South Bank, we see a group of teenagers tend three ponies tethered on the grass. Two perform wheelies on electric scooters while another uses a long stick to scatter rubbish.

On the adjoining estate, more than a dozen homes have boarded-up windows.

On a wall are the words "RIP 2UZZI", said locally to have been the nickname of Jakub Matusiak, who lived one street away.

One 17-year-old boy tells us he knew him. "He was my best mate," he says. "It's sad."

Elsewhere, three letters are repeated: "FTP" - an expletive directed at the police.

I ask the teenager if he would call the police if another young person approached him carrying a knife.

"No," he says. Before adding: "I've never needed the police in my life. I'd rather die than ring the police."

Again and again, the young people we speak to express a profound distrust of the police.

Cleveland's Chief Constable Victoria Fuller said what we'd heard was "horrifying".

"Yes, there are a small minority of people in the Grangetown area who blight those communities. But we will continue relentlessly to serve our communities."

The scale of the challenge facing the force and the community it serves is not new.

The area has some of the highest police-recorded crime rates in England and Wales.

Its leaders have been warning for years that its resources did not match the demands placed upon it.

But recent inspections show Cleveland is one of the most improved forces in England and Wales, with performance levels also judged to be some of the best in the country.

The force has recently arrested 87 people for offences linked to organised crime gangs and over the past two years 16 people have been jailed for such crimes.

Since the crash, more than 200 additional officers have been deployed in Middlesbrough and surrounding communities. Their immediate task is to suppress the violence and identify those directing it.

There is also the question of restoring order and rebuilding trust and confidence.

News.title: Reform promises to increase tax-free personal allowance to £15,000
News.content:
On tax measures, Reform estimates that increasing the tax-free threshold by Â£2,430 would save most taxpayers Â£500 a year and 2.9 million people would stop paying income tax altogether.

It says the policy would cost Â£17.7bn in the first year, rising to Â£21bn by the fifth year and could be paid for through Â£80bn of public spending cuts the party plans to make.

Jenrick told BBC Breakfast Reform would pay for the policy by "cutting out the waste".

Reform has said its spending cuts would include a Â£50bn reduction in welfare spending.

Half of the Â£353bn of welfare spending goes on the state pension, but Reform has said it will not cut this proportion.

The bulk of the funding would come from reducing the cost of welfare, Jenrick said, by not paying benefits to people who are not British citizens and helping people who are off work due to their mental health back into jobs.

Jenrick also said the UK would "stop paying foreign aid to rich countries", adding that "we should be looking after British people first".

"Yes, we'll pay for disaster relief but the vast majority of that budget should be spent on the priorities of our own people," he said.

Reform hopes to raise Â£10bn by scrapping net-zero programmes and Jenrick said, as the UK only amounted to 1% of the world's emissions, it was not sensible to be trying to decarbonise faster than other countries as that was "just impoverishing our own people".

The party hopes to raise Â£8bn by reducing the number of civil servants and Â£7.1bn by capping the foreign aid budget.

The policy is expected to be announced in Jenrick's conference speech later.

"As chancellor, I will wake each morning with one purpose. To make Britain a better place to be a worker than it was the day before," he is expected to say.

He is expected to add: "1.3 million were dragged into paying tax last year alone. Why? Because the tax-free allowance has been stuck at 12 and a half grand since 2021. And Labour has frozen it until 2031.

"That betrayal costs a full-time worker on the minimum wage more than Â£750 a year. And now for the first time, the freeze means they're going to be taxing the state pension. What a disgrace."

In its manifesto before the general election in 2024, Reform said it wanted to lift the threshold to Â£20,000. Jenrick will tell conference activists this remains his long-term aim.

Shortly after becoming prime minister, Andy Burnham told the Times that the "frustration" of people in his Makerfield constituency about the frozen allowance had "lodged in my mind".

He later said that "all of this would be looked at" in the upcoming Budget but that any change would be "difficult given the financial circumstances".

News.title: Disruption at Port of Dover as masked men hold protest
News.content:
There is major disruption at the Port of Dover due to a large group of masked men holding a demonstration.

Kent Police said it was aware of a demonstration currently taking place at the ferry terminal and was "engaging with protesters".

Traffic has been stopped from going in and out of the port.

Images from the scene appear to show hundreds of protesters, all dressed in black and wearing face coverings.

P&O Ferries said it would get passengers on to the next available sailing if they missed their scheduled crossing.

Ferry operator DFDS said it was aware of the "current traffic disruption" and would accommodate passengers on the next departure once they arrived.

Traffic is stopped in both directions on the A20, between the A256 York Street and the A2 Jubilee Way in Dover, according to National Highways.

It is reporting three miles (4.8km) of congestion and delays of up to 30 minutes.

Dover and Deal MP Mike Tapp told the BBC the incident was causing "absolutely awful disruption" for residents.

"My understanding is, a number of individuals have travelled to the area, wearing black, wearing balaclavas, and have blocked a number of roads leading into the port area," he said.

News.title: Lindsay Clancy murder trial has divided US on whether she's victim or criminal
News.content:
Warning: This story contains distressing details and discussion of attempted suicide

Jodi Fournier spent 15 days at the courthouse - sitting, listening and waiting. It was a personal duty, she felt, to show support for Lindsay Clancy, the Massachusetts mother charged with murdering her three children.

Katelyn Kazmirci, from North Carolina, convinced her mother to make a detour to the courthouse in Plymouth on their way to a family funeral, intrigued by the case she had followed on TikTok.

All around them, dozens of women wearing pink rallied in support of Clancy. Not everyone felt the same and across the country, on social media and at dinner tables, Americans have been debating the case with passion.

For nearly seven weeks, the trial transfixed and divided the nation on whether Clancy was a victim or a criminal who deserved to be behind bars.

The 36-year-old nurse's defence team argued she had been suffering from postpartum psychosis when she strangled her young children and so could not be held criminally responsible. The prosecution alleged the killings were intentional and calculated.

The judge declared a mistrial on Friday after jurors - who had heard the testimony of dozens of witnesses and deliberated for 40 hours - failed to come to a uninanimous decision.

News.title: Trump's response is key as Argentina's Falklands demands get louder
News.content:
Domestic politics can rarely be ruled out of the equation when the Falklands issue flares back up. However, Buenos Aires argues that the matter has become urgent: "A clear and urgent danger", as Milei put it.

With two energy companies â the Israeli-owned Navitas Petroleum and Rockhopper Exploration from the UK â due to undertake exploration work on the Sea Lion oilfield off the Falklands coast within two years, the issue has new impetus. Argentina "cannot allow" the companies to "appropriate the oil reserves under our sea", he said. "We will not stand by with our arms folded," he added.

On Saturday morning Milei's office said on X that it was launching sanctions proceedings against 45 people and companies. The announcement did not identify those targeted and it is not yet clear what impact they will have.

In his speech, Javier Milei painted Argentina as a reliable and "trustworthy partner" to Washington and he enjoys Trump's support, both ideologically and personally.

The two men are close allies in a vision of the Western Hemisphere which Trump calls the "Don-roe Doctrine", a play on words on the 19th Century 'Monroe Doctrine' which exerted American domination over the continent. In essence, the two presidents want to see only like-minded leaders in power in the Americas.

Within such a new partnership and a reordering of the spheres of influence, it's more than conceivable that Trump favours the Argentine leader over the British Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, even if the issues at play transcend personality and party politics.

Perhaps the key question for the coming months, then, is whether the strength of the so-called "Don-roe Doctrine" outweighs the lasting history of the "Special Relationship".

News.title: Lauryn Hill, Wyclef and Giggs among surprise guests at Jay-Z's long-awaited UK show
News.content:
Jay-Z's first headline solo show in the UK in more than a decade saw him celebrate hip-hop culture alongside a host of special guests, including Lauryn Hill, Wyclef Jean and Giggs.

The US rap superstar rolled back the years for more than two hours - playing hits like 99 Problems, Empire State of Mind and Dead Presidents - as he took to the stage at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium on Friday night for the first of two shows in London this weekend.

The run is part of his Jay-Z 30 tour, which is marking the 30th anniversary of his debut album, Reasonable Doubt, and his culture-shaping career that followed.

Fans of his wife BeyoncÃ© had hoped she would join him on stage, like she did at two of his three New York shows this summer, as she was also celebrating her 45th birthday on Friday.

News.title: Recipe for success - the Chicken Shop Date moments that created a YouTube star
News.content:
When someone says "we need to talk", it often means one thing - it's time to break up.

After Amelia Dimoldenberg announced on Thursday her hit YouTube series Chicken Shop Date would be turning off the fryers after one last series, some fans were begging for a second chance, while others agreed it was time to move on.

Over more than 10 years and 100 dates, Dimoldenberg's awkward flirting, deadpan silences and willingness to overshare has made her channel an unmissable stop for any celeb, single or not.

Before one last slurp on an orange soda, BBC Newsbeat looks back at some of the talk show's most iconic moments.

News.title: Farage threatens to overhaul Lords and judges to meet his pledges
News.content:
In his speech, which was light on new policy announcements, Farage said the country needed a government "that actually delivers on its promises" and "we're the only people capable of doing it".

He argued the Tories "had 14 years in power and failed absolutely miserably", while Labour's new Prime Minister Andy Burnham "says he needs 10 years", a reference to the PM's promise to set out a 10-year plan for the country later this year.

If Reform wins the next general election, Farage pledged to sack ministers who fail to deliver on their promises in their first 100 days in the job "and replace them with somebody else with the courage to do it".

Setting out his plans to call a "national emergency" if Reform wins power, Farage said: "Parliament will sit, if necessary, for 24 hours a day, for six days a week until we pass the necessary legislation."

He said he expected the House of Lords to "honour" Reform's policy pledges but if they refused to do so threatened to appoint hundreds of new peers so the party had a majority in the upper chamber.

"And if that proves difficult, we will hold a referendum on the current composition of the House of Lords, and they would be swept away by a British public appalled by them," he added.

Identifying the judiciary as another possible "obstacle", Farage promised to remove the ability of judges to rely on conventions like the European Convention of Human Rights (ECHR), which critics blame for hindering some deportations.

"We don't want the courts striking down, do we, the will of the people," he said.

"Parliament makes the law, judges interpret the law. We will do whatever it takes, and perhaps have to consider how judicial appointments work in the future."

Meanwhile, he said civil servants who "try to obstruct us" would be removed from their posts and replaced by people from the world of business.

"I'm tired of being told what can't be done," the Reform leader said.

"That is not what the public want. The public want action, the public want genuine change, the public do not want any more of the same. And our attitude is can do, and will do."

Predicting that Burnham would call an early general election in spring 2027, Farage attempted to use his speech to convince the public Reform was ready to govern.

Stressing he now had a team of spokespeople with "frontline experience", he said the party was planning to broaden its expertise.

"There are more big jobs to fill, and I'm looking and working on defence, health, and the other areas," he added.

In his speech, Farage also hailed a "historic agreement" on small boat returns, signed earlier between Reform and France's hard-right National Rally party.

The deal sets out how a Reform government would intercept boats in the English Channel and return them to France using the Navy, with France "ordinarily" accepting those on board.

It was signed by the National Rally President Jordan Bardella, whose party is currently leading in opinion polls ahead of French presidential elections in April next year, after he gave a speech to the main conference hall.

Farage took to the stage after a long delay, which he told delegates was due to a "security alert".

He took the opportunity to walk through the crowd and greet delegates during the delay.

His speech was also interrupted several times by protesters, including two women who held up a banner reading "Reform works for billionaires".

They were booed by audience members who shouted "out", as they were removed by security.

Farage laughed off the disruption, chanting "boring, boring, boring".

Reform is no longer consistently topping national opinion polls, after more than a year of enjoying a comfortable lead.

Meanwhile, Labour's ratings have risen since Burnham entered Downing Street, and Reform has lost some support to Restore Britain, the new right-wing party founded by former Reform MP Rupert Lowe.

News.title: UK support for Falkland Islands 'unwavering' after Argentina restates claims, No 10 says
News.content:
It is not yet clear how or to what extent the sanctions will be imposed or tightened. In Argentina, a current law already allows for restrictions of activities of oil companies participating in projects considered unauthorised on the islands.

Two oil companies â Britain's Rockhopper Exploration and Israel's Navitas Petroleum â are due to begin extracting oil in the Sea Lion oilfield off the Falklands coast within two years, something Milei said Argentina could not allow.

A joint statement from the two firms on Friday said it had the valid licences granted by the government of the Falkland Islands, "and with the full support of the UK government."

The project is due to deliver its first oil in 2028, Rockhopper and Navitas said the partnerships' timetable would not be affected.

The Sea Lion oilfield, around 130 miles from the islands, contains an estimated 1.7 billion barrels of oil - described by Rockhopper as a field containing "highly marketable crude".

Milei also announced plans for a naval base in Tierra del Fuego in the south of Argentina, saying Trump and the US were "assessing their historical position in regard to the Falklands", which Argentina refers to as Las Malvinas.

"That is not empty words as they understand that Argentina is a reliable partner and a valuable ally for decades to come," he said, describing the UK as a nation "in decline".

On Thursday, President Trump hinted the US would not help the UK in any future Falklands conflict because Britain "had not been there to help me" during his war with Iran.

Trump's latest remarks on the islands come after he previously said the US position on the Falklands is one of many under review.

On Friday, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said the UK would "resolutely uphold" the self-determination of the islands.

Writing on X on Friday, Miliband said the Islands would remain British as that is the "overwhelming position of the islanders."

Defence Secretary Wes Streeting also said Britain's commitment to the Falkland Islands was "absolute and unshakeable".

"Milei's statement overnight tells us more about domestic politics in Argentina than it does about the Falkland Islands," he wrote in his own post on X.

In an earlier statement, Downing Street said it was "not the first time" the Argentine government had made economic threats against the Falkland Islands.

"We are clear that the Falkland Islanders' right of self-determination extends to the right to exploit their own natural resources," it said.

Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch said "Britain does not surrender to bullies".

"If (Milei) wants a stronger Argentina, he should build its economy, not threaten others."

Although the US is formally neutral, Washington provided support for Britain's campaign to retake the islands after the Argentinian invasion in 1982.

Argentine forces landed on the Falklands to stake a territorial claim in 1982, sparking a 74-day war over the territory as a British military task force ejected them.

The conflict led to the deaths of 255 British military personnel, three islanders and 649 Argentine military personnel.

In a sign of the ongoing tensions between the two countries over the issue, Argentina players celebrated their victory over England in the World Cup by waving a banner in support of their country's territorial claim.

News.title: Woman whose XL bully dog killed her cousin given suspended prison sentence
News.content:
A woman has been given a suspended prison sentence after her XL bully dog attacked and killed her cousin.

Kelcie Reed, 24, of Bristol, previously admitted being in charge of a dog dangerously out control, causing the death of Morgan Dorsett.

The 19-year-old, from Shrewsbury, died from neck injuries caused by the attack, which happened at Reed's flat in south Bristol in February 2025.

At Bristol Crown Court, Judge Anna Richardson sentenced Reed to 18 weeks in prison, suspended for 18 months. She will also be required to undergo mental health treatment.

Emergency services were called to the dog attack at a flat in Cobhorn Drive, Bishopsworth, but despite their best efforts, Morgan died from bites to her neck and face, a post-mortem examination ruled.

The dog, named Prince, which belonged to Reed and her boyfriend, was sedated at the scene and later "humanely destroyed", police said.

News.title: The Grand Tour's new presenters: 'I hope we prove the critics wrong'
News.content:
For more than two decades, Top Gear and The Grand Tour were defined as much by the three men presenting them as by the cars they drove.

Jeremy Clarkson, Richard Hammond and James May built one of television's most recognisable partnerships, meaning anyone taking over The Grand Tour was always going to face a daunting task.

Now YouTubers James Engelsman and Thomas Holland and, perhaps most unexpectedly, train enthusiast-turned-internet star Francis Bourgeois are stepping into their shoes for the new series.

And, with initial reviews generally mixed, they knew they had some convincing to do.

"They literally changed the car world," Holland says of the previous trio.

He understands why some fans have questions about whether the show should continue with anyone else.

"They're completely justified to feel that, because they did the same thing that we did - which is grow up watching Clarkson, Hammond and May.

"The show was a very important part of our lives as car enthusiasts."

News.title: Rock stars gather on tiny Scottish island for world stone skimming championships
News.content:
Contenders from around the world are converging on a tiny Scottish island for one of the country's most unlikely international sporting events - the world stone skimming championships.

The annual contest on the isle of Easdale, in the Inner Hebrides, has attracted a record number of international entries, representing more than 30 nations, with some flying in from New Zealand and Canada.

Last year's competition was rocked by a cheating scandal after some contestants were accused of stone tampering.

Toss Master Kyle Mathews, co-organiser of the event, said an official tournament geologist had been appointed this year, leaving no stone unturned in keeping the 400 challengers in order.

The contest was first held in 1983, inspired by an alcohol-fuelled conversation in a pub, and has been held every year since 1997 apart from an interlude during Covid.

Traditionally a male-dominated sport, efforts have been made to make it more inclusive, with this year's event attracting a record number of women and under-16s.

News.title: Cambridge launches review into support for Jason Arday before death
News.content:
The University of Cambridge has launched an independent review into its "decision-making and actions" in the period leading up to former professor Jason Arday's death.

The review will examine the support available to Arday before his death, as well as the wider context of his time at the university.

Arday, 41, was found dead at his home in London on 14 August, the week after resigning from his position as professor of sociology of education amid intense scrutiny over allegations of plagiarism. He had denied the claims.

Announcing the review on Friday, Vice-Chancellor Prof Deborah Prentice said the time since his death had been a "period of profound sadness and reflection for the university".

"We worked very hard to support Professor Arday during an appalling period of external criticism and focus, but given the devastating outcome, we are still asking ourselves whether we could have and should have done more," she said.

"This review will help us answer that question."

In a post on social media, the University of Cambridge said: "University Council took the necessary steps to launch an independent review into the university's decision-making and actions, with a focus on identifying shortcomings and areas for improvement."

The first part of the review will look at the "support, interventions and protections" available to Arday in the period before his death.

Those findings will be reported within three months, allowing recommendations for "urgent action" to be considered and implemented "without delay".

It will be led by Nazir Afzal, chancellor of the University of Manchester and former chief crown prosecutor for the North West of England.

Afzal said in a statement that "it is important that we approach this work with both rigour and humanity", adding "we must be willing to ask difficult questions".

The second part of the review will examine the wider circumstances of Arday's time at Cambridge, including the recruitment of senior academic staff, mentoring and support arrangements.

It will also look at the university's response to allegations of research misconduct and the support available to academics facing "extraordinary public and media scrutiny".

An independent external chair will be appointed to lead the second part of the review, with an expert panel "including individuals with lived experience" advising it.

It is expected to conclude within six months of the panel being established.

In a video message, Prentice said: "I am conscious that Professor Arday's death has deeply affected black staff and students, as well as our neurodiverse community.

"There has also been an unacceptable rise in racist, hateful, and abusive attacks on our staff and students in online forums and on social media."

In 2023, the sociologist, then 37, became the youngest ever black professor at Cambridge.

Arday had faced allegations of plagiarism and questions about some of his achievements. He denied the claims, but admitted errors in his work.

Arday said some errors arose because of his autism, as he relied on using mimicry to make sense of information. He said similar scrutiny would find comparable errors in the work of other academics.

The allegations emerged after another academic - self-defined "race realist" Nathan Cofnas, who was sacked from his Cambridge role in 2024 - said he found numerous instances of plagiarism in the professor's work.

Arday said the criticism had gone "far beyond scholarly disagreement".

Resigning from his post in August, he added: "The relentless accusations, speculation and public commentary have taken a profound toll on me and those I love."

Following his death, his family said they were "in shock to have lost this amazing father, partner, brother, uncle and son".

They added: "The campaign of misinformation was too much for Jason, who was a gentle man and who always wanted to see the best in everyone."

A vigil held in Trafalgar Square was attended by thousands, according to its organisers.

There have been calls for a public inquiry into media coverage of Arday before his death.

News.title: Clock starts ticking on race to buy Scotland's 'forgotten Einstein' church
News.content:
The move follows a meeting in the village earlier this week where it was decided to push ahead with the plans.

A steering group has been set up along with a fundraising page.

Community council chairman Paul Hodson said they were optimistic that they could gather the funds needed to meet the deadline agreed with the Church of Scotland.

"Several individuals and families in the village have already pledged to donate," he said.

"So we are hopeful that with wider help we will be able to meet our target, hovever the deadline of 1 November gives us less than 60 days to do so."

He said that if they were successful in their plans it could have a major impact on the area.

"If we do manage to secure the building this will give us hope that the project to celebrate the life and work of this great scientist can become a vibrant centre and help reverse the slow rural decline of communities like ours and provide a boost for the whole region," he added.

News.title: Transgender surgery halted over concerns patients were not properly assessed
News.content:
Gender-affirming surgery was halted because of concerns from an NHS committee over whether patients had been "appropriately assessed".

After meeting Welsh government ministers on Friday the NHS Wales Joint Commissioning Committee (NWJCC) said data showed the rate of surgery referrals made by the Welsh Gender Service was "significantly higher" than in England.

It also said the proportion of Welsh patients progressing from referral for some types of surgery was "significantly lower" than across the border.

The NWJCC is the body which instructed Cardiff and Vale University Health Board to halt new referrals and planned surgeries.

The health board is responsible for the running of the NHS gender identity clinic which provides specialist care and support for adults in Wales.

It confirmed on Tuesday that some patients who had been awaiting gender-affirming surgery were already in hospital for their procedures when they were told of the suspension.

The Welsh Gender Service provides referrals for patients living in Wales, but all NHS surgeries are carried out in England.

Gender-affirming surgery includes both masculinising and feminising procedures. They are not reversible.

News.content:

Officers are currently “engaging” with protesters clad in balaclavas blocking access to the Port of Dover, Kent Police has said.

In a brief statement, the force said: “We are aware of a protest currently taking place at the Port of Dover. Officers are in attendance and engaging with protesters.”

Videos circulating online show several protesters, dressed in black and wearing balaclavas, gathered at the port. They are milling around roads and roundabouts near the major port, forcing vehicles to a halt.

In a statement on X, the port said: “The Port of Dover can confirm that there is an ongoing public order incident happening around the town of Dover. This is affecting all routes in and out the port and the town.

“We are in contact with Kent Police to understand the situation. This situation is impacting our local community and our customers, so of course we are hoping for a swift resolution.”

The demonstration is being streamed on social media.The Telegraph reports that those in attendance were heard saying they were part of the hard-right group Patriot Platform.

They said the blockade is planned for three days, the newspaper adds.

Dover and Deal’s Labour MP Mike Tapp wrote on Facebook that he was in contact with the police regarding the situation.

He said: “I am fed up with idiots coming to Dover to cause disruption.

open image in gallery The Port of Dover (file photo) ( Getty )

“I bet if you asked any one of those “protesters” they wouldn’t know small boat crossing are down by 40 per cent and we are working hard to fix the mess.”

Councillor Chris Vinson, leader of the Conservative group and member for Walmer on Dover District Council said: “Overnight, clearly what appears to be several hundred masked men wearing black clothing and balaclavas seem to have co-ordinated and loaded into rental vans and then descended on roads leading in and out of Dover with the intent to block them, and that’s what they’ve successfully done, and it’s brought the town to a standstill.

“There are stacks of people who are stuck in their cars or in their workplaces as a result.”

Cllr Vinson said the protest appears to be “illegal migration-related”, but said that the demonstrators do not appear to have placards or banners.

He added: “I’m not aware that there’s been any violence, although clearly, having the path of your vehicle blocked by men wearing black paramilitary gear and balaclavas is extremely intimidating, especially when it’s not clear why they’re there and the police weren’t aware, and so haven’t been able to warn people in advance and make sure that they are made to feel safe.

“I know people who have worked night shifts in the port who are being prevented from leaving for fears for their safety.

“Women who are in cars feeling intimidated, people stuck in traffic – who obviously are without toilet facilities – queues way back on the A20 and the other approach roads into Dover.”

National Highways said the A20 is facing delays in both directions between the A256 (York Street) and A2 (Jubilee Way).

It added: “A large number of protesters are blocking three separate locations bringing all traffic entering the Port of Dover to a standstill.”

Drivers can expect delays of 45 minutes on approach and there are four miles of congestion.

Shipping company DFDS said: “We are aware of the current traffic disruption affecting access to the port.

“Rest assured we will accommodate you onto the next departure once you arrive.”

P&O Ferries said its sailings are “still going ahead as scheduled”, adding that those who miss their departure will be offered the next available crossing.

Rail operator Southeastern reshared a Port of Dover travel update on X, adding: “If you’re delayed into the UK and miss your booked train, you can use the next available at no extra cost.”

Something is stirring in West Sussex. Over the past year, a crop of new pubs, restaurants and rural openings has quietly appeared between the chalky hills and flint villages of the South Downs, adding fresh momentum to an already impressive food scene.

The Black Horse in Amberley is among the latest arrivals, while the newly opened Isca at Borde Hill is bringing ambitious, garden-led dining to the Sussex countryside. And Woodcote in the tiny village of Graffham is an understated, produce-focused addition.

Stretching from the Surrey border to the English Channel, with the South Downs rolling through its middle, West Sussex has long attracted a stylish crowd – from artists and actors to designers and musicians – but compared with the Cotswolds, there is refreshingly little fanfare. It’s just not that kind of place. And I should know since I officially joined the ranks of the “Down From Londoners” and moved here myself six months ago after, numerous weekends spent visiting the area had me longing to call it home.

So far, during what is turning out to be one of the warmest summers on record, I’m realising the sheer brilliance of what’s on my doorstep, from excellent vineyards, higgledy-piggledy market towns, smashing pubs and sandy beaches – all within an easy hop of London and its impressive transport links.

There’s no better time to head to the Downs. Here’s my pick of the hottest happenings in West Sussex for 2026 and beyond.



Where to stay

open image in gallery The 14th-century Swan Inn in Fittleworth reopened in 2025 ( Swan Inn )

First things first, if you really want to experience proper Sussex, swap the generic hotel for something more authentic. In this part of the world, it’s all about pubs with rooms, or, increasingly: restaurants where you can bed down.

Last year saw the 14th-century Swan Inn in Fittleworth re-open. The former drinking hole for the likes of JMW Turner and John Constable is still one of the county’s chicest pubs with rooms (think walls painted with Edward Bulmer colours, Penny Morrison curtains, Birdie Fortescue bedspreads and handmade lampshades by Imogen Pope) with a great Provence-inspired garden at the back.

Amberley is one of my favourite villages in the South Downs and perhaps the prettiest (it has bucolic, Cotswolds-esque vibes, minus the coach tours that no one wants). Conveniently it has its own train station with direct services from London Victoria but more importantly – here lies the Black Horse pub, recently revived by brothers, the Gladwin trio (of the Local & Wild restaurant group), who grew up on a family farm five miles away.

Upstairs are 11 deliciously designed bedrooms, with upholstered headboards, blinds by textile designer Molly Mahon and freestanding Albion slipper baths. Downstairs, beneath the frilly Alice Palmer pantry shades, local produce reigns supreme – puffy finger-licking Marmite eclairs, Nutbourne cucumber (from the family farm) and mint gazpacho, buttery just-caught grilled lobster, and a sticky, torched marshmallow chocolate tart.

open image in gallery The Black Horse pub was recently revamped by the Gladwin trio ( The Black Horse )

Elsewhere in Amberley, if you’re searching for solitude, there’s a magical hideaway with sweeping views over the Arun valley named Upper Barn. This self-contained off-grid barn conversion sleeps up to four, and the rental also encompasses a shepherd’s hut, which is the perfect place to dig into the last remaining chapters of your yet-to-be-completed bestseller. In the summer, its part-walled garden is wrapped in a meadow of wild flowers, with the backdrop of the spectacular South Downs Way walking and biking trail.

In the village of Graffham, on the northern slopes of the Downs, lies another new restaurant with rooms that is worth shouting about; The Woodcote is a place that manages to be smart-as-a-pin but not at all fussy. New chef director Nathan Cornwell (of The Silver Birch, Moor Hall, Kadeau), whips up celebration-worthy dishes with Sussex produce – from Goodwood lamb to Duncton Mill trout. You can rest your head in elegant rooms swathed in pieces by a roll call of great British designers: wallpaper from Robert Kime, bedside tables by Alfred Newall and fabrics from Caroline Inchyra. During the summer months, there’s also a pop-up summer cafe for laidback coffees and pastries, with views worth lingering over.



Eat and drink

Alongside the brilliant line-up of pubs and restaurants with rooms, great places to eat and drink are not hard to winkle out among the hills and valleys of West Sussex.

You’ll want to hotfoot it to the just-opened Isca at Borde Hill, on a 400-acre estate dating back to the 16th century. In a handsome glasshouse overlooking a walled garden, estate-plucked herbs, flowers, fruit and vegetables find their way onto plates and into cocktails, from chalk stream trout to a pea-pod martini. Nicola Harding’s plant-filled interiors are suitably polished, while a seasonal kids’ club with Treehoppers Forest School (running from July until September in 2026) offers parents the ultimate golden ticket: an uninterrupted meal.

open image in gallery Michelin Green Star Wilding Kitchen puts Knepp Estate at the heart of the menu ( Knepp Rewilding )

Another West Sussex estate offering impressive dining is Knepp, the pioneering rewilding project near Horsham. Its Michelin Green Star Wilding Kitchen puts the estate itself at the heart of the menu, with meat from its free-roaming herds, and vegetables from the market garden appearing alongside sustainably-sourced British fish, while much of the cooking is done over fire. In summer, nab a table in the courtyard and combine lunch with a wander along one of the estate’s walking trails.

For something more low-key, there are plenty of independents worth seeking out. In Amberley, locals rallied to save community-run The Sportsman when its future was threatened in 2024. Today, its spectacular views across the RSPB Wild Brooks make it one of the loveliest spots for a pint. Nearby, The Boathouse Amberley, which was a long-popular riverside spot before it closed earlier this year, is set to open under new management in the coming months, this time as an easy-going neighbourhood Italian. Watch this space.

Over in South Harting, rustic La Follia, owned by former fashion creative director Mariana Newton, is perennially packed with locals, who settle beneath the hanging baskets and fairy lights for coffee and cicchetti. And in Arundel, tiny independent Juniper is part cafe, part bakery and part restaurant, turning out freshly baked pastries, including its famous cinnamon buns alongside seasonal breakfasts and lunches. On Friday evenings there are wine and snacks.

What to do

The South Downs are made for exploring on foot, with trails unspooling across chalk ridges, through ancient woodland and along the banks of the River Arun. The 100-mile South Downs Way cuts straight through the county, but fear not, you needn’t commit to the whole thing: there are plenty of gentler circular walks linking villages and pubs. One of my favourites takes you from Bignor Hill through rolling downland towards The Pig in the South Downs, where a cold drink on the sweeping terrace is a fitting finish.

open image in gallery Finish your South Downs walk at The Pig ( The Pig )

If pedal-pushing and lycra is your idea of a fun day out, take to the Downs Link, a 37-mile bike-friendly trail largely following the course of two former railway lines, or try the shorter family-friendly Centurion Way, which runs along a dismantled railway between Chichester, Lavant and West Dean.

If you prefer to get out on the water, hire a self-drive boat from Riverside South Downs at Amberley, or a kayak or paddle board from Pulborough Paddles at Stopham Bridge and potter along the River Arun, spotting kingfishers and rare dragonflies as you go.

Coming to this part of Sussex without sampling its wine is practically illegal. Family-run Nutbourne Vineyards, near Pulborough, offers tours and tastings among its vines, wildflowers and lakes, followed by a tasting of its still and sparkling wines. Better still, order one of its picnics or sharing platters and settle in with a bottle.

The grand estates could occupy a weekend in themselves. At Cowdray pick up a walking map and yomp the 16,500-acre estate, taking in the historic Cowdray Ruins and deer park before refuelling at the cafe.

If you’re visiting in summer, expect polo, the annual Maize Maze (which has a new theme every year) and wildflower picking patch (every August).

Over at Goodwood, there’s horse racing, including family race days, alongside the estate’s packed calendar of motoring events.

Treasure hunters (with deep pockets) will love mooching around the cobbled streets of Petworth, packed to the rafters with antique shops and excellent independent boutiques. Two of my favourites are Tallulah Fox, where shelves are laden with pretty linens, glassware and decorative finds, and Maker’s Barn, a beautifully curated showcase of contemporary British craft, from ceramics and textiles to furniture and art. It also hosts a brilliantly eclectic roster of workshops, spanning everything from making traditional gate hurdles and stools to basket weaving and paper flowers.

For a lungful of fresh sea air, hop aboard Chichester Harbour Charter’s newly launched ferry from Sparkes Marina on Hayling Island to East Head at West Wittering (running until 25 October), where the sandy Blue Flag beaches and coastal walks await.

Nearly 2,000 people, most of them students, fell ill in suspected food poisoning outbreaks linked to President Prabowo Subianto ’s flagship Free Nutritious Meals program this week, raising fresh concerns about food safety as the government rapidly expands the multibillion-dollar initiative nationwide, officials said Saturday.

The incidents, reported between Tuesday and Thursday in East Java, Central Java, West Sumatra, Aceh and South Sulawesi, affected about 1,950 students, teachers and Islamic boarding school pupils who became sick after consuming meals distributed under the government program, known by its Indonesian acronym MBG.

The outbreaks are the latest setback for Prabowo’s signature free meals program, which has been rolled out across the archipelago despite repeated food poisoning incidents and corruption allegations.

The largest outbreak was reported in Central Java’s Rembang regency, where 752 students and 25 teachers at State Senior High School 1 Lasem, suffered diarrhea, nausea, vomiting and stomach pain after eating meals provided through the program, according to Rembang Health Office head Ali Syofi'i.

In Sidoarjo, East Java, 730 people, most of them students at the Manbaul Hikam Islamic boarding school, were affected in another suspected food poisoning incident linked to the program. Sidoarjo health office chief Lakhsmie Herawati Yuwantina said 706 victims had been discharged and were recovering at home.

Authorities also reported 276 suspected cases involving students and teachers in Agam regency, West Sumatra, where food distribution from the local nutrition service center was suspended pending an investigation. In Aceh’s Bener Meriah regency, 15 elementary school students and a school principal were treated after experiencing dizziness, nausea and other symptoms following a school meal.

Another 152 students from two junior high schools in Tana Toraja, South Sulawesi, were treated at three hospitals after developing symptoms consistent with food poisoning. Regent Zadrak Tombeq ordered hospitals and health centers to prioritize treatment for the victims.

No deaths have been reported, and authorities are investigating the causes of the outbreaks.

The latest incidents add to a growing number of food poisoning cases linked to the program since its launch in January 2025. According to Health Ministry surveillance data as of Sept. 2, food poisoning incidents associated with MBG have affected 50,059 people in 560 cases across 245 districts and cities in 36 provinces.

In a hearing with the House's Commission IX overseeing health issues, National Nutrition Agency chief Sudaryono said internal reviews found that roughly 80% to 90% of previous food poisoning incidents were linked to failures to follow food safety procedures, including rules governing food storage, receipt of ingredients, temperature control and consumption deadlines.

“The recent incidents in Sidoarjo, Agam, Rembang and other areas have been a major blow for us,” said Sudaryono, who like many Indonesians uses a single name.

He said the agency was tightening oversight of meal providers and reviewing about 27,000 meal distribution centers nationwide. Inspectors have found hundreds of allegedly fictitious facilities, while at least 833 kitchens have been shut down for failing to meet hygiene and sanitation standards.

The free meals program aims to combat malnutrition and reduce childhood stunting by providing meals to nearly 90 million students, toddlers and pregnant women. The initiative, expected to cost about $28 billion through 2029, is a cornerstone of Prabowo’s administration and one of his key campaign promises.

This year’s rapidly intensifying, climate change-fuelled “super” El Niño is on course to be the strongest on record – and potentially the most powerful in centuries.

“We should be clear that this is an unprecedented event”, said Professor Adam Scaife, head of long range forecasting at the Met Office. “I have never seen an El Niño signal this intense in our forecasts.” Others have described the event as “ truly mind-blowing ” and “ Godzilla-level ”.

Tens of millions of the world’s poorest people are also expected to be plunged into humanitarian crisis as the extreme weather event hits - just as vital support for health, nutrition and disaster response is being gutted by devastating foreign aid cuts from wealthy countries. Britain, for example, is currently slashing bilateral aid to eight African countries by more than 80 per cent.

Torrential rains and flooding are expected to come to parts of East Africa, while droughts are expected to intensify across southern Africa - threatening food supplies and livelihoods on both sides of the continent.

Already, the impacts are being felt in other parts of the world, from unusually weak monsoon rains in India, to catastrophic wildfires in Indonesia.

In the UK, still reeling from a summer of heatwaves that has killed thousands and pushed water levels to critically low levels, the Met office has forecast a particularly wet and stormy winter due to the El Niño. But perhaps the biggest impact will be felt in people’s pockets. Around one quarter of UK food imports – including rice, coffee, cocoa, and tropical fruits – are from parts of the world most exposed to the El Niño, according to research from the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit.

The impacts will come on top of an ongoing cost of living crisis that experts say has been exacerbated by climate change. Poor harvests drove a 77 per cent rise in the price of coffee imported into the UK from Brazil in 2025, while cocoa bean prices from Côte d’Ivoire have doubled.

But it is people on the ground across Africa and Asia that will feel the most critical impacts.

“The world is heading into this El Niño at precisely the wrong moment,” Dr Philip Goodwin, CEO of Unicef UK, told The Independent. “We can see the warning signs coming, yet humanitarian agencies are being asked to prepare with fewer resources.”

MPs from across the political divide are now calling on the government to step up its support, as aid groups warn that countries set to be most impacted by the super El Niño are also those bearing the brunt of the global aid squeeze.

“We must change course in order to meet the scale of this crisis,” Dr Ellie Chowns, Green MP for North Herefordshire, told The Independent. “The government must turn all of their efforts to urgently reducing emissions at home… and restore development aid to ensure the Global South is not abandoned to face the worst realities of a crisis they did so little to cause.”

Wildfires, which scientists say are being fuelled by El Niño, are seen burning across Indonesia earlier this month ( AFP/Getty )

Andrew Mitchell, Conservative MP for Sutton Coldfield and a former development minister, added: “It is the poorest in the world who suffer first and hardest from climate change and this summer has shown the rich world, too, the grave climate threats that await us .

“Cuts to Britain’s development budget - as both Prime Ministers Johnson and Starmer did - were acts of the greatest folly… Britain needs to reinvigorate this international leadership if we are to tackle at their roots the threatening evils of climate change, illegal migration, starvation, water shortage and pandemics.”

Comments come as this week the UN warned that this year’s El Niño - an event caused by unusually warm temperatures in the central and eastern tropical Pacific - is already exceptionally strong. “El Niño is being supersized before our eyes… The science leaves no room for doubt: the planet is in uncharted waters, and those waters are heating up,” said UN secretary general António Guterres.

Occurring on average every two to seven years, a typical El Niño will see sea surface temperatures in a specific patch of the tropical Pacific rise by 1-2C, with 2C considered a very big event.

This year, the temperature has already crossed 2.6C above the El Niño - and current forecasts suggest it could peak at around 4C in November.

Speaking of the super coming El Niño, Dejene Dadi, the general manger of a coffee-growing cooperative in Ethiopia, said: “We aren't ready for this kind of disaster… We can do climate adaptation activities like soil and water conservation, shade management, managing pests and diseases, and water harvesting and irrigation. But it is not possible without more help from coffee companies and governments like the UK.”

For its part, the UK government carried out a “responsible business conduct review” as part of its trade strategy published last year, which advocacy groups understand contains plans that would compel companies to better respond to environmental and human rights concerns in their supply chains. However, the publication of that review has been continually delayed.

“The super El Niño urgently need businesses to invest in their supply chains: paying fair prices, tackling human rights abuses, and safeguarding the environment. And the UK Government must also stop delaying publication of its Responsible Business Conduct review,” said Dr Carley-Jane Stanton, from the Fairtrade Foundation.

The most urgent El Niño concern, however, remains around the impact that El Niño-fuelled weather events will have on food systems at a time when there is very little money available to help the world’s poorest.

The UN’s World Food Programme (WFP) has projected that an additional 49 million more people could be pushed into hunger globally.

“The places most affected by El Niño are often those already facing some of the worst food crises - and over the past year we have already had to make incredible choices on prioritising populations on the brink of famine and starvation,” Richard Choularton, director of WFP's Climate and Resilience Service, told The Independent.

“We simply do not have enough resources. This year we estimate that we need around $13bn to meet emergency food needs around the world, but we expect to only get around six and a half billion,” he added.

A major WFP appeal to donors for $200m to fund “anticipatory action” – programmes that provide families with cash ahead of climate shocks, allowing them to weather the crisis without leaving their communities – has also met with a muted response. “We asked for 200 million for about 22 countries… and we still need over 150 million. And the window for putting those funds to good use is rapidly closing,” said Mr Choularton.

Ummy Dubow, the country director for Somalia at the global development charity CARE, described the super El Niño as a “disaster” for her country during a briefing with journalists this week - in which she emphasised how Somalia is already reeling from crises including the impact of aid cuts as well as the knock-on effects of the War in Iran.

“Somalia is facing a very severe and compounding humanitarian crisis… 3.3 million people are already internally displaced, and 1.88 million children under five in Somalia are acutely malnourished,” she said. “Meanwhile, while CARE used to operate 150 health facilities, this has come down to 50 due to the aid cuts - and food prices have risen between 10 and 20 per cent and fuel costs have gone up by 10 per cent due to the War in the Middle East .”

Unicef’s Dr Philip Goodwin added that it is “children who are paying the highest price” despite the fact that they did not create the climate crisis.

Pippa Heylings, Liberal Democrat MP for South Cambridgeshire and net zero spokesperson, also called on the government to better prepare for the climate crisis and restore the foreign aid budget.

“We cannot afford to abandon our reputation as a global climate leader by betraying our pledges to countries that desperately need climate resilience,” she said.

“The Liberal Democrats want to see the government reverse their cuts. Burnham must set out a roadmap to restore the aid budget back to 0.7 per cent [of Gross National Income, GNI], as well as convening cross-party talks on climate resilience."

The UK retained its aid budget at 0.7 per cent of GNI for a number of years, before Boris Johnson cut it to 0.5 per cent in 2021, and Keir Starmer announced further cuts to 0.3 per cent last year, cutting billions of pounds from the budget.

Sarah Champion, Labour MP for Rotherham and chair of the International Development Committee, echoed warnings that cuts to the UK aid budget are misguided at a time of such severe global danger.

"Climate change is rapidly undermining development gains across vulnerable countries, as we have recently witnessed with the disaster in Nepal,” she said. “We must recognise El Niño risks further worsening food and water security, and will exacerbate poverty and humanitarian need.

"Successive cuts to overseas development aid... are increasingly undermining good intent, at a time when the climate crisis is rapidly intensifying,” she added.

Both the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office, and the Department for Business and Trade, have been approached for comment.

Russian attacks killed four people in Ukraine overnight, as Moscow and Kyiv await the arrival of U.S. envoys to begin a new push for peace in the Kremlin’s 4 1/2-year-old invasion.

The planned visit by Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, who is also U.S. President Donald Trump’s son-in-law, is hoped to revive peace talks amid escalating aerial attacks by both sides.

The air war between Russia and Ukraine has intensified as troops have struggled to make progress along the 1,250-kilometer (775-mile) front line. Russia has recently been using fast-flying, jet-powered drones, and the recurring wail of air-raid sirens has become part of daily life in Kyiv.

The strikes come despite a message from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy Friday saying that Ukraine would halt air attacks during Witkoff and Kushner’s visit and urging Moscow to do the same.

“Just as we did during previous diplomatic visits by the American side, we will ensure the normal functioning of Russian airspace so that the negotiators can arrive safely,” Zelenskyy said in a post on social media. “There will be no airstrikes from our side, and Russia must do the same, ensuring there are no airstrikes from its side for the time needed to hold these talks and handle the logistical matters related to this American visit.”

Russian attacks killed four people and wounded five more at an industrial facility in Ukraine’s southern Dnipropetrovsk region, local military administration head Oleksandr Hanzha said. A 62-year-old man was also wounded and several private homes and an apartment building were damaged in a separate attack on the region’s Nikopol district, he said.

In a statement Saturday, Russia’s Ministry of Defense said it had carried out strikes on two metallurgical plants in the region, describing them as “major suppliers of metal products for Ukraine’s military production.”

A further two people were wounded in an overnight Russian attack on Ukraine’s Kyiv region, said Tymur Tkachenko, head of the regional military administration. In the Boryspil district, a fire sparked by a strike partially destroyed a nine-story residential building.

Russian forces also repeatedly struck a shopping center in the southern Mykolaiv region with drones overnight, damaging retail premises and sparking fires, Ukraine’s state emergency services said. A 72-year-old man and a 17-year-old girl were hurt.

Emergency crews responding to the incident were repeatedly forced to withdraw to safety because of the threat of further strikes, returning whenever conditions allowed, the emergency services said.

Russia launched ballistic missiles from its Rostov and Voronezh regions and deployed 167 attack drones overnight, Ukraine’s Air Force said. The drones included Shahed-type aircraft — around half of them jet-powered — as well as Geran and decoy drones. Ukrainian air defenses shot down or suppressed 128 drones, according to the Air Force.

Elsewhere, Ukrainian attacks wounded three people, including a 14-year-old girl, in Russia’s border region of Belgorod, local officials said.

In a statement, Russia’s Ministry of Defense said that its forces had shot down 53 Ukrainian drones overnight.

News.content:

Penny Lancaster has shared a health update on her husband Sir Rod Stewart, saying he will “come back stronger than ever” following a heart operation and the cancellation of his 2026 US tour.

The 81-year-old singer had embarked on his final world tour when he underwent a coronary stent procedure and was forced to take four weeks off to recover. The development arrived after a year of health issues for “Maggie May” singer Stewart.

His wife Lancaster has reassured fans worried that “he’s back at full speed in his day-to-day activities, but doctor’s orders were to kind of postpone or cancel the current tour, because you know the risk factors involved”.

She added that she “did have to explain to the doctor what Rod’s performances are like”, as “he doesn’t just sit down on a stool or behind a piano, he runs around for nearly two hours with four different costume changes because he’s sweating through everything”.

open image in gallery Sir Rod Stewart cancelled his US tour due to ill health ( PA )

Lancaster, 55, continued: “So, I compared him to either a boxer coming out of his dressing room on the way to the ring, or a horse coming out the blocks, I mean, he runs on and he’s like, you know, straight into it, 100 miles an hour and doesn’t stop.

“It’s like running a sprint for him, so just for precaution, that tour unfortunately had to be cancelled, which he was devastated about.”

Stewart, who called off a string of US and Mexico tour dates, including six nights at Caesars Palace in Las Vegas, “can’t wait to see his fans again”, having had “so many wonderful well wishes and support”.

She also said the doctor’s orders have stretched to home life, and he’s received “strict instructions about the level of workout he could do”.

“I mean, he does not sit down,” Lancaster said. “I can never find him, he’s, you know, he’s got his hobbies.

“But he’s going to come back stronger than ever. He feels like he’s got a new lease of life.”

open image in gallery Rod Stewart with wife Penny Lancaster, whom he married in 2007 ( PA )

The singer has had a series of health issues this year, which have led to him cancelling a string of tour dates. In May, the “Do Ya Think I’m Sexy?” singer sent “apologies to my family of fans” after cancelling performances in Nevada, adding: “I am on vocal rest as I recover from a sinus infection.”

Less than a month later, he cancelled his San Diego show after being diagnosed with a respiratory infection that resulted in laryngitis. However, a day later, he was spotted at a FIFA World Cup game just one day later in Boston with his two sons.

Stewart later admitted that attending the football “wasn’t a good look”, telling talkSPORT: “I really shouldn’t have gone to the Haiti game. I had to cancel a show the night before because I just had no voice left.

“But the truth is, I wasn’t going to let my two sons down. I promised them since they were born that we’re going to go to a World Cup, and this is the first one that’s come about. And it wasn’t a good look, I admit, but I’m going to just have to take the stick. So, I did it for the boys.”

Days later, while performing in Utah, he returned to the stage – but almost fainted while performing. The singer paused the June gig and breathed from an oxygen tank, having become noticeably winded during the performance. “The show must go on. I nearly f***ing fainted there. Would you mind if I sit down for this one?” he told the crowd when he resumed the show. He performed the rest of the gig from a chair.

After undergoing the coronary stent procedure weeks later, he said in a statement: “I’m already feeling better and very much on the mend. I want to thank the doctors, nurses and everyone who has taken such wonderful care of me.

“I am deeply disappointed to miss these shows and sorry to let my fans down, but I look forward to getting back on stage and having a good time with you all again soon.”

While One Last Time was intended to be Stewart’s farewell tour, he suggested back in 2024 that he truly did feel “Forever Young” – a reference to his 1988 hit song – and would want to continue performing on a smaller scale.

“This will be the end of large scale world tours for me, but I have no desire to retire. I love what I do, and I do what I love,” he said in an Instagram post at the time.

“I’m fit, have a full head of hair, and can run 100 metres in 18 seconds at the jolly age of 79. I’d like to move onto a Great American Songbook, Swing Fever tour the year after next – smaller venues and more intimacy. But then again, I may not...”

open image in gallery Rod Stewart is ‘back at full speed in his day-to-day activities’ after cancelling tour dates due to ill health ( AFP/Getty )

Lancaster, who married Stewart in 2007, was speaking as she backed the Street Child charity’s Back To School campaign, which aims to get the public to pledge £4 per month to support a child’s education for a whole year, with the charity claiming that 79 million children around the world do not have access to education.

The charity says those who set up a gift before September will directly help Street Child commit to getting a child back to school this term.

Those wishing to donate can do so from the charity’s website.

Additional reporting by Agencies
