Troy Parrott’s late winner ended Real Madrid’s perfect start ​to the LaLiga season, with the Republic of Ireland striker scoring nine minutes from time before Real Betis goalkeeper Alvaro Valles saved ⁠a stoppage-time penalty from Kylian Mbappe.

Parrott, introduced in the 68th minute, broke the deadlock in the 81st when he reacted quickly after Madrid goalkeeper Thibaut Courtois parried a header into his path.

Mbappe struck the crossbar four minutes later before substitute ⁠Carlos Espi met a cross from Vinicius Junior with a ​spectacular ⁠bicycle kick, only for the ‌equaliser to be ruled out for offside following a VAR review.

open image in gallery Mourinho is back at Real Madrid for a second spell ( AP )

Nelson Deossa then nearly sealed the victory for hosts Betis with a long-range effort after spotting Courtois off his line, but the goalkeeper recovered to make the save.

Madrid got one final opportunity when Natan brought down Vinicius inside the area deep ⁠into stoppage time, but Valles saved Mbappe's spot kick to preserve Betis's lead and secure the three points.

“I don’t know how we lost because we played very well collectively. I cannot fault the attitude of any of my players. We deserved to win but deserving to win does not give you points,” Mourinho said.

open image in gallery Mbappe’s penalty was saved ( Reuters )

“I’m very happy with my ​players, all of them. I cannot fault any of ‌them individually. As for ⁠the penalty, when one of us steps up to ⁠take it, we all stand together.

"The Betis players are more streetwise than the Madrid players, who are very honest. With the backing of a fantastic crowd, they manage to gain these kinds of advantage.”

Elsewhere, Paris Saint-Germain looked to be on their way to a first win of the Ligue 1 season when Marquinhos put the hosts ahead in the 31st minute, but Monaco rallied with goals by Flavio Nazinho in the 58th and Stanis Idumbo in the 72nd.

Monaco leads Ligue 1 as the only team to win its first three games.PSG had already drawn 2-2 with Rennes and Lille in its first two games. They also lost the French Super Cup to Lens 1-0 last month.

PSG’s first league defeat came hours after the French champions announced contract extensions for coach Luis Enrique and several players. João Neves, Lucas Beraldo, Senny Mayulu and Willian Pacho all got new deals through 2031, while Fabian Ruiz had his contract extended through 2028.

Striker Folarin Balogun was left out of Monaco’s squad after the collapse of his proposed transfer to Everton this week.

News.title: DiCaprio’s Amazonian warrior queen
News.content:
It was while she was in hiding after recovering from the sixth attempt on her life, that the activist Juma Xipaia got a call asking if she would agree to be the subject of a documentary. The first female chief of the Middle Xingu region of the Brazilian Amazon, Xipaia was well known in Brazil for her passionate attempts to protect her indigenous community from the effects of deforestation, illegal gold-mining and – in particular – the catastrophic environmental consequences of the $11 billion Belo Monte hydroelectric dam project, a wildly ambitious and destructive endeavour that has affected livelihoods, fish stocks, ecosystems and biodiversity, with legal challenges still ongoing today.

Thirty-four-year-old Xipaia’s outspoken resistance and exposure of corruption relating to the dam’s construction led to the threats on her life. The last attempt was by poisoning, via a food delivery company, which resulted in her being on a ventilator with 70 per cent organ failure. She was on the verge of death, when, she says, she had a dream that she was given a choice – to take the easy path of dying, or the difficult path of coming back, and because she’s a fighter, that’s the one she chose. And a week later she walked out of the hospital.

Leonardo DiCaprio described the activist as one of the most incredible people he’d ever met Credit : Lalo de Almeida/Folhapress, FSP

Like many activists representing indigenous communities she walked a tightrope between protecting the interests and traditions of her people, and not being perceived as standing in the way of progress in terms of the economic development that benefits Brazil as a whole, a paradox that was defined when President Lula da Silva regained power in 2023, and brought Xipaia into government.

Richard Ladkani, a film director who has made vibrant environmental documentaries such as The Ivory Game (about poaching) and Sea of Shadows (marine activists), was the man who called her. It was 2019, when Brazil was still under the brutal rule of Jair Bolsonaro and destruction of the Amazon was at its peak – an area of rainforest the size of Belgium was burned during his presidency, and thousands of illegal goldmines flourished, contaminating the forest, polluting the river with mercury (mercury is used to bind gold) and bringing crime and disruption to previously pristine areas.

Film-maker Richard Ladkani in the Brazilian Amazon Credit : Courtesy of Malaika Pictures

“All summer long we had seen these dramatic apocalyptic images,” says Ladkani. “And I was posing for photos at the premiere of Sea of Shadows, with [executive producers] Leo DiCaprio and Jane Goodall, when Leo leaned over and whispered, ‘So Richard, what’s next?’

“And I said, 'We've got to do something about the Amazon.’”

DiCaprio came onboard as producer, and Goodall as an ambassador. Ladkani knew he had to find a powerful central figure to provide human and emotional context, someone who would be the voice of the Amazon. He drew up a list of possible candidates, until the Brazilian journalist Eliane Brum told him “do not make a decision until you have spoken to Juma Xipaia – when she speaks, the world listens. She can silence a whole room with her energy.”

‘For a long time I had been seen as a soldier, an army of one’

Right now, in a small restaurant in New York, Xipaia is not really in the mood to talk. It is February, and it’s snowing, and Ladkani, Xipaia and her husband, Hugo Loss, are here to publicise the resulting documentary, Yanuni – which took six years to make – at a screening attended by UN representatives and Brazilian diplomats. The recent news about Trump’s exploits in Venezuela has shaken them all and, more specifically, Juma has had a bad experience with American food which doesn’t really agree with her. She is a little reticent at first, but soon opens up with the help of an interpreter, and explains to me what it meant to be a cacique (chief), and how she was selected.

Indigenous leader Juma Xipaia and her husband Hugo Loss in the city of Aracaju, Brazil Credit : Lalo de Almeida/Folhapress, FSP

“I never chose to be a cacique,” she says, “but I couldn’t stay quiet in the face of exploitation of my people – there was violence, and women being harassed and raped.” She is referring to the collateral damage that importing thousands of workers to build a dam inevitably brings. “Usually the role of cacique is given to the oldest male in the community – my dad and my uncles and my brother were all caciques, but the elders knew that they could trust me never to negotiate our rights with corporations or politicians, never to compromise. For a long time I had been seen as a soldier, an army of one. I accepted the position for two years, with the goal of strengthening on our territories and bringing sovereignty to our people.”

Xipaia was born in 1991 and had an idyllic childhood, she says, growing up in Tucumã, a small indigenous community along the Iriri River, about 250 miles west of the city of Altamira. They lived in wooden houses and ate fruit and nuts from the forest and fish from the river, and in 2006 she moved to Altamira for her education. But threats were encroaching her community, with land opened up for mining and farming, and in 2011, a licence was granted to construct the Belo Monte Dam, to stop up parts of the Xingu River, one of the most species-rich areas of the Amazon.

Aged just 21, Xipaia spoke out against the dam at a public hearing, but despite lawsuits, protest from indigenous people and large sections of society, construction went ahead. Xipaia attended law school in Altamira and studied plans put forward by Norte Energia, the company that built Belo Monte, helping to expose corruption that was going on within. In 2015, at the age of 24, she became a cacique, the first female leader of her people. Other communities had been bought off by Norte Energia with gifts of stoves, fridges, TVs.

In November 2019, she led a protest of angry Brazilian landowners and farmers to disrupt the Amazon: Center of the World international conference in Altamira. But by now she had become a target, and by the time Ladkani called her she had survived six attempts on her life, including her car being rammed with children in the back, and a threat to kidnap her son. She went into hiding for a year and she didn’t want to talk to anyone.

“She thought, the only way I’m going to survive is if I stop talking, because when I talk, people want to kill me,” Ladkani says. But she was finally convinced to take a call from him, and from the first moment, he says, he knew he had found the voice for his film. “Her poetry is the thing that stands out – the way she can describe emotions and feelings and put things into context, I felt it was unique. And when she told me the story of how she almost died because of the poisoning, I was in tears.

“I told her I wanted her to be the voice in the film and also offered her the role of producer. Because I knew nothing of indigenous life and I needed her to lead the way.”

An aerial view of the Belo Monte hydroelectric dam in Altamira Credit : CARLOS FABAL

It was a struggle from the word go. Xipaia was not happy about a translator being involved because of security reasons; she couldn’t trust anyone. So Ladkani, who is Austrian, took intensive lessons in Portuguese and within six months was fluent. “It was a key thing to show that I meant business and took her concerns very seriously,” he tells me.

The security budget for the film was huge, they needed the best, most experienced people: safe houses, secure drivers. And the arrangements had to extend for a year after filming was completed – a total of seven years. “Leo was extremely important here because he raised the first third of the budget, and this encouraged other philanthropists to be part of it.”

Filming began in 2020. There was no script and Ladkani didn’t know what he was going to get from it, just that he needed to tell the story of the pillaging of the Amazon via Xipaia’s voice.

And in the end it was a wild ride: it started with Xipaia leading protests against Bolsonaro, but after Lula was elected in 2023, he established a Ministry for Indigenous Rights, of which Xipaia was made state secretary, implementing a series of bills for the protection of the forest and employing lawyers, biologists and engineers to combat the destruction of the Amazon.

Juma Xipata and Leonardo DiCaprio at the Yanuni Premiere during the 2025 Tribeca Festival in New York City. Credit : John Nacion/Getty Images for Tribeca Festival

The film documents her move from her village to set up home in Brasilia with her son; getting together with her husband Hugo Loss, head of special operations for Ibama (the Brazilian Institute of Renewable and Natural Resources), an elite outfit conducting raids on illegal mines; and the birth of their first child, who was called Yanuni.

It was a lengthy, exciting journey, an improvisation which resulted in thousands of hours of film. “I just had to go with the unpredictable. The strength of any documentary is when unforeseen things happen, because a twist in direction is the greatest thing of any film structure.

“And we had that multiple times. I had chosen a woman to be the voice of the Amazon and two years later she became the second most powerful woman in the Indigenous Ministry – I get goosebumps now at the sheer luck. That was the first twist, and then Hugo enters her life, who happens to be this charismatic soldier of an elite force who would take me to the frontline of the Amazon resistance, and then Juma becomes pregnant and gives birth to Yanuni. Holy s**t. If I had written that as a script, everyone would have thrown it out as complete fiction.”

‘I said, how dangerous is it? And he said, “Well, the risk of you dying is 50 per cent”’

Leo DiCaprio was a producer on the film (rather than his usual role of executive producer), which meant he was far more involved. “He not only provided the money, but he gave me meaningful support throughout the production,” says Ladkani. In November 2021 DiCaprio attended Cop 26 in Glasgow, where he met Xipaia for the first time. “That meeting was spectacular – Leo posted a picture of the two of them together and said that she was one of the most incredible people he’d ever met.” The resulting attention helped to protect Xipaia, because a public profile is to some extent a safeguard. “There she is next to DiCaprio, so she’s not just a voiceless indigenous person from somewhere in the Amazon.”

There were many technical challenges. Because of security, Ladkani couldn’t film in the normal way, with lighting and a crew. “I had a second cinematographer, a brilliant guy from Brazil, called Fábio Nascimento, and I took him with me when I could – but that was only 30 per cent of the time. The rest I shot alone. I downsized my gear and basically shot the film with a DSLR, like a photo camera, so I looked like a tourist. To an outsider, I was just a white gringo taking pictures.” Xipaia had a hidden microphone beneath her shirt. If Ladkani was ever confronted, he claimed to be a YouTuber.

“Security demanded that we shot the film incognito, and that became its strength, because I was embedded within the family to the extent that they stopped noticing me,” says Ladkani.

An illegal gold-mining ship destroyed by Ibama in the Brazilian Amazon – it is dangerous work, with agents risking serious injury and even their lives Credit : Courtesy of Malaika Pictures

Hugo Loss’s job involved protecting indigenous communities and flying over the forest and rivers of the Amazon routing out illegal goldmines, dredgers and excavators. His small team lands, arrests the miners and sets fire to all the expensive equipment, which is too bulky to confiscate. In the film we see massive plumes of thick black smoke rising above the forest. Penalties for environmental crime are insubstantial, but, says Loss, “It’s not for President Lula to change those things, it’s Congress, and it’s hard to change the law. But destroying the equipment is a real deterrent, because the machines are expensive, so it’s a risky investment.”

An illegal gold mine in the Brazilian Amazon Credit : Courtesy of Malaika Pictures

Loss and Xipaia met when her village was attacked in 2020 by illegal goldminers; she was in Altamira, a two-day boat ride away. She put out a cry for help on social media and Loss, who was also in Altamira, saw it and responded right away. He picked Xipaia up in a helicopter and asked her to take him to the exact location of the miners’ dredger. The attackers spotted them and ran, but Ibama were able to seize their boat and secure the area. “He saved her village and her people and her parents from an immediate attack and they fell in love and have been together ever since,” says Ladkani.

“I’m usually very shy about these things but from the first time I saw her in the helicopter I couldn’t stop thinking about her,” admits Loss. “Three months later I was doing an Ibama operation on land to remove some illegal loggers and I saw a hawk’s nest and I took a picture of it and sent it to her,” says Loss.

“It’s the bird whose feather I wear in my headdress,” interrupts Xipaia, shyly. She admits that she had first met Loss before the helicopter ride, at a meeting, but he was leaving as she arrived. “He shook my hand and I made eye contact with him and something told me – I can’t really explain what – that he was going to be my husband.”

Loss holds a Master’s degree in social anthropology from the University of Brasília and is one of Ibama’s most experienced field agents, yet he spent a good part of his career sidelined by Bolsonaro, who had no interest in protecting the environment. In February 2023, under Lula, he was appointed Ibama’s coordinator of enforcement.

Loss has taken part in hundreds of operations. His job is a dangerous one. We watch him flying helicopters over swathes of forest to spot mines, or patrolling the rivers looking for dredgers. Recently one of his team was killed in an ambush, another got burns over 60 per cent of his body.

Hugo Loss, Xipaia’s husband, on a mission to destroy illegal mining equipment for Ibama, Brazil’s government enforcement agency

Ladkani asked to accompany Loss on a raid. “Hugo told me, it's too dangerous, the risk of you dying is too high. It’s a small team, and you would be taking the place of a soldier on the helicopter so we would be down one security man, which means our job is much harder, and by the way, if we get into a gun fight, we are not your bodyguards, we are there to finish a job. You would have to save yourself.

“I said, how dangerous is it? And he said, ‘Well, the risk of you dying is 50 per cent.’ I laughed – and then I realised he wasn’t joking.

Film-maker Richard Ladkani in the Brazilian Amazon Credit : Courtesy of Malaika Pictures

“Of course I had to think about that – I have a wife and two daughters. My wife and I discussed it. She grew up in a war zone in Beirut, so she understands threats, and how you can mitigate risks as well. She is also the producer of this film. We have had a long journey together – making conflict zone films like Sea of Shadows and The Ivory Game was no joke. But this one felt like a different level because of the 50 per cent quote.” He smiles.”‘I did hostile-environment training and we augmented the security to a degree where I felt it wasn’t 50 per cent any more.”

An illegal airbase in the Brazilian Amazon being destroyed Credit : Courtesy of Malaika Pictures

So Ladkani joined the team, and the resulting episode is terrifying: they are patrolling the river when they find a huge illegal dredger, used for gold mining. They board the dredger, its crew of illegal miners are put in a small boat and dispatched, and Loss’s team set fire to it. Attempting to get away, they realise their boat is still attached to the dredger by a chain, and they have only moments before an oxygen tank below the deck of the dredger explodes. Loss has to shoot the chain, but he has to hit it while it is taut, or the bullet would glance off. “The oxygen tank is steel and if it had exploded we would have been killed by the fragments if we were within 100 metres of that boat – and we were six metres away. It was Hugo who shot the chain – it took 50 shots at least. When Juma saw that footage she broke down and sobbed,” says Ladkani.

Do you like your job? I ask Loss.

He smiles. “Yes I do.”

Back in the 1970s, when two major roads were originally carved into the Amazon rainforest, of which 60 per cent is in Brazil, it opened it up for settlers to devastating effects – the population of the Brazilian Amazon quadrupled and millions of acres of trees were cut down for timber or land clearance and farming, and the rivers became polluted. Thousands of garimpeiros (prospectors) arrived, bringing disease, destruction and violence.

Indigenous people from the Mura tribe in a deforested area inside the Amazon rainforest near Humaita, Amazonas State, Brazil Credit : Ueslei Marcelino/REUTERS

Despite the protected reserves created by Lula during his first tenure (2003 to 2011), when Bolsonaro took over, he vowed that he would not demarcate a single millimetre of Indigenous land.

There was reason to be hopeful when Lula was re-elected in 2023, especially when he created the Ministry for Indigenous People. But it was an uphill struggle, and Xipaia left the post of State Secretary after about two years, and retired to her territory, where she still is. “She realised that it would be years, if not decades, before change could happen and she felt that her power was with activism from the front lines rather than being in an office in the city,” says Ladkani. “And what really hurt was her children having to grow up in the city and not having the connection to nature that she had.”

Smoke from illegal fires lit by farmers rises in Manaquiri, Amazonas state Credit : MICHAEL DANTAS

There has been a lot of progress, Juma says, compared to the Bolsonaro years “when it was genocide”. “It is hard to quantify all the changes because even though there was a change in the administration, it is important to understand that the government structure is very colonialist, no matter who is in power, and everything takes time. I entered the ministry when it was just being born.

“It was hard working in an office every day and not spending time with my children, and my son Tuppak [eight] told me that he wanted to go back to the forest, he was having a hard time at school in the city. I did not want to rob my son of that kind of childhood – being in the territory and getting his knowledge from the forest.”

I ask Loss and Xipaia if, with the way things are now, they are more inclined to hope or despair. “Most of the time I don’t think about the future,” says Loss. “I just focus on doing my work, one operation at a time.”

A wildfire consumes land deforested by cattle farmers near Novo Progresso, Para state, Brazil Credit : MICHAEL DANTAS/AFP via Getty Images

Xipaia thinks. “It depends where I am. When I’m in the forest with my family, there is immense fulfilment which is hard to explain; it gives me the hope and energy to keep wanting to protect it, and I want the whole world to get to know it.

“When I walk through the forest and harvest food there with my family and my people, it reminds me of what my ancestors were doing. The innocence of children, the idea of clean water, food without toxins – this gives me hope.”

“I don’t feel despair,” says Ladkani. “I feel like we’re in a war. There are plenty of good people fighting back, and that gives me hope. And there are lives on the line that we need to care about, which is the indigenous people, who are the frontline of our defence. They are defending nature for us so we need to make sure that they are heard and seen and respected. And we hope that the film puts a human face to that.

“We can’t pretend that destroying the biggest ecosystem on the planet is OK. If we lose the Amazon, we all lose.”

Yanuni will be released later this year

News.title: Alexander Isak finally starts to justify £125m price tag with fine double
News.content:
Emersonn, Ipswich’s Brazilian striker, did not see the ball in the opening exchanges and, by the time he did, Liverpool had zoomed into the distance to such an extent that you felt it was going to be impossible for them to peg their visitors back.

“I hate having to talk about good performances when you do not get points,” O’Neil declared to a room full of raised eyebrows and you can only assume his message was to ensure that morale in the dressing room was not drooping.

What damage was inflicted with Liverpool’s first significant attack. Gakpo, the subject of an £80m bid from Manchester City, was never going to allow transfer speculation to disrupt his focus and he nudged a perfect little ball into Isak’s path in the sixth minute to show his wellbeing.

The next move announced the return of Isak. One touch gave him an avenue to shoot, the next was a shot with his right foot that was so hard from 16 yards, on an angle, it bent the wrists of Kjell Scherpen as it howled into the net. Critics will feel Ipswich’s keeper should have done better.

Your first thought was to think of the first goal Isak scored in English football in September 2022, a similarly venomous drive, against Liverpool at Anfield. He oozed quality that evening, his pace and skill had Jürgen Klopp’s defenders persistently fretting and this is what he was doing again.

It was no coincidence that three minutes later, he came up with another wonderful goal. This one owed much to the beautiful pass Gakpo presented to him, an inch-perfect through ball with the outside of his right foot, but Isak still showed great poise to bamboozle Scherpen.

News.title: Forced displacement in the West Bank could be ‘crime against humanity’, says UN report
News.content:
Israel’s forced displacement of more than 33,000 Palestinians in the West Bank could amount to a “crime against humanity” and involves “ethnic cleansing”, according to a report published by the UN.

A report by the UN Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) said that Israeli actions in the area had sparked the “largest and longest displacement crisis in the West Bank since 1967” – the year in which Israel captured the territory.

The report said “large-scale, long-term and systematic displacement of over 33,000 Palestinians from refugee camps … during Israel’s Operation Iron Wall [which] raises serious concerns of the crime against humanity of forcible transfer”.

It added: “The documented use of airstrikes, armoured bulldozers and controlled detonations, to render entire camps uninhabitable, to force the displacement of their residents and to prevent their return, in the absence of imperative military necessity to justify such destruction and displacement, are not permissible under international law, appear to amount to collective punishment and raise concerns of ethnic cleansing.”

The 27-page report covers the period December 5, 2024 to January 31, 2026.

In January 2025, Israeli forces launched “Operation Iron Wall” in the northern West Bank in a bid to counter what they said were terrorist threats.

They destroyed hundreds of homes, cut off water and electricity, and barred humanitarian access to the Jenin, Nur Sham and Tulkarm refugee camps.

By October 2025, 52 per cent of structures in Jenin camp, 48 per cent in Nur Shams and 36 percent in Tulkarm had been destroyed or damaged.

The three camps are among 19 in the West Bank established to shelter Palestinians after the 1948 Nakba, and are administered by the UN Relief and Works Agency (UNRWA).

Although still referred to as refugee camps, they are in fact now densely packed towns.

News.title: When is Black Friday 2026? This year’s dates and what to expect
News.content:
Five tips for finding genuine Black Friday discounts and deals

Learning how to find the best Black Friday discounts can make a meaningful difference to your festive budget, especially if you’re a keen sale shopper. The following five tips are a good starting point.

1. Don’t over-fixate on Black Friday itself

Although the day of Black Friday brings some of the best discounts of the festive sale season, good deals are likely to be available both before and after it – and some items may sell out.

“When we look at our pricing data on a daily level, you have certain events such as Amazon’s October Prime sale [not yet confirmed for 2026] that are an earlier vector for change in prices,” says Vivek Pandya, a director at Adobe for Business.

“We typically see more significant discounts starting to emerge as we get into late October or early November, and these really kick up a notch as we get into Black Friday week.”

So, while interest in Black Friday deals will peak around the day itself, some of the best deals may have been available since the beginning of the week, or earlier.

2. Expand your search to everyday essentials

At Telegraph Recommended, we’ve picked up on a proliferation of discounts on everyday household items during recent Black Friday sales (and during other occasional events such as Prime Day). If you need a top-up of items such as cleaning products or pet supplies, this could be a thrifty time to buy them.

“These sales have become a spending spree on what retailers frame as ‘everyday essentials’, as well as bigger items and gifts,” says Pandya. Last year’s Cyber Weekend saw a 260 per cent spike in sales of “personal care” items including cosmetics, shampoos, fragrances and toothbrushes, according to Adobe.

3. Use a price tracker

Free price tracking tools such as camelcamelcamel can show you how the price of a product has changed over time. This allows you to identify when a Black Friday deal has actually brought a product’s price significantly lower than usual, or when the retailer’s pricing strategy has artificially made a deal appear to be generous.

Gabrielė Vitkė, product marketing team lead at data-gathering specialist Decodo, warns shoppers to watch out for “anchoring”, where a product’s price is set high prior to Black Friday, allowing the retailer then to reduce it sharply and advertise an eye-catching reduction.

“Discounts on items such as electronics and computing products can seem steep, sometimes exceeding 50 per cent against the list price,” says Vitkė. “However, our data shows that prices in this category rose in the run-up to Black Friday 2025, which is a sign of anchor pricing before the ‘discount’ is applied.”

News.title: Indonesia wildfires trigger 50,000 respiratory infections
News.content:
More than 50,000 people have contracted respiratory infections in Indonesia, as raging wild fires blanket huge swathes of the country in a thick, toxic smoke.

The vast archipelago is only a month into its fire season, but intense blazes have proven hard to control across Sumatra and Indonesian Borneo. There are fears the situation will only get worse, because the “Godzilla” El Niño is set to suppress rains that would normally have helped extinguish the flames.

“Our problems are not over. September is the peak of El Niño,” said Raja Juli Antoni, the forestry minister. “September is the main fight for us.”

Already the toxic haze has spread across Southeast Asia. On Friday Kuching, a city in Malaysian Borneo, was the most polluted city in the world on the IQ Air Index, followed by Jakarta and Singapore.

The wildfires have brought memories of record-breaking blazes in 2015. Then, the smoke was linked to roughly 100,000 excess deaths in Indonesia, Malaysia and Singapore, according to one study. The World Bank said Indonesia alone saw economic losses of $16.1bn, or 2 per cent of GDP.

News.title: Global hunger is a threat to Britain’s national security, report says
News.content:
Global hunger poses a direct threat to Britain’s national security, and tackling it should be a government priority, a new report from the London School of Economics has warned.

It says hunger is a major driver of mass migration, extreme violence and war – events that threaten significant repercussions for Britain and Europe’s national security.

“Hunger prevention is an important part of national security policy, not an optional act of charity,” Stuart Gordon, professor of International Development at LSE and author of the report, told The Telegraph.

Recent hunger crises in places like Sudan, Afghanistan and across North Africa have contributed significantly to rising numbers of people moving to the West.

Between January and November 2025 alone, 12,684 migrants from Sudan – which is facing what has been described as the worst hunger crisis in Africa’s history – arrived in Europe, roughly three times as many as the previous year.

Last year, an estimated 155,000 African refugees arrived in Europe.

“Food insecurity tests one of the most basic expectations people have of government: that it will protect access to the essentials of life,” said Prof Gordon.

“Food price shocks can rapidly escalate into political instability when governments are perceived to have failed to protect access to basic subsistence goods,” he added.

News.title: Congo’s Ebola outbreak slows at epicentre but widens elsewhere, modelling suggests
News.content:
Congo’s Ebola outbreak shows signs of slowing at the epicentre of the flare-up, but is widening as the infection spreads further afield, modelling suggests.

The daily tally of new cases in Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) was falling at the end of August, but more cases were being found outside Ituri province, where the infection burst out.

Latest official figures say the outbreak has now killed more than 3,000 people out of over 6,100 confirmed cases, with the infection spreading faster than any previous epidemic of the viral haemorrhagic fever.

Modelling by Airfinity, a health analytics firm, suggests the true toll of cases could be more than four times higher than reported.

The outbreak remains on track to eclipse the 2014 West Africa outbreak later this month, to become the largest ever recorded.

Airfinity said that data from late August showed the seven-day averages of reported cases and reported deaths had fallen by 16 per cent and 18 per cent respectively.

The firm said it was “too early to confirm the decline will hold, and it may mask subnational variation: The outbreak has fluctuated before and a week of falling case and death counts does not rule out another surge.

“Even if the decline continues at this current pace, low case levels remain weeks away.”

News.title: Bank of England must raise interest rates, says chief economist
News.content:
Thanks for joining me. Government borrowing costs edged lower on Thursday as Andy Burnham continues to face scrutiny over the public finances.

The yield on 10-year US treasury bonds – considered a benchmark for what governments pay to borrow money – declined slightly to 4.78pc on Thursday after a drop in oil prices.

Pre-market trading of bonds in Britain, France and Germany suggested the market was poised to rally after a brutal first half of the week.

However, Mr Burnham and Chancellor John Healey remain under intense pressure, with analysts estimating that as much as half of the country’s fiscal headroom has been wiped out by the jump in bond yields.

Borrowing costs surged after a jump in oil prices caused by fresh strikes between the US and Iran.

The yield on 10-year gilts, as UK bonds are known, hit levels not seen since the global financial crisis in 2007, while longer-term debt costs hit their highest point since 1998.

It means the Chancellor will have less room for manoeuvre in the Budget next month, with some economists predicting the rise in borrowing costs has wiped out up to £14bn of breathing room.

The rise in bond yields across major economies had deepened concerns about deteriorating financial conditions.

Central banks in the US and Europe are increasingly expected to raise interest rates this month to combat inflation caused by the Iran war, although the Bank of England is expected to hold rates steady for now.

Gavin Friend, an analyst at NAB, said: “If this war ‌were to be ‌put to bed, then that ⁠would certainly be something very positive to bring yields back down again across the board.” Here is what you need to know.

5 things to start your day

What happened overnight

Oil prices slipped, helping boost stocks and bonds.

Renewed fighting between the US and Iran pushed oil prices sharply higher earlier in the week.

However, Brent crude was trading near $94 a barrel after Donald Trump said he does not expect the US bombing campaign to last “much longer”.

Tokyo’s Nikkei 225 advanced 0.2pc to 64,455.83. Among major gainers, OpenAI investor SoftBank Group rose 2.9pc, memory chipmaker Kioxia rose 0.6pc, and chip equipment manufacturer Tokyo Electron gained 0.8pc.

South Korea’s Kospi rose 1.4pc to 6,656.81. Samsung was 1.3pc higher, while memory chipmaker SK Hynix was up 1.4pc.

In Hong Kong, the Hang Seng edged 0.1pc higher, to 25,344.80. The Shanghai Composite index climbed 0.4pc to 3,958.79.

Australia’s S&P/ASX 200 gained 0.5pc to 9,025.10.

The Taiex in Taiwan rose 0.6pc, while India’s Sensex climbed 0.3pc.

It comes after Wall Street bounced back after its sharp sell-off at the start of September, as investors snapped up shares that had fallen in recent days.

The S&P 500 rose, with almost 350 companies ending higher. Dell was among the biggest winners, jumping 14pc after giving an upbeat outlook, while investors were also looking ahead to results from chipmaker Broadcom.

The recovery came despite continued concerns over inflation, with oil prices remaining high as fighting between the US and Iran escalated. Brent crude briefly climbed close to $97 a barrel before easing back after Donald Trump said he did not expect the renewed bombing campaign to last “too long”.

US government bond yields were little changed after surging to their highest levels in several years earlier in the week.

Investors also got a mixed picture from the Federal Reserve’s latest assessment of the US economy. Economic activity increased modestly over the past two months, helped by strong demand from data centres, while companies added jobs at a slower pace in August.

The figures come ahead of Friday’s closely watched US jobs report, which could influence expectations for the next move in interest rates.

Sports.title: Premier League side complete shock transfer THREE DAYS after window closed thanks to little-known Fifa rule
Sports.content:
COVENTRY have announced the signing of Yann Ghobo THREE DAYS after the transfer window shut.

The Sky Blues have added the winger from Toulouse in what has turned out to be one of the more surprising deals of the summer.



The shock factor comes simply from the lateness of the transfer, with the window already being shut for days.

Gboho, 25, has signed a five-year contract with Coventry and could make his debut against Manchester City today.



The club were able to complete the deal despite being 72 hours past the deadline due to a little-known rule.

The Daily Mail have reported that the deal was agreed before the 11pm deadline on September 1.

The deal was subjected to a delay as Fifa checked that all of the documents were in order.

Fifa were eventually able to ratify the transfer subject to his UK Visa approval.

Gboho cost Coventry a reported £10.8million taking their summer spend over £100m.

The winger is a cousin of Paris Saint-Germain and France superstar Desire Doue.



SUN VEGAS WELCOME OFFER: GET UP TO £100 BONUS

He has impressed during his spell with Toulouse as he has scored 19 goals and assisted 12 more.

Gboho’s arrival will be a boost to Lampard and Coventry, who are yet to score in the Premier League this season.

The club have lost both of their first two games this season, with defeats coming at Arsenal and to Hull.

Lampard will be hoping Gboho can make an immediate impact and help the Sky Blues cause a shock at the Etihad.

Sports.title: Betting column: SunSport picks for a big weekend of Premier League action
Sports.content:
Commercial content notice: Taking one of the betting offers featured in this article may result in a payment to The Sun. 18+. T&Cs apply. gambleaware.org.

THERE’S the Havertz and the Havertz nots and it turns out Viktor Gyokeres falls into the latter category.

Arsenal’s showcase signing from last summer has now been reduced to the role of £64million benchwarmer, after being an unused sub in the Gunners’ opening two Premier League wins.

Displaced by German sort-of-striker Kai Havertz, Mikel Arteta has decided that the Swede is not the answer to the club’s 20-year search for the next Thierry Henry, even after his 22 goals in all competitions last season.

Nor was Julian Alvarez, Vinicius Jr or Lautaro Martinez. Despite being the champions of England and Champions League runners-up, Arsenal could not attract the kind of world class hitman that would have been a genuine next-step upgrade.

Sports.content:
MARCUS RASHFORD made his Manchester United debut a decade ago and has gone on to forge an incredible career in football.

The forward marked the Europa League 5-1 win against Midtjylland with a brace in 2016.



The match was memorable to someone else on the team as Joe Riley made his first-ever start for the club.

The former defender was handed the opportunity at left-back as United were suffering an injury crisis.



Rashford, 28, has since earned multiple contracts and earns a reported £325,000-per-week.

But Riley’s career seemed to go the other way as he retired from football in 2026.

He now works as a financial protection advisor selling life insurance, income protection, critical illness and injury cover.

The former defender still plays football but only in non-league with his current team being Warrington Rylands.

Riley has admitted that he would have liked to have played more at the highest level but is enjoying his new chapter.

He told BBC Sport: “I lived with Scott McTominay for six years, and Marcus and I also came through the academy together.

“These people were like family to me.

“I don’t dwell on the past – I’m just happy that it happened. I’ve now got my foot in the door for the next chapter of my life.

“I’m progressing with another career that’s setting me up for the rest of my life.”



Riley left United in 2018 as he spent two years at Bradford before joining Carlisle.

He then went on to have spells at Walsall, AFC Fylde and Tamworth.

As Riley plays in non-league football he is able to take defeats on the chin more than when he was at United.

He said: “A few years back I wouldn’t speak for 24 hours if I lost.

“Now if we lose, it’s not ideal, but there’s always another game around the corner.”



Louis van Gaal was the manager who gave Riley his chance at United and he still remembers the moment his name went on the teamsheet.

Sports.title: ‘There’s no selling Chelsea’ – Katie McCabe reveals why she left Arsenal to join rivals after 11 years in north London
Sports.content:
WHEN Chelsea came calling, Katie McCabe needed no persuading.

After spending 11 years with Arsenal and winning every club trophy available, she decided at the end of last season that it was time to move on.



Only that move saw her join the Gunners’ biggest rivals.

The 30-year-old says it was an easy decision to make when Chelsea entered the picture, despite also being linked with a move to WSL champions Manchester City.



McCabe told SunSport: “Coming to the end of my contract, I knew it was the right time for a new challenge and a new chapter in my career. I think having spoken to Sonia (Bompastor, head coach) and had those conversations with her, I think she’s an excellent manager in terms of what she’s won, but also as a player too.

“She’s been there and done it as a top player, so having had those conversations, understanding what she wants and the expectations as well was really important for me. I think it suited both of us and I was happy to get the deal over the line and get going as a Chelsea player.”



Blues head coach Bompastor didn’t even have to convince the full-back to make the switch, because the illustrious history of Chelsea speaks for itself.

“There’s no selling Chelsea as a football club,” she added. “Chelsea have built up over the years with the amount of trophies they’ve won, how big they are in the WSL and in Europe obviously.

“There was no selling Chelsea, it was just more so understanding what Sonia wanted, the expectations and obviously me being able to bring what I bring to the team as a player. It fitted both of us and I’m here now.”

But why Chelsea? McCabe says it was important to maintain her level of football, especially with the Women’s World Cup on the horizon next summer.



CASINO SPECIAL – BEST CASINO BONUSES FROM £10 DEPOSITS

WSL opening weekend fixtures 4th September – London City Lionesses vs Manchester United

5th September – Chelsea vs Aston Villa

6th September – Brighton vs Arsenal

6th September – Tottenham vs West Ham

6th September – Charlton vs Liverpool

6th September – Crystal Palace vs Everton

6th September – Manchester City vs Birmingham City

She continued: “I wanted to maintain the level I was at in terms of challenging for the Champions League, the league, the FA Cup.

“That was the most important thing for me and having spoken to the club, spoken to Sonia, it was the best for me.”

McCabe officially began training with her new team-mates in July and was welcomed with open arms.

And just a matter of weeks later, they jetted off to Australia and New Zealand for a pre-season tour.

It provided the perfect opportunity for McCabe to get to know her fellow Chelsea stars.



Initiations took place – although the Ireland captain would not let slip what exactly happened.

“For me it’s a new thing coming into a new team, but the girls have been excellent in terms of welcoming me in,” she said.

“It’s been all go from the start really, just getting to know each other on and off the pitch.

“Obviously I’ve come up against these players a lot in the last few years, so I know a lot of their strengths and weaknesses as players.

“But I think that’s the beauty of pre-season, just getting to know team-mates on a more personal level as well, which is what the tour as well helps towards for a couple of the new players in the team.



“So it’s been really good. The girls have been great. And yeah, we’re just excited to get going.”

McCabe became popular at Arsenal partly because of her leadership qualities both on and off the pitch – qualities that also saw her become the youngest-ever Ireland captain at the age of 21 almost a decade ago.

She is hoping to bring that leadership to Stamford Bridge when fully settled into the Chelsea first team.

The defender said: “For me, it’s coming in and getting my head down and getting to work, earning the respect of my team-mates and showing everybody that I want to work hard for the club and for each one of my team-mates as well.



“I want to step on the pitch and with that you grow into your role, whatever that may be in the team.

“Obviously we haven’t started the season yet so it’s hard to predict what that will be, but for me when I get the opportunity on the pitch I’ll always bring my experience and my leadership and qualities on the ball.

“We’ll obviously see how things go over the next few weeks once we kick-start the season but it was definitely just making sure I was getting to work and earning the respect of each one of my team-mates.”

Chelsea kick off their WSL season at home against Aston Villa on September 5.



Games against Manchester United and Birmingham follow before they welcome Arsenal to Stamford Bridge.

However, McCabe isn’t thinking about facing her old team just yet.

In terms of goals for the new campaign, she is fully focused on the team.

“For me it’s all about the team. It’s about getting momentum at the start of the season and trying to get wins under our belt.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“Progressing in the Champions League and getting through that early round which is going to be difficult.



“It’s always about trophies and how well we’re performing as a team.”

Sports.title: Sky Sports and Audi launch unique 'Flying Lap' track guide series
Sports.content:
Get closer than ever before to the technical and physical demands of an Formula 1 race circuit in a series combining real-life driving in an Audi RS5 road car with advanced simulation data

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Powered by Audi: Martin Brundle takes to the iconic Monza track in a high-performance Audi, combining real laps with advanced sim data to break down racing lines, braking points, and elite-level performance.

Sky Sports and their official Innovation partner Audi have launched a new series, combining real-world driving with Audi's R26 simulation technology to deliver a storytelling experience from the race track never seen before.

At the heart of Flying Lap is Audi's cutting-edge simulation technology, placing the brand directly into the narrative of performance. By integrating Audi Sim data with Sky Sports' world-class production, the series brings fans closer than ever to the technical and physical demands of the circuit.

Fronted by Sky Sports pundit and former Formula 1 driver Karun Chandhok, each episode sees the driver take to an iconic track in a high-performance Audi road car, delivering a full-throttle lap guide enriched with immersive data visualisation.

As they navigate the circuit, viewers are guided through key sections of the track inside the high-performance all-new Audi RS5 with highlighted hotspots. At pivotal moments, the experience shifts seamlessly into a fully rendered virtual environment - where an Audi R26 F1 car screams to life.

Within this graphical world, Audi's simulation data is used to break down the intricacies of elite performance, from braking zones and racing lines to gear changes, cornering speeds, and overtaking opportunities. The camera moves dynamically around the virtual car - from exterior angles to the driver's cockpit - offering perspectives never possible before.

The format then transitions back to real-world driving, maintaining continuity as the Sky Sports driver progresses through the lap, creating a seamless fusion of physical and digital storytelling.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Powered by Audi: Karun Chandhok takes to the iconic Miami track in a high-performance Audi, combining real laps with advanced sim data to break down racing lines, braking points, and elite-level performance.

The first Flying Lap episode took on Miami, one of the fastest and most technically demanding circuits on the calendar, while the second headed to the iconic Silverstone in Great Britain.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Powered by Audi: Karun Chandhok takes to the iconic Silverstone track in a high-performance Audi, combining real laps with advanced sim data to break down racing lines, braking points, and elite-level performance.

The third features motorsport's Temple of Speed - Monza in Italy.

Launched across Sky Sports platforms from May 2026, Flying Lap represents the next evolution of the Sky Sports and Audi Innovation partnership - pushing the boundaries of broadcast innovation and creating new opportunities for storytelling beyond live coverage.

Sports.title: Erasmus and Rennie's war of words escalates ahead of third Test
Sports.content:
The four-match series is finely poised at 1-1, with Rugby’s Greatest Rivalry seemingly reaching new heights of tension as Rassie Erasmus and Dave Rennie’s war of words escalates.

Picture the scene: The touring All Blacks win the opening Test with a 33-16 at Ellis Park. Then, the Springboks hit back with a thrilling 33-26 victory over New Zealand in Cape Town.

Named in the front row for the Springboks for that contest were Ox Nche, Malcolm Marx and Wilco Louw. Just one hour before kick-off, that was changed to Gerhard Steenekamp, Deon Fourie and Thomas du Toit with the original three dropping to the bench.

Erasmus said this was down to conditions and a chance of rain not materialising.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights of the Greatest Rivalry second Test between South Africa and New Zealand.

"We thought it was going to be wet and that's why we picked the front row, Erasmus said after the match. "The whole weather prediction, the whole week, was it was going to be wet."

On this matter, Rennie refused to criticise.

"We stuck with the team we named and it doesn't worry me at all," Rennie said on the matter.

"They named their team on Monday. That had no bearing on the team that we named. So, yeah - no drama from my perspective."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights as New Zealand scored five tries to beat South Africa 33-16 at Ellis Park and take a 1-0 lead in the four-Test series of Rugby's Greatest Rivalry.

It is important to note that, under World Rugby regulations, medical dispensation is usually required for a team to be permitted to be make changes within 48 hours of the game kicking-off.

However, with Rugby's Greatest Rivalry independently administered, Erasmus can chop and change as much as he pleases.

In total, Erasmus made five changes from the squad he named on Monday for the second Test, including a complete change to the front row. During the week, Handre Pollard went from fit to injured and was eventually withdrawn, while Cheslin Kolbe went from injured to fit and was ultimately named on the wing.

That is why he is keeping it under his hat ahead of the third Test in Johannesburg - if conditions require it, of course.

"If it's clear and dry this will be the team that's starting, but if it rains we might make a change or two," Erasmus said.

Scrum disagreement erupts: 'Don't come with that nonsense'

While there have been no real arguments over late changes, with diplomacy reigning supreme, one issue that has erupted is a disagreement over scrums.

Rennie has accused the Springboks of "walking around" during scrums, alleging they are illegally angling sideways rather than staying square and driving straight. He believes this gives them an unfair advantage by allowing them to get around the All Blacks' front row.

The New Zealand head coach is so irked by the issue that he said he had provided feedback to World Rugby.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player The All Blacks perform a spine-chilling haka at Ellis Park ahead of the opening Test against South Africa in the four-match Rugby's Greatest Rivalry series. New Zealand are touring South Africa for a full series for the first time in 30 years.

"The scrums were better tonight. I think the referee [Angus Gardner] was pretty strong around setting a mark and trying to keep hookers in the same sort of space. The Springboks moved across further left and he stopped them," Rennie said.

"We will give a bit of feedback around that. It is still a bit of an issue for us because they are able to walk around and then go straight through our tighthead.

"There are a couple of little technical things we will share, again, but I thought at the end, both teams were able to play off them. So, I think Angus did a reasonable job there."

Of course Erasmus responded to Rennie's comments saying "don't come with that nonsense" in a fired-up response.

"We've been playing with the pack of these guys together. It's the first time ever in history that people are talking about us walking around. Why would we, all of a sudden, walk around?

"I wouldn't come with that nonsense and say we are walking around and try to put those things out in the media. If I'm starting to put things out, the last lineout was skew and we contested. I'm not going to moan my a--- off about that.

"If they just want to start moaning about stuff like that, then they are under pressure."

Is it pressure? Is it mind games? Whatever it is, it has set the stage for a third Test that promises to be even spicier, more dramatic, and a further reminder of why this series was dubbed Rugby's Greatest Rivalry.

Sports.title: Chelsea 2.0: How transitional Blues are rebuilding for WSL and WCL success
Sports.content:
"Chelsea are going through a transitional moment and it takes time for the club to rebuild."

Not pundit analysis, but the thoughts of Chelsea head coach Sonia Bompastor to Sky Sports ahead of the new WSL season.

And despite the hint of cliché, it works. There has been plenty upheaval over the last two years, starting with Bompastor replacing Emma Hayes.

Then, there was the shock departure of Paul Green as head of women's football in February. Alongside Hayes, the duo oversaw years of unprecedented success. It is something hard to sustain and even harder to replicate.

But that is the task that falls at Bompastor's feet. She managed to keep it going in her first season with an unbeaten domestic treble - some may say with Hayes' influence still in play - but her second campaign exposed the realties. Chelsea were not the team of old and a new era was beckoning.

Now in her third pre-season with the Blues, Bompastor believes she has the backing of the club to do just that.

"I think now I understand what the club is about a lot more," she said. "I also understand what we want to achieve and bringing my input into that.

"It's good to be in a place where I feel the confidence and the trust coming from the hierarchy in the club. As much as I know my job, we need to get good results in order for me to stay as long as possible, but it's also important to feel like we also have time to rebuild the team in order for us to compete against the best."

How last season informs the next

Chelsea only won the League Cup last season and finished third in the league behind Manchester City and Arsenal. It was the first time in six years they had not walked away with the WSL title.

Bompastor reflected: "We wanted last season to be a more successful season because Chelsea is a club who is used to winning. We only won one trophy, but if you analyse it, we have some good learnings to take and that's really important for us to reflect on.

"We spoke a lot about the environment and the culture we want to create here at Chelsea.

"It's a lot about standards, behaviours, how you show up every day, how much you are committing to work hard to achieve your goals and what are the type of behaviours you want to show up every day, off and on pitch.

"Who do we want to be as a team? How do we want people to talk about Chelsea? These things are really important for us to be able to achieve the goals we have.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights of the Women's League Cup final between Chelsea and Manchester United.

"Chelsea are a club who are used to winning and we need to make sure we put everything together in order for us to achieve that.

"I'm quite happy with the squad of players I have, the quality we have, but it's also important alongside that quality to bring the right mentality."

Experience and youth informing transfer policy

This summer does have the air of a new start about it, especially in terms of playing personnel.

Players who have been the face of Chelsea for years have left. Former captain Millie Bright retired, legendary goalscorer Sam Kerr moved to the USA. Niamh Charles, Guro Reiten and Johanna Rytting Kaneryd also departed. They represent years of service, experience and trophies.

"We lost some really important players in terms of the environment and culture," Bompastor said. "Some of them had been here for many years and it's difficult to replace them.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player With both leaving Chelsea, Sam Kerr and Millie Bright were given a guard of honour following the final WSL game of the season

"So it's for us, the staff and club, to think about how and what is the best way to replace them. It's about the recruitment, but also again linked back to the environment and the culture we want to create.

"We have also great leaders who have the right mentality about when you are on pitch, it's about winning games. Off the pitch, it's about the behaviours you need and showing up every day in order for us to work hard on the pitch to achieve the goals."

Chelsea's transfer strategy of mixing experience and youth is clear and epitomised by two of their four summer signings so far in Katie McCabe and Nelly Las.

McCabe needs little introduction. Indeed, Bompastor herself told Sky Sports she did not need to speak on the defender's quality, and it is clear she goes a long way in replacing some of the leadership Chelsea lost.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Katie McCabe gives her first interview after joining Women's Super League team Chelsea. Video credit: Chelsea FC

"She has already started to impact the squad in terms of the behaviours and the standards," Bompastor added. "I'm really pleased she's a Chelsea player now."

Las, meanwhile, is an exciting 18-year-old prospect who joined from Leicester. She made 16 WSL appearances across the last two seasons, and has featured for England's youth teams.

"It's important to have the right balance between experienced players, but also the youth into the squad," Bompastor said. "Players having versatility to play in different positions is also really important for me.

"I'm a manager who really loves to work with young players, to invest time to develop them and I'm really keen to bring these players into the squad and see how they can develop to contribute to the success we will have in the future."

Carrying on a legacy

There will always be pressure to win at Chelsea given their history, and they now have a balance to strike - maintaining that legacy while also forging a new way forward and meeting the standards Bompastor has set out.

That falls, in part, to the team's senior players - no matter how long they have played for the club.

One of those is defender Ellie Carpenter. She may have only been at Chelsea for a year, but as a multiple-trophy winner and regular starter, she will likely now step into a leadership role among the group.

Image: Ellie Carpenter (left) joined Chelsea last summer

"Chelsea are going through a bit of a transition phase at the moment. A lot of legends have gone and they left such a great legacy," she told Sky Sports. "Now it's our turn to do that, follow in their footsteps and to build on what Chelsea is as a club.

"As a footballer, you love those opportunities and moments in your career and it's a perfect time to be stepping into that role for this club.

"Our aim this season is to fight for those trophies back and show what Chelsea is about. We want to do it as a team, winning in that way and enjoying it and hopefully getting the results on the way as well.

"We have a great team this season and pre-season has felt good so I'm excited."

Champions League - is this the year?

Image: Sonia Bompastor won the Champions League with Lyon - as did new Chelsea striker, Melvine Malard (right)

One way this squad can cement themselves into Chelsea history is by winning the one trophy that continues to elude them - the Champions League.

For a long time, the Blues' recruitment strategy has been geared towards European glory while the domestic trophies took care of themselves.

Bompastor won it as a manager with Lyon and was a key reason for her appointment in 2024. Carpenter was in her victorious squad, as was new striker Melvine Malard and defender Kadeisha Buchanan. McCabe won it with Arsenal. Lucy Bronze - who signed a new Chelsea deal this summer - has been crowned Europe champion five times.

Image: Lucy Bronze and Keira Walsh - now both at Chelsea - won the Champions League with Barcelona

But none of those have come in Chelsea blue and every year, we ask the same question: is this the year the wait is over?

"Winning the Champions League is one of the main goals for us," Bompastor said. "We'll work as hard as possible to achieve that and I know everyone is expecting Chelsea to always be at their best.

"But the competition now in Europe is getting higher and higher. Many clubs now are in a position where they can compete to win the Champions League. I don't want to shy away from us and our ambitions, but I also know it's difficult.

"But that's the one trophy we're missing in the club and we will try as hard as possible to fight for that."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sky Sports' Anton Toloui explains why the WSL have decided to change some of their kick-off times this season.

"It's always what Chelsea want," Carpenter added. "It's what their ambition is, what the fans want, what everyone here wants and what we work towards every day.

"This squad is young, but multiple people have won it in the team, so that helps a lot to bring the experience and what it takes to win.

"But we're just going to go game-by-game this season. We don't want to put too much pressure on ourselves. When we're enjoying football, we're playing our best football."

Getting comfortable with scrutiny

While it may seem a tedious back and forth on the Champions League each year, that is the kind of scrutiny that comes with being at Chelsea and despite changes elsewhere, will never alter.

It has perhaps been one of the learnings for Bompastor in her two years at the club, and something she must instil in the squad she is assembling.

"I've never been in a place before where the scrutiny is so high like at Chelsea, but I'm comfortable with it," she reflected.

"It means people care about us and really think we are a really important club. That's what comes with our standards and Chelsea being one of the best clubs in the world, so we need to get comfortable with that.

"We need to make sure when we go into the season, we don't have any regrets and we give our all any time we step into the pitch."

What is for sure is the Blues are in the process of morphing into something new. Consistent evolution was one of the secrets to Hayes' success, and Bompastor will be hoping the same is true now.

Sports.title: St Helens 'need a clear out' as recruitment questioned after Leigh defeat
Sports.content:
Jamie Jones-Buchanan believes St Helens need a big rebuild as Eamon O’Carroll’s side missed out on making the Super League play-offs for the first time in the club's history.

St Helens' standing at seventh on the Super League ladder for the 2026 season was confirmed on Friday night after they were thumped 48-10 by Leigh Leopards, while Hull KR's 36-6 win against Huddersfield confirmed the top six.

It was Saints' seventh defeat in their last 10 matches and second heavy loss in a row, having suffered a 28-point reverse to Leeds a week ago.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Leigh Leopards secured their Super League play-off spot with the victory

O'Carroll is due to be replaced by former Brisbane Broncos and Australia head coach Kevin Walters ahead of the 2027 season, and the experienced coach will hope to galvanise the Saints back to their best next season.

But eyebrows have been raised over the team's recruitment decisions this year, with the club also struggling with a big injury crisis. At one stage in July, 16 players were sidelined with injuries.

Paul Rowley stepped down as the Saints coach that same month. Saints had been six points behind league leaders Leeds Rhinos at the time, but had suffered a 46-0 demolition by Toulouse earlier in July - the first time the club have gone scoreless at home in a league match since 1980.

The Saints, who won four titles in a row between 2019 and 2022, have experienced a sudden slump, and questions are being raised over the club's recruitment.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player The Saints' day went from bad to worse after Mark Percival was ssent off for a high tackle

"Nothing is given in sport," Jamie Jones-Buchanan said on Sky Sports.

"You certainly can't copy and paste from one generation to another because context is king. St Helens probably need a clear out.

"They have some exceptional young talents coming through, but they're arriving at the wrong time, not having the best of experiences.

"Older players there too, who have maybe stayed a bit too long. Contextually, there are some players playing out of position.

"Tristan Sailor and Jack Welsby were really good against Leigh Leopards, you see moments of genius within it. But it's where they are playing and how it all fits together. The jigsaw has just not been great for St Helens."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Josh Charnley opened the scoring for Leigh and celebrated by holding up a signed contract, after penning a new deal

Over the off-season, St Helens added experienced Australian players Shane Wright, Jacob Host and David Klemmer, while Jackson Hastings and Joe Shorrocks also arrived.

Saints also signed Daniel Suluka-Fifita midway through the campaign, but have struggled to make more acquisitions due to salary cap constraints.

It came after players including Konrad Hurrell, Morgan Knowles, Moses Mbye and Joe Bennison, left over the off-season, while Kyle Feldt was released mid-season.

The club has announced one new signing for the 2027 season, with Solomona Faataape joining from Catalans.

Sky Sports pundit and St Helens legend Jon Wilkin believes they have not replaced like-for-like and have made "short-term" recruitment choices.

"I've said it a number of times but Saints' recruitment has been shocking," Wilkin said.

"It's been terrible. They've made convenient and short-term recruitment choices. They've not replaced like-for-like and they need to rethink their recruitment strategy.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Meanwhile, Hull KR beat Huddersfield Giants t oalso secure their spot in the post-season Play-Offs

"There's a lot of young guys who have gone out into Super League who aren't ready. I'm loving that, it is great for them and for their future.

"But the reason they're out there was because you had an old squad at the start of the year that wasn't durable enough to get through a year, and then you signed shoddy replacements for guys who moved on.

"That's why young guys are having to put a Saints shirt on and are getting flogged by Leigh.

"I'm buying the message that it's all positive: 'Hey, we've got a great youth system and some young lads are getting a chance.' But if you look at the underlying reason why they are getting a chance, that's the issue. It's the root cause of their problem, sloppy recruitment over a period of three or four years."

O'Carroll: Missing out on play-offs disappointing

Reflecting on his side's season, and missing out on a spot in the Play-Offs, O'Carroll admitted that learning from this adversity may help his team move forwards in the future.

"I've just mentioned it to the group - it's obviously really disappointing," O'Carroll said after Friday's match.

"It doesn't sit well with me that I've been a part of that, I won't shy away from it.

"This group has had a lot of success, consistent success, so to experience a bit of adversity is good in some respects.

"Moving on now, I feel the conversations with Eamon and Abi, they have absolute clarity in terms of what needs to be done and I've every confidence they'll do that.

"For Kevin Walters to come in, it's probably a great time to come in now and for the club to accelerate forward."

Sky Sports will show every game of the Super League live this season, including two matches each round exclusively live. The remaining five matches will be broadcast on Sky Sports+.
