“But they are with us. I believe they are with us. I love Everton and always have done. It’s reinvigorated me being back and now there’s a little bump in the road. I need to get over the bump quickly and start looking at how I can make it go smoothly.”

Sports.title: Nottingham Forest’s Liam Delap: ‘I play at my best on the edge of being horrible’
Sports.content:
“You can imagine it: he’s a centre-back, I’m a striker,” says Liam Delap, Nottingham Forest’s £45m club-record signing, smiling as he sets the scene. He is reliving taking on his younger brother, Finn, in the garden. These days, they are each other’s biggest supporters – Liam attended Finn’s victory for third-tier Burton on Wednesday – but as kids there was a friendly rivalry. The elder brother says: “There were probably a lot of tears, a lot of fights … whether it was playing Monopoly or football, it always ended in either the table being flipped or kicking the shit out of each other.”

It is a competitive streak that has stuck and Delap is determined to make his presence felt at Forest, for whom he could make his full debut against Tottenham on Saturday. It has been a testing 16 months; he left Chelsea a season into a six-year contract and after one goal in 28 top-flight appearances, a dozen of those starts. “It is never a linear path straight to the top,” Delap says, his right hand taking flight in the City Ground boardroom, the 1979 and 1980 European Cups shimmering behind him. “I just want to get my head down, focus and keep improving because I’m still so young and I have so much to learn. I even at times probably think I’ve been in football a lot longer than I have. I’ve still, hopefully, got a long career ahead.

“I think you just have to accept that sometimes things go bad, things happen … it might [prove to] be a good thing, I think. My first loans to Stoke and Preston [from Manchester City, across 2022-23] didn’t really go well at all and it was probably one of the best things that happened because I learnt so much from that season and went to Hull [for 2023-24] and kicked on from there. I’m still young, I’ve still got a lot of learning to do. Sometimes injuries happen, sometimes you don’t play. I don’t think anything is lost … Everyone has rocky moments. I’ve just got to use them to learn and kick on.”

Last summer, Delap was hot property. Oliver Glasner tells a story of Delap having proposals from 18 Premier League clubs and jests that the 23-year-old knows every top-flight manager owing to the various Zoom calls he held while deciding his next move. After all, one of those was with Glasner, then at Crystal Palace. Forest wanted him then, too. “It was a tough decision,” recalls Delap. “I remember the conversation we had, I was really impressed and I thought: ‘This guy [Glasner] is really good.’ He spoke incredibly well and you can see he has done really well with the strikers he has had in the past. That definitely stuck in my mind.”

Glasner wants Delap to play to his strengths: physicality, power and finishing. He doesn’t mean the forward’s hidden talent: cube roots. At the start of the year a clip of Delap showing off his maths skills went viral. “I didn’t enjoy maths one bit but I was always quite good at it. One of my friends taught me in school how to do it and I didn’t forget it. I hated school, [the] work, but I was always quite intelligent.”

The Austrian head coach said it was apparent in conversations with Delap this summer that the player had learnt lessons from a trying year: “I think it shows his attitude and his character that he said: ‘Yeah, I want a team and a club that values my strengths and wants to play to my strengths.’ Because I never want to change a player: it doesn’t make sense to say: ‘OK, now you should play like Messi: false nine, drop into midfield and combine play with one or two touches.”

View image in fullscreen Liam Delap scored once in 28 league appearances for Chelsea. Photograph: Adam Davy/PA

A tally of 12 goals in the Ipswich side relegated in 2024-25 triggered widespread interest. At that point Delap was talked up as a potential heir to Harry Kane as England’s No 9. He has been capped by his country at every age group and was in the same under-16s team as Jude Bellingham. “As a little kid, all you want to do is play for your country,” Delap says. “So, of course, in my mind that’s where I want to get to. But it’s not as easy as that. I have to work hard and improve and that’s all I can do.”

An imposing 6ft 2in striker, Delap has long been viewed as the next big thing. He spearheaded Manchester City to FA Youth Cup victory over Chelsea in 2020, a couple of months after Pep Guardiola handed him his senior City debut aged 17. Cole Palmer and Morgan Rogers, now teammates at Chelsea, were part of that same under-18s side, together with the new Aston Villa defender Taylor Harwood-Bellis and James McAtee, one of his best friends and now a clubmate again.

“He was a No 10 and quite often he would give me the ball and we just had that really good relationship off the pitch and it translated on to the pitch,” Delap says of McAtee. “If we didn’t win, we’d all be fuming. It probably instilled that winning mentality into us early. I think it’s worked because you can see from that team that almost everyone is playing somewhere in the Premier League, abroad, the Championship and that is probably because we pushed each other so much.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Delap made his Forest debut as a substitute at Anfield last weekend, his first notable action a quick throw-in that led to the penalty scored by Morgan Gibbs-White to earn a second-half lead. Only after the 2-2 draw did Glasner discover that Delap’s father, Rory, who played for Southampton and Stoke among others, knew a thing or two about throws. “I said: your father will be proud of you,” says Forest’s head coach. So, has Liam got a mammoth throw in his armoury? “No, I don’t think so,” he replies. “I would never, anyway: I’m a striker, I need to be in the box.”

View image in fullscreen Liam Delap was much in demand after impressing with a 12-goal league season at Ipswich. Photograph: Ryan Pierse/Getty Images

Delap relishes the blood and thunder of battle. Glasner loves how Forest’s marquee signing stands up to centre-backs, making the point that defenders are hardly “hugging and kissing you all the time” in the heat of duels. But Delap, who spent a decade at Derby before joining City, says he has learned to harness his aggression on the field, after periods of getting into trouble when he was a youngster.

“You have to be careful, but not shy away from who you are,” he says. “I’m always going to fight for everything, always be aggressive, determined. It goes back to the point about my brother, being little kids in the garden, going at each other: that’s me. Sometimes you need to control it and sometimes you need to be careful, but I think I play at my best when I’m on that edge of being … being horrible.”

Sports.title: RIATH AL-SAMARRAI: This is the untold behind-the-scenes story of the rumbling Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua fight talks - and how much the pair stood to lose under disgraceful idea to stage bout in New York
Sports.content:
I remember the first time I reported that cogs were turning on a fight between Anthony Joshua and Tyson Fury. It was a good while ago – almost 12 years, actually.

The date was December 2, 2014. I’d spoken that evening to Joshua’s promoter, Eddie Hearn, when both his guy and Fury were unbeaten and neither had fought for a world title.

Hearn, then and now, was bullish in spelling out his plan. ‘It is a fight I would love to make next summer,’ he told me. ‘People ask if AJ is ready to fight Fury but, to be honest, is Fury ready to fight AJ?’

It was a nice line for the back page and ultimately good for one thing alone – proving the timeless point that, in boxing, you should only believe it when you see it.

But here we are, trapped in a different version of the same dance all these years on.

Because as of Friday, the fight was on and, according to Hearn, talks had been resurrected to take it to Wembley Stadium. A day earlier it was heading to New York’s Madison Square Garden on November 20 and Joshua’s team were floating the possibility of canning the whole thing in protest.

They were furious that a contract signed three months ago, stipulating a UK venue, was being broken so that Netflix could have a cosier fit with American viewing hours. The Saudi powerbrokers for the fight, led by Turki Alalshikh, were evidently happy to side with the broadcaster, to hell with the British audience for a British fight, and ostensibly that is what sent Hearn and Joshua into a spin.

Twelve years on from when I reported that Anthony Joshua and Tyson Fury were in talks to fight each other, the pair are still yet to touch gloves

Fury and Joshua are closer than ever to trading blows, with signatures on contracts, but they are still squabbling on the details

Time will tell if they get their way – Wembley conversations may have reopened, but it isn’t the only factor at play in this game of brinksmanship. Far from it.

I’ve had conversations this week with people around the deal and can flesh out a few of the details behind the chaos, which boils down to a boring three-letter word. Tax.

It’s something Hearn himself has alluded to in interviews this week – he mentioned that tax conditions in the US were unfavourable for Joshua. The information I’ve since received illustrates what that would look like in real language.

In short, it is my understanding that Joshua’s team have somewhere close to 10 million reasons not to want the fight in New York. Explained in a slightly longer form: if it is staged in London, the tax for a pair of non-UK residents would be around 20 per cent and in the US ‘withholding tax’ is around 30 per cent.

That is a significant jump with the purses involved – I’m told Joshua and Fury are in line to receive approximately $100m each (around £74m), so a $10m shortfall on the net amounts they would take back to Dubai and the Isle of Man respectively has not gone unnoticed.

As far as we can tell, Fury has not kicked up a fuss on the US tax. Publicly, anyway. But Joshua’s team viewed it as a hefty pay cut on what he signed, which fed into their wider anger that the fight was being shifted abroad.

Irrespective of which motivation weighed more, it seems that some level of sense might yet prevail – if the fight lands in the UK, that can only be a good thing. Hearn was very much in the right to paint it as a disgrace if it goes anywhere else.

But, again, we are in the realms of believing it when we see it. And especially in consideration of the individuals who hold true power behind this fight. That would be Netflix, who presumably still see greater value in the US, and the Saudi organisers, Sela, who have been steered on this fight by Alalshikh.

If fight is staged in the US, Joshua and Fury are set to pay millions more in tax. Fury and his promoter Frank Warren have not kicked up a fuss on issue - publicly at least

Turki Alalshikh (centre) claimed that he was trying to stage the fight in London back in July, though this may only have been lip service

Alalshikh, you might note, has already performed a curious role in the London saga. It was early July when he began applying pressure to City Hall, flagging that curfews in the capital would need tweaking to enable a US-friendly start time.

Writing on X, his favoured means of communication, he posted: ‘Hopefully a positive statement from the Mayor of London’s office about a later start time if Fury v Joshua is in London, as so far we have been told it is not possible.’

I might add here that the latter sentiment landed as something of a surprise to those on the receiving end – I’m told no request was made by Sela to mayor Sadiq Khan until mid-August. When those conversations did finally occur, sources tell me it was made clear by the mayor’s office that a late start wouldn’t be a hurdle. Khan has since gone public in saying he wants the fight in London.

A plausible theory, held by a few parties, is that the Sela overture was a gesture. A means of being able to claim: ‘We tried.' Lip-service, in other words, and flapping lips in boxing tend to serve no one.

Hopefully this fight proves the exception to the rule. Hopefully it does go to London. Hopefully the pressure applied by Hearn and Joshua, for whatever reason they prioritised, is decisive. Anything else would be an utter sham and a betrayal of British sport.

But this is boxing. And for more than a decade, one excuse after another has been found to keep these two fighters apart – the threshold for tedium was breached long before any contract. If that extends indefinitely, the question of New York or London might be rendered slightly irrelevant.

Sports.title: 'The most competitive league in the world? Don't be ridiculous. It's rigged': Angry insiders doubt whether Aston Villa, Newcastle, Everton and Co can ever break the Premier League's glass ceiling and challenge the 'arrogant', free-spending 'Big Six'
Sports.content:
More than anything, it’s the utter sense of resignation that strikes you. There is anger, too.

After a summer that has seen our big Premier League clubs spend and exchange players with all the dignity of the Wolf of Wall Street trading floor, the mood among many of our rank and file top-flight clubs is unanimous.

‘It feels like it’s over for us,’ says one Premier League executive. ‘They say this is the most competitive league in the world. Don’t be ridiculous. It’s not allowed to be. The rules make sure of that.’

The spend in the Premier League this summer was a record £3.49billion. Half of that was spent in deals between top-flight clubs. It’s a story of a league that is now so extraordinarily wealthy that – outside of Paris Saint-Germain, Bayern Munich, Real Madrid and Barcelona – the only clubs rich enough to buy its players are its own.

What that says about the competitiveness of the big European competitions going forward is one thing – English clubs dominated last year – but it’s the increasingly skewed landscape of the Premier League that is now concerning many.

Across English football this week – from executives to coaches to scouts and recruitment specialists – the mood has reflected an environment that has perhaps changed for ever.

Chelsea paid £117million to take the England international Morgan Rogers from Aston Villa

While Arsenal took Newcastle talisman Bruno Guimaraes for £75m

Recruitment from the pyramid of the English game, for example, is now desperately low. Of those players taken from the Championship by Premier League clubs this window, the vast majority were from the three clubs relegated last season.

‘Clubs no longer have the patience to see investments in EFL players pay off over time,’ explains one recruiter at a big club. ‘They want results immediately and they want impact and star names. There is an arrogance from our big clubs and it’s damaging.

‘Signing players is about taking a chance but modern clubs would rather spend £130m on a big name or take someone from clubs lower down in the Premier League who have already done the hard work for them.’

That in itself is an emerging trend. Clubs like Brentford, Bournemouth and Brighton have established recruitment models that are the envy of the so-called 'Big Six'. They sign unknown players for small sums before selling them to top-end rivals for vast numbers. Jan Paul van Hecke from Brighton to Spurs is a good recent example.

It’s a practice that on the surface works at both ends. Big clubs get oven-ready players and the smaller clubs make handsome transfer profits. But it’s also a trend that serves to keep the status quo in place on the field. It’s here that the frustration turns to anger.

‘There are well-run clubs doing things the right way who have owners with money yet they are not allowed to spend it,’ adds another Premier League executive. ‘Brentford and Brighton got more points than Chelsea last season. But they are not allowed to spend as much even if they have it.

‘You should never confuse sustainability with competitiveness. We are not competitive. We are not allowed to be by the rules that are essentially endorsed by the big clubs.’

Current spending rules are complicated but broadly speaking allow clubs to spend 85 per cent of what they earn on players, wages and football staff. If you play in Europe, it’s 70 per cent under UEFA’s regulations. It’s this that causes the resentment.

Clubs like Brighton sign unknown players for small sums before selling them to top-end rivals for vast numbers. Jan Paul van Hecke to Spurs is a good recent example

Brentford got more points than Chelsea last season. But they are not allowed to spend as much as them

‘Brighton have got very close,’ says a source who has worked at three top-flight clubs. ‘But they are stuck in a cycle of relative success which is not really success at all in terms of winning things. They are a great club. Well run with a fabulous stadium and training ground.

‘But there is no point anybody buying them because no matter how much money is pumped into it, they wouldn’t be able to spend it on the pitch. Clubs like them and Bournemouth have such limited capacity for growth.’

Another source puts it rather more bluntly. ‘The rules were once worthy and designed to stop people behaving like idiots,’ he says. ‘Sadly the rules have now become a device to stop there ever being a level playing field. The big clubs earn big and spend big. The others don’t and can’t. It’s fundamentally rigged.’

Last November’s vote on new spending rules by top-flight clubs was carried by 14-6, the very minimum required. The dissenters were, not surprisingly, Brighton, Brentford, Bournemouth, Crystal Palace, Fulham and Leeds.

At the same time, a proposal to introduce a system of 'anchoring' – where spending by any club could not exceed five times the money earned in the previous season by the league's bottom club from prize money, TV fees and collective commercial income – was supported by only seven clubs and therefore thrown out. The dissenters viewed it as in effect a wage cap.

'The votes are hard,’ reveals someone from inside the room. ‘You have the top six clubs who vote the way it suits them and then the ones who think they may have a chance of becoming one.

‘Everton are a great example of that. The new stadium they think will lead to new revenues and new commercials. And then the new clubs who have been promoted will understandably vote that way too.

‘They just want their £100m for coming up and don’t wanna p*** off Man United as they may need to loan a player from them. It’s a mess and all of this is accelerated and compounded by the media.

‘They say, “They haven’t spent” or “They have had a bad window”. We will spend right up the limit but the truth is that our limits are different and that isn’t fair is it?’

‘Brighton have got very close (to the big teams),’ says a source who has worked at three top-flight clubs. ‘But they are stuck in a cycle of relative success which is not really success at all'

Everton believe they can crash the Big Six thanks to their new stadium, which will lead to new revenues and new commercial opportunities

In an interview with the True Faith Newcastle United Podcast this week, the Magpies’ chief executive David Hopkinson attempted to outline the way forward for a club awash with Saudi Arabian riches that it cannot spend.

Having lost Anthony Gordon, Bruno Guimaraes and Sandro Tonali this summer, Newcastle are perhaps the best example of a club that feels it’s being held back on a short lead by the league in which it plays.

Hopkinson talked of growing revenues by 50 per cent between now and 2030. He talked of new commercial revenue streams and sponsorship deals but that figure feels wildly optimistic. ‘We are going to catch up from behind,’ he said bullishly. ‘We have a plan.’

Inevitably that plan must include a new stadium at some stage. This is what has launched Tottenham into the stratosphere when it comes to income and this is what Everton are hanging a blue hat on too. ‘We need more stadium capacity because that capacity is revenue,’ Hopkinson said.

Buried within all this, however, was something else that impacts directly on supporters and not in a good way. It’s another direct trickle down of the League’s restrictions on spending.

Hopkinson talked of ‘VIP hosting opportunities’ and a demand for a ‘higher priced product’. Often what this means is a move to ease out regular fans in a bid to squeeze in those wiling to pay through the nose for what they view as a premium corporate match-day experience.

It is symptomatic of a need to push at the edges of what clubs feel they can get away with in a bid to eke a few more quid from their paying customers.

‘We have had to put regular ticket prices up so that means our fans suffer,’ says a third Premier League chief. ‘We have to do anything we can to try and create a little more revenue that we can then invest in the squad. But it’s still nowhere near what the big clubs can do.

Newcastle's chief executive David Hopkinson is bullish about his club's hopes. ‘We are going to catch up from behind. We have a plan,' he said this week

But the club sold midfielder Sandro Tonali to Tottenham this summer, along with Anthony Gordon to Barcelona and Guimaraes to Arsenal

‘And this pressure to compete can promote clubs gambling with that they have and pushing at the margins. It leads clubs into trouble.’

Maybe the best example of this is Aston Villa, a club whose manager Unai Emery spoke eloquently about the limitations of the rules last season.

‘Financial control rules came to football to avoid bankruptcies and payment defaults with a good purpose,’ said Emery. ‘But this good tool will become a limitation.’

Villa have been successful under Emery. They won the Europa League last season and are about to play Champions League football for a second time in recent years. But their wage bill has rocketed in that time – breaching 90 per cent wages to turnover ratio at one point – while they, along with Chelsea, Nottingham Forest and Newcastle, have all been found to be in breach of UEFA’s spending rules last July.

It’s this that contributes to the kind of boom-bust experience of some of our more ambitious clubs. Successful one season, less so the next. Villa have, for example, lost more than half of their Europa League winning team in the recent window.

Villa – in the process of increasing the capacity of Villa Park from 43,000 to more than 50,000 – voted in favour of the new rules last November and amid all the rancour a question that often goes unanswered is what spending rules in England’s top division actually should look like.

One suggestion from a southern club was for all squads to have the same wage bill ceiling. The 'anchoring' system would have been a step towards that but that idea never got very far.

Meanwhile, another of our insiders adds: ‘I don’t think subsidies are the answer. I agree with the big clubs on that. Why should Tesco give its profits to the corner shop?

'But I do think owners should be allowed to inject money as equity that can then be spent on the football. It’s not debt. Debt comes with interest and must be repaid. It’s damaging. Equity is not the same at all. It should be allowed.’

‘Financial control rules came to football to avoid bankruptcies and payment defaults with a good purpose,’ says Aston Villa boss Unai Emery. ‘But this good tool will become a limitation’

Finally, a third small suggestion from a club in the midlands.

‘We suggested the wages of a home-grown player be added on the balance sheet as a positive,’ a staffer explains. ‘In other words, not included on your expenditure. That wage could then be spent on another player. It would act as a reward for growing your own. It never got past first base.’

When the Premier League announced their amended spending rules last season, they talked of ‘competitive balance’ and ‘promoting opportunities’. Looking across the landscape today, it’s hard to see evidence of it.

With the league having virtually annexed the fifth Champions League spot for the foreseeable future, seasonal revenues of at least £100m from that competition serves to widen the gap further.

Underpinning it all, meanwhile, is a nagging feeling among many with Premier League experience that the bubble has to burst at some point. The current TV deal is worth £6.7bn and runs until 2028 but with the way football fans consume their favourite sport ever changing, there is likely to be a shifting in the sands at some point.

Those numbers cannot be relied upon for ever and already this season the Premier League are experimenting in Singapore with producing and selling their own content direct to viewers.

Speaking on the Athletic FC podcast this week, Tim Bridge of the Deloitte Sports Business Group said: ‘I feel as though the League is banking on the ability to have the next new revenue kick – either a new broadcast contract or new commercial partner.

‘If that happens, then it’s rosy. But there is an awful lot being predicated on that (positive) future change and that feels new for the Premier League. I would suggest an appropriate approach for the 20 clubs would be to work more closely together to think about what the League is going to look like in 2035.’

This weekend, Dan Ndoye's Nottingham Forest will have hopes of beating Tottenham. In the long-term, however, it is hard to see much interference in the general order of things

Villa lost more than half of their Europa League-winning team in the recent window

Given that we are only five years on from the failed attempts by England’s big clubs to join a European Super League, the prospects of such a collegiate approach being taken feels unlikely.

And so the Premier League rolls on. So the gap between the top and the middle grows wider.

This weekend, Nottingham Forest will have hopes of beating Tottenham and Everton may have a real go at Manchester United. In the long-term, however, it is hard to see much interference in the general order of things, not when the richest six clubs earn more than the rest of the other 14 put together.

‘At past Premier League meetings we have scoffed at the way some Championship clubs work,’ one of our Premier League sources adds. ‘They have been reckless, blowing their own brains out.

‘Are we now on the way to doing the same?’

Sports.title: Tyson Fury attacks Anthony Joshua and questions his 'love' of England over his speech calling for a block on spending in white-owned shops - in bitter feud over moving their fight away from the UK
Sports.content:
Tyson Fury attacks Anthony Joshua and questions his 'love' of England over his speech calling for a block on spending in white-owned shops - in bitter feud over moving their fight away from the UK

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Tyson Fury has picked apart Anthony Joshua's 'love' of England and desire to fight his great boxing rival on home soil - by dredging up his speech appearing to call for a block on spending in white-owned shops.

Fury, 38, and 36-year-old Joshua are embroiled in a bitter tug-of-war over their heavyweight superfight - largely centring on a debate around hosting it at London's Wembley Stadium or broadcaster Netflix's choice of Madison Square Garden in New York City.

Yesterday, Joshua's promoter Eddie Hearn said Wembley talks had 're-opened', weeks after the fight looked set to be signed off in New York in November - in what has become a crusade towards keeping the event at 'home' for the two fighters.

But today, Fury was keen to make clear Joshua is not motivated by a love of his country. Earlier this year Daily Mail Sport revealed Joshua had in fact quit the UK to move to Dubai - even as thousands tried to flee amid rising panic in the Middle East warzone.

And Fury, a tax exile to the Isle of Man himself, brought up a 2020 speech at a Black Lives Matter march, where Joshua read out a letter from his friend Reece Campbell to urge attendees to stop spending money with white-owned shops and businesses.

'Show them where it hurts,' Joshua had said. 'Abstain from spending your money in their shops and economies, and invest in black-owned businesses.'

Anthony Joshua's 2020 Black Lives Matter speech has been brought back up by his great boxing rival Tyson Fury

A shirtless Fury was relentless in his criticism of Joshua and his perceived dodging of the fight

Fury re-posted the video of the speech, writing: 'This is the man who loves England, absolute s*** bag! Total peice of s*** bully with zero guts! Don't let them deceive you! & Living in Dubai.'

In an address to camera, Fury accused Joshua of trying to derail their fight to avoid being embarrassed: 'If I agreed to tie both hands behind my back and wear solid cement boots, Anthony Joshua would never get in the ring with me because I'll annihilate him.

'And he's a piece of s*** bully, and that's his game—bullying people like he tried to do to Daniel Dubois, and he got knocked spark dead out.

'The latest news from them is, "Tyson don't want to fight in England". Why the f*** wouldn't I want to fight in England, you sausage? "Tyson only wants to fight in America". Are you joking or what?

'Tyson is not in charge of this fight. Tyson didn't put the money up for this fight. Tyson is not the paymaster. Netflix are and Turki Al-Sheikh. Lovely. If it's in England, even better. I'll knock the motherf***er out even quicker. Prime time England, 10 o'clock, Wembley Stadium, 100,000 people. Why the f*** wouldn't I want it in England? Doesn't make any sense, does it?

'Like I said, who do you think you are? You and your little pathetic puppet Eddie Hearn trying to save you. There's no escaping, you know. I'll come to Watford (Joshua's hometown) and I'll set about you. I'll batter you in your own front garden, you piece of s***.'

'There is no getting out of this one. There is no getting out of this one. Get ready for this fight. I've had enough of your sauce to last me 11 years. I'm battering the f*** out of you, you useless dosser, piece of s***. That's what you are. And you know it as well, and everybody else knows what you are: a coward.'

Fury posted this video where Joshua called for 'abstaining on spending' from a friend's letter

Roaring out his title of the 'Gypsy King', Fury added: 'You's are going down, and the cash cow is getting knocked out. Because after this, he won't be able to show his face in public ever again.

'You're a useless dosser, a big bodybuilding piece of s***. Too many weights, not enough speed. When I crack a big right hook off it, you'll go over like spaghetti legs Deontay Wilder. But he's 10 times the man you'll ever be, because he's got a pair of b*****ks like King Kong, and you've got a pair of b*****ks like two f***ing garden peas, you piece of s***.'

Joshua has still not signed his contract for the Battle of Britain fight. Promoter Frank Warren, who suggested that in reality boxing's longest hatching deal had to be finalised by this weekend, told Daily Mail Sport's Jeff Powell: 'AJ hasn't signed yet.

'Tyson signed in January. He's training in Miami for the fight in early November and doesn't care where it takes place.'

The original agreement stipulated England, putting Wembley Stadium on alert.

But Netflix, the mega-paymasters for the broadcast, have joined their Saudi partners in insisting on New York's fabled Madison Square Garden so as to maximise US revenue.

Joshua will need at least a two-month training camp for a fight of this magnitude and ideally nine to ten weeks.

It comes after Joshua was given 10 days to agree a deal on August 26 with Warren previously warning: 'Unless AJ commits by the end of next week I'm afraid this will slip away like so many of those great fights which never happened.'

He added: 'At some point everyone has to say the most important thing is that it happens. Not this bulls*** about money.

'That everyone wants the fight. Does AJ really want it? I don't know. He's been through that tragedy of the car crash which killed two of his closest friends. Only he knows what he wants.'

Much of the discussions around Wembley centre on a willingness to allow a late start time - and late curfew - to suit the American TV market. Mayor Sadiq Khan this week stated that he is keen to host the fight and find a solution.

Sports.title: Sarcastic Jose Mourinho hits out after Real Madrid's controversial defeat: Kylian Mbappe has 94TH-MINUTE penalty saved - which should have been retaken - as ex-Spurs star scores the winner for Real Betis
Sports.content:
Sarcastic Jose Mourinho hits out after Real Madrid's controversial defeat: Kylian Mbappe has 94TH-MINUTE penalty saved - which should have been retaken - as ex-Spurs star scores the winner for Real Betis

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Jose Mourinho suffered the first setback of his second spell as Real Madrid manager as his side were beaten 1-0 by Real Betis, with Kylian Mbappe missing a last-minute penalty.

Real Madrid had won three consecutive league matches to begin the season, following Mourinho's high-profile return to the club.

Mourinho said his opponents 'won the lottery' by picking up the three points despite the fact Real Madrid had 58 per cent possession and 3.16 expected goals compared to Betis' 0.96.

'Congrats to Betis, they won the lottery tonight.

'The game was all Real Madrid, we created so many chances, if we drew tonight, we would have been disappointed.

'I might change my mind tomorrow, but today, judging by the feeling on the bench, I don't know why we lost because collectively we played well.'

The first defeat came at the hands of one of Mourinho's former players in Troy Parrott, who he gave his Premier League debut to in 2019 when in charge of Tottenham.

Parrott, who joined Real Betis in a £17million summer move, was on hand to score on the rebound in the 80th minute after Nelson Deossa's header from a corner had been saved by Thibaut Courtois.

Jose Mourinho suffered the first defeat of his second spell at Real Madrid on Friday night

Kylian Mbappe missed a stoppage time penalty as Real Madrid were beaten 1-0 by Real Betis

Troy Parrott, who was given his Premier League debut by Mourinho, scored an 80th minute winner

Mourinho, who was booked in the 54th minute, thought his side had levelled in the closing stages.

A superb acrobatic volley from Espi from a Vinicius Jnr cross was ruled out after VAR adjudged the forward was offside.

Real Madrid, however, were then given the chance to preserve their unbeaten start to the campaign when they were awarded a stoppage-time penalty after a foul on Vinicius.

Mbappe was denied from the spot by a diving save from Alvaro Valles, with the goalkeeper then squaring up and pushing the Real Madrid star as he celebrated the stop.

Footage showed the penalty should have been retaken after a Real Betis player had encroached into the box as Mbappe was striking the ball.

Mourinho insisted post match that his side had deserved to win, while he sarcastically congratulated Betis players and suggested they had been 'smarter' in committing fouls after five Real Madrid players were booked.

Mourinho sarcastically congratulated Real Betis players following the match

'I have nothing to reproach any player for regarding their attitude,' Mourinho added.

'We deserved to win, but deserving doesn't get you points.

'Betis players are smarter than Real Madrid players, who are more straightforward.

'In the first play of the game, there was a clear yellow card for a player who fouled Valverde, but Fede stays on his feet, he doesn't even fall.

'Meanwhile Betis players exaggerated every foul so much, that you'd think they need an ambulance from their reactions.'

On his own yellow card, Mourinho added: 'I don't know why I saw a yellow card.

'I accept it.

'I stood up because a Betis player looked like he'd died in front of the bench. I saw a lot of people frustrated with the plays, but I didn't see it myself and I can't comment.'

The slip-up gives rivals Barcelona the chance to establish an early three-point lead on Real Madrid, with the Catalans looking to clinch a third successive LaLiga title.

Barcelona travel to Valencia on Sunday afternoon.

Sports.title: Alexander Isak and Liverpool's Red Arrows give the Andoni Iraola era a true lift off - they were not perfect but the manner of the win over Ipswich sends a warning to their rivals, writes LEWIS STEELE
Sports.content:
Alexander Isak and Liverpool's Red Arrows give the Andoni Iraola era a true lift off - they were not perfect but the manner of the win over Ipswich sends a warning to their rivals, writes LEWIS STEELE

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Liverpool were so mesmerisingly impressive in the first half at Portman Road, it was easy to forget they had their showpiece signing keeping warm on the bench.

Bradley Barcola, all £123million of him, was limited to a watching brief for the first hour of this game and, from his padded seat, the Frenchman may have been pondering just how he gets into this team.

Alexander Isak led the charge with two goals in the first nine minutes to help Liverpool to their first win of the Andoni Iraola era, as the Swede closes in on matching his tally from last season already.

Iraola’s front four resembled the Red Arrows, flying forward at breakneck speed, with Cody Gakpo and the rapid bundle of joy Victor Munoz causing all sorts of problems for Ipswich.

Off the ball, Liverpool strangled their opposition into submission and barely gave them a second to breathe, in scenes that would delight boss Iraola who prides himself on intensity, relentless pressing and constant energy.

This was the true lift-off, then, for the Iraola era after two iffy draws to begin left him with more questions than answers. Just like the Arne Slot era which began here two years ago, Portman Road was the location of the first victory for Iraola.

Alexander Isak struck twice in the opening nine minutes to giver Liverpool the lead

Isak produced a smart piece of play to double the lead in a dominant start from the Reds

The result gave Andoni Iraola's era a true lift off after draws in Liverpool's opening two games

‘With Alex, if he’s fit, if he’s available, if he’s in good shape, he will produce the numbers,’ said the boss. ‘My demands with him will not be about the goals, it will be about other things so we can play well.

‘Cody knows how much we value him, there is no doubt. I rate him very highly. I will demand him obviously, he has strong competition with minutes because we have good players in those positions. It’s a matter of pushing each other.’

Tougher tests than newly-promoted Ipswich await ahead and Liverpool were not perfect, either – as the home team created problems at the other end – but this evidence sent a warning to Premier League rivals: do not write off Liverpool.

With £125m man Isak firing with two instinctive finishes, £116m Florian Wirtz causing issues and Gakpo looking like a new man, Liverpool’s attack is frightening.

Gakpo, of course, is well worth a mention. Had the last seven days gone ever so slightly differently, the winger would have been a Manchester City player. The two clubs were in advanced discussions over sanctioning that move.

Some Reds fans might not have lost too much sleep over Gakpo leaving, given his form was inconsistent and frustrating last term. Maybe, too, they would have happily seen him depart given it would have meant the club signed a replacement.

But the grass is not always greener on the other side and Gakpo is now resembling the flying Dutchman everyone knows he can be. A thunderous goal against Newcastle, setting one up against Nottingham Forest last week and now two exquisite assists here.

It was Gakpo’s pick-out that helped Isak open the scoring after six minutes at Portman Road. The winger skipped past a challenge then punched a pass through a tight angle into Isak’s path. Not a breath later, the former Newcastle man was wheeling away in celebration.

Without even pausing for thought, Isak fired a powerful shot past Kjell Scherpen. The goalkeeper should have done better but Isak did not care a jot after an instinctive finish, the sort we have not seen since his acrimonious Newcastle exit.

Liverpool's new £123m signing Bradley Barcola was given a watching brief for the first hour

If Liverpool's attacking signings hit the heights, there sky is the limit for Iraola's side

Three minutes later, the Gakpo-Isak duo combined again. This one was less about power and more about ingenuity, as Isak danced away from Jacob Greaves, worked himself an angle and poked a shot past Scherpen. Again, it was an inch-perfect assist from Gakpo.

Given Isak spent the majority of last season unfit, it is easy to forget just how talented he is. He was worth £125m for a reason, after all, but as old boss Arne Slot used to say: he was signed for six years, not six months.

Season one was a slog but the early signs are that his sophomore year at Anfield will be much better. Indeed, the sky is the limit for the striker if he can keep fit and then reach the form that saw him become the most expensive signing in British history in the first place.

It was not just Isak’s goals but his overall play that would have delighted Iraola. Even when he was in the team last year, one could argue he never truly looked sharp. Maybe when he finally did look fit after having no pre-season for Newcastle, Isak broke his leg in December.

But with a goal last week and a brace here, the £125m man is looking fitter and stronger than at any point last term. He is playing with a smile on his face and foxed defenders by dropping deep or at wide, interchanging positions with Gakpo and Wirtz.

The German is another who is desperate for an improvement after a poor debut campaign and he also shone here. Indeed, Wirtz thought he had teed up Isak for a hat-trick later in the first half but the Swede was marginally offside.

Ipswich looked shellshocked in the opening exchanges but Gary O’Neil’s side settled well and had a number of chances, ending the first 45 minutes with more expected goals (xG) than dominant Liverpool.

Julio Enciso went close several times and overlapping left back Leif Davis caused problems but, unlike in the two 2-2 draws to start the season, Liverpool looked more comfortable at the back and answered all of Ipswich’s questions.

If Isak, Wirtz and Co can hit the heights and fulfil their potential, the sky is the limit for Iraola and Liverpool, especially with £123m Barcola still to break into the side.

The Frenchman, a back-to-back Champions League winner, enjoyed a second-half cameo and was serenaded by the away end. With Iraola’s Red Arrows playing like this, Barcola is not guaranteed to waltz into the starting XI just yet.

Sports.title: 'Seeing every boxing gym in the country packed with female fighters... that's the legacy I want': KATIE TAYLOR reflects on changing the face of her sport as she prepares to bids farewell in front of 82,000 at Croke Park
Sports.content:
'Seeing every boxing gym in the country packed with female fighters... that's the legacy I want': KATIE TAYLOR reflects on changing the face of her sport as she prepares to bids farewell in front of 82,000 at Croke Park

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

There is something beautifully fitting about the way Katie Taylor's extraordinary boxing story is coming to an end.

Thirty years ago, a little girl from Bray had to hide her hair under headgear and pretend to be a boy simply to pursue the sport she loved.

On Saturday night, that same girl – now 40, a five-time world champion, Olympic gold medallist and three-time undisputed champion-in-waiting – will walk into Croke Park for the final fight of her career, with 82,000 people watching.

It is, Taylor admits, the ending she always dreamed of.

'To be honest, I was saying after the last fight against Serrano, nothing can get bigger than MSG, so I think I'm going to just hang up the gloves,' Taylor tells Daily Mail Sport. 'The only thing that could be bigger than MSG is actually Croke Park, but that looked unlikely to happen.

'So when I got the phone call then from Brian that it was actually going to happen, I couldn't believe it. I was so excited and so emotional. This is really the fairy-tale ending I was actually looking for.'

Katie Taylor is set to bid her final farewell to boxing at Croke Park on Saturday night

Taylore takes on Flora Pili in a bid to finish her incredible career as undisputed light-welterweight champion

Taylor has spent her entire life chasing impossible things. At 10, she began boxing with her father Peter, a former Irish champion, but girls were not allowed to compete. So she found a way.

She disguised herself as a boy and fought wherever she could. When women's boxing was finally sanctioned in Ireland, Taylor made history by taking part in the country's first officially recognised female bout in 2001.

What followed was beyond even the wildest dreams of that stubborn little girl: Olympic gold at London 2012, five world titles, six European titles, undisputed crowns at lightweight and super-lightweight, and history-making nights at Madison Square Garden. Now Croke Park.

'This was an impossibility a few months ago, and I don't think people outside of Ireland really understand the importance of Croke Park and the fact that it's there. It's a part of Irish culture and it's our national stadium. Politically, it's been so hard to get this fight over the line for many years, and we're here now. It's actually happening, and not only that, but it's in front of a sold-out crowd.'

Yet beneath the excitement is the realisation that this really is goodbye. Asked about making her final ring walk, entering the dressing room for the last time and knowing there will never be another fight camp, Taylor becomes emotional.

'You're making me emotional here, Charlotte,' she laughs, trying to hold back the tears. 'Yeah, it's... I'm trying not to get too emotional, but even just talking about it, I'm starting to choke up. It's all becoming a bit too real now, honestly. Just give me a minute.'

After pulling herself together she continued: 'I have to obviously hold my emotions together because I have a very important job to do. And I'm trying not to reflect too much on the whole journey because I actually have to go in and perform, and the most important part is that I get my hand raised.

'But every now and then I do think about it, and I do get a bit emotional. I have given my life to this sport and it's everything I know and I love, so the idea of not doing it anymore hurts but I have to actually focus on not thinking too much about it. It's also too dangerous a sport to have your body in the ring, your heart out of it, thinking of retirement.'

Taylor has been a major icon for young women in the boxing community over the years

Flora Pili is intent on ruining the fairytale. The unbeaten Frenchwoman is 12-0 and will challenge Taylor for her WBO, WBA and IBF titles, with the vacant WBC belt also at stake.

'She's a young, hungry fighter. She's undefeated. She's big, she's strong, she's going to come to fight. She looks a bit awkward as well. She has long arms and will look to pressure me. She's obviously trying to ruin my night. She's trying to ruin the fairytale end, and so I have to be at my very, very best to win this fight.'

That competitive instinct remains, but the decision to retire has been coming for some time.

'What else is there to chase after?' Taylor asks.

'It’s been such an amazing journey, but it’s been a long and hard journey as well. It’s been difficult on the body, and my whole life has basically been one big training camp after training camp after training camp. Even as an amateur boxer, I gave so much of my life and so much of my time to amateur boxing. It was gruelling, and I have a lot of wear and tear on my body. There have been little niggles here and there that have popped up over the last few years, so I knew physically it was time.

'And then mentally, I think an athlete’s life is a life full of sacrifice, and usually the casualty of those sacrifices are your relationships. It’s not always the case, but it was the case for me. I found it very hard to focus on relationships when I’m actually in the middle of these big, amazing moments in my career. So I think it is the right time to bow out. I get a chance to actually invest in my marriage now, just pour my energy into that and enjoy the fruits of my labour.'

Then comes the familiar Taylor humour.

'I'll also look forward to not getting punched in the face again after this fight. It doesn't help I don't know how to actually box and move,' she jokes. 'I have to turn it into a war.'

But Taylor's greatest legacy will not be measured in belts.

Taylor's opponent Pili is 12-0 and intent on ruining the Irishwoman's fairytale ending in Dublin

When she looks back, she remembers the pioneers who helped pave the way – Laila Ali, Christy Martin, Lucia Rijker, Ann Wolfe and her childhood hero Deirdre Gogarty – but she also understands what her own journey has meant.

'I want to be remembered as a great fighter, but I also think the one thing I want to be remembered as is that I left my sport in a better place,' she says.

'I think that's probably the proudest moment of my whole career, inspiring a new generation of young female fighters, and seeing every boxing gym in the country just packed with female fighters not having the same struggles or the same obstacles that I had."

Taylor does not know exactly what comes next, although she cannot imagine staying away from boxing entirely.

'I've been involved in boxing for the last 30 years of my life, so I think it would be strange just to walk away and not have a part to play,' she says.

'I do love my sport, and I love the boxing gym environment. And I think that's something that I'm always going to be involved in but I am actually looking forward to being able to just enjoy my life after this fight.

'I've been boxing since I was 10 or 11 years of age. It's been a gruelling and tough journey. It's been an amazing journey, but it has been very, very tough. And I am looking forward to not feeling the pressure of fights again, the pressure of expectation, and not having to prepare for these brutal matches again, and just kind of enjoy life for a change.

'It's been a lot on my family too. Even my siblings’ lives were scheduled around my training growing up because of my Olympic dream. I look back and think how supportive and amazing they were. If I was in their shoes, I’d be so bitter because their lives revolved around me and my schedule. So, it will be nice to enjoy life together now.'

First, though, there is one final war. One final ring walk. One final chance to have her hand raised.

Sports.title: Serena and Venus Williams implode at the US Open as iconic sisters are knocked out of women's doubles in heartbreaking fashion
Sports.content:
Serena and Venus Williams were sensationally knocked out in the first round of the women's doubles at the US Open on Friday night, blowing a 5-0 lead in the decisive 10-point tiebreaker.

The legendary sisters accepted a wildcard into the women's draw in New York at the eleventh hour after previously partnering up at the Cincinnati Open this summer on the heels of Serena's return to competition.

The 23-time Grand Slam singles champion had previously stepped back from competition four years ago, when she played for what tennis fans believed would be the last time on the US Open's Arthur Ashe show court.

Earlier in the summer, Serena accepted a singles wildcard to Wimbledon, but in a twist of fate was beaten in three competitive sets by Joint, her opponent once again in New York.

Two months later, Serena was unable to get her revenge on the Australian world No. 72, who now holds a surprising 2-0 record against the serial champion, with the American favorites falling 3-6, 7-6(6), 6-7(7).

The Williams sisters received a hero's welcome as they kicked off the night session, with the stadium fast to fill up with fans eager to see the blockbuster siblings back in action for the first time on Arthur Ashe since 2022.

Venus and Serena Williams were dumped out of the US Open women's doubles in round one

Serena and her sister were partnering at the US Open for the first time in four years on Friday

They battled well to win the second set before forcing their higher-ranked opponents to a third

But they could not get the better of Australia's Maya Joint (left) and Taiwan's Chan Hao-ching

While both sisters were laser-focused on their evening's work ahead, Serena let her fashion do the talking, sporting a bomber jacket to walk onto court which listed the years she won singles and doubles titles at the US Open.

And after complaints had been made all week about the noise during play on the over 23,000-capacity stadium, you might have been able to hear a proverbial pin drop as Joint prepared her first serve to kick-off the match.

The Australian must have learned a lot from her match-up this year against Serena, after admitting that she had been 'intimidated' by the 44-year-old due to the iconic position she occupies within the sport. Joint was composed as she held serve, with both the 20-year-old and her partner Chan admirably calm under the lights of Arthur Ashe.

The two pairs passed the opening games between one another, with the occasion perhaps top of mind for all four women on court.

But Serena and Venus had an explosive crowd on their side, who provided an enormous roar at the sight of the first real moment of Serena brilliance - a thunderous backhand which could only force an error.

The Williams sisters indisputably have history, but Chan and Joint are a tested recent pair, in July reaching a final together in Memphis. Their partnership felt sharp and familiar, and it was no surprised when they pinched the early break.

Under the gaze of New York Knicks hero Karl-Anthony Towns and his new wife Jordyn Woods, Williams Squared were full of fight, and strong net play.

A bullish break-back for 2-3 ensued, with the crowd firmly onside. They continued to fend off break points too as Chan and Joint grew into the game - but eventually succumbed at 5-3, with their opponents navigating a tricky service game to pull off the opening set.

They would find the second set far thornier to deal with. Although their games on serve stretched, Venus and Serena were able to knuckle down and hold serve, keeping pace with Chan and Joint all the way to a 4-3 lead.

The sisters blew a 5-0 lead in the 10-point tiebreaker before eventually losing 6-3, 6-7, 7-6

Venus looked a far cry from the singles player who lost her 15th match in a row this week

The thousands of fans on Arthur Ashe were raucous in their support of the sisters

Among the stars in attendance were newly married Jordyn Woods and Karl-Anthony Towns

Their run continued. 5-4 up, Serena's excellent backhand down-the-line won the sisters the opening point. Joint's serving, which was capable of causing a lot of problems for Serena and Williams, had to be pinpoint-accurate.

But Joint and Chan tightened up, a fine return from Serena brought up deuce, and advantage - it was set point Williams. They had two, and were even assisted by a rare Joint double fault, but they could not convert, and somehow, their opponents clung on.

A strong serving game from Serena, as expected, steadied the ship for 6-5, and after Joint and Chan did the same for a tiebreak. As the stakes rose, so did the Williamses levels, and it was the sibling duo who had the lead, handing Serena the opportunity to serve out the set. She double-faulted the first time, but as Joint hit wildly out into the stands, Serena and Venus took it to the decider.

This was the last time that Serena and Venus would lead. A particularly strong bit of net play from Chan in the third game helped hand their opponents the early break. But the Williams sisters broke back to make it 4-3 in the third and confirmed it with a confident hold that had Chan flinging her racquet on the court in frustration.

In a third set filled with vintage shot making, Venus and Serena wrenched momentum from their rivals with the older Williams sister in particular looking a far cry from the singles player who lost her 15th match in a row at the beginning of this tournament.

Another tiebreak beckoned. The result, however, looked a little different, with the sisters building a strong early lead, only for Joint and Chan to pull off an almighty comeback.

All in, the match lasted just over three hours. Venus and Serena more than proved that they can be competitive against doubles players on the tour in 2026. But their wait for a win this year goes on.

Sports.title: Unused in the Premier League and almost replaced in the transfer market, Viktor Gyokeres' Arsenal career is at a crossroads. But this is why you'd be foolish to write him off
Sports.content:
Unused in the Premier League and almost replaced in the transfer market, Viktor Gyokeres' Arsenal career is at a crossroads. But this is why you'd be foolish to write him off

The career of Arsenal’s Viktor Gyokeres has reached a crossroads. Even he, a man with a piercing gaze and fierce determination, has been unable to hide his unease of late.

An image of a forlorn Gyokeres arriving at Arsenal’s London Colney training base on Thursday was widely circulated online.

Clutching a black washbag, his demeanour spoke of a man lingering on the outside, searching for a way into Mikel Arteta’s first XI plans.

A more telling example of his frustration came in a pre-season friendly away in Girona last month, when he screamed ‘Max!’ at Max Dowman for failing to pass to him.

Gyokeres is in uncharted territory, more generally. The Swede has not played a single minute in either of Arsenal’s two league matches thus far, against Coventry and Aston Villa.

Villa away, for example, seemed tailor-made for the introduction of the 28-year-old in the second period, Kai Havertz having underwhelmed and with the opposition backline flagging.

It's been a disappointing season so far for Viktor Gyokeres, and an image of the forlorn Swede arriving at Arsenal’s London Colney training base on Thursday was widely circulated online

Gyokeres has been left on the bench in Arsenal's first two Premier League games, with Kai Havertz (left) preferred up front

But, no, he stayed put on the bench. It went against the grain for Arteta. Of the 36 league matches last season in which Gyokeres made the Arsenal squad, the striker featured in every single game.

Twenty-six were starts, the other 10 appearances off the bench. It makes his treatment thus far at odds with how Arteta previously used the forward, who struck 21 goals across all competitions last season.

Chelsea at home on Sunday – a fixture that may well have enormous significance in this season's title race – feels a significant moment for the Swede’s Gunners career.

If he were not to feature in any capacity, the experiences of Aaron Ramsdale and Gabriel Martinelli come to mind.

David Raya’s move to Arsenal in 2023 – initially on loan before signing a long-term contract – saw Ramsdale frozen out and eventually sold to Southampton. Ramsdale had been an important player for Arteta, a mainstay of the first XI. And then he wasn't.

Martinelli, meanwhile, only made 11 league starts last season and was sold to Al Hilal for £60million earlier this week.

With Gyokeres, an interesting subplot was Arsenal’s keenness to bring in a striker this summer.

As Daily Mail Sport reported on Wednesday, it is understood assistant manager Gabriel Heinze reached out to Inter Milan’s Lautaro Martinez – a fellow Argentine – early last week over a potential move.

Inter refused to entertain any kind of deal, the attacker still having three years left on his contract.

The Gunners’ pursuit of Julian Alvarez has been well-documented. That, of course, failed to come off.

So, Arsenal were actively trying to bring a striker into the club, aware of the need for one to supplement Havertz and Gyokeres with Gabriel Jesus out the door.

Write off Gyokeres at your peril. It is easy to forget this is a striker who scored 21 goals in all competitions last season

He also has a track record of overcoming adversity, navigating a difficult start to life in England at Brighton (pictured in 2018) by flourishing at Coventry

It’s now crunch time for Gyokeres, though he can at least tap into his experience of overcoming adversity.

After struggling to break through at Brighton aged 19, the Swede went on loan to Coventry, where he would go on to sign a three-year deal and score 41 goals across 110 appearances in the Championship.

That earned him a move to Sporting Lisbon, taking the Portuguese league by storm, striking 97 goals in 102 matches across all competitions.

He will need to summon that same resilience now to reassert himself in an Arsenal frontline shallow in depth. The route back into Arteta’s plans remains firmly within his grasp.

Tellingly, when Arteta was asked on Friday whether his frontline is ‘world class’, he replied: ‘I love my players, that's all I can say. In the bracket, how you want to put them, I don't know.

‘I think at the end of the season we'll put everybody in their place, and let's trust them. Let's make sure that we are right behind them and we'll do everything we can to help the incredible talent that they have.’

Those words offer little in the way of guarantees for Gyokeres. But they do underline the opportunity in front of him.

Chelsea at home on Sunday could provide the clearest opportunity yet to change the narrative, to remind Arteta and the Arsenal supporters why the club pushed so hard to bring him to north London, battling off Manchester United and others for his signature.

Gyokeres has been here before, overlooked and forced to fight for his place. Soon we will discover whether he can do it again.

Sports.title: Inside Jose Mourinho's £17k-a-month Real Madrid mansion as he returns home after 13 years
Sports.content:
Inside Jose Mourinho's £17k-a-month Real Madrid mansion as he returns home after 13 years

Jose Mourinho is back at Real Madrid for a second spell in charge and is living at the exact same place

View 3 Images Jose Mourinho has returned to the same property he lived in during his first Real Madrid spell (Image: Maximiliano Poch Poch)

It has taken more than a decade, but Jose Mourinho has finally returned to Real Madrid. The Portuguese left the Bernabeu in 2013 after a 103-goal season wasn't enough to deny Barcelona the title, but he is now back in the Spanish capital for a second stint.

‌



In the intervening years, he has won a third Premier League title with Chelsea and managed fellow Premier League sides Manchester United and Arsenal, as well as taking jobs in Italy, Turkey and Portugal. Now, though, he's picked up where he left off in Madrid - even moving into the exact same mansion he lived in last time.

‌



Mourinho has returned to La Finca, a gated community in the Spanish capital. As reported by Mundo Deportivo, the 1,400 square metre property will set him back around £17,000 per month, but that's something he'll easily be able to afford on his hefty Madrid salary.

‌



The same report makes particular reference to the tranquillity offered by the home, as well as to the 5,000-square-metre grounds with plenty of outdoor space. In addition to a large swimming pool, there are said to be several relaxation areas to ensure the 63-year-old can make full use of them when it's warm enough to spend time outside.

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

According to A Bola, the property also includes a dedicated space for Mourinho to hold meetings with his staff and discuss team matters, using video analysis where required. The location is private, away from the hustle and bustle of the city and unreachable via public roads alone.

‌



It marks a notable change from his living arrangement when he was Manchester United manager. Back then, he lived in a luxury apartment at the Lowry Hotel, with the riverside suite setting him back £816 per night.

View 3 Images The home has a massive swimming pool and plenty of outdoor space

In June, Mourinho spoke to Vanity Fair about returning to Madrid and why the club was different to any other. The history. Real Madrid’s history you cannot compare with anybody," he said.

‌



"I think the white shirts, they have something magic. But the reality is that the shirts could be black, green, or blue, it wouldn't change. Because what made Real Madrid what Real Madrid is, is the history.

"The story of Real Madrid is different. It’s not the story of so many amazing players that played for Real Madrid. It's about the club. It's about the titles. Of course, there are periods of difficulties. There are periods where they cannot win—like serial winners, like they do all the time. There are always periods where you have to build, you have to rebuild."

View 3 Images The home is setting Mourinho back a reported £17,000 per month (Image: Maximiliano Poch Poch)

‌



Mourinho began his second Real Madrid spell in dramatic fashion, with Carlos Espi scoring a last-minute winner at Espanyol on the opening weekend of the season. Two home wins followed, but Los Blancos suffered their first defeat of the campaign against Real Betis on Friday.

Troy Parrott scored for the hosts inside the final 10 minutes before Espi saw a leveller ruled out for offside and Mbappe missed a last-gasp penalty. "I might change my mind after watching the game tomorrow, but today, from the bench, I don’t know why we lost. I can’t justify it," Mourinho said after the game.

"Collectively, the team played very well in every aspect. Individually, they played very well too. I have nothing to criticise about any player’s attitude, quite the opposite. The players gave their all. We clearly deserved to win, but deserving doesn’t get you points.”

Sports.title: David Moyes drops bombshell about Everton owners after disastrous window
Sports.content:
David Moyes drops bombshell about Everton owners after disastrous window

Everton endured a miserable summer transfer window, with the collapsed £40million move on deadline day for Monaco striker Folarin Balogun leaving David Moyes with a headache

View 2 Images David Moyes has been left with a tiny squad (Image: AFP/Getty Images)

David Moyes has admitted that he has never spoken to Dan Friedkin, the chief executive of Everton owners the Friedkin Group, following a shambolic end to the summer transfer window.

‌



Everton have been left with a threadbare squad after failing to sign a striker on transfer deadline day. The Toffees sold Beto to Fiorentina and then saw Folarin Balogun reject a move to become his replacement, while late bids for Manchester United's Joshua Zirkzee and Aston Villa's Tammy Abraham also failed. It leaves Thierno Barry as Everton's only senior striker.

‌



While Everton did get some cheer, with Jack Grealish returning on loan from Manchester City, the sale of Iliman Ndiaye to City for £65million further weakened their squad.

‌



The farcical end to the window, in which Balogun U-turned on a move from Monaco after arriving at the Everton training ground, has put the club under scrutiny. Moyes' admission that he has no contact with Friedkin only adds weight to those criticisms.

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

Man Utd striker transfer confirmed despite summer window closing READ MORE :

Liverpool transfer call vindicated as Alexander Isak downs Ipswich - 5 talking points READ MORE :

“My real contact is Angus [Kinnear, Everton CEO]. Angus is the one who I would go to see," Moyes said ahead of Sunday's game against Manchester United. "Rishi [Majithia, TFG representative] is the next one and then the head of the Friedkin family in America. I don’t really get any direct conversations with them, but I do through Rishi, he is the one I would speak to.”

‌



Speaking in a press conference, as reported by the Liverpool Echo, Moyes was diplomatic when assessing the wreckage of the window, saying the collapse of the £40m deal for Balogun "wasn't anyone's fault".

“It was a difficult transfer window generally," he added. "I know how it culminated in the end but it was a difficult window all the way through for us. The last couple of days were difficult because we were pushing hard, we had made bids for several players on bank holiday Monday and it would be hard to believe the outcome got to where it was.

"Lots of things just didn’t fall in line but we probably shouldn’t have been as late as that, we should probably have tried to get the work done a lot earlier than that.”

‌



View 2 Images Folarin Balogun pulled out of a move to Everton (Image: Getty Images)

Asked if his job had been made harder by the transfer window, he said: “Look, I think the Everton job is always a hard job and it’s a club that is used to having some difficult times. I can understand how difficult it must have been for Dychey [former manager, Sean Dyche] and many of the managers in front of him, through different periods.

“It is going to be difficult. We don’t have a huge squad of players, it is not a number we would ideally want, but sometimes you need to do something special in football and we will attempt to do something special. I’ve never wanted a huge squad, I’ve always preferred it when the squad is tighter, but maybe not as tight as this.”

‌



Moyes has a huge amount of experience and is ready to fight on with reduced numbers. “My aim is just to be as good as we've tried to be in the recent seasons," he said. "I think some things will hinder it. There'll be days we don't get it right. But I'll tell you what there won’t be, I'll do my best not to make any excuses for what's happened. And the players are fully aware of that.

"There are no excuses from the players on what we've got, what we need, and there's two or three players who probably get mentioned quite a lot - they are going to have to come with the fore, they're all going to have to be the ones who see if they can really deal with this football club.

“And for me personally, it's a great job, I love Everton and always have done. It's actually invigorated me over the last year, getting back at it again because I was probably going to say I wasn't going to do it again, or I might have taken an international job or I might have done something else.

Article continues below

"I actually think we've had a good year and a half together, I really do. I think if you looked over the year and a half you'd have to say there'd been a lot more positives and negatives. So now, there’s a little bit of a bump in the road. I need to try and get over the bump quickly and start looking how I can make it go smoothly.”

Sports.title: Four players Man Utd were glad to see leave after 'bad attitude' and 'unprofessional' claims
Sports.content:
Four players Man Utd were glad to see leave after 'bad attitude' and 'unprofessional' claims

There's rarely a quiet season at Manchester United, particularly when it comes to high-profile players who can prove a challenge to manage

View 5 Images Michael Carrick has worked hard to restore the culture at Manchester United (Image: Michael Campanella/Getty Images)

Some big personalities have joined Manchester United in decades past, and some have left swiftly to the relief of those at the club. In recent years, Alejandro Garnacho and Jadon Sancho were told they had "bad attitudes" and were "lazy" by managers and squad players alike.

‌



Other, more experienced stars who felt the wrath of their teammates and pundits included the iconic Cristiano Ronaldo and Romelu Lukaku. Current manager Michael Carrick starred alongside Ronaldo during his playing career and hopes to avoid any major dressing-room issues, as have often plagued the club in recent years.

‌



The United boss has started off with one win and one loss for the 2026/27 Premier League season and also has the return of Champions League football to look forward to. He will aim to maintain the feel-good factor around Old Trafford following his initial interim period last season, during which he led a struggling team to third place and European football.

‌



Here, Mirror Football has taken a look back at four former United players that the club were glad to see the back of.

Man Utd loan out Chido Obi as youngster risks following concerning Old Trafford pattern READ MORE :

Fenerbahce issue Mason Greenwood statement as UEFA investigate ex-Man Utd star READ MORE :

Alejandro Garnacho

Garnacho had a bright start at United, making 10 goal contributions in his first full season as a senior Red Devil. However, club captain Bruno Fernandes suggested that the Argentina international lacked a good attitude during his progression into the first team under Erik ten Hag.

Speaking in November 2022, Fernandes told BT Sport: "He was good but he knows we expect a lot from him. He's still really young, doing really well. At the beginning of the season, he was not at his best.

‌



"On the [pre-season] tour he did not have the best attitude. That's why he didn't get his chance until now. He's getting his chances because he's training better, he's having the correct attitude."

View 5 Images Alejandro Garnacho was accused of not 'having the correct attitude' (Image: Gareth Copley/Getty Images)

These words had the opposite effect on Garnacho. He fell out of favour under new manager Ruben Amorim and even criticised his decision to keep him off the pitch during the Europa League final loss against Tottenham.

‌



Garnacho said: "Until we reached the final, I played every round. And I played 20 minutes today – I don't know. I'm going to try to enjoy the summer and see what happens next.

"Obviously it's hard for everyone. Our season was s***. We didn't beat anyone in the league. We lacked a lot of things. When you don't score goals, you always need more."

The 22-year-old departed United and signed for Chelsea in a deal worth £40m. Garnacho failed to impress in west London and this summer joined Aston Villa on loan with an obligation to buy for a similar sum.

‌



Cristiano Ronaldo

View 5 Images Cristiano Ronaldo's return to United ended on a sour note (Image: ADRIAN DENNIS/AFP via Getty Images)

Ronaldo will forever be remembered for his first stint in Manchester, but his homecoming in 2021 ended in disaster. After a year where he scored 24 goals and brought back nostalgia for many, he fell out with Ten Hag and had his contract terminated before the 2022 World Cup.

The striker took part in a controversial interview with Piers Morgan where he stated there was "no evolution" at the club since Sir Alex Ferguson left. Christian Eriksen spoke out following Ronaldo's exit and claimed that "football will go on" without the Portugal international.

‌



He said: "First of all we are sad that Ronaldo is not part of it, his legacy and his name at any club is special, for me to be fortunate to play with him in my career was very nice. The football goes on. You feel that the next game after, people will forget what it was like before and now our focus is really like he is not here."

Highlighting an improvement in the dressing room, Eriksen added: "The atmosphere is good, we have a lot of people coming back from the World Cup, the last guys are coming back and everyone is coming together. The atmosphere is good. It helps winning games and also before we went away for the World Cup, we had a few good games and good wins and it makes it easier to come back and start like this."

Jadon Sancho

View 5 Images Jadon Sancho fell out of favour under Erik ten Hag (Image: Michael Regan/Getty Images)

‌



Sancho joined in a £73m deal from Borussia Dortmund in 2021 and arrived to much fanfare. However, he ended up on loan three times and left the club at the expiry of his contract this summer.

Once again, the player butted heads with Ten Hag, with Sancho left out of the matchday squad for his "lazy" tendencies in training. Speaking after a 3-1 defeat to Arsenal in 2023, the manager said: "Jadon, on his performances in training we did not select him. You have to reach a level every day at Manchester United and we can make choices in the front line. So for this game he was not selected."

Sancho hit back on social media, effectively claiming in a post that was later deleted that the Dutchman was lying. He said: "Please don’t believe everything you read! I will not allow people saying things that is completely untrue, I have conducted myself in training very well this week. I believe there are other reasons for this matter that I won’t go into, I’ve been a scapegoat for a long time which isn’t fair!"

‌
