World.title: Constitutional Court snubs Dikgang Moseneke in Mandela artifacts case
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG – The Constitutional Court has declined retired Deputy Chief Justice Dikgang Moseneke’s request to join as a friend of the court in a legal battle involving an auction of former President Nelson Mandela’s belongings.

Moseneke is the last surviving executor of Madiba’s estate, after Judge Temba Sangoni and advocate George Bizos SC died.

Mandela died in December 2013 and his estate is yet to be wound up.

Moseneke said he ought to be allowed to join the case as a friend of the court because he still has an interest in Madiba’s affairs.

Mandela’s eldest daughter, Dr Makaziwe Mandela, wants to put her father’s possessions on the block at Guernsey’s Auction House in New York.

However, the South African Heritage Resources Agency, Robben Island Museum and the Arts and Culture Department approached the court to stop the export and sale of the items.

The artifacts include Madiba’s green barcoded ID, which he used to vote in 1994, his hearing aid, 11 Madiba shirts, a suit, three briefcases, four walking sticks, one pair of shoes, hand-written letters, two pairs of sunglasses, a tea set, the tennis racket he used on Robben Island and gifts he received from different governments around the world.

In his founding affidavit, Moseneke said in terms of the National Heritage Resources Act 25 of 1999, the exporting of items linked to heritage is regulated.

“The 2019 Heritage Declaration includes ‘objects related to significant political processes, events, figures and leaders in South Africa’ ... Section 32(19) prohibits the export of a heritage object without a permit issued by SAHRA,” part of the papers read.

Moseneke said the belongings were to be auctioned off because of Madiba’s historical significance. This relates to his Robben Island incarceration, his release from prison and his post democratic legacy.

“The first and fourth respondents (Makaziwe and Christo Brand, a former Robben Island prison warden) did not purport to put the Mandela Objects for lease or sale in the auction abroad as their personal property without associating them with the above historical image, role and contribution as well as the enduring legacy of President Mandela.”

Moseneke alleges that in his will, Madiba bequeathed the Houghton property to the Nelson Mandela Trust and that some of his belongings were removed without the knowledge of the Trust, the executors and his widow, Graca Machel.

“In terms of the will, all the movable assets of Mr Mandela, in particular the personal effects were bequeathed to Mrs Machel.”

In addition to these submissions, Moseneke told the court of his close relationship with Madiba, which they formed after Moseneke was jailed at Robben Island as a 15-year-old.

Moseneke said their friendship continued even after he was released and Madiba remained.

“The case before this court raises issues of considerable public in importance which transcends the present dispute. The issues have a direct impact on the preservation of South Africa’s cultural, social and political memory and history.

“It is not hyperbole to say that this court’s findings will influence the national estate that this generation bequeaths to future generations of South Africans and people of the world.”

Despite this, the Apex Court declined the application.

“The Constitutional Court has considered the application of admission as amicus curiae. It has concluded that the application should be dismissed as the applicant has failed to make out a case for admission as an amicus curiae.”

The matter returns to court on 8 September.

World.title: Apartheid-era cop labels Steve Biko as 'aggressive'
World.content:
GQEBERHA - Former apartheid-era police officer Daniel Siebert claimed Steve Biko was aggressive during his detention.

Siebert testified virtually at the Gqeberha High Court on Friday, at the reopened inquest into the 1977 death of the anti-apartheid activist.

"On the said date, the deceased was brought from the police station where he was detained to the offices of the security branch in the Sanlam building in PE ( Port Elizabeth) for the purposes of questioning. "The deceased was, according to my recollection, aggressive and reluctant and refused to answer pertinent questions," Siebert said.

Siebert is one of only two surviving Security Branch officers who witnessed Biko's death.

But as his evidence is being heard, Biko family saed the reopened inquest is moving ahead before it has had enough time to prepare.

This has led the family to challenge the process in court by filing a formal application for the proceedings to be temporarily stopped.

In court, Biko’s son, Nkosinathi Biko, said they have repeatedly raised concerns about the timing of the proceedings.

"I think it's clear from the proceedings of today the point we have been raising consistently that it would be best for this court to give itself the time to get all the relevant material, including the investigation process, completed before it hears this matter. "And I think we are on record as to the struggles that we have encountered to have that point registered,” he said.

With the legal process underway, Nkosinathi said the family would continue to attend proceedings

“We continue to be in this court because, of course, we cannot disrespect a court. We will await the judge to excuse us from this process. And you will have seen from the tactics that have been played that the parties of interest in this matter are awaiting the opportunity for us to have abandoned this. We are not,” he said.

Nkosinathi said he notes Siebert, but said the family would have preferred him to appear in person to face them the same way he faced Biko.

The inquest has been postponed to Monday.

World.title: ANC eyes Electoral Court over IEC candidate lists
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - The ANC's number one has repeated an already dismissed claim of glitches in the Independent Electoral Commission's system.

ANC President Cyril Ramaphosa said the party remains open to exercising its right to approach the Electoral Court over its candidate list registration saga.

He was speaking while on the campaign trail in Ekurhuleni, Gauteng.

READ: IEC denies giving ANC extra time for 2026 election candidate lists

The party missed the IEC’s deadline to submit councillor candidates in the Eastern Cape, KwaZulu-Natal and Free State.

The ANC blames technical glitches on the IEC’s system, but the Electoral Commission has denied experiencing any such problems.

"So there should be a solution to be found because the technical glitches should not, in the end, deprive our people from being able to vote for their candidates and I'm certain that a solution will be found," Ramaphosa said.

"The political party liaison committee, as well as the IEC and the parties themselves, will be able to find a solution, and I'm certain that a solution will be found."

World.title: The US wants to manage the stalemate in the Strait of Hormuz. Iran wants to break it
World.content:
The monthlong lull in fighting between Iran and the United States ended this week with a renewed exchange of fire, dragging the region back to a dangerous – and potentially unsustainable – military stalemate.

The US military struck Iran again Tuesday, prompting Tehran to attack Jordan, Bahrain and Kuwait in defiance of a warning from President Donald Trump that any retaliation would see Iran “hit much harder.”

The exchanges were limited, unlike the fiercer attacks that took place over a month ago, which experts say signals an unwillingness from both parties to return to full-scale fighting.

“So far, both have largely concentrated their attacks on military rather than civilian or energy targets. And despite threats from senior Iranian officials, Tehran has not resumed attacks against Saudi Arabia or the UAE,” said Danny Citrinowicz, the former head of the Iran branch of Israeli military intelligence, in a post on X.

Nonetheless, the current situation is perilous, with room for miscalculation that risks pulling both sides back into all-out conflict.

A screengrab from a video obtained from social media on September 1, 2026, shows a view shortly before what US Central Command said was a US strike on an Iranian military target. U.S. Central Command/Reuters

“Neither side wants to return to full-scale war,” Hamidreza Azizi, senior Iran analyst at the International Crisis Group (ICG) think tank, told CNN’s Becky Anderson, adding that Iran’s disruption of traffic in the Strait of Hormuz and the US’ economic pressure on the country are “increasingly becoming unsustainable” for both sides.

The US president has said that he doesn’t care to negotiate with Iran. “I couldn’t care less if they sign a worthless, to them, agreement,” Trump said, adding that he likes America’s position “now much better.”

But beyond the rhetoric, Americans are feeling the cost of the war amid widespread public disapproval for a conflict that reportedly had cost Washington some $40 billion as of July.

In Iran, the impact of the war has been significantly more severe. The US is squeezing an already crippled economy as it struggles to sell its oil. Iranian weapon stockpiles are also likely being depleted, and citizens are struggling to access basic goods – including food and medicine.

The war has rattled Americans

The Trump administration may believe it scored a victory in the Strait of Hormuz. On Tuesday, the US military escorted 40 commercial vessels carrying 18 million barrels of oil through the waterway, marking a wartime high, according to two US officials familiar with the operations.

But that hasn’t remedied the wider situation. While global oil prices dipped slightly Thursday, they remain high.

The current US national average price for gas stands at $4.14 a gallon, compared to $3.19 a year ago, according to the American Automobile Association.

Meanwhile, the amount of oil in the US Strategic Petroleum Reserve has plunged over recent months to its lowest level since 1983, as the Trump administration continues to deploy emergency oil to minimize impacts from the war.

On Thursday, US Vice President J.D. Vance could provide neither a timeline for the Iran war to end nor a date when gas prices might sink below pre-war levels, suggesting instead it was up to Iran to conclude the conflict.

On the military end, the US is burning through weapons stockpiles and deploying costly military assets. Last month, multiple sources familiar with the matter told CNN that the US military had exhausted nearly 80% of its interceptors for a key missile defense system.

The US military has burned through nearly four-fifths of its THAAD missile inventory compared to pre-war numbers and roughly half of its Patriot interceptors since the start of the war, according to two sources familiar with the inventory report.

Trump later claimed that the US has “massive amounts” of munitions, but acknowledged certain munitions are in “tighter” supply.

US President Donald Trump speaks during a Rose Garden Dinner at the White House in Washington, DC, on September 2, 2026. Brendan Smialowski/AFP/Getty Images

The president’s overall approval rating has slumped in recent months, with many taking issue with his handling of the Iran conflict.

A University of Massachusetts (UMass) Amherst poll published Monday found that over two-thirds of Americans surveyed disapprove of Trump’s handling of the war. His overall approval rating is down to 32%, according to the poll.

Over the weekend, the Washington Post reported that several US military leaders have advised Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth that prolonging large-scale operations against Iran is unsustainable and risks weakening the US’ ability to meet threats elsewhere, citing people familiar with a recent assessment prepared for the Pentagon chief. CNN has not independently verified the reporting.

Why Iran may escalate

Meanwhile, in Iran, an already troubled economy is facing major challenges.

Inflation rates have reached “alarming levels,” with many working-class families unable to afford basic food items, according to state-affiliated Iranian media.

Annual inflation, measured over the 12-month period leading up to July, stood at 66%, according to the Iranian Labour News Agency (ILNA).

Like the US, Iran is running through its weapons stockpiles.

Arash Azizi, a US-based Iran expert, said Iran’s economy has taken a massive hit, but “the regime knows that a total capitulation could bring its downfall.”

Tehran may therefore escalate against the United States, calculating that it cannot absorb the economic pressure indefinitely and needs to break the stalemate.

Iranian families eat fast food while sitting along a sidewalk at an outdoor restaurant in downtown Tehran, Iran, on August 30, 2026. Morteza Nikoubazl/NurPhoto/Getty Images

Iran’s behavior – as well as the speed and scope of its response to the last US strikes – shows that Tehran is choosing to respond rather than yield, Hamidreza Azizi from the ICG said.

That’s because Tehran cannot afford to accept the prevailing order that Trump appears to be trying to impose in the Strait of Hormuz, experts say.

“The events of the past several days sharpen the picture in the Strait of Hormuz, and expose a fundamental mismatch between the US and Iranian approaches to the current confrontation,” Citrinowicz said.

While Washington appears to be trying to avoid kinetic escalation and keep the conflict contained to the economic domain, Iran is pursuing the opposite strategy, Citrinowicz wrote on X.

“It will continue trying to disrupt tanker traffic and challenge the US effort to establish a new reality in the Strait,” he said.

Iran has repeatedly said that it is prepared to return to the negotiating table if Washington resumes its commitments under the memorandum of understanding signed in June.

“I state clearly that if the United States returns to its commitments under the aforementioned memorandum of understanding, the Islamic Republic of Iran will immediately reciprocate,” Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said Tuesday on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization summit in Kyrgyzstan.

But Trump has claimed he is happy with the current position.

“I’m not trying to force Iran to the bargaining table,” Trump wrote on Truth Social on Tuesday night, after Iran retaliated following US strikes. “I like our position now much better, with almost total control of the Hormuz Strait, and their economy totally collapsing.”

Citrinowicz said on X that while both Iran and the US “understand the risks of uncontrolled escalation,” they “continue climbing the escalation ladder.”

“The problem is that this equilibrium is unlikely to hold,” he said.

World.title: Russia strikes Ukraine Security Service headquarters in central Kyiv
World.content:
A Russian drone struck the Kyiv headquarters of Ukraine’s Security Service, the SBU, on Friday, in a rare direct hit on a key government building that highlights Ukraine’s dire shortages of air defenses.

The daytime strike – the first time the SBU building has been hit in the four-and-a-half year conflict – came after days of near continuous aerial assaults by Russia on the Ukrainian capital.

Authorities said 12 people were injured in the attack and that emergency services were at the scene.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said the drone was aimed directly at the office of the SBU’s chief Oleksandr Poklad in that building. The SBU said later Poklad was safe and was not injured in the attack.

“I instructed Poklad to deliver an appropriate, tangible response and, where possible, one that mirrors this strike, to the Russians once everything is ready. Our military will support this response,” Zelensky said.

Kyiv has faced eight days of attacks, with strikes hitting multiple buildings inside the city center as well as warehouses and factories – including one making Coca-Cola – in the suburbs.

At least 53 people have been killed and 134 injured in Kyiv city and the wider Kyiv region since the start of these near non-stop attacks last month.

But the strike against the SBU is a major escalation – and a sign that Kyiv is increasingly unable to defend its key assets against Russian attacks as it struggles with critical shortages of interceptor missiles.

Most of the attacks over the past few days were by jet-powered drones.

These killer machines fly at speeds of up to 500 kilometers per hour (310 miles per hour), evading Ukraine’s air defenses. They are also too fast for Kyiv’s mobile fire groups, so the only way to shoot them down is with ground-to-air missiles or fighter jets – both of which are in extremely limited supply in Ukraine.

Russia has been targeting Ukrainian government buildings since the start of the war, regularly launching mass aerial attacks against Kyiv. And while it has hit a handful of them in the past, it has never managed to strike a target of such importance during day time.

Andrii Sybiha, Ukrainian Foreign Minister, said the attack “demanded resolute response.”

“Moscow launched this strike during a renewed push for peace — laying bare its true rejection of diplomacy,” Sybiha said, pointing to the fact that US special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner are planning to visit Moscow and Kyiv in the coming days.

“We call on international partners to unequivocally condemn these actions and step up pressure on the Putin regime,” he said.

The SBU is Ukraine’s internal security agency, akin to the FBI in the US or MI5 in the United Kingdom. Among others, it investigates Russian crimes on Ukrainian territory.

The agency’s building sits right at the heart of historical Kyiv, across the street from the UNESCO-listed Saint Sophia Cathedral and up the road from two other landmarks: the Golden Gate and the National Opera.

This is story has been updated.

World.title: Trump to take Qatari jet on another overseas trip despite questions about its security
World.content:
President Donald Trump is planning to take the Qatari-gifted jet used as Air Force One when he travels to Ireland later this month, a senior White House official told CNN, just two months after he flew it to Turkey and then secretly left the country on an alternate plane because of security concerns.

CNN reported at the time that the luxury Boeing jet from Qatar — an unconditional gift estimated to be worth about $400 million — did not possess the same capabilities to ensure its safety in dangerous international settings as the older Air Force One, according to two sources familiar with the matter. A third source said it was equipped with many of the same features as the older plane.

After that Turkey trip, Trump said in late July that the new Air Force One would soon be “maxed out,” appearing to acknowledge the plane is not as thoroughly outfitted as older aircrafts, when he was asked about its missile-defense capabilities. He reiterated that in the Oval Office on Friday, insisting that while the aircraft is already well-equipped, it will be upgraded further.

“It has a lot of stuff, but to max it out, meaning you can go into any territory, it’ll take about 60 days,” Trump said.

The president has continued to use the new plane – which he said Friday is scheduled to go to his presidential museum at the end of his term – for domestic travel this summer.

The senior White House official, who noted the upgrades to the plane are expected to happen this fall, said the aircraft is safe for non-hostile international travel, including Ireland, and the president has been long planning to take this plane on the trip. Trump said it would be sent for upgrades in October.

Trump has long boasted about the new aircraft, and he’s seethed privately over coverage of its deficiencies, CNN previously reported. He unveiled it over the summer at Joint Base Andrews, calling it “the world’s most luxurious plane.”

Trump’s plan to use the plane on his trip to Ireland was first reported by the Washington Post.

World.title: Trump says Iran conflict, which has killed 18 US service members and injured hundreds more, is ‘small potatoes’
World.content:
President Donald Trump on Friday labeled the Iran war “small potatoes,” the latest attempt to minimize a six-month conflict that caused a spike in gas prices and led to the deaths of 18 American service-members.

“A lot of people don’t call it a war. I call it a military conflict because it’s small potatoes for us. It’s not a big thing,” he said in the Oval Office.

A day earlier, Vice President JD Vance said the conflict shouldn’t be termed a “war” since major combat operations ended months ago.

Trump similarly cast the conflict as periodic and low-grade, despite routine rounds of back-and-forth strikes.

“I would say that it’s intermittent. You know, we do intermittent strikes,” Trump said, adding: “There’s a lot of truth that we’re not fighting right now. There’s no fighting.”

This week the US said it had targeted nearly 60 military targets around the Strait of Hormuz — including air defense sites, radar systems, maritime assets, mine-laying capabilities and communications sites — while simultaneously escorting ships through the waterway.

The administration had signaled it was moving past a military strategy, focusing instead on choking off Iran financially by applying sanctions on its trading partners. So far, however, the US has stopped short of punishing China, Tehran’s biggest economic lifeline.

Trump, who plans to host Chinese President Xi Jinping for a state visit this month, downplayed the assistance Beijing was providing.

“They are not really involved. Very little involvement by China. China could have plenty of involvement,” he said.

He also extolled potential new routes and pipelines that could bypass the Strait of Hormuz, including an overland alternative through Syria.

“They’re going to end up with a horrible strait that’s not really necessary any more,” he said.

Trump also raised the prospect of a new operation soon to take out a suspected Iranian nuclear site south of Tehran.

“We may hit Pickaxe very soon,” he said, referring to the underground facility where Iran is believed to have moved some of its stockpile of highly enriched uranium.

But he still insisted the conflict was not a war.

“It’s a military conflict, but it’s very intermittent. I could see somebody not calling it a war,” he said.

He continued: “I don’t think it matters what you call it. What matters is the fact that we have had tremendous success.”

This story has been updated with additional details.

World.title: European Triathlon Cup in Northern Ireland excludes Israeli team over Palestinian crisis
World.content:
Organizers of the European Triathlon Cup in Londonderry have barred a four-member Israeli delegation from competing in this weekend’s event, citing an outright refusal to normalize Israel’s standing on the global sporting stage while the Palestinian people continue to suffer.

The Northern Ireland Triathlon Club, which hosts the multi-sport competition featuring sequential swimming, cycling, and running legs, pulled the plug on the Israeli athletes immediately after reviewing the provisional entry list published by World Triathlon.

In a formal statement, the host club confirmed it lodged a sharp, unequivocal objection to the World Triathlon governing body, asserting that no Israeli representation would be permitted at the venue. Organizers underscored that the ban does not target individuals based on religion or ethnicity, but rather serves as a principled stand against official state representation during an ongoing humanitarian crisis.

The decision follows mounting security concerns and planned demonstrations near the venue. According to Israeli daily Yedioth Ahronoth, local police in Northern Ireland actively monitored calls on social media rallying protesters against the delegation’s arrival.

The boycott mirrors a broader wave of resistance sweeping international sports fixtures involving Israeli teams. UEFA recently moved upcoming UEFA Nations League matches involving Ireland and Israel to neutral venues, with Ireland’s home leg slated for Serbia behind closed doors and the return fixture scheduled in Hungary.

World.title: Seoul Korea breaks silence on secret Strait of Hormuz deployment reports
World.content:
South Korea’s presidential office dismissed media reports on Friday claiming Seoul is preparing an immediate military deployment to the Strait of Hormuz, clarifying that “nothing has been decided” and that internal evaluations remain underway.

Refuting reports that South Korea was gearing up to send forces to the strategic waterway, a presidential official told The Guardian that the claims “differ from reality,” emphasizing that the government continues to conduct close consultations with international partners to determine practical ways to support freedom of navigation and regional stability.

The denial follows domestic media reports citing military sources that claimed Seoul planned to seek National Assembly approval to deploy a P-8 Poseidon maritime patrol aircraft, a logistics support ship, and an explosive ordnance disposal unit.

The surrounding debate comes against a backdrop of heightened pressure from U.S. President Donald Trump, who criticized South Korea over its reluctance to commit military assets to the region and subsequently scaled back the duration of the joint “Ulchi Freedom Shield” military exercises.

South Korea remains acutely vulnerable to supply disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz, relying on the vital maritime passage for over 90 percent of its primary energy and approximately 70 percent of its crude oil imports. Officials noted that any future military deployment would strictly require a formal review by the National Security Council, cabinet approval, and final ratification by the National Assembly.

World.title: Four-story building collapses in Minya, casualties reported
World.content:
A four-story residential building collapsed on Al-Mu’assasa Street in the Ezbet Shaheen district of Minya city on Friday, triggering a major multi-agency search and rescue operation as casualties were reported, local officials confirmed.

The operational headquarters of the Minya Local Unit raised the alarm following the structural failure, prompting security authorities led by Minya Security Director Major General Ahmed Izzat to immediately deploy civil defense forces, heavy machinery, and fleet ambulances to the scene.

Emergency teams established a security cordon around the perimeter to protect bystanders while heavy equipment cleared debris in a bid to reach survivors. Rescue workers continue to search through the rubble for trapped residents and victims.

Formal legal proceedings have been filed, and investigations into the cause of the collapse are ongoing.

World.title: Egypt to raise entry visa fees starting January 2027
World.content:
The Egyptian government has established a standardized administrative fee of $15—or its equivalent in foreign currencies—for entry visas, transit visas, and select consular services provided by Egyptian diplomatic missions abroad, effective January 1, 2027.

Issued under Prime Minister Decree No. 2553 of 2026 and published in the Official Gazette on Sunday, August 30, the measure unifies consular service fees globally while repealing all conflicting provisions.

Under the new regulatory framework, the $15 administrative surcharge will be levied on top of base visa charges. Consequently, the final cost for travelers will vary depending on the specific visa category and its associated baseline fee. The move follows an earlier adjustment in March 2026, which raised the visa-on-arrival fee for foreign tourists from $25 to $30.

Egypt will continue operating its digital entry infrastructure, issuing electronic visas equipped with a quick response (QR) code for automated border verification. Currently, citizens from 118 nations qualify for visas on arrival as part of broader national initiatives designed to boost international tourism and streamline arrivals.

Officials framed the standardized fee structure as a key step toward simplifying consular procedures across all Egyptian missions overseas prior to the 2027 implementation date.

World.title: Should the Opposition Put Justice or “Bitterness Aside”?: A Moral Critique of Fr. James Phiri of CCZ
World.content:
By Kapya Kaoma

When Father James Phiri, General Secretary of the Council of Churches in Zambia (CCZ), reportedly called on the opposition to “put bitterness aside” and focus on the next election, Jesus’ words came to mind:

“You are the salt of the earth. But if the salt loses its saltiness, how can it be made salty again? It is no longer good for anything, except to be thrown out and trampled underfoot” (Matthew 5:13).

I never thought these words would apply so directly to Zambia’s religious and political reality.

Speaking to ZNBC, Fr. Phiri said that “it is painful to lose elections, but the opposition must set aside their bitterness, as the church is praying for them.” This statement amounts to a major moral betrayal. He expects the opposition to quietly move on to the next electoral cycle without addressing the severe injustices of the vote that just concluded.

Fr. Phiri appears to misunderstand the concept of justice. Courts operate on the principle of injury: there must be an aggrieved party, and the recent election left the opposition with a list of grievances. Asking them to swallow their pain while their leaders remain behind bars and countless supporters face politically motivated charges before biased courts is insulting.

Contrary to Fr. Phiri’s suggestion, the opposition did not just fail despite doing “their best”—they were actively denied justice. As Fr. Phiri himself noted in pre-election statements, the opposition was forced to campaign in a hostile environment, starved of legal protections, and repeatedly persecuted by state security across the nation.

Demanding that the opposition look toward a future vote without addressing the systemic flaws engineered by this regime is both illogical and suspect. Religious leaders would be better off applying directly for political favors than using the church as a shield for a partisan agenda.

Is Fr. Phiri himself not bitter about injustice? Is he not bitter about innocent musicians being arrested simply for performing for their preferred candidates in Mongu? Is he not bitter about citizens being assaulted for exercising their right to vote, courts being locked down, or the military being deployed to tallying centers?

Fr. Phiri knows that Zambians deserve answers and that those responsible must be held accountable. If these immoral violations go unaddressed, what is the point of holding another election at all?

Moreover, it is disgraceful that foreign entities—including the United Nations, the European Union, and the Anglican Church of Southern Africa—have shown the courage to denounce abuses that Zambian church leaders seem too afraid to confront. Why is there such a gaping chasm between the findings of international observers and the narrative Fr. Phiri is pushing? As the old saying goes: “He who pays the piper calls the tune.”

I agree with Fr. Phiri on one point: “It’s not over for them until God says so.” But I refuse to pray for the opposition to quietly bottle up its bitterness. Instead, they must demand justice—from God, through local, regional, and international legal channels, and from the people of Zambia. This is both their democratic duty and their fundamental right.

After all, righteous indignation can be the very foundation of justice; only those who have been wronged can demand redress. Philosophers of liberation have long endorsed Jean-Paul Sartre’s argument that outsiders and beneficiaries of power have no moral right to dictate how victims of oppression should respond to their oppressors.

Fr. Phiri was not the victim of police or military brutality. He did not risk his livelihood on a campaign, nor did he shed blood. He lost nothing. From the comfort of his office, it is easy to tell victims to blindly place everything in God’s hands. But is this what Kafwaya’s widow wants to hear? What about the families of Bishop Trevor Mwamba, Mundubile, or Makebi? Behind these elections are human wounds and shattered lives that can never be rebuilt. Fr. Phiri’s lack of empathy is appalling.

Besides, if prayers alone sufficed, why would we need laws or courts?

As a theologian, Fr. Phiri knows that God demands active justice for the oppressed. Instead of placating the powerful, he should have urged the opposition to seek redress through the legal system. He should have called on the courts to act with strict impartiality—for the law must never wear political regalia. He should have demanded an independent inquiry into the military’s presence at tallying centers, as well as the immediate arrest and prosecution of all perpetrators of political violence, including state security officers.

Furthermore, he should have called for an independent, international investigation into the irregularities surrounding the G20 forms and result tallies to restore a shred of legitimacy to our republic’s democratic processes. Finally, he should have challenged the President to make the ongoing treason trials public, allowing Zambians to see the evidence for themselves.

Had he taken these steps, his interview would have reflected an independent moral voice. As it stands, it was a devastating letdown.

World.title: Democracy and The Incumbency Advantage: The Case of Zambia
World.content:
By Venus N Msyani

On August 13, 2026, Zambians lined up across the country to elect their next president. Election day itself unfolded calmly, with voting generally conducted efficiently. According to the preliminary findings of the EU Election Observer Mission, voters were offered a competitive choice.

However, the mission also noted that restrictions on campaigning and advantages associated with incumbency contributed to an uneven playing field, a challenge familiar in many democracies.

It was after the polls closed that events took a troubling turn. As vote counting and tabulation began, the Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ) abruptly suspended the process nationwide for several hours without providing a clear explanation. The suspension occurred at a moment when President Hakainde Hichilema was reportedly trailing. During this period, the military took control of several tallying centers, officially to secure ballots. Some observers allege they were removed from these centers, raising concerns about transparency.

When counting resumed, Hichilema began to take the lead. Allegations soon surfaced claiming ballot box seals had been tampered with and figures altered to favor the incumbent. These claims, though not yet independently verified, fueled widespread suspicion and deepened public anxiety about the integrity of the process.

Amid these irregularities, opposition leader Brian Mundubile announced his intention to challenge the election results. Immediately afterward, his home was raided by the military in an operation authorities described as targeting an alleged militia group. The raid resulted in the death of former Minister of Transport Hon. Mutotwe Kafwaya. Mundubile and his running mate, Makebi Zulu, were subsequently charged with treason; a move that has prompted the United Nations to call for their release.

The situation escalated further on the final day of the petition window. Courts across the country were closed, preventing Mundubile from filing his challenge. This unprecedented action left many Zambians questioning whether their copper‑rich nation, long regarded as a beacon of democracy in Southern Africa, still holds that reputation.

On September 1, 2026, Hakainde Hichilema was inaugurated. Supporters argue that it is time for the country to move forward, noting that no democracy is perfect. The congratulatory messages Hichilema has received from governments, organizations, and international partners reinforce this view and suggest continued global recognition of Zambia’s leadership.

Others, however, struggle to accept the legitimacy of his presidency. They point to the military’s involvement in the electoral process and the nationwide closure of courts that prevented the election petition. To them, these events amount to military interference. They warn that allowing a president to assume office under such circumstances sets a dangerous precedent for future elections.

They emphasize that Zambia’s constitution must be respected for the country to remain a regional democratic leader. The nation’s election cycle is meant to be straightforward: campaigning, voting, declaration of results, resolution of disputes, and inauguration.

In 2026, they argue, this cycle was broken. Disputes remain unresolved, and the courts were closed at the critical moment when they were meant to address them. From this perspective, Hichilema’s presidency is viewed as constitutionally compromised. And unless Zambia confronts what happened in 2026, the precedent set today may haunt every election to come.

World.title: Zambia Records Progress Against Financial Crimes
World.content:
Zambia has made progress in its fight against money laundering and financial crimes after three areas of its anti-money laundering framework were upgraded under Financial Action Task Force (FATF) standards.

Attorney-General Mulilo Kabesha says the upgrade was secured during the 52nd Eastern and Southern Africa Anti-Money Laundering Group (ESAAMLG) Task Force of Senior Officials Plenary Meeting and the 26th Council of Ministers meeting held in Kigali, Rwanda.

In a statement made available to ZNBC News today, Mr. Kabesha said the development means Zambia is now compliant or largely compliant with 38 of the 40 FATF Recommendations.

The three areas upgraded are transparency and beneficial ownership of legal persons, regulation and supervision of financial institutions, and regulation and supervision of designated non-financial businesses and professions, commonly known as DNFBPs.

Mr. Kabesha, who is also Chairperson of the Anti-Money Laundering Authority, said the progress was the result of efforts by public and private institutions to combat money laundering, terrorism financing and proliferation financing.

He has since challenged Zambian institutions to shift their focus from compliance with requirements to ensuring the effectiveness of measures against financial crimes.

World.title: FRA smashes maize purchase target
World.content:
The Food Reserve Agency (FRA) has beat its maize purchase target in Central Province by more than 150 percent, buying over 102,000 metric tonnes of maize against a target of 40,000 tonnes.

Central Province Principal Public Relations Officer Tobias Phiri says the FRA has so far purchased 102,964.20 metric tonnes of maize through 139 satellite depots across seven districts.

Speaking at a press briefing in Kabwe, Mr Phiri said the province has exceeded its target by 157 percent.

He stated that Serenje is leading in maize purchases with over 23,560 metric tonnes, followed by Kapiri Mposhi with 14,453.20 tonnes, Kabwe with 14,051.40 tonnes and Chibombo with 13,233.20 tonnes.

Luano and Chisamba have contributed 9,355.20 and 8,821.90 metric tonnes, respectively.

Mr Phiri says government has already paid farmers more than K90 million for maize supplied to the FRA.

He has commended farmers for responding positively to the maize marketing programme, but urged them to keep enough grain for household consumption, especially with a drought projected in the coming farming season.

Mr Phiri says the high maize purchases will help strengthen national food security while providing farmers with a ready market for their produce.

World.title: ZCCM-IH announces proposed listing
World.content:
ZCCM Investments Holdings Plc (ZCCM-IH) has announced that it is progressing with its proposed Listing Optimisation Project, which involves the Company’s listings on the Lusaka Securities Exchange (“LuSE”), Euronext Access Paris and the London Stock Exchange (“LSE”).

The Company first announced the proposed project on July 10, 2026 and subsequently issued a further cautionary announcement on August 28, 2026.

ZCCM-IH Chief Executive Officer Kakenenwa Muyangwa explained that as part of the Listing Optimisation Project, the company is considering a proposed Odd-Lot offer for shareholders holding 100 or fewer ZCCM-IH shares.

Mr Muyangwa said as at July 20, 2026, ZCCM-IH had approximately 5,013 shareholders across its three share registers, of whom 3,637 representing 72.55 per cent held 100 or fewer shares, collectively representing approximately 0.05 per cent of the company’s total shares in issue.

He said the proposed Odd-Lot offer is intended to simplify and optimise the shareholder registers.

“What the proposed offer means for small shareholders subject to the required legal, regulatory and shareholder approvals and the final terms of the Offer, eligible shareholders will have the opportunity to either sell their Odd-Lot holdings to ZCCM-IH for cash or retain their shares,” Mr Muyangwa said.

He said the proposed offer is intended to provide shareholders with a straightforward liquidity option where the small size of their holdings may otherwise make it difficult or uneconomic to sell their shares through the market.

Mr. Muyangwa said the move is about making ZCCM-IH simpler, more efficient and easier to invest in.

He added that the proposed Odd-Lot offer is intended to give eligible shareholders a fair and straightforward cash option if they wish to realise their investment, while ensuring that one shareholder who wishes to remain invested in ZCCM-IH can retain their shares.

“Almost three quarters of our shareholders hold 100 shares or fewer, and every one of them matters to us. For holdings of this size, however, the costs and practical considerations associated with selling through the market can be disproportionate to the value of the investment,” he said.

This is contained in a statement issued to the media by ZCCM-IH Corporate Affairs Manager Loisa Mbatha.

World.title: NW Royal Establishment celebrates HH victory
World.content:
The Kapijimpanga Royal Establishment in Solwezi District of North-western Province has congratulated President Hakainde Hichilema on his re-election in the August, 13, 2026 general elections.

Speaking during a media briefing in Solwezi today, where he was flanked by other traditional leaders, Sub-Chief Mbonge said the re-election of President Hichilema is well deserved.

The traditional leader has also commended voters across the province for turning out peacefully and exercising their constitutional right, adding that the conduct of the electorate demonstrated maturity and commitment to peace which must be sustained beyond the election period.

He has also appealed to supporters of all parties to remain calm and remain united and avoid actions that could disrupt peace regardless of their political affiliation.

He has further called for peace and unity among the newly elected leaders, to achieve national development regardless of their political affiliation.

And Sub Chief Kajoba said the election period is over and it is time to develop the province and ensure it has a university and airport infrastructure development among others.

World.title: Mufulira Mayor ready to deliver
World.content:
Mufulira Mayor-Elect Tsindikai Mudemba has pledged to work closely with small-scale traders in the district to ensure that the town maintains high standards of cleanliness.

Mr Mudemba who stood on the National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity (NRPUP) ticket, stated that he greatly acknowledges and appreciates the hard work small-scale traders put into conducting their daily business.

He noted that rather than condemning street vending, he wants to work hand in hand with the vendors to ensure they maintain the town’s cleanliness.

Mr Mudemba explained that his plan involves actively engaging street vendors to reach a mutual agreement, requiring them to keep their trading spaces clean.

“Under this approach, vendors will clean up after themselves at the end of each day’s trading in a given area to ensure no litter remains on the street,” he said.

Mr Mudemba noted that it is important to embrace the traders, as vending serves as the primary livelihood for many vulnerable families and poor women.

Additionally, Mr Mudemba thanked the people of Mufulira district for having confidence in his leadership.

He stated that he is committed to being a servant of the people who listens to their needs, emphasising that he does not want to impose top-down plans for the district.

“I want to listen to the people as they are the ones who understand their needs best and I will work closely with the people,” Mr Mudemba said.

The Mayor pledged to ensure that the district remains clean and green, assuring the electorate that he is fully committed to fulfilling his campaign promises and not letting them down.

World.title: SC encourages Smart Office platform utilisation
World.content:
Secretary to the Cabinet, Patrick Kangwa, has directed all government institutions to prioritise the adoption and utilisation of the Smart Office Platform in their operations.

Mr Kangwa has further instructed the Smart Zambia Institute to submit a progress report to his office by end of October, on the onboarding of ministries, provinces, spending agencies, state-owned enterprises and other public institutions.

He has emphasised that the Smart Office Platform, a flagship digital government solution is designed to transform how public institutions conduct business, manage records, process workflows and deliver services.

Speaking during the handover of the Smart Office Management System to the Zambia Airports Corporation Limited (ZACL) in Chongwe, Mr Kangwa underscored digital transformation as a strategic imperative for national development.

“Ministries, provinces, spending agencies, state-owned enterprises and other public institutions are directed to work closely with the Smart Zambia Institute, towards accelerating the implementation of the smart office and other related digital government solutions”, the Secretary to the Cabinet stressed.

Speaking at the same event, Smart Zambia Institute National Coordinator, Percy Chinyama, explained that the platform will enable seamless workflow automation, secure electronic records management, paperless governance and improve transparency and accountability.

He noted that ZACL stands to benefit from significant operational cost savings by reducing expenditure on stationery, printing and manual records management.

“These benefits demonstrate the value of digital transformation in modernising institutional operations and enhancing organisational performance,” he said.

And ZACL Managing Director, Urvesh Desai, echoed similar sentiments, noting that the system would improve turnaround times while strengthening transparency and accountability at the institution.

He added that it would also support more efficient decision-making and enhance service delivery across the Corporation.

“Technology can only transform an organisation when its people are committed to making it work. I am happy to confirm that 100 percent of head office staff have been trained and 406 more in other stations will be trained by end of November 2026,” he disclosed.

World.title: Africa: Loza Maléombho Is Building An Industry From African Stories
World.content:
Internationally recognised after Beyoncé wore her designs, Ivorian designer Loza Maléombho is now looking beyond fashion. Through Pokou, she is combining Baoulé history, local craftsmanship and artificial intelligence to build an African-owned creative universe spanning clothing, film, art, architecture and digital experiences.

On the fourth floor of a building in Treichville, one of Abidjan’s busiest commercial and cultural districts, the world of Ivorian designer Loza Maléombho is expanding beyond the clothes hanging in her workshop.

Maléombho is developing Pokou, a creative universe inspired by Queen Abla Pokou, the legendary founder of the Baoulé people, and reimagined through science fiction, fashion and digital technology.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

According to tradition, Queen Pokou led her people from the Ashanti Kingdom towards present-day Côte d’Ivoire. When they were unable to cross the Comoé River, Pokou sacrificed her only son to save her people. The story, which symbolises courage, selflessness and communal survival, is also associated with the origin of the name Baoulé, often translated as “the child is dead.”

“It is a story that everyone knows in Côte d’Ivoire so people can identify with it. But it is also a story about sacrifice, and I think that is something any audience can relate to in family, work, and life in general,” she said.

Maléombho drew on this story for her YouTube Pokou series, which launched in June 2026.

Developed using generative artificial intelligence alongside Maléombho’s own research and design work, Pokou is intended to promote the clothing label while opening routes into film, art, architecture, craftsmanship and digital experiences.

The project represents the designer’s attempt to turn African stories into commercially valuable, African-owned intellectual property.

Maléombho is not starting from obscurity. Her international breakthrough came when singer Beyoncé wore pieces from her Spring/Summer 2016 collection in the “ Formation ” music video. She later created a custom outfit for Beyoncé’s 2020 visual album, Black Is King . The appearances introduced her work to a global audience and strengthened her reputation for combining contemporary silhouettes with West African materials and imagery.

Now she wants to take the label beyond celebrity recognition and luxury clothing.

“The idea today is not that we want to dissociate ourselves, but that we are evolving more toward a multicultural creative studio and toward cultural intellectual property,” Maléombho said.

“We are no longer focused solely on producing products for sale, but more on creating a universe as such. There are characters, there are clothes, there are art objects, there are interactive experiences, there are architectural concepts.”

The shift is partly a response to the limitations confronting fashion businesses based in African markets. A conventional label must design collections, source materials, maintain consistent production, organise distribution and find buyers. Maléombho says African brands often have to do this without the supply chains, finance and logistics available to established international companies.

Her own business has encountered difficulties sourcing raw materials, finding specialised workers, maintaining consistent quality, accepting online payments, securing finance and transporting finished products.

Côte d’Ivoire’s cotton industry illustrates one of these structural gaps. The country is a significant West African producer, with output forecast at 590,000 bales of cotton lint in the 2026/27 marketing year. However, only a small proportion is processed by domestic spinning and weaving businesses; most fibre is exported to textile-producing markets in Asia.

That disconnect helps explain why Maléombho can work extensively with Ivorian artisans while still importing some of the cotton used in her collections.

Rather than relying only on selling larger volumes of clothing, she wants to create several commercial entry points into the same cultural universe.

“It is creativity, it is cultural ownership, it is our cultural stories,” she said. Pokou could encompass clothing, art objects, interiors and architectural concepts, while enabling collaborations and licensing agreements with companies in other sectors.

Artificial intelligence has allowed Maléombho to visualise parts of this universe more quickly, but she rejects the suggestion that it is the author of the work.

“What is very important to specify is that I do not give creativity to artificial intelligence,” she said. “People tend to think that AI designs everything, and then creativity is lost. But artificial intelligence makes a huge number of mistakes in terms of storytelling or even mythology in our African traditions.”

The digital ideas eventually become physical objects in the Treichville workshop. Maléombho works with artisans to test fabrics, dyes, embellishments and accessories. Bronze workers make buttons and a signature gold-plated buckle inspired by a Baoulé mask.

Jute, ordinarily used in sacks for packaging and exporting cocoa, is transformed through dyeing, appliqué, beadwork and printing. Raffia, Baoulé cloth, Kita cloth and hand-dyed cotton also form part of the brand’s visual language.

Baoulé is a traditional Ivorian cotton fabric, handwoven in distinctive patterns and colours and often worn at ceremonies, while Kita is a West African textile handwoven in narrow strips of cotton and silk.

For Norou Sow, a leather craftsman and artisan who has worked with Maléombho for more than ten years, the collaboration has changed both his methods of work and his livelihood.

“She taught me to work in a group. She also taught me to develop my experience,” Sow said. “Many things changed in my life when I started working with her.”

The company employs 10 people directly and works with more than 50 artisans in Côte d’Ivoire. Maléombho says 90% of its inputs or production are local, while some cotton and some manufacturing are sourced internationally.

The label sells through outlets or concept stores in Côte d’Ivoire, the United States, Nigeria, South Africa, the United Kingdom and Tanzania.

Côte d’Ivoire-based fashion and tourism specialist Dorine Negou sees the larger challenge as persuading African brands and consumers to recognise the commercial value of their own cultural identities.

“I think the difficulty is that we Africans want to adopt European models too much,” she said. “We have so many things that can enhance our value and attract more attention to us. It is up to us to rely on our brands, on our nature, on where we come from, and know how to showcase what we have.”

Yapo Patrick is a visual and installation artist who has taught colour and textile techniques for more than 20 years at the Centre Technique des Arts Appliqués (CTAA), or Technical Centre for Applied Arts, in Bingerville, Côte d’Ivoire.

Patrick said Maléombho’s journey demonstrates how formal training must be combined with personal commitment and a willingness to take risks: “There will always be limitations and difficulties, but creators have to commit themselves personally. They have to dare and decide to act despite those difficulties.”

However, turning the success of individual designers into a stronger domestic fashion industry will require broader investment in skills and local production. Although Côte d’Ivoire is a major cotton producer, only a limited share of its raw material is transformed locally into finished textiles and clothing.

Patrick believes vocational training for designers, pattern makers and tailors could help expand production and encourage Ivorians to buy locally made fabric and clothing.

“We need more information, more initiatives and more people investing in professional training,” he said. “If Ivorians can produce and consume Ivorian products, including fabrics, that will generate revenue and encourage both the state and the private sector to develop an ecosystem in which the fashion industry can grow.”

Close 

Maléombho believes that Africa possesses a vast narrative and cultural inheritance but captures too little of its commercial value. The opportunity, in her view, is to turn stories, materials and craft traditions into products that retain a distinct identity while meeting international standards.

Her clothing label provides the initial commercial foundation. Its luxury pieces target customers drawn to the house’s craftsmanship and cultural references, while shoes, belts, jewellery and other accessories offer less expensive entry points.

Pokou would extend that model. A consumer might first encounter a garment in a film or digital world. A character could lead into a collection, while an imagined building might inspire furniture or another designed object. The story itself could be licensed or used in collaborations across different industries.

Over the next three to five years, Maléombho hopes to complete the transition from a fashion label into a cultural studio built around intellectual property. She believes the model could create jobs in traditional crafts, film, digital production and artificial intelligence.

“It is not just a clothing brand,” she said. “It is truly a multicultural studio that is in tune with the times and also knows how to innovate while keeping its roots in its history.”

From its base in Treichville, Pokou is attempting to bring Baoulé history into dialogue with artificial intelligence, craftsmanship with cinema, and clothing with architecture.

Maléombho believes the constraints facing African creative businesses can themselves produce innovation.

“The legacy I would like to leave would really be to show that, first of all, with very little, we can create much more value,” she said. “It is even within the constraints that we have the opportunity to innovate.”

World.title: Ethiopia: Ethiopia Connects Climate Solutions From Field To Factory
World.content:
As rainfall becomes less predictable, researchers are developing improved seed, testing more efficient irrigation and using digital tools to track water losses. Getting these solutions to farmers could protect harvests and provide Ethiopia’s textile factories with more locally grown fibre.

When the rains arrive late or stop too soon, cotton farmer Debalkie Abate can no longer depend on the planting calendar he once knew. But researchers and water specialists are working on an alternative: improved seed, better-timed irrigation and more accurate climate information that could help farmers continue producing despite increasingly unpredictable weather.

“The weather has become much less predictable than it was a decade ago,” Abate says. “Sometimes the rains arrive late, sometimes they stop too early. Without irrigation we cannot rely on rainfall alone.”

Ethiopia already possesses tools that could reduce that risk. Research in its cotton-growing lowlands shows how carefully timed irrigation can make better use of limited water. New assessments are identifying irrigation losses, while researchers develop varieties intended to improve productivity and fibre quality.



The challenge is to move those solutions from research centres into farmers’ fields, protecting livelihoods and providing Ethiopia’s textile industry with a more reliable supply of locally grown fibre.

The work reflects a wider continental shift. In February 2026, the African Union called for greater support to help smallholders—particularly women—access climate-resilient seed, irrigation and insurance. It also urged countries to share research and solutions involving digital agriculture, climate information and resilient infrastructure.

Using less water more effectively

The need to adapt is becoming more urgent. The Ethiopian Meteorological Institute’s 2025 climate projections anticipate continued warming under both medium- and high-emissions scenarios. Rainfall outcomes differ by region and season, with some areas potentially receiving more rain while others experience greater variability.

For farmers, the problem is not simply less rain. It is rain that can no longer be assumed to arrive when the crop most needs it.

At an AGRA agrifood-systems retreat in April 2026 , Ethiopia highlighted lessons from cluster-based approaches and digital advisory systems. It also identified stronger agricultural financing and greater climate finance for smallholders as priorities—support needed to move adaptation tools into farmers’ hands.

Research at Melka Werer in the semi-arid Middle Awash offers one possible response. Trials examined how cotton grown on heavy Vertisol soils performed under different irrigation schedules.

The study, available through the UN Food and Agriculture Organization , found that three strategically timed irrigations—at planting, flowering and boll formation—could produce a yield comparable with a far more intensive schedule while using about 40% less irrigation water, provided seasonal rain was normal and well distributed.

The research does not offer a ready-made prescription. The trials were conducted in the 1980s, relied partly on unpublished research-station data and involved specific varieties and soil conditions. Researchers would need to test the approach with current seed, weather patterns and farm conditions before recommending it widely.

Its value lies in showing what may be possible: improving productivity does not necessarily mean applying more water. Timing can matter as much as volume.

Finding where the water goes

More recent work is identifying another part of the solution—reducing losses before water reaches the field.

A 2025 International Water Management Institute assessment found that the Amibara irrigation scheme in the Awash River Basin was operating at just 32% overall efficiency, down from its original 49%.

Researchers combined remote-sensing information, digital mapping and field measurements to identify leakage, poor distribution and operational problems. They found that although water was available at the diversion point, supplies often fell short of crop needs farther along the scheme because of internal bottlenecks.

Digital water accounting can guide repairs and investment. It also shifts some responsibility away from farmers: advice on when to irrigate has limited value if ageing or silted canals cannot deliver water reliably.

IWMI says measures such as canal lining, improved furrows, low-cost moisture sensors and precision irrigation could raise efficiency. These interventions require investment, but could allow farmers to produce more with the water already available.

Getting improved seed to farmers

Water alone will not build resilience. Farmers also need varieties that can cope with heat, drought, pests and, in some irrigated areas, salinity without sacrificing the fibre quality manufacturers require.

At the Werer Agricultural Research Center in Afar, researchers have developed improved cotton varieties intended to raise yields and fibre quality. But limited capacity to multiply the seed has slowed distribution.

“Financial shortages and limited human resources have prevented multiplication of these improved varieties, leaving valuable research results underutilised,” says Berhanu Megersa, director general of the centre.

Recent research illustrates why seed access matters. A 2024 study of irrigated cotton in Ethiopia found that seed source, variety and planting rate significantly affected yields.

But a promising variety at a research station cannot protect Abate’s harvest. Seed must be multiplied and distributed, while extension officers help farmers select the right variety for local conditions. Seasonal forecasts also need to reach producers before planting and be translated into practical decisions about planting dates and irrigation.

Connecting farms and factories

Close 

The benefits could extend along Ethiopia’s value chain. Cotton must be ginned, spun into yarn, woven or knitted, and finished before a clothing factory can use it.

“If farmers cannot produce enough quality cotton, the entire manufacturing chain feels the impact,” Megersa says.

Abeje Menegesha, procurement manager at Amibara Agricultural Development PLC, says local fibre is preferred but its supply remains inconsistent.

“Our first choice is always Ethiopian cotton because it shortens supply chains and supports local farmers,” Menegesha says. “However, domestic production still does not consistently meet our requirements in quantity and quality.”

The work underway suggests Ethiopia does not need to wait for one transformative invention. It needs to connect several practical responses: repair irrigation systems, retest efficient watering schedules, multiply improved seed, deliver usable forecasts and give farmers a predictable market.

Farmer Abeje Selelew sees the opportunity in generational terms.

“I hope my children will see Ethiopian cotton processed into Ethiopian textiles and clothing sold across Africa and beyond,” he says. “When farmers receive fair prices and industries buy more local cotton, everyone along the value chain benefits.”

For Abate, the starting point remains his next planting season. The weather may be less predictable, but Ethiopia’s response does not have to be. Much of the knowledge already exists. The test now is whether it can reach his field in time.

World.title: Tunisia: Upheld Convictions in Mass 'Conspiracy Case' a Travesty of Justice
World.content:
In response to the Tunis Court of Cassation upholding the convictions and lengthy prison sentences against 34 defendants in the politically motivated 'conspiracy case', Yasmine Ahmed, Amnesty International's Senior Director for Regional Human Rights Impact, said:

"The Tunis Court of Cassation's decision to uphold these unjust convictions is a devastating blow to justice and an appalling indictment of the Tunisian justice system. By validating these draconian sentences, ranging up to 45 years, following a sham trial based on unfounded charges, the authorities have doubled down on their relentless campaign to eliminate political dissent and silence independent voices.

The Tunis Court of Cassation's decision to uphold these unjust convictions is a devastating blow to justice and an appalling indictment of the Tunisian justice system.Yasmine Ahmed, Amnesty International

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

"From the outset, this trial was severely compromised by grave due process violations, including forcing defendants to attend hearings remotely and stripping them of their right to be present at their own trial. The Court of Cassation had a final judicial opportunity to correct this injustice and yet instead today's verdict exposes the authorities' chilling determination to silence all remaining opposition.

"Those imprisoned include human rights lawyer Ayachi Hammami, opposition figure Ahmed Nejib Chebbi, and political activist Chaima Issa amongst many others wrongfully imprisoned. Tunisia's authorities must immediately quash these unjust convictions, drop all charges, and unconditionally release all those detained solely for exercising their human rights. The authorities must stop misusing the criminal justice system as a tool for political repression."

Background

The 'conspiracy case' involves the prosecution of prominent opposition figures, lawyers, and human rights defenders on politically motivated charges, primarily "conspiracy against state security." The trial has been widely condemned by international observers for severe fair trial violations, executive interference, and the denial of basic defense rights.

World.title: Kenya: Ruto Fires Back At Critics of New Police Uniforms
World.content:
Nairobi — President William Ruto has defended Kenya's new police uniforms amid criticism over the design, saying the change is part of a wider plan to transform the National Police Service.

Speaking during the 59th Passing-Out Parade for Administration Police recruits at the National Police College in Embakasi, Nairobi, Ruto said the new uniforms should not be viewed as an isolated project.

"The new uniforms for general duty officers that we unveiled last week must be understood within this broader reform program," Ruto said.

"It is not a standalone intervention, but part of the comprehensive transformation of the National Police Service arising from the reform process."



The President said the uniforms were developed after consultations with police officers and members of the public.

According to Ruto, the new design was meant to improve the professional identity of officers while also considering their operational needs and dignity.

"The uniform itself emerged from consultation with police officers and with the Kenyan public," he said.

He acknowledged that a uniform by itself could not change the police service, but argued that it plays a role in building a more professional force.

"A uniform alone cannot transform policing, but professional identity and pride are part of building a modern, disciplined, and effective police service," Ruto said.

The President also appeared to welcome scrutiny of the wider police reform programme, saying public resources must be properly accounted for.

"And because this entire reform program is undertaken in the public interest and financed with public resources, every aspect of it must withstand scrutiny," Ruto said.

"We welcome scrutiny of every decision and every shilling spent."

Ruto said Kenyans should ask questions about government decisions but warned against condemning individuals without evidence.

"We must demand answers without prejudice, question decisions without condemning people unheard, and expose wrongdoing wherever it exists," he said.

"Honest scrutiny strengthens institutions, safeguards public resources, and serves the greater public interest."

Ruto said the uniform changes are only one part of a much wider programme covering police pay, welfare, housing, training, equipment, technology and infrastructure.

He said the government had completed a three-phase salary review that increased the entry-level basic salary of a police constable by 36 per cent.

"There are corresponding adjustments across all the other senior ranks," Ruto said.

Close 

The President also said the government was expanding police housing, including projects in Embakasi, while improving healthcare through the Usalama Cover.

Other reforms, he said, include better mobility, protective equipment, specialised operational assets and air support.

World.title: Zimbabwe: Govt to Procure More Boats After Kariba Ferry Tragedy
World.content:
Government is moving to increase the number of boats operating on Lake Kariba after overcrowding emerged as one of the concerns surrounding the recent ferry tragedy.

Minister of Transport and Infrastructural Development Felix Mhona told the Senate that Government was looking at procuring additional boats through the Rural Infrastructure Development Agency (RIDA), while also opening the route to private operators.

The minister said the ferry involved in the tragedy was a Government vessel operating under RIDA and had been travelling only twice a week.

"When that accident took place, there were a lot of people because some of the people have their homes in Chalala or Mola and the other problem is, those were school holidays; some were trying to travel to visit their relatives, and some were staying on the urban side," Mhona said.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

He said increasing the number of boats would help reduce overcrowding by giving passengers more options.

"I think when there are several boats, people will not wait for one boat," he said.

Mhona said the Government was already working on bringing in more vessels to improve transport for communities around the lake.

"Government is doing something because that boat was a government boat under RIDA. We are not stopping, and we are looking at procuring more boats, but if we have more boats, it means we will not have overcrowding," he added.

He said additional services were expected from both RIDA and the private sector, which could also result in more competitive fares for passengers.

"I think there will be a boat coming up from RIDA as well as the private sector, and the fares will become competitive for the good of the travelling public," Mhona said.

The minister also said Government was stepping up efforts to improve safety measures for water transport.

"When people travel by water, we also campaign and inform them how they should travel," he said.

Mhona said the Government would also caution boat operators and passengers against travelling in dangerous conditions.

"We are going to take those campaigns towards water and urge them to take caution when there are waves and that they should not travel," he said.

The minister said inspections would continue before vessels were allowed to operate, while those found responsible for wrongdoing would face justice.

"Those who are supposed to face justice will do so," he said.

World.title: Africa: Has the AU Successfully Taken Africa's G20 Baton From South Africa?
World.content:
analysis

Africa's G20 priorities have lost ground under the US presidency, with little pushback from the AU or other development-focused members.

Has the African Union (AU) taken up the continent's baton from South Africa after United States (US) President Donald Trump evicted Pretoria from the G20 presidency? That left the AU, which only joined in 2023, as Africa's only voice in the group. South Africa has been a member since the G20's founding in 1999.

The US boycotted South Africa's G20 presidency in 2025 for spurious reasons, then this year jettisoned almost all of Pretoria's developmental, Africa-focused agenda, inherited largely from the previous presidencies of Indonesia, India and Brazil.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

South Africa had proposals to tackle inequality, increase financial inclusion, improve African countries' access to capital, introduce a global minimum corporate tax rate, and address Africa's unsustainable debt burden. Then Trump's administration took over last December declaring that it would return the G20 to its core mission of driving economic growth and prosperity.

That pared-down agenda is starkly evident in the calendar. Last year, South Africa chaired about 130 official meetings, including 25 high-level ministerial ones, before the November leaders' summit. The US programme comprises far fewer, with just four ministerial meetings culminating in the December leaders' summit.

The AU appears to be trying to help fill the vacuum left by South Africa by coordinating its G20 role with Pretoria, which has much deeper G20 experience, says Paul-Simon Handy, Institute for Security Studies (ISS) Regional Director based in Addis Ababa. 'South Africa has been ... helping the AU to frame its contribution in the G20. AU [G20] meetings are organised with South Africa [which is] playing an important role.'

The AU also convened a strategic retreat in Malabo, Equatorial Guinea, in April to align African positions within the US G20 and prepare a roadmap for the AU's participation.

Burundian diplomat Willy Nyamitwe, the AU's G20 sous-sherpa, told the meeting the success of the AU's permanent membership in the G20 would be measured not by its mere presence but by its 'tangible impact' on Africa's industrialisation, debt burdens and inclusive economic growth.

Equatorial Guinea's Foreign Minister Simeón Oyono Esono Angüe said the US themes of growth and deregulation, trade, innovation and energy abundance 'are of profound relevance to [Africa]. They intersect directly with Africa's development aspirations, including industrialisation, infrastructure development, digital transformation and economic diversification.'

Yet the AU doesn't seem to have published the envisaged roadmap or any other outcome document from the retreat.

ISS Senior Research Consultant Priyal Singh said the retreat showed that the AU had sought a more coordinated strategy for its G20 engagements. 'This notably produced an engagement roadmap for the [continental] body. However, what has been missing is sustained public communication of those priorities, its negotiating objectives and its tangible gains.'

The G20 Chair's Statement from this week's G20 finance ministers and central bank governors meeting in Asheville, North Carolina, illustrated the contrast with South Africa's presidency, and raised doubts about the AU's impact.

South Africa's finance priorities included debt sustainability, reducing the high cost of capital, particularly for African countries and mobilising finance for just transitions to renewable energy and greater climate resilience.

They also covered increased lending and wider Multilateral Development Banks reforms, more disaster relief financing, including climate change-caused disasters, a global minimum corporate tax and greater financial inclusion.

This week's Asheville meeting focused instead on 'private sector engagement, productivity growth, global imbalances, financial literacy, sovereign debt, digital assets, and financial sector issues.'

The only developmental item was a reaffirmed commitment to strengthen the implementation of the G20 Common Framework for restructuring unaffordable debt.

Even there, the emphasis fell on fair burden sharing among creditors, with China accused of not taking its fair share of haircuts in previous restructuring deals under the Common Framework.

Beijing seemed to get the hint - withholding its support from that paragraph of the outcome document. It did the same on three others, so the outcome document was a Chair's Statement rather than a consensus communiqué.

China also objected to an agreement on eliminating global imbalances - that countries with excessive and persistent external surpluses should increase domestic consumption and reduce exports. This was clearly aimed at China's over-production flooding international markets with cheap goods and de-industrialising much of the world.

China withheld its support from a paragraph expressing concerns about disruptions to energy trade, the blocking of the Strait of Hormuz and the need to resolve ongoing wars.

All other members, the AU included, agreed to the entire statement.

The AU had little reason to oppose improvements to the G20 Common Framework or to insist on fair treatment for all creditors. One can also imagine that the AU may well share the view that Chinese over-production is causing imbalances and distortions that hurt other countries.

But surely the AU shared China's apparent indignation at the US's evident hypocrisy complaining about energy trade disruptions caused by Strait of Hormuz blockages and the need to resolve ongoing wars? Given its own key role in causing the blockage by attacking Iran? Then again, no other G20 members except China objected to this statement.

Close 

And would the AU have been happy with the statement welcoming the 'successful streamlining' of the G20 finance track's agenda under the US presidency, and its focus on core economic and financial priorities? Wasn't that another way of saying 'we welcome the dumping of almost all of South Africa's development finance agenda'?

Some G20 members, mainly Western, did complain privately that South Africa's agenda was large and unwieldy. So, pruning it might not be altogether bad. It could even encourage new approaches to development funding, like increasing domestic resource mobilisation. Trump's pruning, though, is surely excessive.

Perhaps the AU and other developmentally inclined members are doing by choice what South Africa had to do by force. That is, sit out the US presidency, and be ready to take up the fight again next year under the United Kingdom. The risk is that a year of silence becomes the baseline for what Africa can expect from the G20.
