World.title: Baja California Sur, Nuevo León and Querétaro lead new foreign investment in first half of 2026
World.content:
Baja California Sur, Nuevo León, and Querétaro emerged as the top destinations for new foreign investment in Mexico during the first half of 2026, even as new foreign investment in the country slowed overall.

According to new data from the Economy Ministry (SE), Mexico received US $2.7 billion in new investments from January to June — one of the three components of foreign direct investment (FDI) — down 13.4% compared to the same period in 2025. At the same time, total FDI grew as established ventures reinvested profits.

However, three entities maintained investor confidence.

Baja California Sur topped the list with US $524 million of new FDI, followed by Nuevo León with $473 million, and Querétaro with $410 million. Together, these three states accounted for nearly half of the funds allocated to new projects.

Baja California Sur’s tourism industry pushed it to the top of the list. In the first half of 2026, over 95% of the state’s total FDI was new investment. Of that new investment, over 97% ($511.9 million) went toward lodging services including guesthouses, boarding houses and furnished apartments with hotel services.

Meanwhile, Nuevo León registered a 190.1% annual growth in new FDI. The capital was concentrated in wholesale trade of trucks and auto parts, vehicle manufacturing and the iron and steel industries.

The result reflects the state’s importance as a manufacturing, logistics and automotive hub, favored for its proximity to the U.S. market and the integration of its suppliers into global supply chains.

Finally, Querétaro saw a 158.6% increase in new capital investment after receiving a boost of US $410 million. The main sectors receiving this investment include electricity generation and supply, confectionery, auto parts, and electronic components — sectors that confirm the state’s industrial diversification and its importance within the Bajío economic corridor.

These three states were followed by Jalisco, Quintana Roo, Nayarit, Chihuahua, Baja California, Puebla and Guanajuato, which received between US $100 million to $300 million in new capital investment apiece.

In contrast, Tlaxcala — the smallest state in Mexico — was the only state that saw no foreign investment.

Meanwhile, México state, Zacatecas, Sonora, Aguascalientes and Mexico City registered capital outflows.

With reports from El Economista

World.title: Marie, now a Category 2 hurricane, brings rain and flooding to Baja California Sur and the Pacific coast
World.content:
Rapidly intensifying Hurricane Marie reached Category 2 status off the coast of Baja California Sur on Friday, closing ports and suspending classes across the state.

A 10 a.m. social media post from the National Meteorological Service (SMN) said Marie was located 885 kilometers west-southwest of Cabo San Lucas, at the southern tip of the Baja Peninsula.

“It has maximum sustained winds of 155 km/h, gusts of 195 km/h and is moving west-northwest at 15 km/h,” the National Water Commission (Conagua) reported.

A Tropical Cyclone Advisory was issued by the SMN which forecast intense localized rains for the northwestern coast of Mexico, including the states of Sinaloa, Nayarit, Jalisco, Colima and Michoacán to the south of BCS.

Civil protection authorities urged the public to take extreme precautions and heed the recommendations issued by the authorities of the National Civil Protection System.

Navigation is also severely restricted due to the extreme weather conditions. Maritime authorities have closed ports to small vessels in San José del Cabo and Magdalena Bay.

High waves are another risk factor along the western coastline, with waves of 1.5 to 2.5 meters (5-8 feet) in height forecast for the peninsula.

Conagua said Marie’s main threat is the extensive cloud bands which increase the likelihood of heavy rainfall and could cause more flooding in vulnerable coastal areas. This prompted BCS Governor Víctor Manuel Castro to suspend all school activities in the municipality of Los Cabos.

Cabo San Lucas was battered by high winds and heavy rain on Wednesday while Marie was still a tropical storm.

Legendary rock musician Sammy Hagar — owner of the resort city’s famous Cabo Wabo Cantina — said in an Instagram post that the storm caused a great deal of damage, asking his fans to pray for his club and the city.

In a Thursday Instagram post, Hagar praised the authorities for their quick reaction to the flooding.

“Cabo to the rescue,” he wrote. “Congratulations to the community for pulling the cleanup crew together so quickly.”

Hurricane Marie — along with the Mexican monsoon, low-pressure troughs, cyclonic circulations at high levels of the atmosphere and Tropical Wave Number 36 in southern and western Mexico — was also forecast to generate intense rains in Veracruz, Oaxaca, Chiapas and Tabasco on Friday.

Conagua said Marie is expected to weaken to a Category 1 storm on Saturday as it moves further out to sea.

Though it could soon thereafter be downgraded to a tropical storm, atmospheric instability is likely to continue interacting with low-pressure troughs in the interior of the country into next week.

With reports from Informador, El Universal and N+

World.title: Defense minister responds to US anti-drone border operations: Friday’s mañanera recapped
World.content:
Listen to this article

Sheinbaum’s mañanera in 60 seconds

📉 Zacatecas homicides down 85%: National Public Security System chief Marcela Figueroa reported an average of 0.17 homicides per day in Zacatecas in August, an 85% reduction compared to September 2024, the final month of the López Obrador administration. The 2026 daily average is down 96% versus 2021.

National Public Security System chief Marcela Figueroa reported an average of 0.17 homicides per day in Zacatecas in August, an 85% reduction compared to September 2024, the final month of the López Obrador administration. The 2026 daily average is down 96% versus 2021. 🚔 Thousands arrested since Sheinbaum took office: Security Minister Omar García Harfuch said 3,824 people were arrested in Zacatecas between October 2024 and August 2026 for high-impact crimes. He said that 1,240 firearms and 7.3 tonnes of drugs were seized in the same period, while six meth labs were dismantled.

Security Minister Omar García Harfuch said 3,824 people were arrested in Zacatecas between October 2024 and August 2026 for high-impact crimes. He said that 1,240 firearms and 7.3 tonnes of drugs were seized in the same period, while six meth labs were dismantled. 💰 Atizapán killings tied to money demand: García Harfuch said one of two men arrested over the multiple homicide in México state had a “commercial relationship” with victim Jonathan Meléndez and had been demanding money from him before the killings.

García Harfuch said one of two men arrested over the multiple homicide in México state had a “commercial relationship” with victim Jonathan Meléndez and had been demanding money from him before the killings. 🇲🇽🇺🇸 Defense minister addresses cartel drone reports: Responding to a Fox News report on U.S. operations against cartel drones at the border, Defense Minister Ricardo Trevilla Trejo said the drones are mostly used by migrant smugglers to scout routes free of authorities. He didn’t confirm or deny Mexican military involvement in the U.S. takedown operations.

Why today’s mañanera matters

President Claudia Sheinbaum held her Friday morning press conference in Guadalupe, a municipality that is part of the metropolitan area of Zacatecas city.

She was accompanied by Zacatecas Governor David Monreal and various members of her cabinet, including Interior Minister Rosa Icela Rodríguez and Security Minister Omar García Harfuch.

Among Mexico’s 32 federal entities, Zacatecas has recorded one of the largest reductions in homicides this year.

At today’s mañanera, officials presented the latest security data for the state — statistics that allowed them to portray Zacatecas as an example of the success of the federal government’s national security strategy.

Also of note at today’s mañanera was García Harfuch’s remarks about the motive for a multiple homicide in México state.

Government reports 85% decline in homicides in Zacatecas

National Public Security System chief Marcela Figueroa reported that there was an average of 0.17 homicides per day in Zacatecas in August, a reduction of 85% compared to September 2024, the final month of Andrés Manuel López Obrador’s presidency.

She said that the daily homicide rate so far this year is 0.2, a reduction of 50% compared to 2025.

Figueroa highlighted that the daily homicide rate in 2026 is down 96% compared to 2021, when an average of 4.5 murders per day were committed in Zacatecas.

In the first seven months of 2026, there were 51 homicides in Zacatecas, the eighth lowest total among Mexico’s 32 federal entities.

More than 3,800 arrests in Zacatecas since October 2024

According to data presented by García Harfuch, 3,824 people were arrested in Zacatecas between Oct. 1, 2024 — the date Sheinbaum was sworn in as president — and Aug. 31, 2026, for allegedly committing high-impact crimes such as homicide, kidnapping, extortion and violent robbery.

He also reported that 1,240 firearms and 7.3 tonnes of drugs were seized in the state in the same period. In addition, authorities dismantled six clandestine methamphetamine labs in Zacatecas, García Harfuch said.

photo-harfuch

He acknowledged that “there is still a lot to be done” to improve security in Zacatecas, noting that rival criminal groups continue to fight turf wars in the state. García Harfuch said that federal authorities are “maintaining and strengthening” intelligence and investigation “actions” in the state as well as “territorial presence” and “coordination” with state and municipal authorities. The aim, he said, is to detain “generators of violence” in Zacatecas.

García Harfuch subsequently noted that three people were arrested in connection with a car bomb explosion outside a municipal police station in Ojocaliente, Zacatecas, last Sunday night.

García Harfuch: Multiple homicide in México state related to a demand for money

García Harfuch said that one of two men arrested in connection with a multiple homicide in México state this week had a “commercial relationship” with one of the victims, namely Jonathan Meléndez, keyboard player with the well-known band Camilo Séptimo. The security minister was referring to Diego Sebastián Rosen Ferlini, an Argentine national who was detained in connection with the murders of Mélendez, his pregnant wife, their three-year-old daughter and a domestic worker. The victims were found dead in an apartment in the municipality of Atizapán de Zaragoza late Tuesday.

Asked how much money the alleged murderer was demanding from Mélendez, García Harfuch responded:

“I don’t know but I’ll ask the [México state] Attorney General’s Office. What is a fact is that he was demanding money. There was a demand, there were certain threats and this terrible multiple homicide was committed.”

Defense minister: People smugglers use drones to locate routes that are ‘free’ of US authorities

A reporter asked the president whether she could confirm the “participation” of Mexican authorities in U.S. operations to take down suspected cartel drones at the Mexico-U.S. border.

His question was related to a Fox News report that was published on Thursday.

Citing a senior U.S. War Department official, Fox reported that the U.S. military “took down ‘approximately 100′ suspected cartel drones in August alone” at the United States’ southern border.

Citing the same official, Fox wrote that “each operation was planned and closely coordinated with the Mexican military and border authorities to prevent interference or unintended conflicts between forces operating on either side of the border.”

Operation Ardent Vanguard Update 11 cartel drones defeated by the Army’s Multipurpose High Energy Laser as of Sep. 4. More than 300 defeats using kinetic and non-kinetic systems this year, with more than 100 occurring in August. “JTF Southern Border’s combined arms approach… pic.twitter.com/KexEOvgM9D — U.S. Northern Command (@USNorthernCmd) September 4, 2026

Sheinbaum referred the reporter’s question to her defense minister.

“Firstly I want to highlight that the relationship with the armed forces of the United States has been very good, very positive,” Ricardo Trevilla Trejo said.

He said that U.S. authorities have informed the Mexican government that drones are mainly used in the border region by people who smuggle migrants into the United States.

“They are commercial drones. They only capture images … and what they’re seeking to find are routes that are free, where there is no presence of [U.S.] authorities,” Trevilla said.

The defense minister didn’t confirm or deny Fox’s reporting that the Mexican military was involved in the planning of U.S. operations to take down drones.

World.title: ‘Sexy and hot, like Mexico’: How Mexican beauty brand AORA is taking on the global market
World.content:
Pyramid-inspired palettes, bilingual packaging and vivid shades drawn from Mexico’s streets are just some of the hallmarks of AORA, a Mexican beauty brand that’s challenging the beauty industry with its plastic-free packaging and strong Mexican identity.

“We wanted to bottle the feeling of Mexico,” co-founder Rodrigo Peñafiel told Mexico News Daily. “We wanted to bottle that feeling you get when you visit a beach in Oaxaca; that feeling you experience when you visit Mexico City for the first time.”

Since the opening of its flagship store in Mexico City in 2022, the brand has expanded into major retail chains, landed collaborations with international celebrities including Sofía Vergara, and most recently, served as one of the makeup brands used during Bad Bunny’s 2026 Super Bowl halftime show.

International expansion, however, didn’t come as a surprise. For Peñafiel and his co-founder Nour Tayara, going global was always part of the plan.

“Why would we build a small local brand when we have the opportunity to bring something big into the world?” Peñafiel said.

Combining Tayara’s experience in marketing and innovation roles within L’Oréal with Peñafiel’s background in public relations, the pair set out to create a brand that offered more than just clean, high-quality products. They wanted to create a luxury product with a strong focus on identity.

“We do luxury makeup by working with the best factories in the world. Because if we want to compete, let’s compete with spectacular quality. But what we’re bringing — we’re bringing culture,” Tayara said.

The brand’s DNA: Mexico

Rather than downplaying AORA’s Mexican identity to appeal to international consumers, the founders have made it central to the brand, drawing inspiration from the country’s creativity, colors, architecture and connection to nature.

From the brand’s signature Mírame Eyeshadow Palette to their lipsticks, pencils and accessories, AORA’s products evoke Mexico’s cultural icons, historic landmarks and scenes from everyday life.

“In our palette, you can see a hint of Frida Kahlo, of Matías Goeritz, of Chichén Itzá,” Peñafiel said. “The shades inside our palette could evoke any street in Mexico with a yellow house and a green Volkswagen parked outside,” he added with a chuckle.

Launching the brand from Mexico also meant producing its marketing campaigns in the country. From their photoshoots to their male and female models, everything is done in Mexico with Mexican talent.

“Every detail about the brand reflects Mexico. We could not have created this brand if we hadn’t launched it here,” Tayara remarked.

A retail presence at Sephora

AORA’s authentic vision has propelled the company into a new growth stage after entering Sephora in the United States, making history as the first 100% plastic-free beauty brand sold at the retailer, and the first brand to use both Spanish and English on its packaging.

“Sephora is betting on a brand that’s very colorful from Mexico and is betting on its first plastic-free brand in its portfolio,” Tayara pointed out.

In a competitive market dominated by European and U.S. brands, AORA is disrupting the beauty industry and aims to demonstrate that luxury also stems from cultural heritage.

“We started something that didn’t exist before, which is creating luxury beauty in Mexico,” Tayara said. “We come to challenge the industry in the language, in the visuals, in the products and in sustainability,” he said.

For the co-founders, AORA’s debut in Sephora goes beyond having its products on the shelves of one of the world’s leading beauty retailers. It also signals support for a Mexican brand and recognition for the Latino consumer market in the U.S.

“I think there’s a recognition of the amount of people in the U.S. that are of Latino descent and speak Spanish. It is an amazing message and signal Sephora is sending to the industry,” Tayara acknowledged.

A growing curiosity in Mexican identity and design

AORA isn’t the first brand to place Mexican identity as the center of its appeal. In recent years, global brands have increasingly sought partnerships that draw on Mexico’s visual identity, cultural heritage and creative talent.

In 2025, cosmetic brand Rare Beauty, founded by U.S. actress and singer of Mexican descent Selena Gomez, launched an exclusive, limited-edition makeup kit in collaboration with the Mexican seasoning Tajín.

Back then, Gomez described the collaboration as a “celebration of what makes us unique — our culture, our energy and the moments that bring us together.”

Last year also saw H&M launch a collection in collaboration with fashion designer Lorena Saravia, marking the first time the Swedish brand collaborated with a Mexican designer.

Joining the trend is Mestiz, a design studio founded by Daniel Valero in San Miguel de Allende, which recently collaborated with French design house Hermès to design their shop windows in Mexico.

Mexico’s appeal to consumers

“Mexico is trendy,” Peñafiel said with a smile. “I think there’s a celebration of Mexican culture that hasn’t been seen before. The challenge was to pass the front page of the news that we see every day about the dangers of Mexico, because the reality is that when people come here, they are amazed and fall in love with the food, with the culture, with the colors, the beaches, the brands,” he said.

As AORA seeks to reshape perceptions of Mexican luxury abroad and share a positive image of the country, its founders say the brand’s ultimate purpose is more personal — to make consumers feel attractive.

“We buy beauty because we want to feel good about ourselves. Because we want to feel sexy,” Tayara said.

“Yes, we want our clients to feel sexy and hot, like Mexico,” Peñafiel said.

Gabriela Solis is a Mexican lawyer turned full-time writer. She was born and raised in Guadalajara and covers business, culture, lifestyle and travel for Mexico News Daily. You can follow her lifestyle blog Dunas y Palmeras.

World.title: ‘I nuh juck nobody’: Dalla van driver angry as sex assault charge upgraded to rape of a child over 15-year-old’s allegations
World.content:
‘I nuh juck nobody’: Dalla van driver angry as sex assault charge upgraded to rape of a child over 15-year-old’s allegations

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A Belize City “dalla van” taxi driver who has been on bail since last year on a sexual assault charge was sent to prison on Friday after prosecutors withdrew that charge and replaced it with the considerably more serious offence of rape of a child.

Wenseslao Garrido-Veilz, 43, a Guatemalan national, appeared unrepresented before a Senior Magistrate in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court, where prosecutors informed the court that his previous charge of sexual assault was being withdrawn.

He was then read a single charge of rape of a child stemming from the same alleged incident involving a girl who was 15 years and 10 months old at the time.

The allegation is that on November 22, 2025, Garrido-Veilz had sexual intercourse with the minor without her consent.

Because of the nature of the new charge, the Magistrate explained that the lower court could not take a plea from Garrido-Veilz and could not grant him bail.

Garrido-Veilz repeatedly attempted to address the allegation, telling the court that he lives in Guatemala, has three children and has evidence in his defence.

“I have the evidence,” he told the court before being cautioned not to discuss the facts of the case at that stage of the proceedings.

An interpreter was eventually provided for Garrido-Veilz, who speaks Spanish, and he responded, “Bueno,” after the court explained the process to him.

He was denied bail and remanded to the Belize Central Prison until September 28, 2026.

Garrido-Veilz appeared visibly angry as he was escorted away to begin his remand. While being taken to prison, he was heard protesting in Kriol: “I nuh juck nobody.”

Breaking Belize News first reported on Garrido-Veilz’s case following his November 25, 2025 arraignment. At the time, police alleged that a 15-year-old girl boarded his grey dollar van near New 2 U on Cemetery Road and that, after the other passengers had exited, he drove her to a feeder road between Miles 2 and 3 on the George Price Highway and allegedly touched her inappropriately.

During that first court appearance, Garrido-Veilz pleaded not guilty to sexual assault. BBN reported that he was a Guatemalan national with Belizean residency and that prosecutors objected to bail on the grounds that he could be a flight risk. He told the court then that he had three Belizean sons and family ties in Belize. He was nevertheless granted bail with strict conditions, including that he not leave Belize, contact the minor or her family, or go within 200 yards of her.

That arraignment also produced a memorable courtroom moment when Garrido-Veilz, who had initially communicated through a Spanish interpreter, suddenly exclaimed in English after learning he would receive bail, denying that he had touched the girl.

BBN subsequently reported in August that the sexual assault case had been delayed while the court awaited CCTV footage from law enforcement.

The case took a dramatic turn on Friday, however, after prosecutors withdrew the sexual assault charge and substituted the charge of rape of a child.

The more serious allegation reportedly follows a further statement given by the minor concerning what she alleges occurred during the November 2025 incident.

Garrido-Veilz will now have to seek bail at the High Court if he wishes to be released while the case proceeds.

World.title: The door that slammed in your face this week may have saved your life
World.content:
The door that slammed in your face this week may have saved your life

By Horace Palacio:

It is Friday, the day Belize passes judgment on its week. The deal that died Tuesday. The call that never came. The door that closed Wednesday afternoon. By Friday evening we have the verdicts stamped, good week, bad week, and we carry them into the weekend like sentences.

So Friday is exactly the right day for a line from the American novelist Cormac McCarthy that has been drifting across Belizean timelines.

“You never know what worse luck your bad luck has saved you from.”

For once, the internet attributed correctly. The line is truly his, from No Country for Old Men. But the meme leaves out the detail that gives the sentence its license. In the novel, the words are spoken by an old lawman named Ellis, shot years earlier, living out his days in a wheelchair, as he comforts a sheriff drowning in despair. Hear that clearly. This is not a comfortable man’s philosophy. It is a crippled man’s. From a healthy mouth the line is a greeting card. From his, it is a verdict earned in blood.

Unpack the logic, because it is sturdier than it looks. Every time misfortune strikes, we grade it against an invisible alternative, the week where the bad thing did not happen. But that alternative is pure imagination, and notice how we always imagine it. Perfect. The job we lost would have flourished. The person who left would have loved us forever. The deal that died would have made us rich. We compare our real, wounded week against a fantasy week with the flaws airbrushed out, and of course reality loses. McCarthy’s old man simply points at the fraud. You never saw the real alternative. It might have been worse. It might have been fatal.

History keeps receipts on this. Milton Hershey, the chocolate king, had paid his deposit for passage on a magnificent new ocean liner in 1912, and business forced him to cancel. The ship was the Titanic. Nearly a century later, a young writer named Seth MacFarlane overslept, missed his morning flight, and cursed his luck at the gate. The flight was American 11, the first plane into the towers on September 11. Both men had bad mornings. Both bad mornings were rescues wearing disguises. And here is the humbling part, for every famous case there are millions of invisible ones, because the accident that never happened calls no witnesses. The truck you never met has no headline. The unseen ledger of your life is full of mercies filed under inconvenience.

The old world knew this. There is an ancient Chinese story about a farmer whose horse ran away, and the neighbors cried, what bad luck. Maybe, said the farmer. The horse returned leading wild horses, what good luck. Maybe. His son broke a leg taming one, what bad luck. Maybe. The army came conscripting young men for a doomed war and passed over the boy with the broken leg. The farmer’s entire philosophy was one word, maybe, the discipline of the unfinished verdict. Life, he understood, is graded in pencil, and every Friday we grab the ink.

Now bring it home, because Belize has lived this line at national scale, and some of our luckiest breaks arrived dressed as disasters.

We never struck the great oil gusher, and we cursed those dry wells for decades. Then look at the nations that did strike it, and count how many the black gold made more corrupt, more divided, more broken. Our dry wells may be the luckiest holes we ever drilled. We spent the Cold War decades feeling small and overlooked, while that very smallness was camouflage, the proxy wars that drowned Guatemala, El Salvador and Nicaragua in blood found nothing here worth fighting over, and we held peaceful elections through it all. The superbond years were agony, and that agony was the schoolhouse where this country learned the fiscal discipline that later cut our debt nearly in half. And when 2020 shut the airport and we called it catastrophe, the collapse ran the great sorting this column wrote about, separating the waiting from the working, and forced lessons no boom would ever have taught. You never know what worse luck your bad luck has saved you from. Neither does a nation.

Now, the guardrails, because this column never sells a sedative, and this beautiful line can be abused into one.

Guardrail one. The line is for the rearview mirror, never the windshield. It is medicine for what you cannot change, the grief, the closed door, the hindsight, and it must never anesthetize what you can. Do not bless the blackout, it was negligence, not providence. Do not thank fate for the stolen millions. A wound you can still treat is not a mystery to accept, it is a job to do. Comfort belongs to the past. Effort belongs to Monday. Confusing the two is how the old ghost of resignation sneaks back in wearing philosophy’s coat.

Guardrail two. The symmetry cuts both ways, and this is where the line turns from comfort into wisdom. You also never know what worse luck your good luck is steering you toward. The lottery winners broke by year five. The promotion that fed the pride that caused the fall. So the mature conclusion is not that bad luck is secretly good. It is that all verdicts on fortune are premature. Hold your celebrations loosely and your despair looser. Maybe, says the farmer, about everything.

So here is your practical instruction for this evening, Belize, and it costs nothing. Before you stamp this week’s verdict, take the worst thing that happened, write it down with the date, file it, and reopen the file in two years. You will be astonished how many entries have quietly converted from disaster to rescue. And tonight, spend one minute on the unseen ledger, the crashes that never happened, the wrong turns not taken, the worse luck your ordinary, complaining, imperfect week quietly saved you from. Gratitude for the visible blessings is easy. Gratitude for the invisible ones is faith, and even an old country song figured it out, thanking God for the prayers He declined.

Somewhere behind you, my friend, is a door that shut in your face this very week and saved your life. You will never see the room. You will never meet the truck.

Say thank you anyway.

Then put down the gavel, pick up the pencil, and go enjoy your weekend.

Monday, we build.

The views expressed in this article are those of the author, Horace Palacio, and do not necessarily reflect the views or editorial stance of Breaking Belize News.

World.title: What the $200 electricity GST exemption means for Belizeans
World.content:
What the $200 electricity GST exemption means for Belizeans

By Zoila Palma: Belizean households could see savings on their monthly electricity bills following Cabinet’s decision to double the GST exemption threshold for residential electricity consumption from $100 to $200, effective September 1, 2026.

Under the new measure, residential customers with electricity bills of $200 or less will have GST removed from the applicable electricity consumption, providing direct relief to household budgets.

For example, if a residential electricity bill is $200 before GST, the 12.5 percent GST would amount to $25. With the new exemption, that $25 would no longer be charged, meaning the customer would pay $200 instead of $225.

The change is expected to benefit more than 91,000 residential customers, representing approximately 96 percent of all residential electricity customers in Belize.

The previous $100 threshold had been in place since April 1, 2017, meaning the new measure significantly increases the portion of residential electricity consumption that can qualify for GST relief.

The measure is intended to provide immediate financial relief to families by reducing the tax burden associated with residential electricity costs.

World.title: Cabinet approves Digital Register and new Licensing system for electrical workers
World.content:
Cabinet approves Digital Register and new Licensing system for electrical workers

By Zoila Palma: Cabinet met on September 2, 2026, and approved the introduction of regulations to establish a digital Electrical Workers Register and a searchable public verification system.

The new framework will introduce a class-based licensing system for electrical workers, along with clear application procedures designed to ensure that workers maintain the required level of competence in the field.

The regulations will also provide for supervised apprenticeships, continuing competency requirements and public electronic verification, allowing members of the public to verify the status of licensed electrical workers.

Cabinet said the framework will also establish clearer administrative and disciplinary procedures while providing transitional measures to ensure continuity for existing electrical workers as the new system is implemented.

World.title: Cabinet approves measures to strengthen electricity security
World.content:
Cabinet approves measures to strengthen electricity security

By Zoila Palma: Cabinet has approved a series of measures aimed at strengthening Belize’s electricity security while providing additional relief to residential consumers.

An Emergency Declaration will allow Belize Electricity Limited (BEL) to begin procuring additional generation capacity ahead of a projected electricity supply shortfall in 2027.

Government says the move is intended to ensure Belize has sufficient electricity to meet growing demand and maintain a reliable supply. The procurement of additional generation capacity is being described as a proactive step toward safeguarding the country’s energy security.

Cabinet has also supported an expansion of the Social Rate, increasing eligibility from 60 kWh to 80 kWh per month.

The change is expected to extend the preferential electricity tariff to approximately 17,000 residential customers.

Together, the measures combine immediate assistance for households with longer-term investment in Belize’s electricity supply. Government says the approach is intended to provide relief to consumers today while strengthening the country’s energy security for the years ahead.

World.title: 91,000 households to benefit as Electricity GST exemption doubles to $200
World.content:
91,000 households to benefit as Electricity GST exemption doubles to $200

By Zoila Palma: Cabinet has approved an increase in the GST exemption threshold for residential electricity customers, raising the monthly threshold from $100 to $200, effective September 1, 2026.

The measure is expected to provide direct relief to more than 91,000 residential customers, representing approximately 96 percent of all residential electricity customers in Belize.

The $100 exemption threshold had been in place since April 1, 2017, when it was lowered by the then United Democratic Party administration.

Cabinet’s latest decision effectively doubles the amount of residential electricity consumption covered by the GST exemption.

World.title: New U.S. Ambassador André Bauer confronted by press over infamous ‘stray animals’ remarks as he arrives in Belize
World.content:
New U.S. Ambassador André Bauer confronted by press over infamous ‘stray animals’ remarks as he arrives in Belize

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Newly arrived U.S. Ambassador to Belize André Bauer has again defended controversial remarks he made more than 16 years ago comparing government assistance for poor people to feeding stray animals, arguing that his comments were about breaking generational dependency rather than denying assistance to people in need.

Bauer was confronted about the remarks during his first press encounter in Belize on Friday.

“If I didn’t know the background and the way the press tried to present it, I would feel the same way they did,” Bauer said.

The controversy dates back to January 2010, when Bauer was lieutenant governor of South Carolina and campaigning for governor.

During a town hall discussion about government benefits, Bauer invoked advice from his grandmother about not feeding stray animals “because they breed” while arguing that public assistance programs should include greater personal responsibility requirements. The comparison generated national controversy in the United States.

Bauer later said at the time that he had not meant to call recipients of public assistance animals and argued that the metaphor had been taken out of context.

On Friday, Bauer said the discussion was not about healthcare, as one question suggested, but about whether government programs merely maintain poverty rather than helping people escape it.

He also revealed that his own family had qualified for free school lunches when he was growing up in what he described as a broken home.

“I believe in doing all we can instead of just giveaways,” Bauer said, pointing to healthcare, transportation, childcare and education as examples of assistance that can help people become self-sufficient.

“I’m all about opportunity, access, and lifting people up,” he added.

Bauer argued that public officials sometimes have to engage in politically difficult conversations rather than simply support programs that sound compassionate.

“If you really want to help people, sometimes you have to have very difficult conversations,” he said.

World.title: ‘Judge me by my actions’: New Ambassador responds to concerns over U.S. Embassy influence in Belize
World.content:
‘Judge me by my actions’: New Ambassador responds to concerns over U.S. Embassy influence in Belize

By Breaking Belize News Staff: New United States Ambassador André Bauer says Belizeans should judge him and the U.S. Embassy by their actions after he was questioned about perceptions that Washington sometimes acts as a disciplinary or oversight force over Belizean public officials.

Bauer was questioned Friday about the U.S. Embassy’s role in governance, including the perception among some Belizeans that U.S. visa restrictions, revocations and other diplomatic measures can be used to exert pressure on elected and government officials.

“Everybody… we all have opinions and different perspectives based on life experiences,” Bauer responded.

He said most people he has spoken with appear comfortable with the relationship between Belize and the United States but acknowledged that others may see it differently.

“They’ll be able to judge me by my actions and the actions of what the United States tries to do to work together,” Bauer said.

Pressed specifically on what oversight role he believes the United States should play in Belizean governance, Bauer said he did not have a direct answer.

Instead, he described diplomacy as a process through which countries discuss both shared interests and areas of disagreement.

“We have certain things that are important to our country, and you have certain things that are important in your country,” Bauer said.

He suggested informal and formal engagement with Belizean leaders could help each side better understand the other’s position.

“If leaders in your country break bread with me or we spend time together, I think we’ll get a mutual understanding of places that maybe we don’t agree, and places that we do agree,” he said.

Bauer said he intends to take that approach beyond government officials and meet ordinary Belizeans around the country.

“We don’t have to agree,” he said, adding that a well-made argument has changed his own mind in the past.

Bauer said his objective is for Belizeans to ultimately feel better about the bilateral relationship and see the United States as a partner rather than simply an outside power exercising influence over the country.

World.title: Dancehall veteran Powerman loses second son in 16 months
World.content:
Christopher Davy, the 25-year-old son of veteran dancehall act Powerman who was killed on Friday, September 4, 2026, in Brooklyn, New York.

Dancehall veteran Powerman is reeling from unimaginable grief after his 25-year-old son, Christopher Davey, was fatally stabbed in Brooklyn, New York, on Friday evening — the second son the entertainer has lost in just 16 months.

Observer Online spoke with the distraught deejay, whose given name is Michael Davey, as he remained at the crime scene reviewing surveillance footage and speaking with police officers.

According to Powerman, Christopher had been sent to a nearby laundry by his mother when he became involved in an altercation with two men near the corner of Church and Albany avenues.

“His mother had sent him to the laundry, and he was less than a block away when he got into an altercation with two men armed with a knife and cutlass,” Powerman said. “They stabbed him and killed him.”

Police were processing the scene as investigators examined surveillance footage of the fatal attack.

The killing has reopened a barely healed wound for Powerman. In May last year, he lost another son, a 32-year-old trailer mechanic, in what was described as a case of misadventure.

“This is a lot to deal with,” he said, almost overcome by grief. “Mi just lose a son — Christopher’s older brother — last year May, and now this.”

The identities of the alleged attackers and a possible motive for the stabbing were not immediately known.

An original member of the Monster Shack Crew, Powerman rose to prominence with connections to Shocking Vibes and artistes like Beenie Man and Baby Wayne. He is known for hardcore and raw dancehall anthems like Next, Statue, Serious Thing, and Wrong Sound.

World.title: Market Bag: Sweet pepper hits $600, lettuce $1k as drought sends prices higher
World.content:
KINGSTON, Jamaica — Shoppers at local markets could see higher prices over the next few weeks as vendors report growing shortages of agricultural produce due to drought conditions affecting the island.

According to vendors, several items have become increasingly difficult to source, including Irish potatoes, now selling for $350 per pound; sweet potatoes at $250; pumpkins at $300; and lettuce at $1,000. Carrots, priced at $400 per pound, and sweet peppers ($600) are being imported to help meet demand.

Vendors say the reduced supply has also pushed up the prices of onions ($250) and other produce, with consumers expected to feel the impact.

One vendor told Market Bag host Carlysia Ramdeen that the lack of rainfall has made it difficult for some crops to survive, particularly water-dependent produce such as pumpkins and sweet peppers.

“Pumpkins cannot withstand the heat because pumpkins need water so because of the drought, we don’t have pumpkins. Peppers can’t grow without water. Sweet peppers cannot grow without water. So, the drought is really affecting the market,” she said.

World.title: UPDATE: Mistrial ruling upheld in case of US mother who killed her children
World.content:
Kevin Reddington, defense attorney for Lindsay Clancy, and Lindsay Clancy look on as Judge William Sullivan (out of frame) instructs the jury to continue deliberating, during Lindsay Clancy's murder trial at the Plymouth County Superior Court in Plymouth, Massachusetts, on September 4, 2026. (Photo: AFP)

PLYMOUTH, United States (AFP) — A judge declared a mistrial on Friday in the high-profile case of an American woman who killed her three young children.

Judge William Sullivan declared a mistrial after the jury failed to reach a unanimous verdict in the case of Lindsay Clancy, and an appeals court rejected a last-minute bid by the defence to have a juror replaced.

The jury was deadlocked 11-1, with the majority apparently leaning to find Clancy not guilty by reason of insanity.

World.title: Gift from the heart
World.content:
Minister of Health and Wellness Dr Christopher Tufton (second right) checks out specialised equipment donated to the University Hospital of the West Indies (UHWI) by Abigaye Smythe (second left), founder and managing director of I Have a Heart Foundation, on Thursday, as consultant cardiothoracic surgeon Dr Sunil Stephenson explains its function. Sharing in the moment is chief executive officer at UHWI Dr Sydney Powell. The equipment will give surgeons at the hospital the ability to perform minimally invasive open-heart surgeries. (Photo: Garfield Robinson)

A cardiac patient facing her sixth surgery this December has donated US$4,000 in specialised equipment to the University Hospital of the West Indies (UHWI), directly upgrading its training resources and capabilities for minimally invasive open-heart surgery.

Speaking at the handover ceremony of the medical equipment at UHWI on Thursday, Abigaye Smythe, founder and managing director of I Have a Heart Foundation, revealed that leading this initiative is her life’s purpose.

Describing her connection to the project as lifelong, Smythe shared that she has battled heart disease since the age of seven, when she first began experiencing symptoms.

At 19, Smythe was delivered life-altering news when she was diagnosed with arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy — the same disease that took her mother’s life. The rare genetic condition causes fat and scar tissue to replace healthy heart muscle, disrupting electrical signals and triggering abnormal heart rhythms.

Since her diagnosis, the philanthropist has undergone five surgeries at UHWI, making this donation a profoundly personal milestone.

“Because of my own journey, and understanding the fact that cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of death in Jamaica, I don’t advocate for heart disease patients from a distance. I understand what it means to be one [a cardiac patient], and I understand what it means to lose one. So this is my purpose. And that is why today is so meaningful,” she said.

“I’m not simply donating equipment to a hospital, I’m giving back to an institution that has cared for me, from testing and diagnosis in 2011, through five surgeries between 2012 and 2019, several emergency room visits and hospitalisations in-between, and an institution that will care for me again in December when I undergo my sixth heart surgery. I am investing in my fellow heart disease patients. I’m also investing in my country, in Jamaica,” added Smythe.

The donation builds on a partnership between the I Have a Heart Foundation, the Organisation for International Development, and a medical team from New York’s Montefiore Einstein Hospital. Since 2019, this partnership has provided more than $120 million in free open-heart surgeries at UHWI for 60 financially vulnerable patients.

Smythe noted that while this collaboration has been highly beneficial for both the patients and UHWI, she realised the hospital still lacked the capacity to perform minimally invasive open-heart surgeries without foreign assistance. She highlighted this gap as the driving force behind her efforts to lobby for and secure the new equipment.

“During the 2025 cardiac mission, the international medical team brought their specialised tools to perform minimally invasive open-heart surgery, and this resulted in the first such procedure being performed at UHWI, and possibly the first in Jamaica. They returned [home] and so did their equipment. And they came back in March 2026, for the mission. And when they performed the surgeries, and when they left, so did their equipment again,” she explained.

“So I said, ‘Okay, I want us to be independent, I want us to have our own, I want us to be able to perform minimally invasive open-heart surgeries outside of the mission’. And that is where the begging began. Thanks to our sponsors, we were able to raise the money, and we turned that vision into a reality, and purchased the equipment,” Smythe explained.

Looking ahead, she hopes this contribution will elevate care at UHWI, arguing that the island has no shortage of medical skill or talent but requires some help securing the tools to match that expertise.

“I’m excited to see how this capacity, this capability, will continue to grow. Today is not simply a handover, it is an investment in Jamaican lives, in our health care system, our medical professionals, and the future of cardiac care. My hope is that one day a Jamaican will never have to ask, ‘Can this procedure be done in Jamaica?’ They will simply know that it can be done here, and it can be done here at the University Hospital of the West Indies,” she said.

Expressing gratitude for the donation, Dr Sunil Stephenson, consultant cardiothoracic surgeon at UHWI, told the Jamaica Observer that the equipment was a necessity as the hospital continues to observe an increase in cardiac patients yearly.

“For a year, we perform about 80 to 90 heart surgeries. As a matter of fact, most deaths… in Jamaica are caused by cardiovascular diseases. So we do see quite a bit of patients who require our services and it’s mainly related to lifestyle illnesses. Some are genetic but most of what we do see is related to chronic non-communicable diseases. So there’s definitely an increase,” said Dr Stephenson.

He added that the equipment gave patients greater access to minimally invasive surgery which, he noted, offered significant advantages.

“The benefit in the sense that there’s less pain, they recover much faster. There’s still a shorter time in the ICU, and they need less time on the ventilator. So they recover much quicker and they’re more comfortable. And for females, they prefer the fact that they don’t have an incision in the middle of the chest because they’re very concerned about how the scar would look. So these instruments will actually help us to be able to do these procedures, and extend these procedures to the entire Jamaica, because that’s the population that we serve,” said the doctor.

For his part, Health and Wellness Minister Dr Christopher Tufton thanked Smythe and her team for the donation, and expressed confidence in the quality of staff at UHWI, adding that he had no doubt that the equipment would be put to good use.

“I just want to embrace the concept of ongoing effort to improve, and to make the services more efficient, embrace the concept of volunteerism and charity and gifting, and just say that for health, we have to see ourselves as a community and work together as a community. So thank you again, we appreciate it, and we certainly wish you the very best in terms of your own struggles and work, both as a foundation but also individually,” Tufton said.

World.title: Fit for purpose
World.content:
Mico CARE Centre interventionist Collette Demetrius (right) shows one of the centre’s retrofitted classrooms to (from left) permanent secretary at the Ministry of Education, Skills, Youth, and Information Dr Kasan Troupe; The Mico University College President Dr Asburn Pinnock; and portfolio manager, education and special needs, Digicel Foundation Jamilia Crooks Brown at Thursday’s official opening of the facility that caters to children with special needs. (Photo: Karl Mclarty)

AFTER more than four decades of supporting children with special needs, The Mico University College’s Child Assessment and Research in Education (CARE) Centre has upgraded its learning environment, unveiling renovations to five classrooms aimed at creating better spaces for students to learn, develop, and thrive.

The project, valued at approximately $24 million, was done in collaboration with Digicel Foundation and partners and provides classrooms with specialised sensory and occupational therapy equipment designed to aid concentration, emotional regulation, and physical engagement.

“The classrooms before were just regular classrooms. The rooms were very old, wooden floors, old aluminum windows, and so on, which are from the 1980s. Renovating these rooms makes the learning space more modern, more accommodating. So what we’ve done, we have looked at the needs of the clients that we serve,” Micro CARE Centre Director Dr Sharon Anderson-Morgan explained after the official handing over and ribbon-cutting ceremony on Thursday.

“So the rooms are now fit for purpose, they’re not just a regular classroom. We have children who are fidgety, for example, because they have attention-deficit disorder or any kind of disorder that causes them to want to move all the time. So we have the kick bands on the chair, they can put their feet on the chair. We have the wobbly things at the end of it, so they can rock and can move,” she added.

Anderson-Morgan pointed to several challenges faced by the institution prior to its renovation.

“The rooms were very, very hot. When you have spaces that are hot and you have bodies moving around, people are going to get a little agitated sometimes. So we’ve had children who react terribly to the heat. For example, we had some of our kids with autism and it gets hot and they would just start screaming,” she said.

“Also, we could not move the furniture as we would like to, because the old furniture did not allow for us to. If you’re going to move the chairs, it’s going to scrape the floor, some children are sensitive to that. They didn’t fit together the way these fit together,” Anderson-Morgan said, adding that the lighting at the facility was also an issue.

“We had these old fluorescent lights that also affected some children. There were children who would look up because they’re hypersensitive to visual stimuli. They would get scared because they think they’re seeing patterns in the ceiling. I remember one day we had to cover a portion of the ceiling with paper because the child kept looking up there because he thought he was seeing something else,” said Anderson-Morgan.

She underscored that the renovations will not only benefit students who enter the facility through its intervention programme, but also those who come in for assessment.

“Sometimes children come here for assessment and they are dysregulated. The clinicians now have the centre space to take them, calm them down before they can assess them, because before, sometimes they can’t get to assess them unless they come back because a child is screaming, running all over the place,” Anderson-Morgan said, adding that the centre assesses close to 1,000 children yearly.

She hastened to add that despite the centre being known to conduct assessments, its services extend beyond that.

“We do assessment, we do intervention, not just academic, because we have speech therapy. And we have occupational therapy, behaviour therapy, we have behaviour therapy for one group, and that’s only because we don’t have an on-site behaviour therapist, so we have to bring in the service. And we also have counselling services, we have a counselling centre up there, where even some of our kids in the intervention programme, they also receive counselling as needed, and sometimes their families need it as well,” she explained.

Permanent secretary in the Ministry of Education, Skills, Youth, and Information Kasan Troupe welcomed the upgraded facility and lauded Digicel Foundation and partners for their investment in the special needs sector.

“We’re going to have a room that teachers will be exposed to improve opportunities to train and integrate technology because it is technology-enabled. We’re going to have a room that will build confidence in learners because here they have a safer space, a modern space that they can make mistakes, learn and grow and be strong because they are fully supported with specialists that can train them and support them in the way they should grow,” she said.

“You’re going to have learners who cannot communicate confidently. You’re going to have learners who will learn new skills so they can transform their whole realities in the future. That’s the promise of this investment,” Troupe added.

The Mico University College CARE Centre states on its website that it was established in 1980 as a centre of excellence, dedicated to child assessment and research in education. It was formed through a partnership between The Netherlands and Jamaican governments.

World.title: Malie Donn releases debut album Golden Child
World.content:
Malie Donn.

Dancehall artiste Malie Donn today released his debut studio album, The Golden Child, marking a major milestone for the entertainer who has steadily carved out a place among dancehall’s new generation.

The 21-track project, released through VP Records, follows several years of building his name with songs including Van Cleef, Body Tea, V6, Dirty Mirror, Suspect, Crook and many others.

“The Golden Child represents everything that brought me to this point: the pressure, the growth, the wins and the lessons,” Malie Donn said. “This project gives people a chance to hear more of who I am as an artist, where I want to take the music next and the versatility I bring.”

On Thursday, Malie Donn released the album’s title track, Golden Child, featuring fellow dancehall artiste Squash. The collaboration pairs Malie Donn’s melodic delivery with Squash’s distinctive style, while exploring themes of confidence, ambition and resilience that also run through the wider project.

The official music video for Golden Child also premiered on Thursday, providing the final lead-in to the album. Born Kimalie Hylton, Malie Donn is originally from Jones Avenue, Spanish Town, St Catherine, but grew up in Waterford, Portmore.

His passion for music dates back to his days as a student at Waterford Primary School and developed further while he attended Bridgeport High School. Malie Donn has emerged as one of the acts in dancehall’s newer wave, building a catalogue that has helped expand his audience locally and internationally.

The Golden Child also continues his relationship with VP Records. In 2024, he released The Grand Rising EP through the label, followed by the Leak the Hard Drive EP in 2025.

The album was preceded by Holiday, which arrived on August 7 alongside its official music video and offered listeners an early glimpse of a different side of Malie Donn’s artistry.

For Malie Donn, the release of his first full-length album represents an opportunity to present a more complete picture of himself beyond the individual songs that first brought him attention.

World.title: GOJ TAPS MARKET FOR US$1B
World.content:
The Government of Jamaica (GOJ) has gone to the international capital markets to raise a US$1 billion ($157.62 billion) unsecured bond to support its liability management strategy and budgetary objectives.

The prospectus was published on Wednesday through the United States Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), three weeks after GOJ filed its registration statement to issue debt securities. According to a roadshow document seen by the Jamaica Observer, US$600 million is to be used to fund a tender/exchange offer, with the balance earmarked for general budgetary purposes. A source close to the matter also indicated that the new bond is expected to mature in 2037.

At the same time, GOJ launched the tender/exchange offer for holders of the three existing global bonds, tying the new borrowing directly to its wider effort to manage the country’s external debt.

“The Invitation is part of a broader program of Jamaica to proactively manage its external public debt,” stated the tender invitation to holders of the old bonds/notes.

The Government currently has US$837.53 million outstanding on its April 2028 notes, which carry a 6.75 per cent interest rate. The 2036 and 2039 notes have US$250 million and US$1.24 billion outstanding, respectively.

International Financing Review (ifre.com) reported that GOJ began holding fixed-income investor meetings on September 3, likely in connection with the new bond issuance, which will be listed on the Euro MTF Market of the Luxembourg Stock Exchange. Citigroup Global Markets Inc. and Scotia Capital (USA) Inc. are serving as deal managers and joint lead underwriters for the transaction.

If the value of bonds tendered exceeds GOJ’s maximum purchase amount, the government can determine how much of each series it will accept, applying different proration factors where necessary. This means it could accept less than the full amount tendered by holders of any of the eligible notes.

The new tender offer opened on September 2 and will expire on September 9, unless extended or terminated at GOJ’s discretion. Settlement is expected to be completed by September 17.

“The invitation is not conditioned upon any minimum participation of any series of Old Notes but is conditioned on, among other things, the pricing and closing of an international capital markets transaction in an amount and on terms and conditions acceptable to Jamaica,” stated the GOJ release.

The Government last executed a transaction of this nature in October 2023, when it spent US$237.4 million to redeem three notes with a nominal value of US$233.2 million. At the time, GOJ repurchased approximately US$99.7 million in two separate 2025 notes and US$165.15 million of the April 2028 notes. The tender on the 2028 notes represented 11.6 per cent of the amount outstanding before the GOJ offer.

That tender offer coincided with Jamaica’s first Jamaican dollar (JMD)-linked bond issuance on the international capital markets, worth $46.6 billion, or US$300 million. The instrument carried a 9.625 per cent interest rate and matures in November 2030.

Through the new tender offer, GOJ can extend the maturity profile of its foreign debt and reduce the amount that will need to be refinanced in the near term, in keeping with its broader debt management strategy.

The transaction, however, comes against the backdrop of a difficult start to the government’s 2026/27 fiscal year. According to the central government accounts for April to July 2026, revenue and grants came in eight per cent below budget at $353.84 billion for the four-month period. That was despite $18.04 billion in new taxes being implemented for the current fiscal year, with one company reporting that it paid $454 million in special consumption tax on sweetened drinks for May and June.

The revenue shortfall was largely driven by tax collections coming in $21.32 billion below budget, including a $13.27-billion shortfall in taxes on companies. Expenditure was also six per cent below budget at $387.27 billion. The Government recorded a fiscal deficit of $33.43 billion, wider than the budgeted $30.89 billion.

An overall surplus of $10.28 billion was recorded, compared with a budgeted deficit of $57.86 billion, largely because loan receipts of $130.62 billion were twice the budgeted amount. Based on the roadshow document, a successful bond raise would leave US$400 million, or approximately $63.05 billion, available for general budgetary purposes in the 2026/27 fiscal year.

“The effects of this natural disaster may continue to adversely affect the development and performance of key sectors of the country’s economy,” GOJ’s prospectus stated, regarding the impact of Hurricane Melissa.

The warning was included among the risk factors outlining Jamaica’s exposure to external shocks, including risks to the tourism sector.

The prospectus added that volatility in global energy prices may also contribute to higher domestic energy costs for Jamaica and could place upward pressure on inflation.

“While the full extent of the impact of these conflicts remains to be seen as of the date of this prospectus supplement, the effects of such conflicts could negatively affect Jamaica’s economic growth, inflation and fiscal revenues,” it said.

Final pricing details, including the interest rate on the new GOJ bond, are expected to be revealed in the coming days. Until then, recent sovereign issues elsewhere in teh Caribbean ofer some indication of where borrowing costs have been landing. Trinidad & Tobago refinanced a US$1-billion bond in January at 6.50 per cent for 10 years before issuing a US$800-million bond at 6.20 per cent for 12 years. Trinidad currently carries a higher international credit rating than Jamaica, although S&P Global Ratings has assigned it a negative outlook, compared with Jamaica’s stable outlook.

World.title: ELITE COMPANY!
World.content:
Oblique Seville (Photo: Garfield Robinson)

WORLD champion Oblique Seville will be gunning for his first Wanda Diamond League title when he lines up in the men’s 100m on the opening day of the two-day Diamond League athletics final at King Baudouin Stadium in Brussels, Belgium.

Seville is one of nine Jamaicans down to compete today with another eight set for Saturday.

He is coming off a confidence boosting win in Poland on August 23, and is hoping to join 100m sprinters Usain Bolt, Asafa Powell and Ackeem Blake as Jamaican men who have won the Diamond trophy.

Following his win in Poland, in which he clocked 9.83 seconds to break the meet record, Seville had said he was focused on ending the season on a high.

“I am just having fun. There are great things ahead of me. Many sprinters ran under 10.00s, that is really special. For the rest of the season I would like to keep winning and the next win should be in Brussels.”

He will have his hands full and will need to be at his best as he lines up against a tough field that includes Nigeria’s Kayinsola Ajayi, who has beaten the Jamaican twice this year, Commonwealth Games champion Emmanuel Eseme of Cameroon, Akani Simbine of South Africa and Trayvon Bromell of the United States.

Jamaicans have won at least one Diamond League title in the 16 years that the global series has been contested.

Today, Rushell Clayton, in the women’s 400m hurdles; Orlando Bennett, in the 110m hurdles; Tajay Gayle and Wayne Pinnock, in the men’s long jump; Romaine Beckford, in the men’s high jump; Roje Stona, in the men’s discus throw; Danniel Thomas-Dodd, in the women’s shot put; and Ackelia Smith, in the women’s triple jump, will be hoping to add their names to the list.

Clayton, who is coming off a win at the prestigious ISTAF Berlin on Sunday, has been consistent through the Diamond League series.

The event in Brussels could be decided between points leader Emma Zapletalova of Slovakia, who lost in the series for the first time after she hit a hurdle in Zurich as world leader Anna Cockrell sped to victory.

Veteran American Dalilah Muhammad, who has announced she will retire at the end of this season, and Belgium’s Paulien Couckuyt are expected to challenge for podium places.

Bennett, the World Athletics Championships medallist, is to take on a handful of Americans, led by world record holder Ja’Kobe Tharp in the 110m hurdles.

Tharp’s compatriots Jamal Britt and Trey Cunningham will be expected to give him competition,

Former world champion Tajay Gayle will be hoping to continue his late season improvement after he jumped a season’s best 8.43m in Zurich. There, he challenged world leader Miltiadis Tentoglou of Greece before falling just short.

Gayle and Pinnock will hope to provide robust competition for Tentoglou, who has lost just once in 15 outdoor meets this year.

Beckford is enjoying his best season as a professional and cleared 2.29m in Poland, just off his season’s best 2.30m. He is down to take on world leader JuVaughn Harrison of the United States, Gianmarco Tamberi of Italy, and Oleh Doroshchuk of Ukraine, all of whom have cleared 2.32m this year.

Stona is set to meet world leader Matthew Denny of Australia on Australia in the men’s discus throw, Mykolas Alekna of Lithuania, and Kristjan Ceh of Slovenia, all of whom have thrown over 72.00m this season.

Thomas-Dodd faces two of the best women’s shot-putters in the last decade or so, Jessica Schilder of Netherlands and Chase Jackson of the USA, both of whom have thrown beyond 21 metres this season. Back-to-back Commonwealth Games champion Sahara Mitton of Canada is also expected to feature.

Ackelia Smith is to line up in what is expected to be an explosive women’s triple jump that will see four jumpers who have gone over 15 metres.

World leader Thea Lafond of Dominica will hope to end the series on a high, but will be challenged by Cubans Davisleydi Velazco and Leyanis Perez Hernandez and Senegal’s Saly Sarr.

World.title: Ein Spaziergang mit Sahra Wagenknecht
World.content:
Endspurt im Wahlkampf in Sachsen-Anhalt: Zwischen Plattenbauten in Halle-Neustadt steht für das Bündnis Sahra Wagenknecht (BSW) weit mehr auf dem Spiel als nur der Einzug in den Landtag. Sahra Wagenknecht skizziert ein Klima der extremen Polarisierung, in dem ihre Partei von zwei Seiten unter Beschuss gerät. Fällt die Brandmauer, oder zwingt das BSW die etablierten Parteien in völlig neue Bündnisse?

Im Spannungsfeld zwischen der AfD um Ulrich Siegmund und den Altparteien kämpft das BSW um Sichtbarkeit und beklagt eine mediale Blockade. Wagenknecht zieht scharfe rote Linien zu Björn Höcke, fordert eine leistungsgerechte Aufstiegsgesellschaft und rechnet mit der Agenda-Politik von Gerhard Schröder ab. Was bedeutet der Begriff „links“ heute überhaupt noch, wenn die einstige Linkspartei ihr traditionelles Milieu verliert?

Neben landespolitischen Fragen geht es um die große geopolitische Linie, von der Kritik an teurem US-Gas bis zur Forderung nach mehr Diplomatie. Ein Spaziergang, der die strategischen Ziele des BSW offenlegt und in der Gordon Repinski mit Wagenknecht auch ihre persönliche Prägung zwischen DDR-Vergangenheit und dem Bruch mit ihrer alten Partei beleuchtet.

Das Berlin Playbook als Podcast gibt es jeden Morgen ab 5 Uhr. Rixa Fürsen, Maximilian Stascheit und das POLITICO-Team liefern Politik zum Hören – kompakt, international, hintergründig.

World.title: The lonely crusader against Gianni Infantino
World.content:
That being said, it’s impossible now to bring back the Russian teams. Because of the way they are used, the national teams, it’s so hard to separate from the propaganda. But that is a failure, I’m not happy to say that it’s impossible; it’s sadly so, even though we are in 100 percent solidarity with Ukraine. It’s never good to make kids never play with each other. That is the aim, that they could play with each other and not be affected by the war. But that’s not possible now, football would stop and Ukraine would not play. So then we are there, and that’s a sad situation, but happening because of war.

When it comes to the Israel situation, we have always said, and we will always say, when you have a breach of FIFA statutes, it needs to be treated. It was delayed, delayed, delayed for many years, that they play with teams from [settlements in] Palestinian territories, which is not allowed by FIFA statutes. And then it’s politically very difficult, but legally not so difficult. So then you need sanctions, and then what the sanctions should be. You’ve got to look at precedents. Do you have any similar cases where you play in other people’s territories? What about Crimea? What about former Yugoslavia? Maybe you have some precedent. What’s the sanction? If it’s not changed, you increase the sanctions, because you need a rules-based system. And you need territory lines.

Klaveness at a press conference in Oslo on August 7, 2026. | Terje Bendiksby/NTB via Getty Images

When we played Israel, we gave the money to the victims of Gaza, not because we did not want to give to the victims of October 7th, but because there were ongoing attacks on the kids in Gaza, and they were poor, they needed the money.

In the end, it’s all about having bridges that are actually working when this is over, when people come to terms, you need to be effective bridges that speak to both sides. For us, we have had projects in Palestine for very many years, decades, educating girls and women there to be coaches; also in Jordan, in this area. So it’s an area [where] we know how difficult it is, how many good people live there on both sides. You know, in Israel, Jordan, everywhere. So we feel very connected to the region because of these projects.

Daria Zakharova contributed to this report.

World.title: Why Macron’s space summit risks blowing up on the launchpad
World.content:
Six participants with first-hand knowledge of the summit's organization described it to POLITICO as a poorly coordinated event with an unclear outcome. They were granted anonymity to discuss sensitive matters.

“It’s falling behind schedule, it hasn’t really been coordinated with the major players in the European space sector, and it’s not entirely clear what its purpose is,” said a senior space expert involved in the summit’s preparation.

“And now that the White House has effectively decided to use it against Emmanuel Macron, it’s becoming even more awkward — it shows that, from a diplomatic standpoint, they didn’t do what they should have done,” they added.

Next week’s event aims to gather the international community — including leaders, large corporations, startups and researchers — to discuss issues including the regulation of space activities, competitiveness, security and defense, and space exploration.

Macron is keen to ensure that France and Europe remain credible space powers, with an independent launch capability and their own global satellite communications system, in an effort to reduce dependence on U.S. technology.

The French president's office insisted Friday that the absence of SpaceX and Blue Origin — two of the world's leading space companies — will have little impact on the summit.

World.title: Witkoff and Kushner set to visit Moscow then Kyiv on Sunday
World.content:
Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff listen as Vice President JD Vance speaks during a news conference. | Pool photo by Jacquelyn Martin/Getty Images

The men have been key U.S. mediators in the stalled Ukraine peace talks.

U.S. President Donald Trump’s special envoys Steven Witkoff and Jared Kushner will visit Moscow and Kyiv in the coming days in an apparent attempt to restart stalled negotiations to end the Ukraine war, Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Telegram.

“We discussed today that Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner will visit Moscow and then Kyiv on Sunday,” the Ukrainian president wrote.

No details about the substance of the meetings have been released, but a U.S. official told CNN Friday that Witkoff and Kushner intend to press for a diplomatic solution to end the conflict.

World.title: Farage-Bardella show of unity tries to paper over immigration sticking points
World.content:
The document Farage and Bardella signed is only binding if the two parties come to power, and it says France will “will ordinarily accept” migrants intercepted in the Channel — potentially leaving wiggle room for Paris to reject them in some cases. Farage called the line “legalese” at a press conference alongside Bardella.

“As Australia proved in 2012, once you provide no incentive to pay a trafficker money to be taken across a stretch of water, in very very short order, the business model will be broken,” Farage said.

But Farage was not asked about the fact that the phrase does not even appear in the French version of the agreement. A National Rally official, granted anonymity to discuss the agreement’s finer points, said the French translation is the “final” version of the agreement.

The memorandum in both languages says the French will be responsible for deporting migrants to their countries of origin, and that the costs of policing operations will be assessed later. It adds that that France will do “its upmost” to stop departures.

“If France gains control of its borders there will be no departures [from French shores],” Bardella said in a speech at the conference. “If we end up doing pushbacks, it would be a failure of our government, it would mean that we have let dozens of thousands of people enter France illegally,” he added.

And the National Rally has long vowed to submit its immigration plans to a referendum in France, which is a lengthy and uncertain process that could get derailed even Bardella’s mentor, Marine Le Pen, wins the presidential election next year. Polls have consistently showed she is the front-runner.

World.title: Farage plans fall visit with Le Pen in France
World.content:
The official added that Farage plans a series of other visits to leaders on the European right before the end of 2026.

Farage has had a long association with Marine Le Pen and interviewed her for his radio show in 2017. He said Friday that while he would not have struck a deal with the National Front founded by her father Jean-Marie Le Pen, her rechristened party had moved away from “extreme elements.”

The relationship has not always been so harmonious. Farage said in 2024 that RN’s economic policies would be a “disaster” for France and “even worse for the economy than the current lot.”

However, the two parties have forged closer links over their hard line on immigration issues. Le Pen is the favorite in the first round of voting in France’s 2027 presidential election, while POLITICO’s Poll of Polls now has Farage’s Reform UK one percentage point behind the ruling Labour Party ahead of the next general election, due by 2029.

Farage alluded to a return visit from the conference stage in Birmingham after Bardella’s speech, which he gave in English — a rare move for him in public. Farage said: “The only downside is I think they’re going to invite me to go to Paris and I’ll have to speak in French, but never mind, we’ll get there.”

World.title: Russian drone strike hits security service headquarters in Kyiv
World.content:
Smoke rises above the Kyiv skyline following a drone strike on Sept. 2, 2026. | Sergei Supinsky/AFP via Getty Images

Volodymyr Zelenskyy asked the SBU acting chief to prepare an attack that would “mirror, if possible” the strike on his office.

A Russian drone attack on Friday afternoon struck the central Kyiv headquarters of the Security Service of Ukraine, the state’s top counterintelligence agency, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said.

The attack “directly” targeted the office of Oleksandr Poklad, the acting head of the SBU, Zelenskyy wrote on his Telegram channel.

Kyiv mayor Vitali Klitschko separately said that nine people had been injured in a fire following a drone strike “on a non-residential building in the Shevchenkivskyi district,” where the SBU headquarters are located. Zelenskyy said on Telegram that he spoke with Poklad after the attack, while Ukrainian Pravda reported that he was not in his office at the time of the strike.

World.title: French government promises €1B for drought-stricken farmers
World.content:
Three schemes account for the bulk of the government’s spending under the new plan.

France will speed up payments under its “national solidarity” scheme designed to compensate for crop losses. It will be topped up to a total of €520 million, provided the country's 2027 budget is duly adopted.

An “agricultural recovery fund” of €235 million aims to provide targeted support for the hardest-hit and most vulnerable farms across the produce, cereal and livestock sectors.

Finally, a targeted tax relief scheme on unbuilt land will cut €330 million in tax revenue for the state. The government is also considering extending a program helping farmers to purchase fertilizer and non-road agricultural diesel.

Genevard also suggested that the retail sector could "play its part" by keeping price rises in check.

Part of her plan is already funded for this year, but more cash will need to be allocated in next year's budget, which is set to be presented by Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu at the end of September.
