World.title: Final sprint before Saxony-Anhalt vote: AfD campaign family festival in Magdeburg
World.content:
Supporters queue in lines stretching dozens of metres to get a photo with him: AfD lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund. The 35-year-old is standing for the party in Sunday’s state election in Saxony-Anhalt. The AfD in Saxony-Anhalt is classified by the state Office for the Protection of the Constitution, a department of the CDU-led interior ministry, as a confirmed far-right extremist organisation. Siegmund is the young shooting star of the AfD in the east.

 

"I finally want to make policy for our own country again," Siegmund tells Euronews. He wants to reorganise migration. Money should be freed up that is "currently being handed out around the world, for people who are here illegally, who commit crimes here". It should become a policy "in our own interest for our own country".

Within his first 100 days in office, Siegmund plans to introduce a "work obligation for asylum seekers", he says. Fire service driving licences and the display of flags at schools are also right at the top of his list. "Of course this is not turning the really big wheel, but these are the first concrete steps where you can see the first progress in all areas of this society." What has been destroyed will take a few years to rebuild, the AfD politician goes on to say.

{{image align="center" size="fullwidth" ratio="auto" id="4571232" src="https://images.euronews.com/articles/stories/09/90/21/54/808x454_cmsv2_a1502eed-029e-5b55-bd20-6ac8d2280d70-9902154.jpg" url="https://images.euronews.com/articles/stories/09/90/21/54/{{w}}x{{h}}_cmsv2_a1502eed-029e-5b55-bd20-6ac8d2280d70-9902154.jpg" caption="AfD lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund in Magdeburg, Saxony-Anhalt on 04.09.2026" alt="AfD lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund in Magdeburg, Saxony-Anhalt on 04.09.2026" credit="Donogh McCabe/Euronews" naturalwidth="2000" naturalheight="1125" }}

Here at the "family festival", as the AfD calls it, near the Magdeburg city centre, thousands cheer and celebrate their "Ulli". His likeness is emblazoned on countless T-shirts and placards. Time and again chants of "We are the people" cut through the crowd. Some AfD supporters also chant "We are the Wende". In between, musicians take to the stage or techno beats blare from the speakers.

The party has rolled out the heavy artillery – its best-known politicians fire up the crowd, including Thuringian AfD politician Stephan Brandner and co-chair Tino Chrupalla. Whenever the speakers mention the CDU, SPD or other parties, the crowd boos and whistles. Some shout "Shame".

Visitors are hoping for a 180-degree turnaround in state politics in Saxony-Anhalt, led by Siegmund. "I support the AfD and I love Ulrich. Once you’ve done all sorts of things, rape and stabbings, then you can’t live here, then you have to go and he makes sure of that. That’s already good," Gerda tells Euronews. The pensioner has travelled specially from Berlin. She finally wanted to attend an AfD event in person. She has already watched several on YouTube. Gerda is actually called something else. She does not want to give her real name, like many at the event. The fear of possible consequences is too great.

{{image align="center" size="fullwidth" ratio="auto" id="4571226" src="https://images.euronews.com/articles/stories/09/90/21/54/808x454_cmsv2_6609a7fb-f98d-5b17-a467-a3dabe8a2f9a-9902154.jpg" url="https://images.euronews.com/articles/stories/09/90/21/54/{{w}}x{{h}}_cmsv2_6609a7fb-f98d-5b17-a467-a3dabe8a2f9a-9902154.jpg" caption="Visitors at the AfD " family="" festival="" .09="" .2026="" in="" Magdeburg="" alt="Visitors at the AfD " credit="Donogh McCabe/Euronews" copyrightlink="" sourcetext="" sourcelink="" calltoactiontext="" calltoactionlink="" naturalwidth="1920" naturalheight="1080" }}

Even a heavy downpour does not stop his fans from waiting for Siegmund’s appearance. For them, everything is at stake: for the first time, the AfD could govern at state level – as part of a coalition or possibly even on its own.

CDU politician: working with the AfD would spell the end of the Union

Current polls put the AfD at around 41 percent, according to Forschungsgruppe Wahlen on behalf of ZDF. The CDU trails far behind in second place with 23 percent, the Left party is third with 11.5 percent. In the last election in 2021, the AfD won 20.8 percent. Back then the CDU won by a clear margin (37.1%).

This time the AfD hopes to be able to win the election outright. But that might still not be enough for the state government. The party may get too few votes to govern alone. It rejects any coalition with the CDU. The CDU also rejects a coalition. It has adopted an incompatibility resolution.

Dennis Radtke, the head of the CDU’s workers’ wing (CDA), warns that his party would be doomed if it formed a coalition with the AfD in Saxony-Anhalt. "The moment we start working with this party, bringing it into positions of responsibility, the CDU is finished," Radtke said on ZDF’s "Maybrit Illner" programme.

Only the BSW can imagine tolerating an AfD-led government, meaning supporting an AfD single-party government with its votes. But the BSW is currently on four percent in the polls and could thus fail to clear the five-percent threshold. The SPD and the Greens, too, have in recent weeks been shaky contenders hovering just below the threshold. They have now climbed to 8.5 percent and six percent respectively.

{{image align="center" size="fullwidth" ratio="auto" id="4571227" src="https://images.euronews.com/articles/stories/09/90/21/54/808x454_cmsv2_1107ac14-dc22-51a1-9037-4e44165b8fa4-9902154.jpg" url="https://images.euronews.com/articles/stories/09/90/21/54/{{w}}x{{h}}_cmsv2_1107ac14-dc22-51a1-9037-4e44165b8fa4-9902154.jpg" caption="Election posters in Magdeburg, Saxony-Anhalt on 04.09.2026" alt="Election posters in Magdeburg, Saxony-Anhalt on 04.09.2026" credit="Donogh McCabe/Euronews" copyrightlink="" sourcetext="" sourcelink="" calltoactiontext="" calltoactionlink="" naturalwidth="1920" naturalheight="1080" }}

Lead Left party candidate optimistic

Given the current polling figures, Saxony-Anhalt may face a complicated coalition-building puzzle after the vote. A coalition of AfD and CDU appears to be ruled out. A CDU–Left party alliance as the basis for a majority government with the SPD and Greens also looks unrealistic for now, because the Union’s incompatibility resolution also applies to the Left party.

Just a few days ago, Chancellor Friedrich Merz (CDU) said: "Both with the AfD and with the Left party there are such fundamental differences with the Union that cooperation is out of the question," Merz told the "Magdeburger Volksstimme" and the "Mitteldeutsche Zeitung".

The mood in the state parliament has changed significantly in recent years, explains Eva von Angern, lead Left party politician, speaking to Euronews. She has been a member of the Saxony-Anhalt state parliament since 2002. "The climate is very hostile to women. Hate and incitement are what define a parliamentary sitting." This has now also arrived in society and on social media.

Despite the current forecast, she is looking "optimistically" towards election day, the Left politician says. She is "firmly convinced" that the AfD will not manage to form a single-party AfD government in Saxony-Anhalt. "People have understood. They want to fight for diversity in Saxony-Anhalt."

World.title: Boss of STIHL: Time for reforms – this is how we will safe prosperity and welfare state
World.content:
The opinions expressed in this article are those of the author and do not represent in any way the editorial position of Euronews.

The state of the German economy is serious, very serious. Over the past eight years, we’ve lost approximately 15 percent of our industrial production. Month after month, Germany loses around 15,000 industrial jobs. And the industrial base that underpins our prosperity is starting to erode. Private net investment has fallen to almost zero. On balance, companies are doing nothing more than replacing what wears out. High costs are paralyzing companies’ willingness to invest. Even the special depreciation package (the “Investitionsbooster”) that the German government introduced in mid-2025 has done nothing to change that.

 

And the industrial base that underpins our prosperity is starting to erode. Dr. Nikolas Stihl, Chairman of the STIHL Advisory Board and Supervisory Board

Of course, US tariffs, China’s aggressive industrial policy, and geopolitical tensions weigh on investment too. But the real problems are of our own making: an overregulated economy, high energy costs, high labor costs, high taxes, and falling levels of education and skills.

Planned reforms are not enough to reverse the economic trend

At the beginning of the year, many entrepreneurs had almost lost faith in Germany’s ability to reform. In July, the German government surprised everyone with a reform of statutory health insurance, along with reform plans for pensions, taxes, and the labor market. This package isn’t enough to pull Germany out of its structural crisis. But the current coalition showed it can compromise to help move the country forward. If those compromises were now unpicked and watered down, the damage to business confidence in politics would be devastating. The planned reforms are still not the breakthrough we were hoping for, the one that would actually turn the economy around.

XXXX (c) Stihl

Right now, we need to put everything into the next round of reforms, the ones that deliver real momentum for investment and growth. And that means the governing coalition, employers, and unions all stepping outside their comfort zones to live up to their responsibility for Germany. The special funds for defense and infrastructure will hardly lead to a self-sustaining upswing in the economy unless conditions for doing business here improve noticeably. The next reform steps have to keep cutting bureaucracy, raise the total hours worked, bring labor costs down, and give companies real reasons to invest in research and development.

The next reform steps have to keep cutting bureaucracy, raise the total hours worked, bring labor costs down, and give companies real reasons to invest in research and development. Dr. Nikolas Stihl, Chairman of the STIHL Advisory Board and Supervisory Board

Public authorities should enable, not obstruct

What we should expect from public authorities is nothing less than high-quality administration: rules people can understand, procedures that are lean and fast, reporting requirements that are reasonable. Digital, and supported by artificial intelligence. Clear rules and fast, straightforward decisions should make investment possible, not hold it back.

The draft law presented by the new Baden-Württemberg state government on reducing reporting and documentation requirements could send an important signal. The principle is simple: statutory reporting obligations should be dropped across the board and only retained where their necessity is explicitly justified. If public authorities acted far more as service providers for people and businesses, it would strengthen confidence in Germany as a place to do business – and in politics too.

Increase hours worked

People working in industry are hugely dedicated, responsible, and highly professional. Without that commitment, German companies would not be succeeding the way they do around the world. STIHL is just one example among countless others.

XXX (c) Stihl

But demographics are slowing the whole economy down and putting massive pressure on the welfare state. To protect our prosperity and to ensure high levels of social benefits, the total number of hours worked has to rise. More hours worked means more economic output. So the debate about working more is really a debate about holding on to what we have – and it is in no way a debate about employees being lazy.

XXX (c) Stihl

Germany has to use every lever it has to get those hours up. Dr. Nikolas Stihl, Chairman of the STIHL Advisory Board and Supervisory Board

Germany has to use every lever it has to get those hours up. Incentives to work more hours. A longer working life, with fair exceptions for physically demanding jobs. Better use of the labor we already have, meaning people out of work and people in part-time roles. Skilled immigration. No sick pay for the first day of illness. An end to doctor’s notes issued over the phone. Productivity gains from digitalization and AI won’t offset what demographics are doing to us.

Reduce labor costs

The collective bargaining round in the metal and electrical industry, which will begin in fall 2026, will be a key factor in determining whether Germany remains an industrial nation or falls further behind. The reason is simple: we no longer have the productivity edge over our main competitors that justifies those high labor costs. That’s why I’m calling for a 40-hour workweek – with no increase in pay. I know I’m asking a great deal of unions and employees. But I’m not trying to take anything away from anyone. Quite the opposite. I want industrial companies to be able to compete, production to stay in Germany, and jobs to be safe.

That’s why I’m calling for a 40-hour workweek – with no increase in pay. Dr. Nikolas Stihl, Chairman of the STIHL Advisory Board and Supervisory Board

And the current debate pays far too little attention to non-wage labor costs. Contributions to pension, health, long-term care, and unemployment insurance should not go above 40 percent of gross wages. That is the economic limit. Getting there means overhauling the social security system from the ground up. The German government’s latest reform measures do at least address the stabilization of contribution rates for pension and statutory health insurance. However, the 40 percent limit has already been far exceeded.

Priority for research

The close links between world-class research institutions, universities, innovation clusters, and innovative companies rank among Germany’s greatest strengths as a business location. Give innovative companies better conditions and you speed up the whole chain: knowledge moves faster, and so does the production and marketing of what comes out of it, new business models included. Regulatory leeway would do that. So would higher tax incentives and more venture capital. Overall, innovations and the approvals they need must be given far greater priority than before, and they must not be held back by bureaucracy.

XXX (c) Stihl

Future-oriented fields deserve far more targeted support: the industrial use of AI, robotics, biotechnology, medical technology, space technology, and quantum technologies. Dr. Nikolas Stihl, Chairman of the STIHL Advisory Board and Supervisory Board

XXX (c) Stihl

Future-oriented fields deserve far more targeted support: the industrial use of AI, robotics, biotechnology, medical technology, space technology, and quantum technologies. The Germany Fund, launched at the end of 2025, is only a start, measured against other countries with strong research bases.

Act decisively

We have no more time to lose. Because only a strong, competitive place to do business can secure prosperity and a strong welfare state.

Germany has shown many times that it can reinvent itself. Dr. Nikolas Stihl, Chairman of the STIHL Advisory Board and Supervisory Board

Germany has shown many times that it can reinvent itself. But if people are going to understand what’s coming, we have to start with an unflinching look at where we actually stand. And then set out a plan they can follow, one that spells out what will change for them. With a plan like that, the government can give direction, bring people with it, and win back trust. It’s time to act.

Dr Nikolas Stihl is the grandson of the company’s founder, Andreas Stihl, and represents the third generation at the helm of the world’s leading chainsaw brand and a global technology company. Under his leadership, STIHL has further expanded its international presence and, in 2025, achieved a turnover of 5.48 billion euros with 20,246 employees worldwide. STIHL has been the world’s best-selling chainsaw brand since 1971.

World.title: Berlin cyberattack: hackers leak highly sensitive data across dark web
World.content:
The hacker group "Rhysida" has published almost six terabytes of data from Berlin's state administration on the dark web. Among the data is said to be highly sensitive information.

 

The scale of the leak is enormous: 1,439,893 files. So far, there has been hardly any response from Berlin's administration and political leaders.

Among the published files is a folder titled "AG CBRN-Rahmenplanung." CBRN stands for chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear threats. This means that highly sensitive information about potential threat scenarios may now be publicly accessible and could also be viewed by terrorists or foreign intelligence services.

Investigative journalist Lars Winkelsdorf has sounded the alarm on "X." According to him, the cyberattack is "of a magnitude that threatens the state."

"In addition to LKA documents related to investigations, the files also include plans concerning national defense—ranging from the federal government’s secret communication channels in the event of an apocalypse to defense-related companies and emergency plans developed by government agencies," he wrote.

A large amount of personal data has also been leaked, particularly relating to state civil servants, including birth certificates, what appear to be absence lists, telephone numbers and home addresses.

The hackers had previously threatened to publish the data on their leak site and demanded a ransom of 30 Bitcoin, around two million euros. They set a countdown that expired at about 3.35 pm on Friday. The Berlin Senate had already made it clear before the ultimatum expired that, as a matter of principle, it does not give in to such blackmail demands.

Shortly after the countdown ended, the data package was published on the dark web, and members of the hacker group have already been sharing lists of filenames on social media.

World.title: Medieval manuscripts made from animal skin reveal ancient history of deadly sheep virus
World.content:
In the Middle Ages, most texts were written on sheep, goat and cattle skin, used as a writing material and known as parchment.

 

It is in some of Europe’s famous ancient manuscripts that researchers found clues into the history of the deadly sheep pox virus — a viral disease of sheep that causes fever, skin lesions, and death. Such traces can help scientists to understand how pathogens evolved and how they impacted past societies.

An international team of geneticists, historians, virologists, protein chemists and conservators, led by scientists at University College Dublin, has extracted DNA from the skin used to make these centuries-old documents.

“The recording of ancient DNA of pathogens has completely changed our understanding of infectious disease in the past, and here we show that parchment can also preserve animal pathogen DNA,” said Louis L’Hôte, lead author of the study.

Among the works analysed were the 1,000-year-old York Gospels — one of the finest illuminated manuscripts to survive from the late Anglo-Saxon period — as well as earlier texts such as the Corpus Glossary at Corpus Christi College in Cambridge, regarded as one of the earliest English dictionaries. Other medieval texts examined came from across Britain and continental Europe.

“It is possible that archives and libraries around the world also contain the genetic traces of disease outbreaks in animals in the past”.

Sheep pox is a highly contagious disease that spreads rapidly and can affect large portions of a flock in a short time. It can cause significant economic losses due to decreased milk production, poor quality of hides and wool and trade restrictions. There is no evidence that sheep pox can infect humans.

Related Man lived with pig kidney for nine months before human transplant

The study, published in Science Advances, found that in some cases, multiple pages from the same manuscript contained sheep pox virus DNA, suggesting that infected animals were used to produce them.

The researchers combined the DNA found in the manuscripts with older samples from Bronze Age sheep teeth, and found that the disease has threatened livestock for over 3,700 years.

“Ancient genomes can help us understand how these pathogens affecting us today evolved. We find that unlike the smallpox virus, the sheeppox virus genome was very stable over the last few millennia,” added L’Hôte.

“This might mean that genetic changes before this point were very important to how the sheep pox virus evolved to infect its host, which may help us fight the pathogen in the future.”

World.title: US peace envoys Witkoff and Kushner to visit Kyiv and Moscow with plan to 'end the war'
World.content:
US peace envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner are set to visit Kyiv and Moscow this weekend, armed with a "proposal to end the war," US President Donald Trump has announced, in the latest push to break a diplomatic deadlock over the war in Ukraine.

 

"I sent Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, two great negotiators. They've done a great job, and we sent them over to see whether or not we can get something done. And there may be a good chance that we'll do it," Trump told reporters on Friday.

The pair are expected in Moscow on Saturday before heading to Kyiv on Sunday, in what will be their first visits to the Ukrainian capital since Trump returned to the White house in January last year.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed the planned visit to Ukraine in a post on X.

"We need to look for real options for how to move this war toward an end," Zelenskyy wrote. "We will see what proposals Steve and Jared bring and what they are told in Moscow in response".

He added that Ukrainian forces would ensure the "normal functioning of Russian airspace" to ensure the envoys could make the trip to Moscow safely.

Zelenskyy had warned airlines and insurers on Tuesday that Russian airspace would "effectively be closing" due to the scale of Ukrainian drone operations making flying unsafe.

But the Ukrainian leader said Ukraine would hold off on strikes while Witkoff and Kushner made the trip, while calling on Moscow to do the same.

"We are looking out for them, not for Russia. There will be no air strikes from our side, and Russia must do the same, ensuring there are no air strikes from its side for the time needed to hold these talks and handle the logistical matters related to this American visit," he wrote on social media.

Russian strikes kill four overnight

The announcement came as Russian strikes on the city of Kamianske in Ukraine's Dnipropetrovsk region killed four overnight, per local authorities.

Oleksandr Hanzha, the head of the Dnipropetrovsk Oblast Military Administration, said five people were also injured in the strikes, which hit an industrial facility.

On Friday, Zelenskyy announced that a Russian drone had also hit the headquarters of Ukraine's Security Service (SBU) in central Kyiv, adding that it had been "aimed directly" at the head of the agency's office.

In response to the attack, he said he had ordered the SBU to carry out an "appropriate, tangible response and, where possible, one that mirrors this strike."

World.title: France's literary season: a uniquely French phenomenon?
World.content:
Sonia Devillers, Philippe Jaenada, Amélie Nothomb, Philippe Besson, Ananda Devi. They all have one thing in common: they will be part of the 2026 literary season. Between now and October, some 461 novels, including 344 French titles, will reach bookshops. That is a slight drop compared with the previous year, when 484 books were published.

 

For publishers and booksellers, this period is unmissable, all the more so at a time when reading is playing a smaller and smaller role in our daily lives. "The share of French people who spontaneously describe themselves as readers is falling across all categories, particularly among regular readers (down 5 points vs 2023)", notes the 6th barometer from the Centre national du Livre (CNL), published in 2025. "Over the last 12 months, 63% of French people say they have read at least five books (down 6 points vs 2023) and the share of daily readers is declining (down 4 points vs 2023), reaching its lowest level in 10 years", the study also points out.

"It is our shared duty to reassert the central place of reading in our lives. Reading is a vital time, time for oneself, that absolutely must be protected", argues Régine Hatchondo, president of the CNL.

And the trend is even more pronounced among young people: they spend an average of 3 hours and 1 minute a day in front of screens, but only 18 minutes reading books, according to the study "Les jeunes Français et la lecture" ("Young French people and reading"), published in 2026. "Regular reading is declining and young people very often do something else at the same time as they read", adds the head of the CNL.

In Belgium and Switzerland, all eyes on France

Although it is a particularly big deal in France, the literary season also exists in several other European countries.

In Switzerland, the phenomenon does not have the same impact. "There is far less media hype and fewer prizes [literary] at that time of year too", observes Nicolas Julliard, a literary journalist at RTS, speaking to Euronews. "It is not the same phenomenon."

However, he acknowledges that Switzerland is aligning more closely with the French market. "More and more publishing houses are matching their schedules to this calendar in order to release their biggest titles", the journalist continues. One reason is that this allows Swiss publishers to gain greater visibility in France. "Quite a few books are exported and are even starting to appear in certain prize lists." In short, the Swiss literary season "is increasingly becoming a key date for publishers, particularly for the newer publishing houses", concludes Nicolas Julliard.

In Belgium, it is "quite a paradoxical period", says Nausicaa Dewez, editor-in-chief of the journal "Le Carnet et les Instants", speaking to Euronews. "Driven by the pull of the French literary season, there is intense media and public attention on books and literature, and at the same time the space is saturated by titles published in France. [...] Belgian publishing houses are present during this period, but they also know that commercially they cannot compete with much larger and more powerful structures. So they do not throw all their strength into the autumn season."

Nausicaa Dewez adds another nuance: "For most literary publishers in French-speaking Belgium, the first major moment of the year is the Brussels Book Fair, held in March", which explains why the start of the year is also an important time for Belgian literature.

An important phenomenon across Europe as well

In Spain, this period is known as the "temporada editorial de otoño" ("autumn publishing season"). While the country "does not reach France's level of activity, publishers prepare major titles every year for the beginning of September", explains journalist Pepa Blanes in the pages of the Cadena SER (source in French). "Events also start to fill much of the month."

In Germany too, the end of summer means a wave of new books, though again with less impact than in France. Across the Rhine, this period is called Bücherherbst ("book autumn") or Literaturherbst ("literary autumn"). The press then showcases the big new releases and regards this season as an important one for bookshops. It is an event that is "planned long in advance", reports the Tagesspiegel (source in French).

Above all, this flurry of new releases comes a few weeks before the Frankfurt Book Fair, held every October and a key date for the industry. It is there that the Deutscher Buchpreis is awarded, a prize created along the lines of France's Prix Goncourt, notes Deutsche Welle (source in French).

In Italy, "autumn is when some of the year's most important books are concentrated, although in recent years this market approach has changed and publishers, to avoid an overload of titles in autumn, have started to spread their output more evenly over the rest of the year", explains Paolo Ambrosinin, president of the Associazione librai italiani, speaking to Euronews.

The British literary season perhaps comes closest to what we see in France, even though it follows a different timetable. "'Super Thursday' is an exciting day for booksellers, because hundreds of new books arrive in bookshops on the same day", says Kate Skipper, chief operating officer at the book chain Waterstones, speaking to The Guardian (source in French).

It usually falls on the first or second Thursday in October. "It is always an extremely busy day, but there is a real buzz when you unpack so many big titles for Christmas all at once", Kate Skipper continues. In 2024, more than 1,900 books were published for this "Super Thursday", reported The Guardian (source in French).

That exceptional volume dropped sharply the following year: the number of releases was almost halved, as publishers adopted a strategy summed up by the slogan "publish less, but publish better", reported The Bookseller (source in French) at the time.

World.title: Germany: From emigration to immigration destination
World.content:
Migration is a sensitive topic in Germany, with public debate dominated by the fear of uncontrolled immigration. But over two centuries, millions of Germans emigrated in search of a better life.

"Why should [they] be suffered to swarm into our Settlements, and by herding together establish their Language and Manners to the Exclusion of ours? [...] [They] will shortly be so numerous [...] and will never adopt our Language or Customs."

These defamatory comments about refugees and asylum-seekers sound as if they might have been made today by the right-wing populist Alternative for Germany party (AfD). Yet in this instance, the people vilified and accused of refusing to integrate are Germans — and the harsh judgement was made in the 18th century by none other than Benjamin Franklin, one of the Founding Fathers of the United States.

The pursuit of happiness and a better life are mentioned in the American Declaration of Independence, which Franklin helped write. Over the centuries, they have been the motivation for countless people to turn their backs on their respective homelands.

Benjamin Franklin, one of the Founding Fathers of the United States, warned against accepting German immigrants Image: Public Domain

The Germans who emigrated to America in Franklin's lifetime were actually fairly limited in number. By 1820, only about 150,000 had successfully made the journey. Often, they were persuaded by compatriots who told tales of their tremendous success in their new homeland and celebrated the prosperity they had supposedly attained in a very short space of time. What most people back home didn't know was that these recruiters received a commission for every migrant.

"The crossing on a sailing ship cost about what a tradesman would earn in a year," said Simone Blaschka of the German Emigration Center in Bremerhaven . "To be able to afford that, families had to sell all their worldly goods."

A journey into the unknown

They would have had no idea what awaited them on board the ship. During the crossing, which took several weeks, they were packed together below deck in a very confined space, plagued by bedbugs, fleas and rats. Many fell sick with dysentery, typhoid, smallpox or scurvy.

In his book "Journey to Pennsylvania in the Year 1750," the schoolmaster and organist Gottlieb Mittelberger described what he had experienced on the voyage: "Many people whimper, sigh and cry piteously for their homes; most of them get home-sick. Many hundred people necessarily die and perish in such misery, and must be cast into the sea."

Many European immigrants who came to the US in the 20th century arrived by boat in New York Image: Raimund Franken/imageBROKER/picture alliance

On arrival in America, Mittelberger wrote, the majority of his fellow passengers were effectively auctioned off. These were people without means who were granted free passage after undertaking to work for years as bonded laborers in exchange. In the US, their contracts were sold off. Mittelberger saw families torn apart and parents forced to sell their children.

An invitation from Russia

As these early migrants were traveling to America, there was simultaneously a big wave of emigration from Germany to the east. People followed the call of the Russian czarina, Catherine the Great, herself a German princess by birth.

On July 22, 1763, she issued a manifesto inviting people to come to Russia, with the aim of cultivating uninhabited regions for arable farming. She promised the new arrivals free transport to their chosen place of residence, land, also free of charge, the first year tax-free, schooling, exemption from military service, and a special political status that would allow them to maintain the German language and, for the most part, govern themselves.

Catherine the Great officially invited Germans to immigrate to Russia in the late 18th century Image: akg-images/picture-alliance

However, in the 19th century the American continent once again became the dream destination. "The German population almost doubled in the 19th century, so you can imagine what the job market was like," said Blaschka from the German Emigration Center. The situation was exacerbated by failed harvests and famines.

"People didn't see any future for themselves or their children, and decided to emigrate," she said. In this way, around 6 million Germans were drawn to the New World.

Migration: A burden or an asset?

Germans were far from the only ones who left their homeland.

"Between the beginning of the 19th century and the World War I, there were probably around 60 million Europeans who left their homes," said Jochen Oltmer, a professor at the Institute for Migration Research and Intercultural Studies in Osnabrück. Then, in the mid-20th century, this trend reversed and Europe went from being a continent of emigration to one of immigration.

Migration researcher Jochen Oltmer has studied the immigration waves to and from Europe in the 19th and 20th centuries Image: Michael Gründel/NOZ

In the 1950s and '60s, the future looked rosy for postwar West Germany and its "economic miracle." From 1956 onward, so-called "guest worker trains" arrived in stations like Stuttgart, Dortmund and Cologne, carrying Italians, Greeks, Spaniards, Portuguese, Yugoslavs and Turks, attracted by the promise of well-paid jobs in the new Federal Republic.

By the time the ban on recruiting foreign labor came into force in 1973, around 14 million people had come to West Germany as "guest workers." Around 3 million stayed permanently.

Yet Germany still did not consider itself an immigration country. "For a very long time, we were dealing with the mindset: It doesn't matter why people came to the Federal Republic; they don't belong, because in any case they'll leave the country again and disappear," said Oltmer.

Between 1956 and 1973, around 14 million 'guest workers' came to Germany from other European countries Image: Hans Heckmann/dpa/picture alliance

In 2025, according to Germany's Federal Statistical Office, more than 30% of Germany's total population had a migrant background. Yet many third- and fourth-generation citizens still don't feel they belong, which has to do with the perspective of the society in which they live.

Who's welcome – and who isn't?

These days, Germany is keen to attract skilled workers, but refugees are only granted asylum if they are politically persecuted in their homeland, or are fleeing war.

As a migration researcher, Oltmer is constantly examining the reasons why some migrants are accepted and others are not. This question was especially relevant in 2015, when refugees came to Germany in very large numbers.

"The attitude was: 'OK, you people from Syria, in light of the Syrian civil war, you are entitled to protection.' But at the same time this society says of people from Afghanistan, 'In your case, we're a bit more sceptical,'" he said.

Germany took in hundreds of thousands of refugees in 2015, above all people fleeing the civil war in Syria Image: Johannes Simon/Getty Images

Yet asylum accounts for barely 10% of immigration to Germany, Oltmer explained. The majority of immigrants are not people fleeing their country. "This means that when it comes to scandalization and the creation of certain negative images, we are seeing a massive distortion of the debate." And the descendants of the German emigrants Benjamin Franklin once reviled as "Palatine boors" have long since perfectly integrated into American society.

In Germany, however, integration is taking much longer. "Many people have no possibility of regularizing their status and obtaining a stable residence permit, even though everyone involved knows they can stay, and will stay," said Oltmer. He believes people urgently need to sit down and clarify how they want German society to look in future.

"It may be a very hard, even hurtful discussion. But it's the only way."

World.title: Why many Syrians feel Assad's death sentence isn't enough
World.content:
In July, a Syrian court sentenced former dictator Bashar Assad to death for crimes against his own people. But after 14 years of civil war, many survivors are demanding more when it comes to transitional justice.

Huda Khayti often finds herself returning to the place where she lost almost everything. Khayti, a Syrian women's rights activist, survived a 2013 chemical weapons attack on the east Ghouta region by forces of the former Syrian dictator Bashar Assad.

Her brother was killed by the bombs of the Assad regime and its allies. Her women's center was destroyed along with her home and in 2018, she had to leave her hometown of Douma — a major city in Ghouta — and flee to Idlib, a rebel stronghold in northern Syria.

Today, Khayti regularly visits her hometown, which is about 10 kilometers (about 6 miles) northeast of the country's capital, Damascus. Since the Assad regime was overthrown in late 2024, Khayti has traveled regularly between Idlib and Douma, where she's even working on opening a new women's center.

"Ghouta means so much to me emotionally," she told DW. But every time she returns there, she is also confronted with remnants of the civil war. "When I'm traveling through the country I see traces of war everywhere, so many houses and so much infrastructure destroyed. So much suffering. So much trauma."

In Douma, Huda Khayti visits the grave of her murdered brother Image: privat

Almost two years since the overthrow of the Assad regime, Syria has started a process to examine the crimes of the regime in court. In mid-August a Damascus court sentenced Bashar Assad and other high-ranking members of his regime to death in absentia. Assad is currently living in Russia, where he fled after his government was overthrown. Many senior officials are also there or hiding elsewhere.

Among other things, Assad was found guilty of premeditated murder, torture and depriving individuals of their liberty. The court said these were war crimes and crimes against humanity.

"Of course, this conviction of Assad is a good thing," Khayti said. "Even if it's only on paper. Bashar Assad may have been convicted but he just continues to live his life in Russia — like so many other Syrian criminals who fled to Russia."

Justice served in Syria?

The court's conviction had a big impact in Syria anyway. "The verdict had a lot of echoes by people, they were so happy," said Lina Chawaf, a Syrian journalist, media expert and researcher at Harvard University's Center for Middle Eastern Studies. "Many media celebrated the verdict on the statement day as a victory and consider it as part of transitional justice."

Still, it remains unclear whether there will be any actual punishment following the conviction. Although Russia and Syria agreed on an extradition treaty in 2023, observers say it's unlikely Russia would send Assad, a long-time ally, back to Syria. Additionally, according to the treaty, if the death penalty is likely, that could prevent extradition too.

In August, Syria's Deputy Justice Minister Mustafa al-Qassem said the country had established a commission to cooperate with Interpol and that cooperation with other countries in extraditing fugitive suspects would speed up legal proceedings.

Syria still scarred after 14-year civil war To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Rana Sheikh-Ali, founder of Daret Salam (Peace Circuit in English), which uses technology to build peace and empower women, believes the Assad trial in August should be seen as largely symbolic. From a human rights perspective, she opposes the death penalty, but at the same time she says many locals saw the death sentences as just.

But the prosecution of high-ranking regime members is only one aspect of the transitional justice process.

Transitional justice isn't just about criminal trials. Other aspects include searching for missing people, investigating crimes, deciding on reparations and formulating institutional reforms. With all that, the focus should be on victims and survivors.

Numbers supplied by the Syrian Network for Human Rights indicate just how big the task is. In an article, the advocacy network reports that over 234,805 civilians were killed during the civil war, at least 202,000 of them by the Assad regime and its allies.

In addition, there are also at least 181,312 cases of arbitrary arrest and enforced disappearance to investigate as well as 45,339 deaths resulting from torture. It's thought that the actual numbers are likely far higher. The network has also documented 217 chemical weapons attacks by the Assad regime.

Victim-centered process needed

Women's rights activist Khayti was just a few kilometers from the epicenter of one of those attacks in eastern Ghouta in 2013. "I remember it like it was yesterday," she recounted. "I can't forget the screams of the victims. I kept thinking we were next. I felt that scratchiness in my throat, that burning in my eyes."

For a system of transitional justice that is truly victim-centered, it's not enough to just have survivors act as witnesses in court. "Victims must also participate in every detail related to the transitional justice process," she explained.

Additionally, those who were impacted by the crimes must be able to participate voluntarily and be protected as they do, Sheikh-Ali added. They should be able to talk about their experiences and should also be heard on topics like compensation, financial support and public recognition.

For survivors like Khayti, this means not just making Assad and a few top regime officials the primary targets of justice.

"I also want to see convictions for individuals who wrote reports that led to people ending up in the Saydnaya torture prison," Khayti said. "These individuals are just as guilty as the torturers themselves."

Huda Khayti also runs a women's center in Idlib and works with people in refugee camps on the Turkish border Image: privat

At the moment, though, it's unclear exactly how thoroughly Syria will confront its past.

"Convictions in absentia against Assad and other officials send an important signal after decades of impunity," said Sophie Bischoff, managing director of Adopt a Revolution, a German-Syrian human rights organization that supports civil society initiatives. "But for survivors like Huda Khayti, these sentences remain symbolic as long as those convicted are not actually held accountable — and it's also still not transparent exactly who is to be held accountable and on what legal basis, and who would be granted immunity."

Bischoff also noted that the new Syrian state has yet to fully and comprehensively investigate crimes against humanity and war crimes committed in Syria.

"So far it's primarily been Syrian civil society organizations and human rights activists who have been researching and documenting these cases for years," she told DW. "Systematic state documentation of violent crimes committed during the Assad regime era is only just beginning."

The new Syrian government has created two commissions to work on issues of transitional justice. In late August, one of these — the National Commission for Missing Persons — launched a platform called Athar, where families of the missing can submit information.

The other organization, the National Commission for Transitional Justice, was established in May 2025 but has so far dealt only with crimes committed by the Assad regime. It has not dealt with crimes committed by militias fighting the war or the extremist group known as the "Islamic State".

Return to Syria: Rebuilding and seeking justice in Yarmouk To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Investigating all war crimes

"This falls far short," said Bischoff. "For a comprehensive reckoning and a new beginning in a Syria for all, the war crimes of all warring parties must be included."

For Khayti, the requirement to place victims at the center of the process of transitional justice also has another difficult aspect. Her testimony is being heard, but at the same time she is forced to return to the original trauma.

"It's difficult for me to talk about it and I often feel like I'm reliving it," Khayti explained.

Sheikh-Ali said centering the victims means those impacted play a meaningful role in the process. But as they do so, she added, they should also be protected.

It's also important to remember these events, Khayti added. In Douma, she is working on ways to preserve recollections of the war. "We need to inform younger people about it so that the memory doesn't fade," she said.

In Syria, she said now it's about finding the missing, holding all perpetrators to account, fully investigating all crimes and giving survivors a voice.

"We will continue to be loud," Khayti said. "And we will continue to demand justice."

This article was originally written in German.

09/05/2026 September 5, 2026 India marks Teachers' Day

India is celebrating its national Teachers' Day on Saturday.

Every year on September 5, educational institutions across the country hold cultural events and programs honoring teachers for their contributions to the society.

Teachers' Day in India is celebrated on the birth anniversary of renowned scholar and philosopher Dr. Sarvepalli Radhakrishnan who was born on September 5, 1888 and served as the second president of the nation.

The commemoration dates back to 1962, a few months after he became president.

According to a popular anecdote, some of Radhakrishnan's students wanted to celebrate his birthday but the academic-turned-statesman is believed to have told them that it would be his "proud privilege" if the day was observed as Teachers' Day instead.

On Saturday, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi extended Teachers’ Day greetings.

"#TeachersDay is about appreciating the strong contribution of teachers to our society. It is also a day to pay homage to Dr. S. Radhakrishnan," he wrote on X as he shared visuals of his meeting with the recipients of the annual National Teachers' Awards that were presented on Friday.

Police believe the same man may have been responsible for several attacks on the power grid this week Image: Thilo Schmuelgen/REUTERS

Police in Germany continue to hunt for a 48-year-old man suspected of causing deliberate damage to the country's electricity grid.

The most serious incident was on Tuesday evening at a substation in Bergheim, west of Cologne.

Launch devices were used to fire cables across overhead lines, causing a short circuit that forced five units of the nearby Niederaussem coal plant to temporarily disconnect from the network.

Earlier the same day, a similar attack was carried out near the Jänschwalde plant in eastern Brandenburg. More than a dozen launch devices were found.

On Thursday, a passer-by found similar unused devices at a substation in Dormagen, between Cologne and Düsseldorf.

Police say the objects matched the launch gear used in the other incidents.

Sabotage fears hit Germany's power grid To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Germany's DPA news agency reported on Friday that a man from a town near Dortmund claimed responsibility for the incidents in two letters.

His motive is reportedly to draw attention to the use of fossil fuels in electricity production, which he called a "crime."

This week, officers found explosives in the 48-year-old's home, while a special operations unit stormed a truck in a wood, some 100 kilometers (62 miles) away. The suspect was not found.

Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt has described the acts as "climate extremism."

World.title: What would an AfD government in Saxony-Anhalt really mean?
World.content:
Detention centers for deportation, mandatory work for asylum-seekers, vigilante groups — the AfD wants to drastically overhaul Saxony-Anhalt. What does the party have planned?

The Alternative for Germany (AfD) could bring in massive changes should it form a government in Saxony-Anhalt. The far-right party, currently way ahead in opinion polls, is hoping to form a single-party government and have its lead candidate, Ulrich Siegmund, serve as state premier.

The Saxony-Anhalt chapter of the AfD is classified by the domestic intelligence agency as "confirmed far-right."

Radical tightening of asylum laws

In its draft government program , the AfD has promised "deportation from minute one!" if it wins the election in Saxony-Anhalt. The stated goal, according to the party's election program, is simply to deport as many immigrants who have no residency permits as possible.

The party has also pledged much stricter asylum rules at all levels: It wants more detention pending deportation, mandatory work for asylum-seekers, and intends to cut all state funding for integration programs, which it refers to as an "asylum industry."

What if Germany's far-right AfD party wins in Saxony-Anhalt? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Furthermore, it wants to exclude children and adolescents who do not have permanent residency in Germany from attending regular schools. On top of that, a "Remigration Task Force" is to be established within the state government to coordinate the state's asylum policy.

Exactly how many of these measures an AfD state government would be legally able to implement remains unclear. Creating special classes for refugees could, for example, be a violation of international and European law.

And the question of who can and can't be deported falls under the jurisdiction of the federal government, not that of an individual state.

Anti-immigration policy

The AfD opposes immigration to Germany. In its government platform, the party calls for a "180-degree turnaround in migration policy," and its stated goal is to reduce the number of immigrants in Saxony-Anhalt.

However, the region has been suffering for years from a shortage of skilled workers, particularly in nursing and care for the elderly. The AfD's plan to end this shortage is to encourage Germans who live abroad to come back.

To this end, it plans to launch a "return program," including a proposed "return bonus" to help find housing and daycare spots for children. It is unclear how many returnees the AfD anticipates and how much money it has budgeted for the "return program."

Germany looks to India to address skilled labor shortage To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Saxony-Anhalt has been severely affected by depopulation for over 30 years. No other German state population has shrunk more since reunification in 1990 — from around 2.9 million people then to 2.1 million today.

Economic researchers like Reint Gropp, president of the Halle Institute for Economic Research, have warned that an AfD government is likely to exacerbate the skilled worker shortage.

"Highly qualified professionals, in particular, have options," he told Die Welt newspaper on Tuesday. "If they feel they are unwelcome or can expect hostility, they will choose other regions."

Rapprochement with Russia

The 16 state governments have virtually no authority over Germany's foreign and defense policy, though they can influence political debates via the Bundesrat, the chamber of parliament that represents the states. In that context, an AfD state premier would carry considerable political weight.

For example, since the start of Russia's full-scale war against Ukraine in 2022, Germany has largely halted oil imports, but the AfD's election platform calls for a rapprochement with Russia and an end to sanctions.

The call is largely symbolic, as Saxony-Anhalt is bound by federal sanctions, but an AfD state premier could set a new tone in the Bundesrat.

Threat from the far right: Never quite German enough? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The AfD also wants to expand Russian language instruction in schools and specifically recruit native Russian speakers for this purpose.

On Ukraine, meanwhile, the AfD is taking a harder line, calling for a "return offensive" for Ukrainian refugees. Again, a state government cannot deport Ukrainians from Germany — that is regulated by federal policy.

Establishing citizen patrols

Particularly controversial is the AfD's call for a kind of auxiliary police force. The regular police are "overwhelmed" by the task of ensuring security, according to the AfD's program for Saxony-Anhalt: "We will therefore establish a voluntary citizen patrol as a third pillar of the local security architecture."

Legal scholar and criminologist Thomas Feltes, of Ruhr University Bochum, warns against the idea. "It is the police's duty to ward off dangers and ensure the protection of the public. Only the police are authorized to use force in doing so," he wrote in a column for the outlet Legal Tribune Online.

Germany's freedom of art under threat? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

A "citizen patrol," he said, would basically be a vigilante group that would have a negative effect on public safety: "Where such groups are active, the fear of crime is only stoked — not only among the participants, but above all among everyone else, and not just among 'concerned' citizens," he wrote.

Radical change in social policy

A central tenet of the AfD's governing platform is so-called identity politics. It aims to promote a positive image of German history, and advocates a fundamentally different view of the country's past. The party describes the process of coming to terms with German crimes during the Nazi era as the "perpetuation of a guilt complex" and wants to change school curricula accordingly.

It has also declared war on social diversity: Rainbow flags, as symbols of diversity, are to be banned in schools. It rejects the world-famous Bauhaus architecture — which flourished in Saxony-Anhalt — as "too globalist" and calls for a "patriotic cultural policy."

To that end, it wants to redirect funding away from the many pro-democracy projects that receive state funding for their work. In its platform, the AfD has rejected any continuation of these payments.

World.title: Tunisia: Judge orders arrest of journalist Mohamed Yousfi
World.content:
A journalist and vocal critic of the Tunisian president, Mohamed Yousfi has been taken into custody ahead of an interview. A union called the arrest an attack on all journalists' rights.

A judge in Tunisia ordered the detention of prominent journalist Mohamed Yousfi on Friday. Police had taken him into custody as he arrived at a radio station to give an interview, according to Zied Dabbar, president of the journalist syndicate SNJT.

Dabbar said it was unclear why Yousfi was detained outside Radio Express FM , but he believed it was related to Yousfi's criticism of the authorities.

The judge ordered Yousfi detained on charges of illicit enrichment and money laundering, the state news agency reported, citing a judicial source.

No reason provided for detention

Yousfi, editor-in-chief of investigative news website Al-Qatiba, has been an outspoken critic of President Kais Saied. Al-Qatiba is known for investigative reporting and coverage of political, economic, social and environmental issues.

Radio Express FM host Walid Ben Rhouma said no reason was given for Yousfi's detention.

"He was barred from entering to participate in the program as a guest and was taken away for questioning, according to those who stopped him," Rhouma said in a Facebook post.

The SNJT said Yousfi's detention shows the erosion of press freedoms in Tunisia, where reporters, lawyers, opposition figures and activists have recently faced prosecution.

Attack on freedom of the press

SNJT called Yousfi's arrest not only an attack on him but also on all journalists and Tunisians' right to a free and independent media.

Rights ⁠groups ​warn of efforts to close Tunisia's remaining independent ​voices since Saied suspended parliament in 2021 and dissolved it in 2022. Saied says he will not be a dictator and that freedoms are guaranteed in Tunisia.

In August, protesters took the streets to demonstrate in support of jailed activists and journalists, as well as to call for Saied's removal from power.

Media figures jailed this year include Zied Heni, Mourad Zghidi and Borhen Bsaies. Khaoula Boukrim was sentenced in June to four years in ​absentia.

On Thursday, lawyer Ghazi Mrabet, known for handling politically sensitive and civil liberties cases, was arrested and placed in custody, according to local media reports.

The case reportedly involves alleged drug trafficking, although there are conflicting accounts of the circumstances.

Edited by: Dmytro Hubenko

World.title: Bolivia: Deadly explosion rocks military base in Viacha
World.content:
The explosion occurred at an army base where fireworks were stored. The exact cause of the blast is under investigation.

At least 2 people were killed, and more than 50 were injured after two explosions occurred at an army barracks in Bolivia on Friday, local authorities said.

Earlier, the police reported at least two deaths and several missing persons.

What do we know about the blast?

According to authorities, the blast occurred at around 2:30 p.m. (1830 GMT) local ​time in an area used to store pyrotechnic materials.

The explosion occurred in the western city of Viacha, about 30 kilometers (19 miles) from the capital, La Paz, at the military base where fireworks were stored. However, the authorities have yet to determine the cause of the explosion.

In a Facebook post, Defense Minister Ernesto Justiniano said that 52 of the injured were civilians and the rest were military personnel.

Justiniano said "pyrotechnic material" was stored at the base in Viacha, southwest of Bolivia's administrative capital La Paz.

The Defense Ministry said that 14 people were missing.

The fatalities could be between 10 and 15 people, Viacha health director Rita Nebraska had earlier told ‌local television.

Fourteen of the wounded were transferred to hospitals ​in La Paz, including a girl with third-degree burns, she said.

Police spokesman Roger Roca said that seven people are missing.

Several homes were damaged as windows broke in the blast, according to the police.

Threat of another blast looms

Nebraska ⁠said firefighters had warned that a heat source remained at ⁠the site, raising ​the risk of another explosion, and urged residents to stay at least 150 meters away.

Rescuers, medical teams and ambulances have been deployed at the site to help the injured and assess the damage.
