"Now take the case of drugs. It's not just in big cities or universities anymore, nobody even knows what it is; someone just comes and gives it. Teachers should watch for behavioural changes in children," he added.

Saturday marks the 138th birth anniversary of Dr Sarvepalli Radhakrishnan, who also served as Vice President of India. Later in the day, PM Modi will visit Shri Ram College of Commerce, which is celebrating its centenary.

World.title: Cash-for-jobs scam: Former Tamil Nadu minister KN Nehru’s home, other premises searched
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Tamil Nadu's Directorate of Vigilance and Anti-Corruption (DVAC) on Saturday conducted searches at the residence and premises linked to DMK leader and former minister KN Nehru in connection with alleged irregularities in the Municipal Administration and Water Supply (MAWS) Department.

The searches were conducted in Thillai Nagar, Tiruchirappalli.

DMK cadres gathered outside Nehru's residence during the searches. Former minister Anbil Mahesh Poyyamozhi also visited Nehru's home.

The case relates to allegations of corruption in recruitment, contract allocation and transfers during Nehru's tenure as the minister in charge of the department.

Join conversation Commentsâ Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

The DVAC registered an FIR after the Madras high court directed it to initiate a probe into allegations related to the department.

The agency named Nehru, his relatives and several officials as accused.

The allegations include a Rs 888-crore cash-for-jobs scam, in which money was allegedly collected from candidates in exchange for government jobs, as well as irregularities in contracts worth around Rs 1,020 crore and illegal transfers and postings linked to the department.

The Enforcement Directorate (ED) had earlier shared details of the alleged irregularities with Tamil Nadu authorities, following which the matter came under scrutiny.

However, the Madras high court later granted an interim stay on further action by the vigilance agency and proceedings against the accused. Legal proceedings in the matter are continuing.

(With ANI inputs)

World.title: Razing of illegal mosque sparks row in UP's Saharanpur, SP MP put under house arrest
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Authorities on Saturday demolished a mosque located inside the district magistrate's office complex in Uttar Pradesh's Saharanpur after a court upheld an earlier order declaring the structure illegal.

Senior administrative officials, including the district magistrate and sub-divisional magistrate, reached the site as bulldozers began demolishing the structure. The collectorate complex was placed under heavy security, with Provincial Armed Constabulary (PAC) personnel deployed and all gates shut as a precaution.

SP MP Iqra Hasan claims she was placed under house arrest

Meanwhile, Samajawadi Party MP Iqra Hussain claimed that she was put under house arrest at her residence ahead of her scheduled visit to Saharanpur.

Hasan said that a large police force was deployed outside her residence overnight and prevented her from leaving for Saharanpur.

"A large police force was deployed at my Kairana residence overnight, and I was placed under house arrest to prevent me from going to Saharanpur. I intended to visit Saharanpur to meet officials regarding the Collectorate mosque issue and to voice the concerns of the people of my constituency, but I was not even allowed to leave my home," Hasan told news agency ANI.





"In a democracy, public representatives are elected to raise the voice of the people. That voice cannot be suppressed by stopping me," she added.

The demolition came a day after the district judge's court dismissed an appeal filed by the Muslim side challenging the City Magistrate's order.

On September 4, the district judge's court, after hearing arguments from both sides and examining the evidence presented, upheld the city magistrate's order declaring the mosque illegal.

The city magistrate's court had on July 17 ordered the demolition of the mosque and imposed compensation of around Rs 6.41 crore on the occupants over alleged illegal encroachment and misuse of government land.

The case was initiated following a complaint by Vikas Tyagi, former provincial coordinator of Bajrang Dal, who alleged that the mosque had been built illegally inside the DM office complex, a sensitive government premises where confidential administrative work is carried out.

The complaint also alleged that the premises were being used for commercial purposes apart from religious activities. According to the allegations, a post office was operating from the site and some rooms had been rented out to outsiders, with the mosque committee allegedly collecting monthly rent.

The district administration had argued that the alleged encroachment and commercial use of the premises raised security concerns, particularly given the sensitive nature of government operations conducted there.

The development comes amid similar administrative action against alleged illegal religious structures in various parts of Uttar Pradesh.

World.title: Punjab government to hike DA of 85,000 employees from 42 to 60 pc: Minister Aman Arora
World.content:
Punjab government will raise the Dearness Allowance of around 85,000 government employees

Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

Chandigarh, Punjab government will raise the Dearness Allowance of around 85,000 government employees recruited after July 17, 2020 by 18 per cent to 60 per cent, Cabinet Minister Aman Arora said on Friday.Speaking to mediapersons here, Arora said a recommendation in this regard was made by the Cabinet Sub-Committee formed to examine the issues of employees.The announcement is significant as employees recruited after July 17, 2020 were getting a pay equivalent to the Central pay scales, along with 42 per cent Dearness Allowance (DA). These were much lower than the pay scales of employees recruited before July 2020, who were paid as per the Punjab Pay Commission.Arora said there were two pay scales in Punjab, which was leading to conflicting interests and confusion: the Punjab basic pay scales and the one equivalent to the Central basic pay scales (as per the 7th Central Pay Commission)."Punjab basic pay scales, which traditionally are higher, range from 30 to 70 per cent more than the Central basic pay. And when DA is added to it, which is currently 42 per cent, the salary increases much above the Central pay scales," he said."When we calculate and compare, even with 60 per cent DA added to Central basic pay, the Punjab pay scales and take-home salaries are higher," he said.Arora said the previous Congress government had decided to hire employees on the Central pay scales after July 17, 2020.In the last six years, 85,000 employees have been recruited.The Mann government will give them a "Janmashtami gift" as the three-member Cabinet Sub-Committee has decided that the DA of these employees will be raised from 42 to 60 per cent. The committee's recommendation will be sent to the chief minister, Arora said.He, however, said that this hike will not benefit employees recruited before July 2020."From day one, the Bhagwant Mann government has been talking about the welfare of every section. We cannot imagine good governance without our employees," he said.The development comes amid over 3 lakh government employees, who went on a statewide strike on August 27, pressing the state government to accept their various demands, including the release of their pending 18 per cent DA.They have also threatened to go on mass casual leave on September 8 if the state government does not withdraw a recent notice imposing disciplinary action against those who remained on "unauthorised absence" on August 27.The employees have given the state government time till September 7 to withdraw the notice issued to protesting employees.Punjab government on Thursday appealed to employee unions to engage with it through dialogue rather than confrontation, calling employees the backbone of good governance.

World.title: Munnar plantation worker narrowly escapes wild elephant attack
World.content:
A man had a narrow escape after two wild elephants charged at him in Munnar on Friday (September 4, 2026).

According to local residents, the incident occurred at the Lower Division of the Kannimala estate, under Kanan Devan Hills Plantations (KDHP). The worker, identified as Muniyandi, was standing outside his plantation quarters (layam) when two wild elephants suddenly charged at him. Muniyandi fled immediately, managing to escape unhurt. Residents reported that the herd entered the residential area around early Friday morning.

Elephant sightings are frequent across the Munnar hill tracts, where recurring human-wildlife conflict continues to stoke fear among labourers. Workers stated that persistent elephant presence has made them afraid to step outdoors or report to work in the tea estates.

Munnar Range Officer S. Biju said that upon receiving the information, the forest department’s rapid response team (RRT) rushed to the spot and chased the elephants back into the forest. “The RRT members are monitoring the movements of the wild elephants in the area,” said the official.

World.title: KTR warns Congress against seeking KCR’s resignation, recalls 2006 episode
World.content:
Bharat Rashtra Samithi (BRS) working president K.T. Rama Rao hit out at Telangana Chief Minister A. Revanth Reddy and the Congress government and warned that the ruling party would face a political backlash similar to what it encountered in 2006.

Addressing a protest in Karimnagar on Saturday (September 5, 2026) on the 1000-day rule of the Congress, KTR questioned the demand for former Chief Minister K. Chandrashekar Rao’s resignation. “Why should KCR resign? Should the person who brought Telangana resign?” he asked, asserting that Mr. Reddy should step down instead.

Recalling the political developments of 2006, when Congress leaders had demanded Mr. Chandrashekar Rao’s resignation in Karimnagar, KTR said the BRS leader’s resignation from the Lok Sabha and the subsequent political developments had dealt a blow to the Congress. He warned that the ruling party should remember that episode before asking for KCR’s resignation again.

He predicted that the Chief Minister and the Congress would face a similar political outcome if they continued to target the BRS chief.

He said the Chief Minister and Congress leaders should take responsibility for what he described as the government’s “420 promises” and alleged failures. “They should resign 420 times for the 420 promises,” he said.

Reacting to the dismissal of a Minister [Konda Surekha] from the State Cabinet, Mr. KTR said removing one Minister would not resolve the Congress government’s problems. “The days are not far when your government itself will be dismissed,” he warned.

He said the BRS would continue to question the Congress government over its election promises and alleged failures, and issued a warning to the ruling party to “remember” the political consequences of its action.

Challenges Rahul Gandhi

KTR also attacked Congress leader Rahul Gandhi challenging him to come to Telangana with his ‘Chatron ki Ghoonj’ programme to see the reality. “Why is Rahul Gandhi shying away from Telangana. Is he fearing the students’ backlash here?” he asked.

He said Mr. Gandhi should focus on Telangana youngsters’ wishes as well after promising the moon before the Assembly elections.

World.title: Bengaluru-Mangaluru Vande Bharat Express is two hours late during run time trial
World.content:
South Western Railway is carrying out the run time trial of the Bengaluru-Mangaluru Vande Bharat Express on September 5.

A 16-coach rake was deployed for the run time trial, which commenced in Yesvantpur in Bengaluru. The train will reach Mangaluru Central and was expected to commence the return journey on the same day.

Bengaluru Mangaluru Vande Bharat run time trial

During the run time trial, the Vande Bharat Express was scheduled to reach Subrahmanya Road Station, in Dakshina Kannada district of Karnataka, at 12 noon, but pulled in as late as 1.55 p.m.

Tentatively, the train is expected to cover the distance from Bengaluru to Mangaluru in 8 hours and 20 minutes. The return journey is expected to take 8 hours.

In August, railway officials carried out trial runs on the Sakleshpur-Subrahmanya Road ghat section from August 12-20.

Drawing up a schedule for the train

Following successful completion of the trial run of Vande Bharat Express on the Sakleshpur-Subrahmanya Road Ghat section in August second week, the Railway Ministry ordered the timing trial of the VB Express between Bengaluru (Yesvantpur) and Mangaluru Central, on Saturday (September 5, 2026).

While the Ghat section trial was conducted using an automatic emergency brake (AEB)-fitted 20-car VB rake, the timing trial would be conducted using an AEB-fitted 16-car VB rake.

Tentative schedule

Bengaluru-Mangaluru Departure Mangaluru-Bengaluru Departure Yesvantpur (Bengaluru) 6.05 AM Mangaluru Central 3 PM Hassan 9.05 AM Subrahmanya Road 4.35 PM Sakleshpur 10 AM Sakleshpur 6.35 PM Subrahmanya Road 12.35 PM Hassan 7.30 PM Mangaluru Central 2.25 PM Yesvantpur (Bengaluru) 11 PM

As per the schedule issued by the South Western Railway Headquarters (HQ) on Thursday (September 3, 2026), the VB Express would depart Yevantpur at 6.05 a.m. to arrive at Mangaluru Central at 2.25 p.m. (8.20 hours). En-route, it would depart Hassan at 9.05 a.m., Sakleshpur at 10 a.m. and Subrahmanya Road at 12.35 p.m.

In the return run, the trial rake would depart Central at 3 p.m. to reach Yesvantpur at 11 p.m. En-route, it would depart Subrahmanya road at 4.35 p.m., Sakleshpur at 6.35 p.m. and Hassan at 7.30 p.m.

Mudit Mittal, Divisional Railway Manager of Mysuru Division, told The Hindu that the run time trial is being carried out to assess the actual timing taken for the operation of the service. The route, timings, and halts, would be finalised by the Railway Ministry after receiving the results of the run time trial.

World.title: Nepal floods: Indian volunteers take relief to isolated communities
World.content:
For nearly 20 members of a family in Trishuli, one room has become home after devastating floods destroyed homes, cut roads and left several families without basic amenities. A week on, Indian volunteers are travelling up to 10 hours through damaged mountain roads and bridges to take food, bedding and household essentials to such communities, while some areas of Rasuwa remain accessible only by helicopter.

The relief effort is increasingly shifting from accessible flood-hit areas to isolated settlements, where families have lost homes, livestock, belongings and livelihoods, but the terrain and damaged infrastructure make reaching them difficult.

“Almost a week after the floods, some of the more accessible areas are slowly seeing relief reach them, but our biggest concern now is reaching the families who have been most severely affected and remain isolated,” Manohar Naidu, a Khalsa Aid volunteer, told The Hindu from Nepal.

In Trishuli, Tupche and other remote communities, volunteers have found several families living together with little shelter or basic household equipment. Some, they said, have effectively lost everything.

Nepal flash floods: What caused the devastation?

The volunteers also described mass burials being carried out as mortuaries run out of space, with forest land being cleared to accommodate bodies as the death toll rises and many remain unidentified.

“Our immediate support is focused on essential relief such as food, clothing, bedding and basic household requirements. At the same time, we are assessing and documenting what each community will need for longer-term recovery,” Mr. Naidu said.

Reaching the affected communities has become a major logistical challenge. Some journeys from Kathmandu to areas such as Trishuli take nine to 10 hours, with damaged or completely washed-out roads and bridges forcing volunteers to take longer routes. Teams are travelling in trucks carrying supplies, while demand for 4x4 vehicles has surged, making them difficult to arrange and prompting suppliers to raise prices.

The problem is more acute in Rasuwa, where some affected areas have no road connectivity and helicopters are the only practical option. Each trip can cost around $2,000, significantly increasing the cost of delivering relief.

“So the challenge is not simply having relief material available. The biggest challenge is getting that aid to the families who need it most,” Mr. Naidu said.

The organisation is procuring supplies locally, but demand is outstripping availability for mattresses, solar lights and other household items.

“People need much more than food. They are asking how they are going to rebuild their lives,” Mr. Naidu said.

The next phase will require shelter, clean water and sanitation and getting children back into education, followed by restoring livelihoods and rebuilding homes, roads, bridges and community infrastructure.

Khalsa Aid had earlier proposed adopting inaccessible villages for longer-term support. The proposal is being assessed on the extent of damage, families affected, livelihood losses and infrastructure needs, with the aim of concentrating resources in severely affected communities rather than spreading assistance thinly.

The organisation is also considering temporary holding centres with mattresses, portable washroom facilities and cooking arrangements for families living together without basic amenities.

Ten Indian volunteers are currently involved in logistics, assessments, packing and distribution. Many have prior disaster-response experience, including during the recent Assam floods, but Nepal has posed added challenges of mountainous terrain, long journeys and limited electricity and internet connectivity.

The organisation has also sought official permission to clear debris in local areas to restore connectivity and ease access to affected communities.

World.title: ‘Utlotsavam’ steals the show at ISKCON festival
World.content:
‘Utlotsavam’ or ‘Dahi Handi’ turned out to be the major attraction at the three-day ‘Sri Krishna Janmashtami’ festivities at the Lotus Temple maintained by the International Society for Krishna Consciousness (ISKCON) in Tirupati on Friday (September 6, 2026).

Local youths jumped merrily into the ring to try their luck at beating the pot tied at a height, where they formed vertical pyramids to reach the top. The traditional festival is performed every year on the sprawling ground abutting the temple to celebrate the event observed during Lord Krishna’s childhood, which is followed even today in Vrindavan.

The youths, braving the gush of water poured on them in an apparent bid to dissuade them, climbed atop the pyramid and bagged the pot tied at the summit, indicating their victory.

Meanwhile, the ‘Hare Krishna Road’ leading to the temple was tastefully decorated with electrical serial lighting and images representing mythological episodes from Srimad Bhagavatha.

The temple premises were draped with garlands made of rare and exotic flowers. The wide altar at this temple is quite unique in nature, as it depicts the idols of Lord Krishna and Radha along with those of their eight accomplices (Ashtasakhis), which is considered a rare phenomenon in the ISKCON group of temples.

As the temple is thronged by a heavy crowd on these three days, Alipiri police have barricaded the entire street to restrict vehicular movement and also appealed to the crowd to maintain order.

The three-day festivities also coincide with the birth anniversary of ISKCON founder Srila Prabhupada, observed in a grand manner over the weekend.

World.title: How three Keralam nuns stitched together clothing venture ‘Stand By Me’ in a struggle for survival after standing up against the Church
World.content:
Sewing was once just another skill they learnt at the convent. Today, it has become their way of stitching together a life of their own.

At St. Francis Mission Home at Kuravilangad in Kottayam district of Keralam, a place that was once at the centre of a storm within the Catholic Church, sewing machines now hum through the day. Fabric is measured and cut, needles run through cloth, and one garment after another takes shape.

Behind the machines are three nuns who, after years of living an isolated life and struggling even to meet their basic needs, are now building something they can call their own, a small clothing venture named ‘Stand By Me’.

Sustained by friends, well-wishers

Nighties, churidar tops, co-ord sets, bags, table mats and runners are among the products that emerge from their workspace. A desperate bid for survival has gradually grown into a fledgling business, sustained by friends and well-wishers who stood by them through some of the most difficult years of their lives.

But every stitch in that little workspace carries the weight of a far more difficult journey.

In 2018, a nun accused former Jalandhar Bishop Franco Mulakkal of rape after repeated attempts to seek redress from senior Church authorities failed. Her complaint set off a chain of events that shook the Church and sparked a nationwide debate over its power structures.

On September 8 that year, five nuns, including the three now at Kuravilangad, staged a sit-in in Kochi demanding justice. It was an unprecedented protest, with a group of nuns publicly challenging the authority of the Church hierarchy. Days later, Bishop Mulakkal, then head of the Latin Catholic Diocese of Jalandhar, was arrested.

But the arrest did not bring their ordeal to an end.

When a local court acquitted Bishop Mulakkal on January 14, 2022, citing lack of evidence, the nuns were left facing an uncertain future within the Church. The survivor has since challenged the verdict in the Kerala High Court.

As the legal battle continued, their lives inside the convent became increasingly difficult. In 2023, the financial assistance available to them was stopped, leaving them struggling to meet even their basic expenses. Their circumstances eventually came to the attention of the Keralam government, which issued them ration cards in January this year (2026).

Two of the nuns, both MSW graduates, tried to find internships. But opportunities proved difficult to come by, which they believed was because of their association with the high-profile case.

“We wondered how we would survive without even a penny in our hands,” one of them recalled.

As the pressure mounted, two of the five eventually left religious life. The remaining three chose to stay together. And it was at this point that they stopped looking for a job and decided to create one for themselves.

With help from well-wishers, they bought sewing machines and revived the tailoring skills they had learnt years ago. The first orders came from friends and supporters. As word spread, the trickle of orders gradually turned into a steady stream.

Exhibition sales

The little venture has since grown enough to employ two workers. The nuns have also taken their products to exhibition sales in different parts of the State and are now preparing to take ‘Stand By Me’ online soon. “The name was suggested by the very people who had stood by them through their most difficult years. We embraced it readily’’, a nun said.

Today, ‘Stand By Me’ carries the story of three women who have gone from struggling to meet even their basic needs to building a life they can sustain on their own.

World.title: Nepal floods: Indian volunteers take relief to isolated communities as access remains a challenge
World.content:
Devastating floods in Nepal have left a 20-member family in Trishuli confined to a single room, cut off from all outside assistance. With no basic facilities and several families struggling to find adequate shelter, the flood emergency has given way to a harder struggle — finding food, bedding and other essentials while waiting for a way to reconnect with the outside world.

A week after the disaster, Indian volunteers trying to reach such families are travelling for up to 10 hours through difficult mountain terrain, navigating damaged roads and bridges, while some affected areas in Rasuwa have no road access at all.

For volunteers, the focus has now shifted from the more accessible flood-hit areas to these isolated communities, where the scale of need is often greatest but reaching help is proving the hardest. “Almost a week after the floods, some of the more accessible areas are slowly seeing relief reach them, but our biggest concern now is reaching the families who have been most severely affected and remain isolated,” Manohar Naidu, a Khalsa Aid volunteer, told The Hindu from Nepal.

Nepal flash floods: What caused the devastation?

In Trishuli, Tupche and other remote affected communities, volunteers have found families who have lost homes, livestock, household belongings and their sources of income. Some, they said, have essentially lost everything.

The volunteers described mass burials being carried out as mortuaries run out of space, with forest lands being cleared to accommodate the bodies as the death toll rises and many remain unidentified.

“Our immediate support is focused on essential relief such as food, clothing, bedding and basic household requirements. At the same time, we are assessing and documenting what each community will need for longer-term recovery,” Mr. Naidu said.

From Kathmandu, reaching some of these communities can take nine to 10 hours by road through difficult mountain terrain, volunteers shared. Roads and bridges damaged by the floods have made the journey even harder, while vehicles travelling into the affected areas are suffering damage.

The volunteers are travelling on trucks to deliver supplies, while demand for 4x4 vehicles has surged. Arranging suitable vehicles is becoming a challenge, with suppliers also raising prices amid the high demand, the volunteers said.

In Rasuwa, the problem is more acute. Some of the affected areas currently have no road connectivity at all, leaving helicopters as the only practical means of reaching them in many cases. But a single helicopter trip can cost around $2,000, making it an expensive proposition for humanitarian organisations trying to move relief into isolated communities.

“So the challenge is not simply having relief material available. The biggest challenge is getting that aid to the families who need it most,” Mr. Naidu said.

The shortage is not limited to transport. Khalsa Aid is procuring supplies locally, but demand has outstripped the available supply of essentials such as mattresses, solar lights and other household items.

The shift in focus has come as the teams have travelled deeper into the affected areas and seen how sharply conditions differ away from the main roads. “People need much more than food. They are asking how they are going to rebuild their lives,” Mr. Naidu said.

For many families, that rebuilding will begin with the most basic necessities — shelter, clean water and sanitation, household items and getting children back into education.

Further ahead lies the more difficult task of restoring livelihoods, while damaged homes, roads, bridges and other community infrastructure will also need to be rebuilt.

Khalsa Aid had earlier proposed adopting some of the inaccessible villages and supporting them through the recovery process.

“The proposal is still being assessed and teams are looking at the extent of damage, the number of families affected, loss of livelihoods and infrastructure requirements before committing resources. The idea is to concentrate resources on severely affected communities where sustained intervention could make a meaningful difference rather than spread assistance thinly across a much larger area,” a volunteer said.

The organisation is also considering temporary holding centres where affected families could be provided mattresses, portable washroom facilities and arrangements for cooking, particularly where several families are currently living together without basic amenities.

For the volunteers from India, the work has meant moving between logistics, assessments, packing and distribution while working directly with communities.

Many of the Indian volunteers have previous experience in disaster-response operations in India, including during the recent Assam floods. But Nepal has presented its own challenges — difficult mountain terrain, long journeys, limited electricity and internet connectivity and difficult transportation. “What stands out is their willingness to travel into difficult and remote locations despite the challenging terrain and conditions,” Mr. Naidu said.

The organisation has also sought official permission to help clear debris in some local areas to restore connectivity and make it easier to reach affected families, the volunteers said.

World.title: ECI bars former Velachery MLA Aassan Maulaana from contesting elections for three years
World.content:
The Election Commission of India (ECI) has disqualified J.M.H. Aassan Maulaana, who was elected from the Velachery Assembly constituency in Chennai on a Congress ticket in the 2021 Assembly elections, from contesting elections for a period of three years from August 2026.

According to the Election Commission’s order, the disqualification bars Mr. Maulaana from contesting elections to become a member of either the House of Parliament or of the Legislative Assembly or Legislative Council of a State or Union Territory. The Order said, Mr. Maulaana failed to lodge a true and correct account of his election expenses within the time and in the manner required under the Representation of the People Act, 1951.

According to the order, Mr. Maulaana had lodged his account of election expenses, declaring a total expenditure of ₹17,03,548, with the District Election Officer (DEO), Chennai, on May 24, 2021, within the prescribed time. However, the EC said the Returning Officer had issued a notice to Mr. Maulaana on March 30, 2021, raising the issue of whether s published by the Tamil Nadu Congress Committee (TNCC) in 10 newspapers were intended to promote his election.

Understatement of expenses

On March 31, 2021, Mr. Maulaana informed the EC that the Tamil Nadu Congress Committee had borne the stated  expenses independently. However, the DEO, Chennai, in his scrutiny report on June 19, 2021, did not accept the account and determined that there had been an understatement of ₹32,05,915 in respect of the s, the order said.

The Commission said with the understated amount of ₹32,05,915 added to the declared expenditure of ₹17,03,548, the total expenditure came to ₹49,09,463, exceeding the then permissible ceiling of ₹30.80 lakh prescribed under Rule 90 of the Conduct of Election Rules, 1961.

Mr. Maulaana unsuccessfully contested the 2026 Assembly election from Velachery Assembly segment and finished third.

World.title: Police charge sheet says building management at fault for Gul Plaza inferno
World.content:
KARACHI: Police on Saturday submitted a charge sheet before the South judicial magistrate on the Gul Plaza fire, blaming the building management’s “negligence”.

The deadly inferno , which erupted on the night of January 17 at the mall and took nearly two days to be fully extinguished , had claimed at least 73 lives and left over 1,100 shops in ruins.

A previous charge sheet submitted in July had named six people — including 11-year-old Huzaifa — as the accused. However, a judicial magistrate had rejected the document, noting that the investigating officer (IO) had not conducted a thorough and satisfactory probe.

The fresh charge sheet, dated September 3 and submitted by the Nabi Bux police, names four of those six as the accused sent for trial: Huzaifa’s father Naimatullah who owned an artificial flower shop; Gul Plaza Traders Association President Tanveer Pasta; along with association members Ammar Ismail and Muhammad Ramzan.

The document stated that the Gul Plaza administration did not have adequate tools to extinguish the fire, considering the scale of the building.

It added that there was “no alternative arrangement for emergency lights, due to which people faced difficulties leaving” the building.

It noted that during the investigation, the complainant in the case said only two of the building’s gates were open at the time of the fire. “People could not leave due to the locks on the grills of the gates,” the charge sheet read.

It went on to say that the iron gates on the third floor were padlocked, which “showed that the Gul Plaza administration had their guards close them”.

The document further pointed out that the building management had K-Electric switch off the power supply “despite knowing that they do not have any other alternative arrangement for lighting”.

More to follow

World.title: Asif says devolution of power is 'inevitable', accuses PPP of having contradictory stance on new provinces
World.content:
Defence Minister Khawaja Asif has said that the devolution of power is “inevitable”, while also accusing the PPP of having a contradictory stance on the issue of new provinces.

“When there is talk of a Saraiki province in Punjab, the PPP supports it or shows a soft corner on this issue. And when there is talk of multiple provinces or administrative units instead of four, talk of ‘Sindhudesh’ begins,” he said in a post on the social media platform X late Friday night.

On Friday, the Muttahida Qaumi Movement-Pakistan (MQM-P) was denied the opportunity to present a resolution against the “Sindhudesh movement”. The PPP had slammed the party for attempting to “mislead the people” by tabling the resolution.

Asif said that he saw “something else” behind this “dual policy” by the PPP, adding that he would delve into this deeper “when the time comes”.

“We are first and foremost Pakistanis. Devolution was decided as a constitutional principle through the 18th Amendment, which was not respected. Time and circumstance demand that it be implemented with integrity,” he said.

He said that concentration of power had made the current system obsolete, which needed to be “corrected”.

“Provinces or administrative units, whatever label you want to apply. You have 36 divisions, use them, or devise some other administrative-geographical scheme. The devolution of power is inevitable,” he said.

Asif’s remarks come as the PPP, a key ally of the PML-N-led ruling coalition, has questioned Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif’s silence over the debate on creating new provinces and sought his stance on the matter.

The PPP had earlier maintained that any move to create additional federating units must follow the procedure laid down in the Constitution. However, the PPP-led Sindh government on Wednesday got a resolution passed by the provincial assembly opposing any further division of the country’s existing four provinces.

A debate over the creation of new federating units has continued for the past couple of months in different circles, although there has been no official confirmation about the origin or contours of any proposal. However, some ruling-party leaders and federal cabinet members have publicly expressed support for the idea at different forums, including parliament.

Media reports have suggested proposals ranging from eight to as many as 30 provinces, though no official plan has been announced.

Talking to Dawn on Friday, PPP Parliamentarians Secretary General Nayyar Hussain Bokhari sought the prime minister’s position on the issue.

Bokhari said that if the government was serious about increasing the number of provinces, it should first bring the matter before the federal cabinet, after which the prime minister should take all stakeholders and political parties on board.

He recalled that consultations between the government and political parties had continued for months during the framing of the 1973 Constitution, while deliberations preceding the 18th Constitutional Amendment had lasted for more than a year.

Bokhari, who also raised the issue during a talk show on DawnNewsTV on Friday, said the consent of the provinces was essential for carving out new federating units. He said any such move would also require the necessary constitutional amendment to be passed by both the National Assembly and Senate with a two-thirds majority.

The PML-N-led government enjoys a two-thirds majority in the National Assembly with the PPP’s support. Therefore, if the PPP pulled back its support, it would become impossible for the government to implement the idea.

Responding to a question about the local government system in the country, Bokhari said any move in that regard must also follow the Constitution, particularly Article 140-A, which provides for the establishment of local governments by the provinces.

Meanwhile, PML-N leader and Adviser to the Prime Minister on Political Affairs Rana Sanaullah on Friday reiterated that no preparations were currently under way for the creation of new provinces.

Sanaullah told a private television channel that no bill or resolution regarding the creation of new provinces had been presented in parliament.

He said consultation and consensus among political parties would be essential before any such bill or resolution could be brought before parliament.

Responding to a question, he said there was currently no discussion under way regarding the division of the existing provinces.

World.title: Skardu by-election: Polling underway at 61 polling stations amid tight security
World.content:
GILGIT: Polling is currently underway at 61 polling stations in the GBA-09 (Skardu-III) constituency amid tight security. The process began at 8am and will continue till 5pm.

State broadcaster PTV said 33,985 voters would exercise their right to franchise, adding that special security arrangement had been made for the occasion.

A local holiday has been declared in the constituency. According to the notification issued by the Skardu district magistrate, the holiday was declared to “facilitate eligible voters in exercising their right to franchise and to ensure the smooth and peaceful conduct of polls”.

The by-election was announced by the Gilgit-Baltistan Election Commission after the GB Supreme Appellate Court disqualified PPP candidate Fida Muhammad Nashad, who had been declared a returned candidate in the June general elections.

Nashad’s son, Akhtar Abbas, is contesting the election on PPP’s ticket, while Mohammad Ajmal is contesting from the PML-N. Former minister Mohammad Saleem, who is contesting as an independent, is also among 10 candidates who have filed their nomination papers.

Analysts said a close contest was expected between PPP’s Abbas and independent candidate Saleem. They said Abbas could retain his father’s vote bank and may benefit from public sympathy following Nashad’s disqualification by the GB Supreme Appellate Court.

District Returning Officer (DRO) Hamza Murad told Dawn on Friday that GBA-09 had 61 polling stations, of which 25 had been declared sensitive under Category A, 11 had been placed in Category B as medium-sensitive, and 25 had been classified as normal under Category C.

World.title: Passport collection counters to remain open on Saturdays for 2 months
World.content:
Passport delivery counters will now be open on Saturdays from 8am to 4pm for the next two months, according to a public notice issued by the Directorate General of Immigration and Passports (DGIP).

The public notice, available on the DGIP’s official website and was also shared on social media, advised citizens to collect their passports as soon as possible.

It called on citizens who were unable to visit during regular office hours to take advantage of the new timings.

The DGIP warned that passports remaining unclaimed for six months would be destroyed, as per government policy.

In July, the DGIP partnered with logistics and courier company TCS to launch “Passport Aapki Dehleez Par” — a home delivery service for passports.

DGIP Director General Muhammad Ali Randhawa said the initiative reflected the department’s commitment to making passport services more accessible and efficient.

In June, the government had also announced that it had decided to phase out machine-readable passports and switch fully to e-passports.

According to Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi, the complete transition to e-passports will “end fraud and forgery related to passports”.

World.title: War has made Tehran more confident, say US intelligence agencies
World.content:
WASHINGTON: Intelli­gence agencies in the United States believe that six months of war may have made Iran more, not less, confident in its ability to withstand American pressure and continue the conflict.

A New York Times report, published on Friday, says “Iran has grown more confident in its ability to attack targets in the Middle East and appears determined to continue the conflict for months to frustrate the United States”.

The assessment comes as clashes resumed this week.

“The new exchanges have been limited so far. But the intelligence reports, according to people who have read them, suggest that Iran’s hardline government might be contemplating a significant escalation,” the newspaper reported.

The intelligence assessments also indicate that reaching an agreement to end the war could prove difficult. Current and former US officials told the NYT that there are few indications Tehran is ready to make a deal with Washington.

Mid-term elections

Some officials believe Tehran may seek to prolong the conflict until at least the US mid-term elections in November, calculating that continued warfare and high energy prices could create difficulties for President Trump and Republicans.

The report notes Donald Trump is currently not pursuing negotiations as he believes that economic pressure can force Tehran to make concessions concerning its control of the Strait of Hormuz and, eventually, its nuclear programme. But officials familiar with the intelligence told the NYT that sanctions could provoke further escalation.

Missile and drone capability

Iran’s military calculations appear shaped by its growing missile and drone capability and by its understanding of how to use the Strait of Hormuz as leverage. The strait carried roughly one-fifth of the world’s oil before the war.

Representative Jason Crow, a Colorado Democrat and member of the House Intelligence Committee, described the Iranian leadership as increasingly confident. “Iranians are feeling pretty bullish about their position,” he said.

But at the same time he acknowledged that Iran has suffered substantial damage.

Other officials briefed on the intelligence said Iran may also believe that the United States will be constrained in launching major new attacks as its ammunition stocks decline.

Representative Josh Gottheimer, a New Jersey Democrat and Intelligence Committee member, said: “The Iranians think they have maximum leverage.”

He suggested that, from Tehran’s perspective, continuing to pressure the Trump administration could serve its interests.

The conflict has also opened a cyber front. According to the Times, US officials believe Iran-linked hackers were probably responsible for attacks on more than 100 American water systems in late July. The attacks did not appear to make drinking water unsafe, although some caused disruptions requiring manual overrides and precautionary boil-water advisories.

Officials said Iranian hackers have also shown interest in US oil and gas infrastructure.

The New York Times reported that Iranian-linked cyber hackers may have regrouped after suffering losses early in the war. Former intelligence officials and cybersecurity experts said such attacks could remain attractive to Tehran because even limited disruptions might weaken American public support for a conflict with no clear end.

Alex Orleans, a former US government cybersecurity contractor who tracks Iranian hacking groups, said Iran’s cyberoperators probably feel emboldened. He warned that even unsuccessful attacks could serve a broader purpose by exhausting public patience with the conflict.

Influencing political scene

The report also describes Iranian efforts to influence US politics, including propaganda and social-media activity focused on mid-term elections. Meta recently identified a small network of Iran-based accounts on Facebook and Instagram that posted material concerning US politics.

Taken together, the intelligence assessments present a picture of an Iranian government that has been damaged but does not regard itself as defeated. Six months of warfare may have strengthened Tehran’s belief that it can absorb punishment, retain important military capabilities and continue imposing costs on the United States and its allies.

Published in Dawn, September 5th, 2026

World.title: Bolivian army base blasts kill 2, wound dozens
World.content:
Two explosions at an army barracks in Bolivia killed at least two people and wounded 81 on Friday, authorities said.

Defence Minister Ernesto Justiniano said “pyrotechnic material” was stored at the base in Viacha, southwest of Bolivia’s administrative capital La Paz.

The exact cause of the blasts, which happened at around 2:30pm (1830 GMT), was under investigation, he said in a statement.

Footage circulated by local media showed a thick column of black smoke rising from the city center.

Houses in the area were damaged by the blasts, with footage showing shattered windows, broken ceilings and scattered debris.

Justiniano said two people were confirmed dead and seven people were missing.

The wounded, including two people in “serious condition,” were taken to medical centres, he added.

The dead and missing were soldiers serving at the base, the defence ministry said.

An earlier police report said 59 people were wounded, at least 52 of them civilians.

Firefighters rushed to the base following the blasts, and residents were evacuated to a temporary shelter.

The power supply was cut off in the area, where dozens of police officers had been deployed, an AFP journalist observed.

President Rodrigo Paz expressed his “deep solidarity with the families of the deceased, the injured and all residents affected by the explosions.” He said he had ordered a “thorough, technical and transparent” investigation.

“We must establish with absolute clarity the causes of this event, verify compliance with safety protocols and determine any responsibilities that may arise,” he said in a post on X.

Viacha’s authorities have declared three days of mourning.

Justiniano said that there were two successive blasts.

The first detonation was believed to have involved “black powder corresponding to pyrotechnic material stored at the site,” he said.

It was followed by a “second detonation of much greater magnitude,” he said, adding that the cause and the material that exploded were still being determined.

The defence ministry said no military weapons had been detonated.

“At this time, our priority is people: caring for the injured, supporting their families, and continuing search and verification efforts,” Justiniano said.

World.title: Govt reduces petrol price by Rs3.13, increases HSD by Rs3.74
World.content:
The government on Friday reduced the price of petrol by Rs3.13 per litre while increasing the price of high-speed diesel (HSD) by Rs3.74 per litre.

Following the revision, petrol will retail at Rs345.87 per litre while HSD will cost Rs378.05 per litre. The government continues to levy Rs114 per litre in taxes and duties on petrol and Rs100 per litre on diesel.

According to the Petroleum Division’s notification, the new prices will remain in effect from Sept 5 (Saturday) to Sept 7 (Monday).

The price of HSD has come down from a peak of Rs520.35 recorded on April 3. Its price had started rising from Rs281 per litre after the US-Iran war broke out on February 28.

The petrol price had peaked at Rs458.41 on April 3 after beginning its upward trajectory from Rs266 in the first week of March.

On July 17, Petroleum Minister Ali Pervaiz Malik announced that fuel prices would now be fixed on a daily basis due to fluctuations in international market prices following renewed hostilities between Iran and the US.

Prior to this, the government had been announcing weekly revisions to fuel prices since early March, alongside measures for the conservation of fuel amid possible oil supply disruptions due to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. The federal government in April also announced targeted relief measures to provide subsidised fuel.

The petroleum minister stated that the cabinet and the prime minister had decided to give the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra) the responsibility of deciding fuel prices on a daily basis based on international market trends.

Petrol is mainly used in private transport, small vehicles, rickshaws and two-wheelers, and changes in its price affect the middle and lower-middle classes.

Similarly, changes in diesel prices also impact the public at large, as it is mainly used in the heavy transport sector, power plants and large generators.

Petrol and high-speed diesel (HSD) are the major revenue earners, with monthly sales of about 700,000 to 800,000 tonnes, compared to just 10,000 tonnes of monthly demand for kerosene.

World.title: 4 abducted Chinese nationals rescued in Islamabad
World.content:
ISLAMABAD: The capital police recovered four Chinese nationals kidnapped for ransom after an encounter with a gang of criminals.

Earlier, the suspect was arrested in connection with a case registered at Shalimar Police Station and was being interrogated by the robbery and dacoity unit of the capital police.

During interrogation, the suspect disclosed that he, along with his accomplices, kidnapped the four Chinese nationals from F-10/4 for ransom. After the kidnapping, the victims were shifted to Bangial area and detained at a dairy farm. The suspect further disclosed that bargaining was in progress over the ransom for the release of the Chinese nationals. The suspect also offered assistance in taking the police to the farm.

A police team was constituted for the raid, and after reaching the area, the team cordoned off the farm. However, the suspect present inside the farm started indiscriminate firing at the police team, and as a result, panic spread in the area.

The police also retaliated and fired. Later, the police succeeded in capturing two kidnappers who were guarding the captives, detained in an adjacent room of the farm. The police found the four Chinese nationals in the room and took them into their safe custody.

Later, the raiding team arrested four more kidnappers and recovered weapons from them. However, the ringleader of the gang managed to escape from the spot.

Published in Dawn, September 5th, 2026

World.title: Ramisa rape and murder: Sohel Rana mentions new name as charges framed
World.content:
A new name has surfaced in the Ramisa rape and murder case, with prime accused Sohel Rana telling reporters today that a man called "Dollar" was responsible for the rape and murder of the eight-year-old girl.

However, no further details about the person were immediately available.

Sohel made the claim while being escorted to the courtroom of the Dhaka Metropolitan Children Violence Suppression Tribunal.

"I am at fault, and Dollar is also at fault. I am not the only culprit," he told reporters.

Standing in the courtroom's dock, he shouted at the lawyers present in the courtroom after the hearing, and said, “I did not commit the rape; I only dismembered the body. A man named Dollar committed the rape. I have sinned, so punish me for that sin.”

At that time, Sohel further claimed that Dollar had promised to pay him Tk 2 lakh if he could bring the girl to him.

However, police officers present immediately stopped him from speaking further.

Sohel also claimed that his wife, Swapna Khatun, was innocent.

Earlier in the day, Sohel and Swapna were brought to the lock-up of the Metropolitan Sessions Judge's Court in Dhaka.

Later, Judge Masrur Salekin of the tribunal framed charges against the couple in the case over the rape and murder of Ramisa in Dhaka's Pallabi area.

Both accused pleaded not guilty after the charges were read out, said Bench Assistant Pankoj Peter Gomes.

The judge also fixed tomorrow for the start of the trial, with the victim's father, Abdul Hannan Mollah, scheduled to testify first, he added.

On May 24, Sub-Inspector Ohiduzzaman of Pallabi Police Station submitted the charge sheet before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate's Court in Dhaka, accusing Sohel of rape, murder and destruction of evidence, and Swapna of destruction of evidence and providing false information.

Several hours later, the CMM Court transferred the case to the Children Violence Suppression Tribunal for trial.

Ramisa, a second-grade student of Popular Model High School, was found beheaded on May 19 in the house of her neighbour, Sohel.

The following day, Ramisa's father filed a case with Pallabi Police Station, accusing the couple and an unidentified person.

According to the case statement, Sohel lured Ramisa into his room and raped her. Investigators said he later slit her throat and attempted to dismember the body to conceal the crime.

On May 20, police produced Sohel and Swapna before a Dhaka court, and court sources said Sohel agreed to give a confessional statement before a magistrate. The third and unidentified accused was on the run. Dhaka Metropolitan Magistrate Aminul Islam Junaid recorded Sohel's confessional statement after police brought him to the magistrate’s chamber, said a court staff member.

Sub-Inspector Ohiduzzaman of Pallabi Police Station told The Daily Star that day, the prime accused had already admitted to the crime during primary interrogation.

On May 22, the Dhaka Bar Association decided not to provide legal assistance to the accused following an emergency virtual meeting of its executive committee, citing the gravity of the allegations.

The next day, the government appointed Supreme Court lawyer Musa Kalimullah as a state defence counsel to represent the accused to ensure a fair trial.

This report has been corrected at 4:43pm. In the earlier version, Sohel Rana’s comment was misreported. We regret the error.

World.title: Why Bangladesh must pivot to renewable energy now
World.content:
There are moments in a nation’s history when a crisis does more than create hardship. It reveals the weakness of an old system and opens the door to a better one. Bangladesh is now standing at such a moment.

The country is facing an energy crisis that no longer centres on power cuts. It is affecting factories, farms, schools, offices, exports, foreign currency reserves, and the daily life of ordinary people. What we are seeing today is not just a temporary shortage of gas or fuel. It is a signal that our energy system has become too dependent on imported fossil fuels.

More than 60 percent of Bangladesh’s energy demand is met through imports. LNG, coal, oil, and other fossil fuels have kept the country running for years, but this dependence has become risky and expensive. Global fuel markets are unstable because of geopolitical tension, supply chain disruption, and price volatility. For a country like Bangladesh, this creates double pressure: fuel supply becomes uncertain while fuel costs keep rising.

The government is now spending more than BDT 200 crore per day in energy subsidies. Annual energy import expenditure remains around USD 12 billion, putting serious pressure on foreign currency reserves. Nearly 70 percent of Bangladesh’s LNG imports come from Qatar. If supply is disrupted, Bangladesh can quickly face a severe shortage. In the power sector, daily gas demand exceeds 2,500 mmcfd, but supply sometimes falls to 850–900 mmcfd. This can create a power generation shortfall of 1,500–1,800 MW. Overall, the daily gas shortage exceeds 1,100 mmcfd, and peak-time electricity shortages may reach nearly 2,000 MW.

Bangladesh also has a weak Strategic Petroleum Reserve. The current reserve capacity is sufficient for only about 35–40 days, well below that of countries such as China and Japan. This makes the national energy system even more vulnerable.

Visual: Teeni and Tuni

The impact is already visible. In the readymade garments sector, gas shortages and load shedding are reducing productivity by 25–30 percent in many cases. This threatens export earnings, foreign currency reserves, and economic stability. The crisis has also reached ordinary households. Although Bangladesh declared 100 percent electrification in 2022, many rural areas still experience 10 to 20 hours of load shedding every day during summer. This affects education, small businesses, agriculture, and people’s dignity.

We have also seen long lines at fuel stations, schools moving online, and offices shortening working hours because of fuel shortages. These are not isolated events. They show how deeply energy insecurity can disturb national life.

Over the last 15 years, electricity tariffs in Bangladesh have been increased on many occasions, including more than 10 rounds of increases at both bulk and retail levels. This path is not sustainable. Fossil-fuel-based electricity depends on imported fuel, global prices, the availability of the dollar, subsidies, and repeated tariff adjustments. Solar power offers a different path. With a one-time investment, solar can provide stable energy for 15–20 years. Once installed, its fuel cost is almost zero.

The economic comparison is clear. A 1 MW HFO-based power plant produces electricity per year at a cost of nearly BDT 190 crore, with much of the cost paid in foreign currency. In contrast, a 5 MW solar project requires a one-time investment of around BDT 25 crore, after which fuel costs are practically zero. Each 1 MW of solar power can save around USD 325,000 per year in foreign currency.

This is why renewable energy should not be discussed solely in technical terms like decarbonisation, emissions, and sustainability. For Bangladesh, renewable energy means jobs, fuel independence, savings in foreign currency, industrial competitiveness, agricultural protection, and economic strength. Policymakers and stakeholders can lead this transformation, inspiring confidence in a sustainable future.

Despite Bangladesh’s potential, renewable energy contributes less than 5 percent to power generation, far below the global 30 percent target by 2030. Clear, measurable goals and timelines are essential for effective policy planning and investment decisions.

Renewable energy equipment imports face around 50–60 percent in duties and taxes, hindering local manufacturing growth. Policy reforms that reduce import duties and support local industry can accelerate renewable deployment and reduce dependency on imports.

For Bangladesh, renewable energy means jobs, fuel independence, savings in foreign currency, industrial competitiveness, agricultural protection, and economic strength. Policymakers and stakeholders can lead this transformation, inspiring confidence in a sustainable future.

Import duty is usually imposed to protect the local industry. But where local production is not yet significant, a high duty only increases project costs, reduces investment returns, and slows renewable energy expansion. Policy reforms can unlock this potential, making stakeholders feel their efforts directly contribute to progress.

India, Pakistan, Vietnam, and China have expanded solar and wind power by offering low or zero import duties, tax exemptions, and low-interest financing. Many countries have also reduced duties on lithium-ion batteries and energy storage systems. Bangladesh should learn from these examples.

The barriers are clear: high duties and VAT, high financing costs of 10–12 percent or more, limited access to easy loans, slow approval processes, net metering delays, high LC margin, weak Merchant Power Policy, lack of clear policies for rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, floating solar, agrivoltaics, solar irrigation, and hybrid solar-storage, weak local manufacturing, and insufficient grid digitalisation. Addressing these collectively can accelerate Bangladesh's renewable journey, uniting stakeholders in a common goal.

One urgent reform is customs assessment. The current weight-based assessment system does not reflect the actual value of solar equipment. It can create artificial overvaluation and raise duties by three to four times. Bangladesh should shift to transaction-value-based assessment using pro forma or commercial invoice values, in line with international practice and WTO customs valuation principles.

The second urgent reform is the elimination of customs duty on renewable energy equipment. This should apply to Solar PV Module, Photovoltaic Cell, Solar Inverter, DC Cable, Data Logger, Aluminium Mounting Structure, Battery Pack, Battery Cell, BMS Circuit Board, PV DG Controller, Hybrid Controller, Solar Plant Safety Aluminium Walkway Mesh, Safety Accessories, and related components.

Current TTI rates are high. Solar PV Module carries 26.90 percent, Photovoltaic Cell 25.75 percent, Solar Inverter 28.73 percent, DC Cable 58.40 percent, Data Logger 37.25 percent, Aluminium Mounting Structure 58.40 percent, Battery Pack and Battery Cell 58.40 percent, BMS Circuit Board 31.50 percent, pack materials 37.25 percent, PV DG Controller or Hybrid Controller 89.08 percent, and Solar Plant Safety Aluminum Walkway Mesh 37.25 percent. These should be reduced to zero percent for renewable energy expansion.

The third reform is a tax holiday. Rooftop solar power producers and project companies should receive benefits comparable to those of utility-scale renewable energy producers. A practical structure could be a 100 percent tax holiday for the first 10 years, 50 percent for the next 3 years, and 25 percent for the next 2 years. This should apply to CAPEX, OPEX, IPP, and MPP models. A broader 10–20 year tax holiday for renewable energy projects should also be considered.

Bangladesh has a remarkable solar opportunity already waiting on its rooftops. About 7 percent of the country’s land is covered with concrete or other built structures. This means more than 10,000 square kilometres, or about 10 billion square meters of built surface. If only 30 percent is usable, that would give around 3 billion square meters. At 10 square meters per kW, this can create nearly 300 GW of solar potential. Bangladesh’s peak demand is only around 16–18 GW. The opportunity already exists on rooftops, factories, warehouses, schools, hospitals, government buildings, and commercial establishments.

Rooftop solar should therefore be relaunched nationwide with a clear business model. Utility-scale solar also needs support through unused khas land, transparent tendering, and grid readiness. Floating solar, river-based solar, agrivoltaics, solar irrigation, and hybrid solar-storage should receive separate policy attention.

The suspended solar projects must also be revisited. A total of 31 solar power projects, with a combined capacity of more than 3,000 MW, were previously suspended or cancelled. Many were being developed by foreign investors, with more than USD 200 million reportedly already invested. If implemented, these projects could save around BDT 10,800 crore annually in energy import costs. They should be reassessed and revived quickly.

Energy storage is another missing pillar. Solar and wind need storage support to become more reliable. Duties on lithium-ion batteries, BESS, and other storage systems should be reduced to zero. This will help stabilise renewable power and support future grid flexibility.

Electric vehicles can also become part of the solution. In China, Japan, and the United States, EVs are increasingly seen as mobile energy storage systems. A typical EV battery has a capacity of 40–70 kWh, enough to power an average household for 1–2 days. If Bangladesh had 1 million EVs, the country would have 40–70 GWh of distributed storage. This is several times higher than the daily peak demand gap. Solar-powered EV charging, vehicle-to-home, and vehicle-to-grid systems should be included in future energy planning.

If Bangladesh had 30–40 percent of the grid powered by solar, along with solar-powered EVs, the country would be far less exposed to global fuel market shocks. Long fuel lines, online schooling, shorter office hours, and industrial disruption could be reduced. Solar, storage, and EVs should now be planned together.

Finance will decide how fast this transition happens. Renewable energy projects cannot grow at interest rates below 10–12 percent. Long-term financing should be available at an interest rate of 3.5–4.5 percent. A 10–15-year financing facility at a maximum interest rate of 5 percent should be introduced. Bangladesh Bank’s green refinancing fund should be expanded. Rooftop and residential solar customers should be eligible for collateral-free loans. The LC margin for renewable equipment should be limited to 5%.

Net metering must be simplified. Approval should be completed within 15–30 days through a one-stop service. Approval, interconnection, inspection, billing adjustment, and utility coordination should all be simple and time-bound. Wheeling charges for renewable energy should also be kept reasonable and low. The Merchant Power Policy should be clear, simple, and investment-friendly so that industries and commercial consumers can directly procure renewable electricity.

Agriculture should also be included in the solar transition. Bangladesh can set a target to convert 1.5 million diesel irrigation pumps into solar pumps. This will reduce diesel imports, lower farmers’ production costs, and protect the environment. The program should include duty-free facilities, low-cost loans, investment support, and local service networks.

Waste-to-energy should also receive policy support. City corporations need clear rules, easy financing, and private-sector participation to enable urban waste management and distributed power generation to work together.

Bangladesh now needs a phased national roadmap for renewable energy.

In the short term, within 0–6 months, customs duty, VAT, and taxes on renewable energy equipment should be reduced to zero. Duties on lithium-ion batteries, BESS, and energy storage should be withdrawn. Approval for net metering should be obtained within 15–30 days. Industrial and commercial solar installations should be eligible for special incentives. The 31 suspended solar projects should be reassessed. Wheeling charges should be rationalised. Solar, storage, and EV charging should receive urgent policy support. Collateral-free lines of credit should be introduced for rooftop solar. NBR should quickly implement assessment reform and a 0 percent duty.

In the medium term, within 1–3 years, renewable energy financing should be available at a maximum interest rate of 5 percent for 10–15 years. The LC margin should be limited to 5 percent. Land banks and grid infrastructure should be developed for utility-scale solar. Merchant Power Policy and MPPA should be simplified. Rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, and hybrid solar-storage projects should receive a 10–15-year tax holiday. A national program should convert 1.5 million diesel pumps into solar pumps. Rooftop solar should be made mandatory or incentive-based for government buildings, industrial zones, EPZs, economic zones, and large commercial buildings. EV solar charging and distributed storage policies should be developed. Renewable energy skill development and employment programs should also be launched.

In the long term, within 3–10 years, Bangladesh should aim to reach more than 10,000 MW of solar power by 2030. Offshore and onshore wind should be developed. Floating solar, river-based solar, and agrivoltaics should be implemented. A National Energy Storage Strategy should be prepared. Smart grid and power sector digitalisation should be accelerated. Local assembly and manufacturing of solar panels, inverters, mounting structures, battery packs, BMS, and EV charging equipment should be encouraged. Regional power trade should be expanded. The Renewable Purchase Obligation should be introduced. Fossil fuel subsidies should be gradually redirected to a renewable energy transition fund.

Image Visual: Anwar Sohel

The benefits can be large. Energy import costs will fall. Pressure on foreign currency reserves will decline. Industrial production costs will reduce. Export competitiveness will improve. The subsidy burden will decrease. New investment will grow. Renewable energy can create 20–25 jobs per MW through rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, solar pumps, EV charging, battery storage, smart grids, manufacturing, installation, operation, and maintenance.

The government may worry about revenue loss from tax and duty exemptions. But this should be seen as an investment. In the short term, there may be a limited impact on revenue. In the long term, Bangladesh can save far more by reducing fuel imports, lowering subsidies, saving foreign currency, strengthening industries, and attracting new investment.

Bangladesh’s energy crisis is a major challenge but also a historic opportunity. The crisis is not only a supply problem. It is a policy framework problem. Renewable energy, especially solar power, storage, and EV integration, can be among the most practical solutions for the country.

The question is no longer whether Bangladesh should adopt renewable energy. The real question is how quickly, how systematically, and how boldly the country can complete this transition.



Mohammad Ataur Rahman Sarker is a renewable energy entrepreneur and the secretary of the Bangladesh Sustainable and Renewable Energy Association.

Md. Tanvir Siraj is a renewable energy researcher.

World.title: The forgotten art of Bengali advertising
World.content:
I have never seen someone at a rustic village market, anklets jingling, shouting slogans for "Khol Company’s Ringworm Ointment." No smooth-talker has ever leaned in, fanning out thin booklets like a deck of cards, whispering rhythmically, "Here are the mysteries of Gopal Bhar, and here—the secret love letters."

I never hid colourful s of a reclining Gauhar Jaan, cigarette in hand, between the folds of shirts in my drawer. I did indeed rummage through my grandfather’s pockets to collect old tram tickets, but none of them bore that curious notice for "Ashtavakra Toothpowder." Perhaps the elders of the house witnessed a tram tearing through the heart of a half-awake city, bearing the Khadi Pratisthan’s pledge for cow protection—but there was no question of me witnessing such a sight.

An iconic early 20th-century  for Bukhsh Ellahie & Co., featuring classical maestro Gauhar Jaan holding a cigarette to promote their brand

Someone’s great-grandfather might have known which drummers came beating the kara and nakara to announce, "Tonight at seven, the Chaitanya-lila folk play commences." I never heard the name of a young "lad" like Dhiren Bal, who reportedly painted the  for "Himkalyan Hair Oil" at a three-way junction in Dinajpur.

While searching the Panjika (almanac) for the auspicious moment of a wedding, I never had the chance to chuckle at the suggestive illustrations for "Libido-Enhancing Tablets." On a morning shortly after Mahatma Gandhi’s assassination, I didn't sit with a newspaper wondering which artist, known only as "Munshi," had used swirling brushstrokes to sketch a portrait as a final tribute on behalf of some bankrupt cotton mill.

I saw none of this because I hadn't been born yet. Most of those who witnessed it are now gone forever. Yet, even without being born in that era, I have managed to 'see' it all. The old, withered newspapers and digital archives acted like Alibaba’s cave, revealing to me a lost jewelry box. To me, those vintage s were not just pages of history; they were the precious Sita-har, the Jhumko, and the Nak-chabi themselves. I saw those 'ornaments'—the lost illustrations—and through them, I glimpsed a world that has otherwise vanished.

Actually, on a sudden whim, I spent a long time digging through ancient newspapers and periodicals. My eyes kept getting stuck on the bizarre s still surviving on the faded, brownish-yellow newsprint of yore. I was looking, most of all, at the illustrations.

As I tasted this history, I remembered a book I read long ago: The Lost Tribes of Israel by Tudor Parfitt. Many believe that since the foreign invasions of Israel in the 8th century BC, at least twelve tribes went missing. Mr. Parfitt scoured the planet in search of them—a search that reportedly continues today. Some even believe the signs of those lost people are visible in the Afghans.

Looking at the drawings for old s, I felt I found a resemblance between those legendary lost tribes and these forgotten illustrators. That is why the book came to mind. It also felt as though there was no such mismatch that could prevent us from linking these unknown artists’ ghosts to their successors, even without a DNA test!

The connection might be clear, but can we not grant them even a small corner in the history of Bengal's illustrative arts?

Renowned figures like the artist Raghunath Goswami continue to say—no, those  drawings or ideas are not even worth considering. They claim it is a "mindless and indiscriminate simplification of art objects." They say the expression has neither grace nor form. Artistic value? Far from it!

For some reason, despite respecting the scholars' verdict, I grew stubborn. As I weighed the pros and cons, even the "ugly" artworks of those who drew s for ringworm cures or hair-growth tonics began to pull at my eyes. I saw in them plenty of humour, and plenty of heartache too. Nevertheless, I began looking for a way to have a long conversation with those early advertising artists.

A representative of a "vanishing species" like O.C. Ganguly (Arun Kumar Gangopadhyay) introduced me to a certain "madman." He had a crow's nest of hair. His lower garment was draped over his chest like a shawl. He wore a striped vest. His hands were shackled in massive iron rings.

It is precisely these kinds of s that art critics have referred to as brainless and ugly art. The  regarding the cure for insanity, however, dates back to 1952. Yet, long before that, a group of young artists from agencies had completely transformed the face of Bengali ads.

Apparently, such a madman would no longer need to be restrained. Why? Because the illness would be cured simply by administering "ABD Pills" and "Dutta Oil." Such was the claim of the "Bengali Asylum" of Dutta Nagar, Dum Dum, whose head office was at 29-A Vivekananda Road (Phone: Jorasanko 5220).

Seeing the address "Jorasanko" in that illustrated ad, I was immediately reminded of the Tagore family—specifically, their members who struggled with mental health. One was Birendranath Tagore, the fourth son of Maharshi Debendranath. He was brilliant at mathematics but suddenly fell victim to "wind-disease" (mental instability). The other was Somendranath, another brother of Rabindranath.

The Nobel laureate poet knew well which medicines helped the "insane." I learned of another —not for the ABD Pills of Dum Dum, but a special notice from "S.C. Roy & Co." at 167/3 Cornwallis Street. They advertised Dr. Umesh Chandra Roy’s world-famous "Great Cure for the Mad," priced at five rupees per bottle. The ad claimed that for over 70 years, this medicine had cured "millions of violent madmen and all kinds of nervous patients." This  would appear with a quote from the poet himself, saying: "...I have been aware of its efficacy for a long time." Was the "Great Cure for the Mad" then used on Birendranath or Somendranath? I know bringing up Rabindranath's name is somewhat irrelevant, but seeing these old drawings makes my mind wander in a thousand directions!

The illustrated  I mentioned was published in 1952—the day I saw the picture of the shackled madman in the paper. That drawing was made several years after legendary artists had already begun to dominate Bengali advertising. By then, Bengalis had seen hundreds of fantastic drawings for various products. A legend like O.C. Ganguly was earning forty rupees a month at Calcutta’s "Stronach Advertising" as early as 1937. An agency named "Paradise Advertising" existed in Calcutta in 1928. No one can really speak of agencies in East Bengal (now Bangladesh) before the Partition. We mostly know of the birth of agencies like Bitopi, East Asiatic, or Interspan in the 1960s. Clearly, advertising production in both Bengals (undivided India at the time) was centred in Calcutta. Be that as it may, an agency required an artist—someone to present the matter attractively to lure customers.

But not all sellers went to agencies. Instead, they took "ugly" creations (by today’s standards) made by local artists to make printing blocks for newspaper offices. The madman illustration is a classic example. The calligraphy in that ad was purely amateurish—something no professional agency would ever approve. Whether that ad ran before 1952 or if that was the first, I do not know.

It is undeniable that finding artists from the era before the establishment of agencies (pre-partition) is extremely difficult. Only a handful of artists signed their names on those ads, and even then, it was just a tiny first initial of their name and surname, usually in English. Pranabesh Maity, who drew ads in the 60s and 70s, had a more bitter experience. He claimed that even if artists signed, agency bosses would often erase the signature to imply that the agency was everything and the artist didn't matter.

This makes me think of the "Lost Tribes" and a piece by Premendra Mitra about the Patuas (traditional scroll painters). Premendra once had a great desire to find the lost Patuas of Kalighat. Briefly, the story goes like this—a young boy walking the streets of Kalighat would watch with wonder a specific style of indigenous painting. Ordinary men in dirty clothes sat cross-legged on mats in small roadside shops, painting those pictures. Yet, the walls of the shops were adorned with framed, colourful photographs of gods and goddesses. People coming to the temple preferred to buy the framed photos. Even so, the Patuas would sit down to paint whenever they found a moment’s respite between sales.

Then came a day when not only the scroll paintings but even the expensive printed pictures of deities vanished from those shops. The Patuas disappeared too. I don't know if that young boy was Premendra himself—since his childhood was spent in North India, having been born in Varanasi. But for a creative man like him to imagine that boy while thinking of the Patuas is not far-fetched. When a kind soul eventually went looking for those Patuas, he was utterly disappointed. He learned that they had been pushed out of the city. Their descendants had not become "useless" painters; some took jobs as labourers in jute mills or chose other professions. At most, unable to ignore the "blood connection," some practised their hand at painting the chalchitra (background canopy) of idols.
