World.title: Wilson declares abortion laws off-limits as scare campaign grows
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsVictoriaVictorian election Wilson declares abortion laws off-limits as scare campaign grows Chip Le Grand September 5, 2026 — 7:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Victoria’s abortion laws providing legal access to terminations at any stage of pregnancy would not be changed by a Coalition government, Opposition Leader Jess Wilson has declared. Wilson issued the statement, which also makes clear her personal, pro-choice view that abortion is a healthcare issue best left to women and their doctors, in an attempt to defuse a Queensland-style scare campaign about what a change of government could mean for reproductive rights. “Abortion law will not change under a Liberal and Nationals government. Full stop,” Wilson told The Sunday Age. “Anyone that claims otherwise is simply wrong. Victorian Opposition Leader Jess Wilson says abortion law won’t change under a government led by her. Louis Trerise “Abortion is a personal decision that should be made by women in consultation with their healthcare professionals.”



A promotional video for the Carroll government circulated last week by a market research company with strong ALP links raised the spectre of a Coalition government, in partnership with One Nation, dismantling reproductive rights that women in Victoria have had since 2008, when abortion was decriminalised and regulated. A version of the video claimed without evidence that Wilson “handpicked Liberal candidates who want abortion banned” and stated that One Nation state leader Warren Pickering wanted to make abortion a crime. “Victorians can’t risk a Liberal One Nation government and the polls show the Liberals can’t govern without One Nation,” it claimed. Premier Ben Carroll doubled down on Saturday, saying Wilson “won’t be calling the shots” on abortion law. “I will stand against any assault on the dignity and rights of women, and will always support a woman’s right to access safe abortion,” he said. Victorian Premier Ben Carroll. Photograph by Chris Hopkins



“One Nation have said they want to make abortion a criminal offence. Jess Wilson cannot form government without One Nation — it doesn’t matter what she says, she won’t be calling the shots on this.” Sophie Torney, a teal candidate running against Wilson in the opposition leader’s seat of Kew, is also seeking to put abortion on the ballot at the November 28 election. Loading In June, after a Family First bill restricting abortions after 25 weeks gestation passed the upper house of the South Australian parliament, Torney published a statement on Instagram questioning Wilson’s support for Victoria’s current laws. “Why would any Victorian voter believe a single word Jess Wilson says when it comes to abortion?” Torney told The Sunday Age.



“Under her leadership, the Liberals have already caved in and accepted One Nation’s energy policy and in the Nepean byelection they preferenced One Nation. Until Moira Deeming blew up her candidacy, Ms Wilson said nothing about Mrs Deeming’s determination to undermine access to abortion.” Deeming, a former Liberal MP who quit the party after being disendorsed as a candidate for the November election, has described abortion as a “terrible evil”. The South Australian abortion reform bill was defeated in the lower house on a conscience vote but supported by Premier Peter Malinauskas, a former state secretary of the socially conservative Shop, Distributive and Allied Employees Association, and Opposition Leader Ashton Hurn. South Australian Premier Peter Malinauskas this year voted to restrict abortion after 25 weeks’ gestation. The bill failed. Roy VanDerVegt



At the 2024 Queensland election, the ALP waged a determined scare campaign on abortion against LNP leader David Crisafulli. Despite Crisafulli repeatedly insisting he had no plans to change the abortion regulations he voted against six years earlier, the issue dogged him throughout the campaign. He has since taken the unusual step of prohibiting any debate or legislation to change Queensland’s abortion laws in the current term of parliament. Queensland Premier David Crisafulli. Cameron Atfield The campaign against Crisafulli was partly based on a false assumption that the LNP would have to rely on support from the pro-life Katter’s Australia Party to govern. In Victoria, the most recent Resolve Political Monitor results published by this masthead, if replicated at the state election, would result in a change of government but most likely leave the Coalition short of an outright majority. Emily’s List chief executive Pamela Anderson, whose pro-choice organisation was established 30 years ago to boost the number of Labor women in parliament, said she had “genuine concerns” about what could happen to Victoria’s abortion laws under a Coalition government.



“Jess may have a particular view, but she may not have the numbers in the party room,” Anderson said. “She is a moderate, and there are not a lot of moderates left in the Liberal Party. “I don’t think the Liberals are going to be in a position to govern on their own. They are going to have to negotiate with One Nation, who have a very forward, pro-life position. I think it is absolutely something we should be worried about.” Related Article Exclusive

Victorian election Revealed: How leadership coup has changed Labor’s electoral fortunes A pro-choice Labor MP, speaking confidentially to discuss internal party matters, said the uncertain make-up of the state’s next parliament meant that women could not feel secure about their abortion rights – irrespective of who governs. “Both political parties have conservative rumps with different views on this,” the MP said. “If One Nation win too many seats, everything is up for grabs.”



Wilson has ruled out forming a coalition with One Nation but left open the possibility of relying on Pauline Hanson’s party for confidence and supply. She is the first woman to lead the Victorian Liberal Party, the first Millennial leader of either major party and, since joining parliament in 2022, has made no public comment suggesting she wants to restrict abortion. One Nation is explicitly pro-life. Its national policy platform commits the party to “seek every opportunity to roll back brutal and extreme abortion law”, and Hanson this year told the National Press Club that once a woman reaches her 20th week of pregnancy, it should be too late for an abortion. Pickering in 2024 joined pro-life activists at a “March for Babies” and has described Victoria’s abortion laws as among the world’s most draconian. “We, as a society, must have the conversation to decide exactly what constitutes a reasonable term for abortion,” he said after the march. One Nation founder Pauline Hanson with the party’s Victorian leader Warren Pickering. Eamon Gallagher Victoria’s 2008 Abortion Law Reform Act, which was passed under the Brumby government with the support of pro-choice MPs across the party divide, removed abortion from the Crimes Act and provided women the right to an abortion up to the 24th week of gestation.



After 24 weeks, two medical practitioners must agree that an abortion is “appropriate in all the circumstances”. Animal Justice Party MP Georgie Purcell. Victorian Parliament Abortions in Victoria are lawfully performed with prescription medication up to the ninth week of gestation and surgically in public hospitals and private clinics. Although reliable statistics on surgical abortions are not readily accessible, the Victorian Women’s Health Atlas published by Women’s Health Victoria reports that in 2025, abortion scripts were issued to 13,108 women living in the state. Animal Justice Party MP Georgie Purcell, the co-author of a report that identified concerns about affordability and scarcity of abortion services in parts of the state, said accessibility to abortion was a more pressing problem than its regulation. Purcell has spoken previously about her experience in having to pay $1000 for an abortion – a cost not affordable to many women. She said more women in parliament needed to speak up for reproductive rights.



“I have a great fear that in a few years’ time you won’t be able to get an abortion in Victoria whether or not it is legal,” she said. “Despite us having more women than ever before in parliament, nobody is talking about it. Everyone is scared to say the word. We need more politicians championing choice.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: A Cinderella story: Why most women are wearing the wrong size shoes
World.content:
NationalScience A Cinderella story: Why most women are wearing the wrong size shoes Liam Mannix September 5, 2026 — 7:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

More than two-thirds of Australian women are wearing shoes that do not match the size of their feet, a study suggests. The discrepancy is likely to have several causes, including baffling inconsistencies between brands for the same sizes. But the central problem seems to be that most shoes are sized for length, not width, according to researchers. And wearing the wrong-sized shoe can have significant health costs. Carol Tan and Saniyat Islam, two of the paper’s co-authors. Simon Schluter “There are serious health implications if you’re not wearing proper-sized shoes,” says Associate Professor Saniyat Islam, a fashion researcher at RMIT and co-author of the study.



“Women are not bad at shopping. This is a universal problem with our industry.” The research, published earlier this year in the International Journal of Fashion Design, Technology and Education, began with an insight by lead author Barbara Pallaspuro, who was working at the time in shoe retail. Women kept coming in and telling her they wore a certain size shoe – but when Pallaspuro measured their feet, the results were strikingly different. Could the problem be widespread? To test her hunch, Pallaspuro and a team from RMIT recruited 107 women who volunteered their usual shoe size. Then they measured their feet in the lab.



Related Article Cancer Sydney scientist behind ‘moon landing’ cancer vaccine wins top science prize Seventy-two per cent of women were in the wrong shoe size, according to the lab measurements. “It shocked us,” says Islam. The size differences varied widely: some women were out by only half a size, others were putting size 4 feet in size 7 shoes. One woman was trying to cram size 8.5 feet into size 7 shoes, but most of the women studied were wearing shoes that were slightly too large.



If the shoe fits ... Historically, shoes were custom-made. That makes sense given the wide variation in foot width (known as girth, measured at the ball of the foot), length and shape. For example, 93 of the 107 volunteers had left and right feet of different sizes. But the bigger problem, Islam says, is that EU and British shoe sizes are delineated in length, not girth. The Nike sneakers worn by Caitlin Clark of the Indiana Fever during their game against the Golden State Valkyries in San Francisco in May. Getty Images Nike lists its size 5 women’s shoes as 22 centimetres long and its size 14.5 as 30 centimetres long. Each size in between increases by .4 or .5 centimetres.



As length increases, so does a shoe’s width (to complicate matters, different brands’ sizes vary by up to 3.5 centimetres for the same size). Related Article Explainer

Health Bunions, corns, plantar fasciitis: How to nail foot trouble before it’s too late Human feet do not work the same way. Long feet can be narrow and short feet can be wide. “Feet are not one-dimensional. It’s as 3D object,” says Islam. “We are trying to compensate for everything with a single measure – length. There lies the problem. We do not provide the girth or the arch size.” To get the right width, women are forced to choose shoes of an incorrect length or vice versa, says Islam.



This problem is less acute for men, who often wear shoes with laces. “We can compensate the girth problem with the laces,” says Islam. “You can tighten it up or loosen it up.” Health effects The results don’t surprise podiatrist Laura Kelly, spokeswoman for the Australian Podiatry Association. “It would be one of the most common problems we see,” she says. “And often, they think they are wearing the right size shoe.” She ticks off a list of problems linked to ill-fitting shoes: bunions, wounds, ingrown nails, nerve compression, an increased risk of falls. Some of these conditions are driven by genetic risk factors, but are triggered or worsened by ill-fitting shoes. “Lots of quite serious things can come from this,” says Kelly. “A lot of people, I think, put up with a certain level of discomfort. They think it’s normal. It’s not normal to have discomfort, neuromas, corns, ingrown nails. There is a lot you can do about it. Maybe people put up with things they shouldn’t.”



What to do? Not all shoe systems have the same problem. Japanese and Chinese shoe size charts include foot girth; China’s system even allows shoes to be sized according to width. Companies selling in Australia know the width of the shoe they are selling – they just don’t report it to consumers. “It baffles me,” says Islam. “They take the measurements, but they don’t disclose it. Consumers need that data to fit their feet properly.” Several Australian brands have started making shoes of differing widths, says Dr Alexandra Sherlock, founder of the Footwear Research Network (she was not involved in the study). But they are much more expensive than mass-produced shoes. “We have got into a habit of buying very cheap shoes, cheaply produced, out of cheap non-renewable materials,” says Sherlock. “We’ve got into really bad habits, and we don’t even realise.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Three children injured in jumping castle accident as 80km/h winds hit Sydney
World.content:
Updated NationalNSWEmergency services Three children injured in jumping castle accident as 80km/h winds hit Sydney Max Maddison Updated September 5, 2026 — 6:38pm ,first published 4:41pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Three young children have been taken to hospital after powerful winds lifted a jumping castle into the air in Sydney’s inner south, as wild weather caused widespread power outages in the city’s west and left more than 90,000 households without electricity. Ausgrid confirmed about 40,000 customers had been left in the dark, as swaths of Sydney’s west suffered outages after high winds damaged one of the company’s substations. Another 50,000 customers on Endeavour Energy’s network were also without power. Three children were injured when a jumping castle became airborne in Banksia, in Sydney’s south, amid ferocious wind gusts on Saturday. Nine News The outages came after a cool change ripped through NSW, with gusts of wind surpassing 80km/h recorded at Sydney Airport late on Saturday afternoon. The temperature in Sydney had hovered about 30 degrees, accompanied by strong north-westerly winds. The Bureau of Meteorology has issued a severe weather warning for damaging winds, with peak gusts of up to 100km/h expected across parts of the state.



Emergency services were called to Gardiner Park in Banksia, about 12 kilometres south of the CBD, about 1.20pm on Saturday after the jumping castle became airborne, a NSW Ambulance spokeswoman said. The children were taken to Sydney Children’s Hospital after being treated by paramedics at the scene. A preschool-aged boy and girl suffered head injuries, while a baby was treated for minor injuries. A woman was also taken to hospital with minor injuries, the spokeswoman said. All three children were in a stable condition. Loading This was the second incident involving an airborne jumping castle recorded in a matter of hours on Saturday. Two children were injured at a party near Geelong in Victoria in the morning. Both children were taken to hospital with injuries to their upper bodies and were in a stable condition. Greater Western Sydney and the Blue Mountains were the areas worst hit by the wild winds.



“There’s currently over 250 fault sites. Crews are currently working to make damaged areas safe before restoration work can commence,” an Endeavour Energy spokeswoman said. The company’s website estimated that power would not be restored until the early hours of Sunday morning. In a statement, an Ausgrid spokeswoman said most customers were expected to have their power restored by 7pm with the remainder by 11pm. “There are currently approximately 40,000 customers without power after strong winds moved through Sydney and the Central Coast this afternoon,” she said. “Hardest-hit areas include Bankstown, Milperra and Revesby where high winds have caused some damage to one of our substations.”



Outages were being experienced right across Sydney, including in Mosman, St Ives, Bellevue Hill, Rosebery and Summer Hill. Get alerts on breaking news as it happens.

World.title: ‘Survivable pockets’: Australian tunnel expert arrives in Nepal, hopeful of more rescues
World.content:
WorldAsiaFloods ‘Survivable pockets’: Australian tunnel expert arrives in Nepal, hopeful of more rescues Michael McGowan Updated September 5, 2026 — 6:31pm ,first published 4:50pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Kathmandu: An Australian tunnelling expert who helped to orchestrate the extraordinary rescue of two workers from a hydropower tunnel in northern Nepal is headed for the disaster zone, firmly believing there is still hope of finding more survivors trapped hundreds of metres below the earth. After helping to lead the rescue operation remotely from his home in Victoria this week, engineer and geologist Arnold Dix flew into Nepal’s capital, Kathmandu, late on Friday night (Nepal time). Australian tunnelling expert Arnold Dix has arrived in disaster-stricken Nepal believing there is still hope of finding survivors. Justin McManus It comes as rescuers in Nepal pulled a Chinese national alive from a hydropower tunnel on Saturday, according to a social media post by the country’s prime minister’s office, and in a separate effort, rescuers pulled a woman out alive from a house 10 days after floods hit Nuwakot town, a Nepalese army spokesperson said. The latest tunnel rescue brings the total to three workers pulled alive from the Trishuli hydropower project. Two Nepalese workers were rescued from a tunnel at the Trishuli 3A hydropower plant on Friday.



Nepal’s army said the man was pulled alive from a 225-metre tunnel and is undergoing a health assessment. Images showed him being evacuated by helicopter, with an army medic checking on him during the flight. View post on X While the odds are against Dix and the rest of the global team of experts providing advice to Nepalese authorities on the ongoing rescue mission, he said that he absolutely believed there was hope of finding more survivors under the earth some 10 days after the devastating floods. “In the game of paper, scissor, rock, human, the odds aren’t good. But yeah [there are] survivable pockets, absolutely, and that’s what we’re aiming for,” he said. A helicopter drops search and rescue teams at the exit tunnel of the Chilime Hydropower Plant during the week. Kate Geraghty



On Saturday morning, he boarded a helicopter for the Chilime Hydropower Plant, high in the Himalayan valley and close to the Chinese border. There he will meet with members of the Indian rescue team he worked with after 41 men were trapped in the Silkyara Bend-Barkot tunnel in the Himalayas in 2023. Dix has also worked on other rescue missions, including at Ground Zero after September 11. Loading “We’re just like the underground rescue buddies,” he told this masthead just ahead of his flight on Saturday. It has been more than a week since devastating floods tore through Nepal, causing tsunami-like waves of water, rock and debris that has resulted in 1294 confirmed deaths. More than 5000 people are still missing, including 583 foreign nationals. The Chinese government has reported 31 confirmed deaths and 531 missing – including 261 foreign nationals – on the Tibet side of the border.



Among those still unaccounted for are workers believed to be trapped inside the hydropower tunnels that Nepal has used to harness the fast-flowing waters of the Himalayas and increase the blackout-prone country’s power generation. Related Article Floods Boots on the ground as first Australian rescue team arrives in Nepal Nepal’s Independent Power Producers’ Association said during the week that it believed ​at least eight people could be trapped in the Chilime tunnel. It is one of seven hydropower tunnels at which rescue operations are taking place, with hundreds of workers believed to have been trapped. Until Friday, Dix had helped the effort remotely from Australia, unable to board a plane during the crucial hours and days after the disaster. “Time was of the essence,” he said. “I couldn’t lose two days because I knew they had to start digging.”



They had focused on the Trishuli 3A ­hydropower project, and he said the rescue of mechanical foreman Sanjay Sah and mechanical supervisor Kabir Maharjan from the tunnel on Friday was confirmation of the work he and others had been doing throughout the week. Related Article Graphic content

Floods ‘I saw many dead bodies’: The harrowing escape from a flooded Nepal tunnel “[It means] we’ve got survivable zones in there,” Dix said. “That confirms our theory, if you like. Until that, it was a theory. We really didn’t know if it was survivable in there.” It makes him believe there could “absolutely” be more workers still alive inside. “Of course, the odds are against us. Like, you wouldn’t, you know, go to the casino and play the house on these things normally,” he said.



Dix and his team had relied on engineering drawings of the massive hydropower structures that Nepal uses to generate electricity, as well as satellite imagery, to identify the survivable pockets inside. “The world has never had something like this,” he said. Arnold Dix has previously helped to orchestrate the rescue of 41 Indian workers who were trapped for 17 days after a landslide in the Himalayas. “We’re not dealing with tunnels that might’ve collapsed. They won’t have. We’re dealing with tunnels that are filled up with stuff. “It’s this explosive inrush. It just turns the textbook on its head … that’s why the rescue yesterday was so important because we’ve never dealt with anything like this.”



While they were confident in their theory, the challenge of digging into the deep, unstable earth, where “rocks the size of cars” had barrelled into the tunnels, presented many challenges of its own. Related Article Floods At first, the smell is overwhelming. Then, they open the book of the dead “That’s on the one hand, and the other hand, [the question was] how the hell are we going to get in there to get them?” he said. “You have to find a reason to use your resources, which is where might people be alive? That’s the first question, and then your second question is, ‘OK, now, how do we get them?’ “You can’t just dig everywhere. You’ve seen the destruction here, so you’ve got to be very specific in what you do.”

World.title: AFL LIVE: Fagan lashes Lions, says Swans showed ‘human spirit’ in finals win; Dogs, Crows prepare in SA
World.content:
Many questions have been asked in relation to the Sydney Swans since that fateful Monday morning at the Pullman Hotel in East Melbourne three weeks ago.

Here’s one nobody bothered to ask: what happens if they actually win?

Logan McDonald of the Swans celebrates a goal. via Getty Images

Nobody bothered to ask because, before Saturday, the idea was preposterous. Outside of the Swans themselves, nobody genuinely thought they could win this game. Not a qualifying final against two-time reigning premiers Brisbane, who have lost only one game since May. Not without five of their best players. Not after everything that’s happened in the last month.

As soon as the Swans suspended the ‘Pullman Five’, a line was drawn through the club’s name by virtually the entire AFL industry. Their odds blew out with bookmakers and they sunk to the bottom of everyone’s finals power rankings.

Their own chairman, Andrew Pridham, seemed to think they were as good as done: their season had been “torpedoed”, in his words, when those season-ending bans were meted out to Isaac Heeney, Nick Blakey, Chad Warner, Riley Bice and James Jordon for breaching club standards. Even their own fans seemed to agree, with only 37,261 turning up at the SCG on Saturday afternoon. It was the Swans’ lowest finals crowd at home in more than a decade.

Perhaps the Lions believed it, too. Because only that could explain the way they turned up, as if they expected the Swans to simply roll over and accept their assigned fate. They did not.

And now, after Sydney’s stirring 53-point victory, one of the great AFL finals upsets, we are in uncharted territory: this crisis-torn football club is somehow just one win away from a grand final appearance, having absorbed every bit of angst and scrutiny directed their way and channelled it to their advantage.

“I’d be writing them off at your peril,” Alastair Clarkson said here two weeks ago in what proved to be one of his final utterances as North Melbourne coach. Prophetic words.

The Lions simply could not handle Sydney’s hunger, intent and efficiency, which overwhelmed Brisbane’s most celebrated names and punched massive holes in their much-vaunted defence. The Swans kicked six of the first seven goals of the match to leave the visitors stunned; that margin remained intact for practically the whole afternoon and proved to be the difference. They prevailed 21.15 (141) to 13.10 (88).

Kai Lohmann gets into a tangle with the Swans Getty Images

Every time Brisbane tried to reel them in, the swarming Swans had a response of some kind that kept alive the belief that was sustaining them. They simply wanted it more, whereas the Lions, having tasted the ultimate success twice before, resembled a champion boxer who got old overnight. Lachie Neale, the pre-eminent example, had just 18 disposals and two clearances, none of them important. Brisbane have overcome bad finals defeats before, but this one was a doozy.

Tom Papley started the day under an injury cloud after appearing to tweak his calf in the warm-up. He finished it with five goals, each of them somehow worth more than six points because of the energy he generated with his celebrations. Two came in a blitz at the end of the third quarter which pushed Sydney’s lead to a scarcely believable 46 points at three-quarter time, capped by Errol Gulden’s sensational individual effort from the centre bounce.

Logan McDonald produced the game of his career, bagging six goals. His first was the first of the match, and came at the end of a chain which featured a one-handed grab in the middle by Charlie Curnow over Darcy Gardiner. The last came from a set shot on the boundary in the dying moments. (Curnow also booted five.)

Charlie Curnow celebrates for the Swans. AFL Photos via Getty Images

Almost everything went right for the Swans. Almost. Something went very wrong midway through the opening term, when captain Callum Mills twisted his knee in ominous fashion as he tried to corral Will Ashcroft on the boundary line.

Confirmation that he would take no further part in the game suitably arrived, via the club’s X account, with a crying emoji at the end of the sentence as punctuation. Coach Dean Cox spoke about what losing the skipper to the team after the game.

“To lose your captain early, to rally, execute the roles they wanted to play at. I couldn’t be prouder,” Cox told Kayo Sports.

“We’ve worked hard on this game style for 10 months and we want to make sure that anyone that comes into the team can execute their role and do what is required, when it is required and they did that in spades.”

That Sydney still won without him, and after seeing his shattered visage on the big screen, further underlined the value of this performance. But a more cruel twist of fate was hard to imagine. Mills had risen to the moment as the Pullman scandal had demanded, leading admirably with both his words in press conferences and his actions on the field. He also missed Sydney’s last grand final appearance through injury in 2024; this was his first consistent season of football in three years.

In the absence of the five banned players, for all sorts of reasons, Mills was one of Sydney’s most important players.

Whatever they do next, they will almost certainly have to do in his absence. But you’d be crazy to put a limit on what that could be.

World.title: Swans v Lions player ratings: How the reigning premiers fared in their stunning Swans loss
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 Opinion Swans v Lions player ratings: How the reigning premiers fared in their stunning Swans loss Scott Spits Sports writer and editor September 5, 2026 — 7:07pm

September 5, 2026 — 7:07pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Loading

No one gave the Swans a chance. Winning a qualifying final against the two-time reigning premiers was a hard enough task, let alone doing it without the five first-choice players serving a club-imposed suspension. What transpired at the SCG on Saturday afternoon was nothing short of remarkable, with the Lions dominated by 53 points and forced to enter a semi-final next week still licking their wounds. Scott Spits rates every Lions player’s performance from a stunning game. Brisbane Lions superstar Harris Andrews and Chris Fagan have plenty to sort through after their side’s stunning loss to the undermanned Swans. AFL Photos



Brisbane Lions (1) Kai Lohmann: He had a game to forget – a shocker, really. He didn’t bother the stats-markers until early in the second half and only had three possessions by the final break. 3/10 (2) Sam Draper: Very, very quiet. The big man couldn’t get in the game at all. A third-quarter goal saved a bit of face, but the Swans dominated around him that term. Draper badly misread a marking attempt in tough conditions in the second term. 4/10 (3) Jaspa Fletcher: Far from Brisbane’s worst, but he gave away an important free kick (for Sydney’s sixth goal) in the first quarter when he took the ball over the goal-line. 5.5/10 (4) Oscar Allen: The big man had a quirky kind of game. He did OK from limited opportunities and had three goals from three touches by the final break, and finished with four goals from six. 5/10



(5) Josh Dunkley: The midfield beast never stopped trying. He won plenty of the ball at the coalface, but had almost no one to turn to in the trenches with Lachie Neale and Cam Rayner among those well held. 7.5/10 (6) Hugh McCluggage: He just couldn’t get into the game and was largely ineffective. He had an early chance to kick the Lions’ first goal, but he was off-line. 6/10 (7) Jarrod Berry: He failed to have any real influence. Made one blunder in the second quarter when an errant handball went to Sydney’s Hayden McLean, who took his chance and booted a goal. 5/10 (8) Will Ashcroft: He largely battled in the first half but, to be fair, improved from there. There was one nice moment, in particular, in the first term when he stormed out of the centre and found Eric Hipwood. 5/10 Lachie Neale and the rest of the Brisbane Lions midfield had an uncharacteristically poor day. Getty Images



(9) Lachie Neale: Beaten by James Rowbottom, he didn’t touch the ball until the 20-minute mark of the first term. It was a tough day for Neale (by his usual high standards) and his team. To his credit, he still finished with 18 possessions. 4/10 (10) Levi Ashcroft: He struggled for influence. He booted what looked like a stirring goal on the quarter-time siren when his effort from an angle split the big sticks. But it was a classic false dawn as the Lions never really rallied. 4.5/10 (13) Logan Morris: He didn’t really have an influence, managing two goals from 14 touches. Brisbane badly needed a focal point, but he couldn’t offer it today. 4/10 (15) Dayne Zorko: Did his bit as teammates went missing around him. The veteran got better as the game wore on and finished with a team-high 26 touches. He was easily Brisbane’s best performer with metres gained (822), much more than any other teammate. 7/10 (16) Cam Rayner: Emblematic for the Lions on a shocking day for the two-time reigning premiers. He struggled to even reach double figures with possessions. There was one delightful pass to Conor McKenna in the third term, however. 5/10



The Swans lost captain Callum Mills in the first quarter, but went on to a big win over Dayne Zorko and the Lions. Getty Images (23) Charlie Cameron: The match-winning forward was completely unsighted, finally getting his hands on the ball in the second term but missing his shot at goal. He didn’t even pick up junk stats when the game was gone. 1/10 (26) Conor McKenna: He tried hard but just couldn’t get going. Had two touches for the first term as the Swans jumped them and had a vital goal assist in the third quarter when he kicked one off the ground to Berry. He also booted a final-quarter goal. 5/10 (27) Darcy Gardiner: He got smashed by Charlie Curnow and had an equal team-low four touches. He just had a shocker and the Coleman medallist took complete advantage. 2.5/10 (30) Eric Hipwood: Showed a bit at different stages and gave the Lions a target to kick to. But he was badly off target with a shot deep in the forward pocket after just eight minutes that failed to trouble the scorers. That didn’t help his cause. 4.5/10



View post on X (31) Harris Andrews: For one of the game’s best defenders, the leader of the Lions’ pack won’t look back on this game fondly. He was soundly beaten by Swan Logan McDonald, an opponent who had probably his best match and was a result-shaper. This one will burn for Andrews. 3/10 (32) Darcy Fort: He only played 50 per cent game time. He played a back-up role to Sam Draper in the ruck but just wasn’t a factor and got his hands on the ball just nine times. 3/10 (33) Zac Bailey: He scrapped his way to 21 touches and tried hard, but had a forgettable moment late in the second half when he didn’t allow for the wind with a shot at goal in the tough, swirly conditions. It was telling. 5/10 (35) Ryan Lester: He played a typically solid game. He was far from the Lions’ worst and did OK in defence, recording 21 touches. 6/10



(43) Noah Answerth: Did OK. He picked up eight touches but was off the ground in the first half with injury. 5.5/10



(44) Darcy Wilmot: He was one of the Lions’ better players when their regular stars largely went missing. 6/10 Swans ratings are still to come Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: Wilson declares abortion laws off-limits as scare campaign grows
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsVictoriaVictorian election Wilson declares abortion laws off-limits as scare campaign grows Chip Le Grand September 5, 2026 — 7:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Victoria’s abortion laws providing legal access to terminations at any stage of pregnancy would not be changed by a Coalition government, Opposition Leader Jess Wilson has declared. Wilson issued the statement, which also makes clear her personal, pro-choice view that abortion is a healthcare issue best left to women and their doctors, in an attempt to defuse a Queensland-style scare campaign about what a change of government could mean for reproductive rights. “Abortion law will not change under a Liberal and Nationals government. Full stop,” Wilson told The Sunday Age. “Anyone that claims otherwise is simply wrong. Victorian Opposition Leader Jess Wilson says abortion law won’t change under a government led by her. Louis Trerise “Abortion is a personal decision that should be made by women in consultation with their healthcare professionals.”



A promotional video for the Carroll government circulated last week by a market research company with strong ALP links raised the spectre of a Coalition government, in partnership with One Nation, dismantling reproductive rights that women in Victoria have had since 2008, when abortion was decriminalised and regulated. A version of the video claimed without evidence that Wilson “handpicked Liberal candidates who want abortion banned” and stated that One Nation state leader Warren Pickering wanted to make abortion a crime. “Victorians can’t risk a Liberal One Nation government and the polls show the Liberals can’t govern without One Nation,” it claimed. Premier Ben Carroll doubled down on Saturday, saying Wilson “won’t be calling the shots” on abortion law. “I will stand against any assault on the dignity and rights of women, and will always support a woman’s right to access safe abortion,” he said. Victorian Premier Ben Carroll. Photograph by Chris Hopkins



“One Nation have said they want to make abortion a criminal offence. Jess Wilson cannot form government without One Nation — it doesn’t matter what she says, she won’t be calling the shots on this.” Sophie Torney, a teal candidate running against Wilson in the opposition leader’s seat of Kew, is also seeking to put abortion on the ballot at the November 28 election. Loading In June, after a Family First bill restricting abortions after 25 weeks gestation passed the upper house of the South Australian parliament, Torney published a statement on Instagram questioning Wilson’s support for Victoria’s current laws. “Why would any Victorian voter believe a single word Jess Wilson says when it comes to abortion?” Torney told The Sunday Age.



“Under her leadership, the Liberals have already caved in and accepted One Nation’s energy policy and in the Nepean byelection they preferenced One Nation. Until Moira Deeming blew up her candidacy, Ms Wilson said nothing about Mrs Deeming’s determination to undermine access to abortion.” Deeming, a former Liberal MP who quit the party after being disendorsed as a candidate for the November election, has described abortion as a “terrible evil”. The South Australian abortion reform bill was defeated in the lower house on a conscience vote but supported by Premier Peter Malinauskas, a former state secretary of the socially conservative Shop, Distributive and Allied Employees Association, and Opposition Leader Ashton Hurn. South Australian Premier Peter Malinauskas this year voted to restrict abortion after 25 weeks’ gestation. The bill failed. Roy VanDerVegt



At the 2024 Queensland election, the ALP waged a determined scare campaign on abortion against LNP leader David Crisafulli. Despite Crisafulli repeatedly insisting he had no plans to change the abortion regulations he voted against six years earlier, the issue dogged him throughout the campaign. He has since taken the unusual step of prohibiting any debate or legislation to change Queensland’s abortion laws in the current term of parliament. Queensland Premier David Crisafulli. Cameron Atfield The campaign against Crisafulli was partly based on a false assumption that the LNP would have to rely on support from the pro-life Katter’s Australia Party to govern. In Victoria, the most recent Resolve Political Monitor results published by this masthead, if replicated at the state election, would result in a change of government but most likely leave the Coalition short of an outright majority. Emily’s List chief executive Pamela Anderson, whose pro-choice organisation was established 30 years ago to boost the number of Labor women in parliament, said she had “genuine concerns” about what could happen to Victoria’s abortion laws under a Coalition government.



“Jess may have a particular view, but she may not have the numbers in the party room,” Anderson said. “She is a moderate, and there are not a lot of moderates left in the Liberal Party. “I don’t think the Liberals are going to be in a position to govern on their own. They are going to have to negotiate with One Nation, who have a very forward, pro-life position. I think it is absolutely something we should be worried about.” Related Article Exclusive

Victorian election Revealed: How leadership coup has changed Labor’s electoral fortunes A pro-choice Labor MP, speaking confidentially to discuss internal party matters, said the uncertain make-up of the state’s next parliament meant that women could not feel secure about their abortion rights – irrespective of who governs. “Both political parties have conservative rumps with different views on this,” the MP said. “If One Nation win too many seats, everything is up for grabs.”



Wilson has ruled out forming a coalition with One Nation but left open the possibility of relying on Pauline Hanson’s party for confidence and supply. She is the first woman to lead the Victorian Liberal Party, the first Millennial leader of either major party and, since joining parliament in 2022, has made no public comment suggesting she wants to restrict abortion. One Nation is explicitly pro-life. Its national policy platform commits the party to “seek every opportunity to roll back brutal and extreme abortion law”, and Hanson this year told the National Press Club that once a woman reaches her 20th week of pregnancy, it should be too late for an abortion. Pickering in 2024 joined pro-life activists at a “March for Babies” and has described Victoria’s abortion laws as among the world’s most draconian. “We, as a society, must have the conversation to decide exactly what constitutes a reasonable term for abortion,” he said after the march. One Nation founder Pauline Hanson with the party’s Victorian leader Warren Pickering. Eamon Gallagher Victoria’s 2008 Abortion Law Reform Act, which was passed under the Brumby government with the support of pro-choice MPs across the party divide, removed abortion from the Crimes Act and provided women the right to an abortion up to the 24th week of gestation.



After 24 weeks, two medical practitioners must agree that an abortion is “appropriate in all the circumstances”. Animal Justice Party MP Georgie Purcell. Victorian Parliament Abortions in Victoria are lawfully performed with prescription medication up to the ninth week of gestation and surgically in public hospitals and private clinics. Although reliable statistics on surgical abortions are not readily accessible, the Victorian Women’s Health Atlas published by Women’s Health Victoria reports that in 2025, abortion scripts were issued to 13,108 women living in the state. Animal Justice Party MP Georgie Purcell, the co-author of a report that identified concerns about affordability and scarcity of abortion services in parts of the state, said accessibility to abortion was a more pressing problem than its regulation. Purcell has spoken previously about her experience in having to pay $1000 for an abortion – a cost not affordable to many women. She said more women in parliament needed to speak up for reproductive rights.



“I have a great fear that in a few years’ time you won’t be able to get an abortion in Victoria whether or not it is legal,” she said. “Despite us having more women than ever before in parliament, nobody is talking about it. Everyone is scared to say the word. We need more politicians championing choice.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: A Cinderella story: Why most women are wearing the wrong size shoes
World.content:
NationalScience A Cinderella story: Why most women are wearing the wrong size shoes Liam Mannix September 5, 2026 — 7:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

More than two-thirds of Australian women are wearing shoes that do not match the size of their feet, a study suggests. The discrepancy is likely to have several causes, including baffling inconsistencies between brands for the same sizes. But the central problem seems to be that most shoes are sized for length, not width, according to researchers. And wearing the wrong-sized shoe can have significant health costs. Carol Tan and Saniyat Islam, two of the paper’s co-authors. Simon Schluter “There are serious health implications if you’re not wearing proper-sized shoes,” says Associate Professor Saniyat Islam, a fashion researcher at RMIT and co-author of the study.



“Women are not bad at shopping. This is a universal problem with our industry.” The research, published earlier this year in the International Journal of Fashion Design, Technology and Education, began with an insight by lead author Barbara Pallaspuro, who was working at the time in shoe retail. Women kept coming in and telling her they wore a certain size shoe – but when Pallaspuro measured their feet, the results were strikingly different. Could the problem be widespread? To test her hunch, Pallaspuro and a team from RMIT recruited 107 women who volunteered their usual shoe size. Then they measured their feet in the lab.



Related Article Cancer Sydney scientist behind ‘moon landing’ cancer vaccine wins top science prize Seventy-two per cent of women were in the wrong shoe size, according to the lab measurements. “It shocked us,” says Islam. The size differences varied widely: some women were out by only half a size, others were putting size 4 feet in size 7 shoes. One woman was trying to cram size 8.5 feet into size 7 shoes, but most of the women studied were wearing shoes that were slightly too large.



If the shoe fits ... Historically, shoes were custom-made. That makes sense given the wide variation in foot width (known as girth, measured at the ball of the foot), length and shape. For example, 93 of the 107 volunteers had left and right feet of different sizes. But the bigger problem, Islam says, is that EU and British shoe sizes are delineated in length, not girth. The Nike sneakers worn by Caitlin Clark of the Indiana Fever during their game against the Golden State Valkyries in San Francisco in May. Getty Images Nike lists its size 5 women’s shoes as 22 centimetres long and its size 14.5 as 30 centimetres long. Each size in between increases by .4 or .5 centimetres.



As length increases, so does a shoe’s width (to complicate matters, different brands’ sizes vary by up to 3.5 centimetres for the same size). Related Article Explainer

Health Bunions, corns, plantar fasciitis: How to nail foot trouble before it’s too late Human feet do not work the same way. Long feet can be narrow and short feet can be wide. “Feet are not one-dimensional. It’s as 3D object,” says Islam. “We are trying to compensate for everything with a single measure – length. There lies the problem. We do not provide the girth or the arch size.” To get the right width, women are forced to choose shoes of an incorrect length or vice versa, says Islam.



This problem is less acute for men, who often wear shoes with laces. “We can compensate the girth problem with the laces,” says Islam. “You can tighten it up or loosen it up.” Health effects The results don’t surprise podiatrist Laura Kelly, spokeswoman for the Australian Podiatry Association. “It would be one of the most common problems we see,” she says. “And often, they think they are wearing the right size shoe.” She ticks off a list of problems linked to ill-fitting shoes: bunions, wounds, ingrown nails, nerve compression, an increased risk of falls. Some of these conditions are driven by genetic risk factors, but are triggered or worsened by ill-fitting shoes. “Lots of quite serious things can come from this,” says Kelly. “A lot of people, I think, put up with a certain level of discomfort. They think it’s normal. It’s not normal to have discomfort, neuromas, corns, ingrown nails. There is a lot you can do about it. Maybe people put up with things they shouldn’t.”



What to do? Not all shoe systems have the same problem. Japanese and Chinese shoe size charts include foot girth; China’s system even allows shoes to be sized according to width. Companies selling in Australia know the width of the shoe they are selling – they just don’t report it to consumers. “It baffles me,” says Islam. “They take the measurements, but they don’t disclose it. Consumers need that data to fit their feet properly.” Several Australian brands have started making shoes of differing widths, says Dr Alexandra Sherlock, founder of the Footwear Research Network (she was not involved in the study). But they are much more expensive than mass-produced shoes. “We have got into a habit of buying very cheap shoes, cheaply produced, out of cheap non-renewable materials,” says Sherlock. “We’ve got into really bad habits, and we don’t even realise.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Three children injured in jumping castle accident as 80km/h winds hit Sydney
World.content:
Updated NationalNSWEmergency services Three children injured in jumping castle accident as 80km/h winds hit Sydney Max Maddison Updated September 5, 2026 — 6:38pm ,first published 4:41pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Three young children have been taken to hospital after powerful winds lifted a jumping castle into the air in Sydney’s inner south, as wild weather caused widespread power outages in the city’s west and left more than 90,000 households without electricity. Ausgrid confirmed about 40,000 customers had been left in the dark, as swaths of Sydney’s west suffered outages after high winds damaged one of the company’s substations. Another 50,000 customers on Endeavour Energy’s network were also without power. Three children were injured when a jumping castle became airborne in Banksia, in Sydney’s south, amid ferocious wind gusts on Saturday. Nine News The outages came after a cool change ripped through NSW, with gusts of wind surpassing 80km/h recorded at Sydney Airport late on Saturday afternoon. The temperature in Sydney had hovered about 30 degrees, accompanied by strong north-westerly winds. The Bureau of Meteorology has issued a severe weather warning for damaging winds, with peak gusts of up to 100km/h expected across parts of the state.



Emergency services were called to Gardiner Park in Banksia, about 12 kilometres south of the CBD, about 1.20pm on Saturday after the jumping castle became airborne, a NSW Ambulance spokeswoman said. The children were taken to Sydney Children’s Hospital after being treated by paramedics at the scene. A preschool-aged boy and girl suffered head injuries, while a baby was treated for minor injuries. A woman was also taken to hospital with minor injuries, the spokeswoman said. All three children were in a stable condition. Loading This was the second incident involving an airborne jumping castle recorded in a matter of hours on Saturday. Two children were injured at a party near Geelong in Victoria in the morning. Both children were taken to hospital with injuries to their upper bodies and were in a stable condition. Greater Western Sydney and the Blue Mountains were the areas worst hit by the wild winds.



“There’s currently over 250 fault sites. Crews are currently working to make damaged areas safe before restoration work can commence,” an Endeavour Energy spokeswoman said. The company’s website estimated that power would not be restored until the early hours of Sunday morning. In a statement, an Ausgrid spokeswoman said most customers were expected to have their power restored by 7pm with the remainder by 11pm. “There are currently approximately 40,000 customers without power after strong winds moved through Sydney and the Central Coast this afternoon,” she said. “Hardest-hit areas include Bankstown, Milperra and Revesby where high winds have caused some damage to one of our substations.”



Outages were being experienced right across Sydney, including in Mosman, St Ives, Bellevue Hill, Rosebery and Summer Hill. Get alerts on breaking news as it happens.

World.title: ‘Survivable pockets’: Australian tunnel expert arrives in Nepal, hopeful of more rescues
World.content:
WorldAsiaFloods ‘Survivable pockets’: Australian tunnel expert arrives in Nepal, hopeful of more rescues Michael McGowan Updated September 5, 2026 — 6:31pm ,first published 4:50pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Kathmandu: An Australian tunnelling expert who helped to orchestrate the extraordinary rescue of two workers from a hydropower tunnel in northern Nepal is headed for the disaster zone, firmly believing there is still hope of finding more survivors trapped hundreds of metres below the earth. After helping to lead the rescue operation remotely from his home in Victoria this week, engineer and geologist Arnold Dix flew into Nepal’s capital, Kathmandu, late on Friday night (Nepal time). Australian tunnelling expert Arnold Dix has arrived in disaster-stricken Nepal believing there is still hope of finding survivors. Justin McManus It comes as rescuers in Nepal pulled a Chinese national alive from a hydropower tunnel on Saturday, according to a social media post by the country’s prime minister’s office, and in a separate effort, rescuers pulled a woman out alive from a house 10 days after floods hit Nuwakot town, a Nepalese army spokesperson said. The latest tunnel rescue brings the total to three workers pulled alive from the Trishuli hydropower project. Two Nepalese workers were rescued from a tunnel at the Trishuli 3A hydropower plant on Friday.



Nepal’s army said the man was pulled alive from a 225-metre tunnel and is undergoing a health assessment. Images showed him being evacuated by helicopter, with an army medic checking on him during the flight. View post on X While the odds are against Dix and the rest of the global team of experts providing advice to Nepalese authorities on the ongoing rescue mission, he said that he absolutely believed there was hope of finding more survivors under the earth some 10 days after the devastating floods. “In the game of paper, scissor, rock, human, the odds aren’t good. But yeah [there are] survivable pockets, absolutely, and that’s what we’re aiming for,” he said. A helicopter drops search and rescue teams at the exit tunnel of the Chilime Hydropower Plant during the week. Kate Geraghty



On Saturday morning, he boarded a helicopter for the Chilime Hydropower Plant, high in the Himalayan valley and close to the Chinese border. There he will meet with members of the Indian rescue team he worked with after 41 men were trapped in the Silkyara Bend-Barkot tunnel in the Himalayas in 2023. Dix has also worked on other rescue missions, including at Ground Zero after September 11. Loading “We’re just like the underground rescue buddies,” he told this masthead just ahead of his flight on Saturday. It has been more than a week since devastating floods tore through Nepal, causing tsunami-like waves of water, rock and debris that has resulted in 1294 confirmed deaths. More than 5000 people are still missing, including 583 foreign nationals. The Chinese government has reported 31 confirmed deaths and 531 missing – including 261 foreign nationals – on the Tibet side of the border.



Among those still unaccounted for are workers believed to be trapped inside the hydropower tunnels that Nepal has used to harness the fast-flowing waters of the Himalayas and increase the blackout-prone country’s power generation. Related Article Floods Boots on the ground as first Australian rescue team arrives in Nepal Nepal’s Independent Power Producers’ Association said during the week that it believed ​at least eight people could be trapped in the Chilime tunnel. It is one of seven hydropower tunnels at which rescue operations are taking place, with hundreds of workers believed to have been trapped. Until Friday, Dix had helped the effort remotely from Australia, unable to board a plane during the crucial hours and days after the disaster. “Time was of the essence,” he said. “I couldn’t lose two days because I knew they had to start digging.”



They had focused on the Trishuli 3A ­hydropower project, and he said the rescue of mechanical foreman Sanjay Sah and mechanical supervisor Kabir Maharjan from the tunnel on Friday was confirmation of the work he and others had been doing throughout the week. Related Article Graphic content

Floods ‘I saw many dead bodies’: The harrowing escape from a flooded Nepal tunnel “[It means] we’ve got survivable zones in there,” Dix said. “That confirms our theory, if you like. Until that, it was a theory. We really didn’t know if it was survivable in there.” It makes him believe there could “absolutely” be more workers still alive inside. “Of course, the odds are against us. Like, you wouldn’t, you know, go to the casino and play the house on these things normally,” he said.



Dix and his team had relied on engineering drawings of the massive hydropower structures that Nepal uses to generate electricity, as well as satellite imagery, to identify the survivable pockets inside. “The world has never had something like this,” he said. Arnold Dix has previously helped to orchestrate the rescue of 41 Indian workers who were trapped for 17 days after a landslide in the Himalayas. “We’re not dealing with tunnels that might’ve collapsed. They won’t have. We’re dealing with tunnels that are filled up with stuff. “It’s this explosive inrush. It just turns the textbook on its head … that’s why the rescue yesterday was so important because we’ve never dealt with anything like this.”



While they were confident in their theory, the challenge of digging into the deep, unstable earth, where “rocks the size of cars” had barrelled into the tunnels, presented many challenges of its own. Related Article Floods At first, the smell is overwhelming. Then, they open the book of the dead “That’s on the one hand, and the other hand, [the question was] how the hell are we going to get in there to get them?” he said. “You have to find a reason to use your resources, which is where might people be alive? That’s the first question, and then your second question is, ‘OK, now, how do we get them?’ “You can’t just dig everywhere. You’ve seen the destruction here, so you’ve got to be very specific in what you do.”

World.title: Fullback Taine Tuaupiki saves Warriors with hattrick of tries over Sea Eagles
World.content:
Fullback Taine Tuaupiki - who wasn't originally named to play - has saved NZ Warriors' bacon with a hattrick of tries in a desperate 31-30 win over Manly Sea Eagles to keep their NRL minor premiership hopes alive.

The home side needed a late field goal from Chanel Harris-Tavita to snatch victory from their dogged opponents and now await the result between Penrith Panthers and Wests Tigers on Sunday, which will determine the winners of the regular-season crown.

Off to a slow start, the Warriors trailled 12-4 after 20 minutes, but rattled on the next four tries - two to Tuaupiki - to lead 24-12 just after halftime.

Tuaupiki was initially named on the interchange bench as backline cover, but entered the starting line-up when centre Leka Halasima withdrew with an ankle injury 24 hours out.

His inclusion saw Charnze Nicoll-Klokstad shifted to the wing, where he also had a try double in that 20-point run before the Sea Eagles came charging back.

As the match continued, star fullback Tom Trbojevic started to stamp his class on the game, creating chances for those around him.

Manly scored the next three tries and almost had a fourth, which was disallowed for a penalty back on halfway, to grab a 30-24 advantage late in the second half.

Tuaupiki brought the Warriors back on level terms, slicing against the grain to score next to the posts and then converting from in front.

The Warriors had two tries ruled out in the closing minutes, with Harris-Tavita and prop Tanner Stowers-Smith both crossing, and Harris-Tavita also had a field goal attempt charged down.

With the final seconds ticking down, halfback Te Maire Martin received the ball in front of the posts, but was run off his kick. On the next play, Harris-Tavita had more room to operate and duly slotted in the gamewinner.

Victory sees the Warriors set a club record of 18-6 for the season and puts them two points clear at the top of the NRL table.

Penrith can still secure the minor premiership with a three-point win over the 15th-placed Tigers.
